A neighbourhood in Tokyo popular with foreign tourists will ban visitors from using thousands of short-term rental accommodations after a slew of complaints about behaviour.
In the latest sign that Japan’s patience with mass tourism is wearing thin, Shinjuku ward – home to the notorious Kabukicho nightlife district and the world’s busiest railway station – will prevent visitors from using private lodgings in residential areas and near schools and important cultural sites, Japanese media reported this week.
The measure, to be introduced through a local ordinance, could encourage other local authorities to follow suit. Shinjuku, with a regular population of more than 350,000, is home to 3,775 private lodgings – or minpaku – the largest number anywhere in Japan.
While tourism has boosted sectors of Japan’s economy and raised the country’s profile overseas, the surge in visitor numbers has created tensions with residents in popular destinations such as Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka.
Shinjuku ward believes the measure will affect as many as 2,000 lodgings in residential areas – almost half the total, according to the Mainichi Shimbun. The number of minpaku residences in Shinjuku has almost tripled since 2022.
Reports said officials had been forced to act after receiving more than 1,300 complaints from residents in the 12 months to March. Many cited disruption caused by visitors who did not dispose of their rubbish properly, made too much noise and smoked in areas where it is banned. There have also been reports of trespassing.
Officials said temporarily revoking the licenses of renters whose tenants misbehaved would not address residents’ concerns. “Even if we crack down on badly behaved operators, the number of complaints remains the same,” a ward official told the Japan Times. “So we decided it’s better to change the ordinance.”
Authorities did not single out particular operators for the ban. But it is likely to affect those using popular companies such as Airbnb. The Guardian has contacted Airbnb’s Japan office for comment.
The ward will ask for members of the public to give their feedback on the proposal next month, with a view to submitting revisions to the ordinance in February. It also plans to reduce the number of days per year that minpaku in residential areas can be rented out from 180 to 120.
Authorities in Kyoto – where tourists flock to view temples and shrines, rent kimono and photograph traditional geisha entertainers – limit minpaku operations in residential areas to just 60 days a year, during the off-peak season between January and March.
“Residents are concerned that their communities could be falling apart,” Kyoto’s mayor, Koji Matsui, said earlier this year. “We have strengthened the oversight of operators, but that is not enough. We need to go further,” the Asahi Shimbun quoted him as saying.
A record 42 million people visited Japan last year, spending a combined ¥9.5tn ($62bn) – also an all-time high. The government has set a target of 60 million visitors by 2030 – a goal critics say will exacerbate “tourism pollution”.
Authorities near Mount Fuji have introduced climbing fees and imposed a daily visitor cap in an attempt to reduce overcrowding on Japan’s highest mountain. In February, the town of Fujiyoshida, a popular Fuji viewing spot, decided to cancel this spring’s cherry blossom festival, citing a rise in disruptive behaviour by tourists.
The mayor, Shigeru Horiuchi, said the decision had been taken to “protect the dignity and living environment of our citizens”.

Barclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its financial links to a coal-fired power station near the Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and home to millions of people in Bangladesh and India.
Three complainants from the region have submitted a case to the UK government’s Office for Responsible Business Conduct, alleging that the British bank breached international guidelines by underwriting companies involved in the emission-heavy Maitree super thermal power project, also known as the Rampal power plant.
The coal-fired power station is situated near the Sundarbans, a Unesco world heritage site made up of more than 100 tiny islands across a river delta that supports hundreds of plant and animal species, including the Bengal tiger.
Sharif Jamil, an environmental campaigner based in the Bangladeshi capital, Dhaka, who is one of the complainants, said heavy-metal pollution from the plant and the industrial development surrounding it was entering the Sundarbans through its interconnected rivers and canals.
“The Rampal power plant is right on the bank of the Pasur River, which is the lifeline of the Sundarbans,” he said. “The health of the forest is in trouble.”
Last November, a study found elevated levels of mercury and arsenic in water samples taken from the Sundarbans, with the highest concentrations recorded in the Pasur River.
Researchers identified industrial discharge and port-related activities among the sources of heavy-metal contamination and said the Rampal power station posed “a significant environmental threat due to emissions from coal combustion and increased navigation traffic”.
Millions of people live in the Sundarbans, and many depend on the river and forests for food and other resources.
The claimants allege that Barclays failed to conduct sufficient due diligence on the environmental and human rights risks before providing financial services to organisations connected to the project.
Barclays underwrote debt of India’s state-owned NTPC Ltd (formerly the National Thermal Power Corporation), one of the joint-venture partners behind the plant, according to King’s Legal Clinic, which is assisting the complainants. It also says Barclays underwrote bond issues for the Export-Import Bank of India between 2016 and 2019, which provided a loan for the Rampal project.
The complainants argue that emissions from the plant will contribute to global heating, rising sea levels and extreme weather in a region already highly vulnerable to the climate crisis. Mangroves act as a natural barrier against cyclones and other extreme weather.
The power station faced sustained opposition during its planning and construction, including concerns raised by Unesco in a report in 2016, which concluded that “air and water pollution have a high likelihood to irreversibly damage the … World Heritage property”. Some financial institutions, including banks in France, refused to support the project because of its potential environmental and social effects, the complaint says.
Jamil said Barclays’ international standing obliged it to consider the consequences of financing. “The greater your reputation, the greater your responsibility to behave responsibly towards the planet and its people,” he said. “Barclays is a reputed global organisation, and that is why it also has a responsibility.
“Other banks and financial institutions were divesting from, or declining to finance, this project,” he added. “Barclays and other financial organisations should change their policies and examine how their operations can protect the planet from climate catastrophe.”
Jamil also called on banks to direct more funding towards renewable energy rather than imported fossil fuels. “Bangladesh has sunlight throughout the year,” he said. “Why should we expand fossil fuels when there is enormous potential to produce electricity from renewable energy?”
The other complainants include Animesh Mandal, a farmer and politician, and the Dakshinbanga Matsyajibi Forum, a trade union representing fish workers in West Bengal.
They are being assisted by students and lawyers at King’s Human Rights and Environment Clinic, part of King’s College London’s law school.
Sue Willman, a solicitor at the clinic, said: “Rural communities in the Sundarbans are on the frontline of the climate and nature crisis. We hope to persuade banks and financial institutions to think again before financing oil and coal developments that are contributing to that crisis.”
The Office for Responsible Business Conduct, part of the Department for Business and Trade, will assess whether to consider the complaint.
Barclays Bank and BIFPCL (Bangladesh India Friendship Power Company Ltd), the holding company for the Maitree super thermal power project, declined to comment.

The way you decorate your home is entirely up to you — but there are a few guidelines and design suggestions you may want to keep in mind as you're decorating.
Although there are rare exceptions, here are a few decorating rules that the pros say you should almost never break.
Having curtains that are too short can make your space feel incomplete.
Lauren White, owner and principal designer at Ellen W. Interior Concepts, said curtains should always hit the floor. This generally helps a space look larger and more polished.
"Curtains that are too short are like wearing high-water pants," she said. "It does not look good and makes your space look unfinished."
There are rare exceptions to this — for example, if you're dealing with a window above a sink or bathtub.
A rug that's too small can throw off an entire room.
A high-quality rug isn't cheap — and the bigger you go, the more expensive they become.
Because of this, you may be tempted to choose a smaller, more affordable option, even if it means sacrificing aesthetics.
If that's the case, and your rug won't be properly scaled to your space, you're probably better off skipping a rug altogether, White said.
"A rug that is too small takes away from the space, although you would hope it adds visual value," she told BI.
The "right" size of a rug varies depending on the room. However, at the very least, White said, your rug should at least be able to sit under the front legs of your furniture pieces,
Ordering furniture without measuring your space can lead to expensive mistakes.
It may seem like a no-brainer, but taking the time to measure your space is a crucial first step to creating a successful design, White said.
Even better, try envisioning how an item will sit in your space by using a bit of tape.
"Get the dimensions of the furniture you're interested in, grab some blue painter's tape, and create the shape of the furniture with the painter's tape and dimensions," she said. "This will give you a visual guide to ensure your furniture will be functional in your space."
Choosing stylish pieces without thinking about their function can cause your space to look cluttered.
"When choosing furniture for your home, it is important to not only incorporate pieces you love, but to ensure these pieces work for your lifestyle," Gena Kirk, vice president of design at KB Home, said.
Because of this, you want to avoid buying stylish pieces that aren't functional and instead opt for pieces that have a lot of storage space.
Doing so helps to "keep your home looking beautiful without the clutter," Kirk said.
Having only one source of light in a room can make a space fall flat.
Windows aside, having only one source of light (such as recessed lights) could make a room's ambiance fall flat, Kirk said.
"It's important to layer the lighting in your home by incorporating pendant lighting, chandeliers, or trendy wall sconces to soften the light sources," Kirk said. "This creates a calm and welcoming environment throughout your home and can complement your design style."
When it comes to expensive, tough-to-replace pieces, you might want to stick to timeless colors and designs.
Kirk said she always tells her clients to "play it safe" with items that aren't easy to replace, such as countertops, cabinets, and built-in furniture pieces.
"You can incorporate current trends through accessories and easy-to-replace pieces such as backsplashes, cabinet hardware, or small pieces of furniture," she said, adding that this can help you keep up with trends in an easier, more affordable way.
Your space might feel awkward if you hang artwork too high.
"Art is commonly hung too high and looks best at eye-level," Sara Ray, owner of Sara Ray Interior Design in Nashville, said.
She said the sweet spot tends to be about 57 to 60 inches above the floor.
"There are exceptions to every 'rule,' but this one holds true most of the time," she said.
Buying all your furniture from the same collection can make your home look like a showroom.
It can be tempting — and certainly convenient — to purchase all your furniture, rugs, and accessories from one store.
However, Ray said, you should mix your pieces unless you want the space to feel like a furniture showroom.
"It's better to buy from a variety of sources, as well as from different eras, so you can mix vintage and new pieces," she said. "The space feels more collected when older pieces are used, and it adds to the 'story' of your home.

Climatetech startup Circolife has netted $4.5 Mn (around ₹40.45 Cr) in a pre-Series A round led by Polycab India’s joint MD Bharat Jaisinghani. The round also saw participation from Nazara founder Nitish Mittersain, Intelliquity Ventures, Param Capital, Everest Fleet’s founder Siddharth Ladsariya, Anand Ladsariya of Everest Flavours, Indian Express’ executive director Anant Goenka, Sky Impact Capital, Ideas91’s founder Rohit Dev, and family offices S N Damani and Vyom Wealth, among others. The Thane-based startup plans to deploy the fresh capital to expand its AC (air conditioning) fleet, enter new markets, scale its in-house installation and field-service operations, and invest in its IoT and AI capabilities. Founded in 2023 by Abhishek Murarka, Tushar Patil and Devanshu Mishra, Circolife operates a subscription-based model for commercial AC, allowing businesses to use AC units for a monthly fee while the company handles installation, maintenance and eventual refurbishment or replacement. The startup serves businesses across segments such as restaurants, hotels, gyms, salons and co-living operators. Circolife currently has around 10,000 active subscriptions across five cities. With the fresh capital, it is targeting growing its customer base by 4X over the next two years. Circolife currently operates two refurbishment facilities in Mumbai and Delhi, where AC units are refurbished and redeployed at the end of their lifecycle. Circolife's AC units are connected through an IoT layer that monitors parameters such as temperature, power consumption and gas pressure. The data is used by its predictive-maintenance system to identify potential equipment failures before they result in breakdowns. The startup is also developing digital twins of individual AC units and, subsequently, entire sites. It aims to use the data generated across its fleet to optimise cooling performance and energy efficiency at the unit and property level. Cooling as a Service (CaaS) in India is growing significantly as subscription models, where businesses pay per unit of cooling instead of buying expensive equipment upfront, is picking up steam. Businesses increasingly look for alternatives to outright ownership of energy-intensive equipment, while the CaaS model allows service providers to retain ownership of the equipment and manage its lifecycle. The investment comes amid continued investor interest in India’s climatetech sector across energy, mobility and climate-focused businesses. For instance, Bengaluru-based Newtrace secured $6.3 Mn (₹56.93 Cr) in a Pre-Series A funding round in March, to boost its commercialisation.

A 27-second long video has gone viral on social media over the past week. The clip shows a mob, predominantly comprising men, kicking and attacking a woman in the middle of a busy street, while police personnel in the vicinity do little to nothing to prevent the attack.
The X user, Vikas Pokhariyal (@vikasindiafirst), posted the clip on August 31, claiming that a female Hindu teacher had been attacked by Islamists in Bangladesh. At the time of this article being written, the post had been reshared over 3000 times. (Archive)

Pokhariyal later posted a reply to his tweet, attempting to correct his earlier claim. “Correction: The woman was reportedly assaulted by shopkeepers and salesmen after she complained about the shop under the Consumer Rights Protection Law,” the tweet read.
Another X user, Deepak Sharma (@SonOfBharat7), posted the same clip, with a seperate claim that in Bangladesh, a Dalit teacher had allegedly offered water to an upper-caste Muslim child, following which she was chased down in the streets and thrashed. (Archive)

Fact Check
To verify the authenticity of the claims surrounding the viral clip, Alt News broke it down into keyframes. A reverse image search on one keyframe led us to a news report published by the Bangladeshi news portal BD News 24 on August 30.
According to the report, the incident took place at Bangladesh’s Rajbari clothes market, on August 29. The victim in the video is reportedly a female shop owner, who managed her own clothing shop in the market for 12 years. She had allegedly found that one of her female employees had started working in a different shop on August 22. In response, she dismissed the worker from her role at the shop and asked her collect payment in the following month.
Further, another news report published by The Dhaka Tribune on August 30, identifies the female shop owner as one Zakia Sultana, and the ex-employee as Shahana Parveen Bristy. In another report by the outlet Ajker Patrika, Sultana accused Bristy of turning up at her shop with 15-20 men on August 23 and intimidating and verbally abusing her.
This prompted Sultana to launch a protest at the clothes market on August 29 afternoon, along with her female employees. Enraged by this, several shop-owners from the Rajbari clothes market then attacked her, in the presence of police officers who had turned up at the spot to offer her protection, the report states. However, in the video it is visible the that men continue to kick and attack Sultana despite police presence.
We also found a video report from BBC News Bangla, uploaded on August 31, which shows recorded evidence of the attack.
News reports from Bangla TV, Views Bangladesh, and Jago News 24, dated September 1, also reveal that three people have been arrested in relation to the violent attacks on Sultana, as recorded in the viral video.
In conclusion, the viral clip which shows a woman being violently attack is indeed from Bangladesh, but the woman seen in the clip is Muslim, thereby refuting any allegation of a communal angle at play.
Further, the reason for the attack arises from a business dispute as reported by several credible news outlets, thus the aforementioned claims, including that Sultana is a Dalit teacher who was beaten up for offering water to a Muslim child or that she complained about the other shop under the Consumer Rights Protection Law, are false and misleading.

Sweden pays foreign residents £27k to leave amid right-wing immigration crackdown
Sweden was once known for welcoming migrants – but attitudes have changed over the past decade
Sweden was once known for welcoming migrants.
But over the past decade, the country has not only shut its borders – its right-wing government is now paying some foreign-born residents huge sums to leave.
In 2015, Sweden took in 163,000 asylum seekers. That was the second highest per capita in Europe.
By 2025, that number had fallen by 96 per cent.
And since the start of 2026, the coalition government – which ran on a pledge to cut both immigration and crime – has been offering those with non-EU residency permits up to 350,000 Swedish crowns (£27,100) to leave the country.
The Sweden Democrats, a far-right party that is outside the government but backs it in parliament, has thrown its support behind the scheme.
The party launched ads on buses in July promoting the scheme to Somali immigrants.
“Do you miss Mogadishu?” the ad read, referring to the capital of Somalia. “The remigration grant will help you get home.”
The government has also publicised the scheme, which has a budget of 1.3 billion Swedish crowns (£100 million), on its websites in multiple languages.
“Improving re-migration is high on my government's agenda,” Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson has said.
Germany’s AfD supports the scheme
Anti-immigration rhetoric has surged across Europe since over a million people, mainly Syrian nationals fleeing war, arrived in 2015.
Right-wing nationalist parties have seen a surge in support, and governments across the continent have adopted increasingly restrictive migration policies.
Mary Khan-Hohloch, a European Parliament politician for Alternative for Germany (AfD), which won 44 per cent of the vote in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, welcomed the Swedish initiative.
“Given the considerable financial and social burdens facing many European countries as a result of migration policies to date, interest in effective return and remigration programmes is likely to continue to grow,” she said.
However, Bram Frouws, director of the Mixed Migration Centre, a research body, said that there was no evidence such schemes produce any significant increase in voluntary emigration.
“This is one of those policy proposals where this doesn’t even matter, it’s mainly symbolic, it’s about signalling how tough they are on migration,” he said.
Fewer than 200 migrants opt for the money
So far this year, just 171 people have taken up the offer of cash to leave. The Sweden Democrats now want to extend the offer to immigrants with Swedish citizenship, if they agree to revoke it.
“That's where you find the large numbers,” said Ludvig Aspling, the immigration spokesperson for the party, highlighting citizens who struggle to support themselves financially and speak little Swedish.
The opposition and civil rights groups have accused Mr Kristersson of going too far and call the policy divisive.
Latest opinion polls for the 13 September election show an almost equal split between the government on one side and the Social Democrats and centre-left on the other in the country of 10.6 million, where two million people are foreign-born.
Immigrants want ‘freedom and a good life’
In the working-class Stockholm suburb of Satra, a dozen immigrants have gathered at a community centre to have coffee and practice Swedish. Among them are a Sudanese woman, two people from Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine, one person who fled the Taliban in Afghanistan, and a dissident from China.
They have all heard about the government cash incentive to leave. None are interested.
“I want freedom, to be able to work and live a good life,” said Elena Ibrahim, 42, from Sudan.
She fled her ex-husband and religious oppression eight years ago. Now remarried, she works as an artist. “I will not go back,” she vowed.
Mahmoud Khalfi, the imam at the Stockholm Mosque, Sweden's largest, said the scheme and anti-immigrant rhetoric were divisive and caused anxiety among Sweden's Muslim population.
Those who would have opportunities if they left are the highly educated, such as doctors or professors, he said.
“They can go to London or Dubai...but those with less education have no choice, they can't leave.”
The policy, he said, “doesn't solve any problem. Even if a few thousand leave, it has made it worse for those who have to stay”.
Sweden’s wider immigration crackdown
Sweden has also started tightening other rules for immigrants. It no longer awards permanent residency permits and makes immigrants re-apply for them after three years.
In August, the government launched the first-ever citizenship tests, mandatory for all who apply. At a Stockholm convention centre, 900 immigrants were tested on their knowledge of Sweden, including the line of succession for the monarchy and the midsummer holiday.
“It wasn't that hard,” said Cornelius, 38, originally from Cameroon, who added that citizenship would bring peace of mind.
“Sweden is a very good place. It's safe and there are jobs.”
Migration Minister Johan Forssell said that the tests were important in underlining the value of citizenship and that it came with both rights and demands.
“These are highly reasonable requirements,” he said.
“What's unreasonable is that until now you have been able to become a citizen without knowing anything about Sweden and without speaking a single word of Swedish.”

The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) has initiated an inquiry into allegations concerning advertisements related to Child Sexual Exploitative and Abuse Material (CSEAM) on Meta’s platforms and has summoned the company’s India leadership for questioning.
The child rights body had taken suo motu cognisance of a media report by BBC Eye and issued a notice to Meta Platforms, Inc. on July 3, 2026, seeking an explanation from the social media company over the allegations.
Meta submitted its response to the NCPCR a week after receiving the notice. Following an examination of the company’s reply, the child rights commission has now decided to institute a formal inquiry to determine the facts of the matter.
As part of the inquiry, NCPCR has summoned the Managing Director and Head of Meta India to appear before the commission on September 9, 2026.
The summons marks the next step in the commission’s examination of the allegations and is aimed at establishing the facts and understanding Meta’s position on the matter.
The NCPCR’s decision to institute an inquiry comes after it sought an explanation from Meta following the BBC report. The commission is expected to examine the allegations and the company’s response as part of the proceedings.
The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) had directed the Delhi Police to conduct a comprehensive investigation into allegations that paid advertisements on Meta-owned Instagram promoted Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM) in India.
The human rights body also asked the police to examine whether Meta and other entities concerned had complied with mandatory reporting requirements under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act.
The NHRC took suo motu cognisance of media reports published by the BBC alleging that advertisements on Instagram used specific expressions and redirected users to channels where child sexual abuse material was allegedly being offered for sale.
In a letter dated July 8, the NHRC directed the Commissioner of Police, Delhi, to conduct a comprehensive probe into the allegations and submit an Action Taken Report (ATR) to the Commission.
The inquiry was also expected to examine the compliance of Meta and other concerned entities with their obligations under the POCSO Act, particularly provisions relating to the reporting of offences involving children.
The Commission subsequently wrote to the Delhi Police again on July 29, seeking submission of the requisite report.
The latest communication underlines the NHRC's continued monitoring of the matter and its efforts to ascertain the facts surrounding the alleged advertisements and the response of the concerned entities.
The allegations concern the use of Instagram advertisements to direct users towards channels allegedly offering CSAM, raising questions about child safety on social media platforms and compliance with India's child protection laws.

Mumbai: The city's oldest community Ganeshotsav celebration at Keshavji Naik Chawl in Girgaon will celebrate Warli art, one of Maharashtra's most distinctive traditional art forms, during this year's festival beginning September 14.
The pandal, established in 1893 in response to a call by freedom fighter Lokmanya Tilak, has traditionally kept simplicity and tradition at the heart of its celebrations.
Historic Mandal Continues Tradition While Embracing Change
“This Ganesh mandal is striking a balance between honouring tradition and embracing modern times,” said Kumar Walekar, secretary of the Shree Sarvajanik Ganeshotsav Sanstha, which organises the festival.
The theme was selected after the organisers approached an artist from the Sir J J School of Art, Architecture and Design, who suggested Warli art. “This style is between 2,000 and 3,000 years old. There are very few artists who work with the art form,” Walekar said.
Warli Art Theme Highlights Maharashtra’s Ancient Tribal Heritage
Traditionally practised by women from the Warli tribal community of Palghar district, the art form uses rice paste, gum and water to create paintings on the mud walls of homes. Warli paintings are characterised by geometric forms such as lines, triangles and squares, which are used to depict scenes from everyday life and nature, including the sun, moon and trees.
Alongside the traditional theme, the mandal will organise lectures on artificial intelligence, drawing a connection with Lord Ganesh, who is worshipped as a symbol of wisdom. Residents with expertise in the technology will speak at the sessions. A lecture on Seven Habits of Highly Effective People is also planned.
Website Launch Planned To Connect Devotees Digitally
“The way we communicate has changed with technology. To make our festival more accessible, engaging and connected with devotees, we are launching our website. It is our attempt to blend tradition and culture with new means of interaction with devotees,” Walekar added.
Keshavji Naik Chawl was built as a cluster of four two-storey buildings between 1860 and 1862 by Keshavji Nayak, a shipowner, for his workers. The name underwent a change in spelling after the builder's death. A fifth building was added in 1925. Around 150 families currently live in the chawl.

What to expect as Republicans gather in Dallas for Trump’s midterm convention
Republicans are heading to Dallas this week for a two-day event conceived by President Donald Trump to energize his base prior to the upcoming midterm elections.
Trump said he intended to recreate the scale of traditional quadrennial conventions, where political parties present their vision for the nation and officially select a presidential candidate. The gathering will even feature a large-scale balloon drop at its close.
Although Democrats organized midterm conventions in the 1970s and 1980s, this is the first time Republicans have staged one. Key elements to watch on Wednesday and Thursday include:
Can a Trump-style convention save Republicans from a midterm blowout?
For some time, Trump suggested hosting this type of convention, a proposal his fellow Republicans eagerly turned into a tangible event.
Midterm elections traditionally challenge the governing party in Washington. Trump expects this gathering to energize supporters and drive his base to the polls.
"Pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot," Trump said recently in South Carolina. "Just come and vote."
Party members claim the convention will propel conservative contenders into November while highlighting the achievements of Trump's first two years. Even with sagging approval ratings, the president maintains that campaigning on his record offers Republicans their highest chance of victory.
Is the GOP hosting a true political convention or just a massive Trump rally?
Every four years, presidential nominating conventions hosted by both Republicans and Democrats typically bring together thousands of rank-and-file party members, who serve as delegates to represent their home states in the formal candidate selection process.
No nominations will be awarded at this gathering, however, as the primary contests have already settled the outcome. Because the event is open to the public, it could feel more like a Trump rally than a convention.
More than 100 Republican House members and candidates are expected to gather in Dallas, according to a person familiar with the arrangements who asked to remain anonymous before the event begins. Attendees must pay $25,000 for admission and lodging, which the source described as standard for political conventions.
Meanwhile, several lawmakers facing competitive races have stated they will not attend or remain undecided less than a week before the convention.
Who is taking the stage?
Trump is scheduled to speak every evening, giving a keynote address on Wednesday and returning to the stage Thursday following a speech by Vice President JD Vance.
The expansive roster includes Cabinet members such as Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, as well as Attorney General Todd Blanche. Addresses will also be delivered by the president’s son Donald Trump Jr., former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt, Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxon, and Mike Rogers, the party’s Senate nominee in Michigan.
House Speaker Mike Johnson and Texas Sen. Ted Cruz are slated to speak, alongside numerous incumbents and contenders running in critical, competitive House and Senate races nationwide.
Everyday Americans will also offer remarks, sharing personal accounts of how they have gained from the president’s policies.
Organizers plan for as many as 50 speakers or presentations each night, keeping speeches concise to maintain a rapid pace suited for viewers and online sharing. Trump has teased "lots of Great Entertainment" and described the event as "a RALLY like none other."
Can tax cuts, border crackdowns, and fierce partisan attacks propel conservative candidates?
The party’s slate of candidates will take center stage, featuring Texas Senate contender Paxton, who secured Trump’s contentious endorsement over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn. Despite enduring years of scandals, Paxton prevailed with Trump’s backing, offering Democrats a rival they view as more vulnerable in an otherwise conservative state. Trump stated that helping Paxton win election remains a primary focus of the Texas convention, calling him "he’s a good man."
However, the convention program concentrates heavily on Trump’s broader agenda, highlighting his immigration crackdown, efforts to reduce prescription drug costs, last year’s broad tax cuts and spending legislation, and trade tariffs.
The schedule also presents a partisan argument against Democrats, with speakers anticipated to mirror Trump’s rhetorical attacks that frame Democrats as communists.

South African among workers abducted after attack on hunting camp in Mozambique
A South African national was among a group of workers abducted in Mozambique during an attack by insurgents on a hunting camp, South Africa’s foreign ministry said on Monday
JOHANNESBURG -- A South African man was among a group of up to 20 workers abducted in Mozambique during an attack by insurgents on a hunting camp, South Africa’s foreign ministry said Monday.
The Department of International Relations and Cooperation said the 30-year-old man was among five South Africans working at the wildlife reserve who were caught up in last week's attack. Of the other four, two had returned to South Africa, and two remained safe in Mozambique.
“Embassy officials are working with Mozambican authorities and are monitoring the situation and developments in Niassa Province,” the department told told The Associated Press.
Three U.S. citizens are thought to have been evacuated from the area.
The attack is thought to have been carried out by militants linked to the Islamic State group, which launched an insurgency in neighboring Cabo Delgado province in 2017.
The U.S. Embassy in Mozambique, which acknowledged the attack in a statement, did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Local police said at least 11 people, including children, were abducted during the attack on the town of Marangira, in Niassa province. It wasn't immediately clear why there was a discrepancy in the number of people abducted between South African and Mozambican authorities.
Police spokesperson Osvaldo Mahando told local media that one person was killed, another slightly injured, and vehicles were burned in the attack.
Security forces were patrolling nearby forests, he said.
The insurgency has destabilized northern Mozambique, killing thousands and forcing more than 1 million people to flee their homes, according to the United Nations. The militants have also carried out attacks in the neighboring Niassa and Nampula provinces.
Mozambique’s state news agency, Agencia de Informacao de Mocambique (AIM), reported that the attackers looted and burned a hunting camp and damaged a health center, police post and telecommunications tower.
Citing provincial government figures, AIM said the attack forced thousands to flee and about 2,000 people were initially given shelter.
The attack prompted the U.S. Embassy to advise Americans to avoid the Niassa Special Reserve and areas near the Niassa-Cabo Delgado border.
Peter Bofin, a regional expert at the conflict monitoring group Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, said the latest attack marked the group’s first incursion into Niassa since May 2025.
Although Bofin said the raid was probably an isolated operation rather than evidence of a sustained presence in Niassa, he said it demonstrated the militants’ mobility.
“The ability of one group of ISM (Islamic State Mozambique) fighters to enter Niassa and undertake that attack highlights that ISM still has an advantage in maneuverability in rural areas,” he said.
Bofin said the camp offered an opportunity to seize supplies and strike an important economic target, undermining confidence in the government’s control of the region.

A Chinese rescue team has reached the all-but-obliterated Gyirong border crossing complex for the first time and found “nothing but ruins” as Nepal and China continue their arduous rescue operations in the flood-hit Himalayas.
Surveillance camera footage from the worst-hit Gyirong border crossing complex showed huge torrents of water and debris on Wednesday engulfing buildings and people trying to flee. Only on Friday were rescuers able to reach that area.
State media reported that the Chinese team of 21 rescuers and a search-and-rescue dog crossed mountains and valleys and used ropes to navigate forests and cliffs after roads to the complex, hemmed in by steep Himalayan slopes, were destroyed.
“There was no road … it was all virgin forest and sheer cliffs,” rescue worker Zou Mingqi said. At the complex, “as far as the eye could see, there was nothing but ruins.”
The glacier collapse which unleashed a deadly torrent through Himalayan mountain river systems has killed at least 579 people in Nepal and seven in China’s Tibet. The number of missing in Nepal has nearly doubled to 1,924, officials said on Friday. At least 558 were missing in Tibet’s Gyirong County, Chinese state media said. Among the missing are at least 540 foreigners, many of them Hindu pilgrims from India.
More than 90,000 people have been affected by the disaster, the Red Cross estimated.
Amid the deepening crisis, Nepal has now said it needs foreign help in specialised and technical areas in which it does not have expertise, but not in search and rescue.
Earlier on Friday, Nepal’s foreign ministry had said that Kathmandu could manage the rescue efforts on its own for now and declined foreign involvement.
The areas Nepal is seeking help include opening transport and communication services in places where bridges have been destroyed, identification of dead bodies, DNA testing and storing bodies for longer durations, foreign minister Shisir Khanal said late on Friday.
Asked about that stance of his government, Khanal said there was no need for assistance in general search and rescue which was being done by Nepali rescuers. “We think there is no need for repetition in this,” he said.
India and China, between whom Nepal is wedged, have been requested to supply bailey bridges to reopen transport and communication in an area where about two dozen bridges had been destroyed.
Nepal is continuing to monitor two barrier lakes upstream of the flood zone, with an official warning that flood risks will persist until both lakes fully drain.
Satellite imagery showed the second lake growing larger with no visible outlet, raising concerns that water pressure could still be building.
China’s state-run Xinhua news agency said that the first barrier lake was reducing in size, citing analysis by the water resources ministry. A Chinese government geo-hazards expert warned, however, that the lake may be unstable and that over 100 glacial lakes scattered throughout the area could pose a threat.
In Beijing, a politburo meeting chaired by President Xi Jinping called for stronger monitoring of glacier lakes and landslide risks, and for closer international disaster cooperation, Xinhua reported.
China’s Premier Li Qiang, the country’s No. 2 official, arrived in the area of Gyirong on Thursday afternoon, Xinhua said. The visit suggested Beijing was treating the disaster as a matter of the highest national priority.
In China, strict controls on the flow of information from one of its most sensitive regions are hampering the public’s understanding of events.
The BBC and NY Times have reported videos of the catastrophic floods, widely shared globally, have not appeared on Chinese social media sites.
Chinese state media has carried several broadcasts about the floods and dispatched their own journalists to the area, but reports have focused on the rescue efforts rather than the scale of the devastation. In one broadcast from a relief centre in Tibet, the journalist did not speak to any of the people sitting behind him.
Tibet, brought under Chinese control in the 1950s, is the most sensitive and tightly controlled region in the country.
The Gyirong border port plays a key role in China’s Belt and Road network linking the country to South Asia, with logistics zones and parking lots built there in the past decade.

Can Kane buck history and win Ballon d'Or?
- Published
With the Ballon d'Or shortlist to be announced tomorrow, Harry Kane heads the field as the bookmakers' favourite after a prolific season for club and country. History, however, suggests football's biggest individual prize is rarely decided on goals alone.
Since the Ballon d'Or was first awarded in 1956, performances in the game's biggest competitions have consistently shaped the outcome.
World Cup years, in particular, have followed a remarkably clear pattern and recent editions have shown just how difficult it is to win the award without lifting a major global or continental tournament.
Once the nominees are announced, an international jury of specialised journalists will cast their votes, with one representative per country from the men's top 100 having their say.
So, can Kane, who has never finished higher than 10th in the battle to be the world's best player, become one of the rare exceptions?
- This could be year I win Ballon d'Or, says Mbappe 
  - Published3 hours ago
- 73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it 
  - Published3 days ago
The World Cup effect
Created by France Football journalist Gabriel Hanot, the Ballon d'Or was first presented in 1956, with England's Sir Stanley Matthews the inaugural winner. Originally voted for by journalists, the award was restricted to European players until eligibility was expanded to all nationalities in 1995.
Raymond Kopa became the first Ballon d'Or winner in a World Cup year after helping France reach the 1958 semi-finals. To mark the award's 60th anniversary in 2016, France Football revisited every pre-1995 edition, external. Its retrospective review concluded Pele would have claimed the award after inspiring Brazil to their first World Cup triumph at the age of 17.
Four years later, Josef Masopust officially won the Ballon d'Or after captaining Czechoslovakia to the World Cup final. Again, France Football judged Brazil's Garrincha to have been the standout performer after leading his country to successive World Cup titles.
It reached the same verdict for Pele in 1970 after he inspired Brazil to a third World Cup crown. By then, a clear pattern had emerged. Bobby Charlton (1966), Paolo Rossi (1982), Lothar Matthaus (1990), Zinedine Zidane (1998), Ronaldo (2002) and Fabio Cannavaro (2006) all won the Ballon d'Or after lifting the World Cup.
Even among the official exceptions, players still tended to enjoy deep runs at the tournament. Johan Cruyff collected the Ballon d'Or after leading the Netherlands to the 1974 World Cup final, while Luka Modric repeated the feat with Croatia in 2018.
World Cup success has never been an absolute requirement. Kevin Keegan won the 1978 Ballon d'Or despite England failing to qualify for the World Cup, although France Football later concluded Argentina striker Mario Kempes would have been the deserving winner after finishing as the tournament's top scorer and helping the hosts lift the trophy. The publication reached the same verdict for World Cup winners Diego Maradona in 1986 and Romario in 1994.
France Football's review ultimately reinforced the World Cup's influence on the Ballon d'Or. In essence, had the prize always been open to players from all countries, each South American World Cup-winning side between 1958 and 1994 would have supplied the winner.
The biggest prizes matter
The World Cup is not the only competition to shape Ballon d'Or voting.
Recent history suggests success in one of football's biggest tournaments has become almost a prerequisite. Only four of the previous 19 Ballon d'Or winners failed to lift either the Champions League, World Cup, European Championship or Copa America during the year of their triumph.
Those exceptions underline just how extraordinary Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo had to be. Messi won despite Argentina's quarter-final exit at the 2010 World Cup, and again in 2012 and 2019 without lifting a major international or continental trophy.
Ronaldo also prevailed in 2013 after Portugal failed to progress beyond the World Cup play-offs, thanks largely to another remarkable individual season with Real Madrid.
Conversely, Wesley Sneijder's treble with Inter Milan and run to the 2010 World Cup final, Franck Ribery's role in Bayern Munich's 2013 treble and Mohamed Salah's record-breaking 2017-18 season all proved insufficient when voters favoured different narratives.
Rightly or wrongly, modern Ballon d'Or voting has consistently rewarded football's biggest occasions. That presents Kane with another obstacle.
Unlike Ronaldo in 2014 or Luka Modric in 2018, he cannot point to Champions League glory as Bayern Munich's European campaign ended in the semi-finals against eventual winners Paris St-Germain.
Nor is he alone, with Erling Haaland, Kylian Mbappe, Michael Olise, Declan Rice and Jude Bellingham all potential rivals and attempting to buck one of the award's strongest recent trends.
Why Kane's case is different
History points towards major honours being important to winning the Ballon d'Or but Kane's 2025-26 season suggests this may not be a typical race.
The England captain scored 73 goals for club and country - 61 for Bayern Munich and 12 for England - in a season in which Bayern won the Bundesliga and DFB-Pokal and England finished third at the World Cup.
Among players representing clubs from Europe's top five leagues, only Messi has scored more goals for club and country in a single season, the Argentine striking 82 times for Barcelona and Argentina in 2011-12.
Kane's tally places him ahead of Bayern great Gerd Muller (72 in 1972-73), Cristiano Ronaldo (66 in both 2011-12 and 2014-15), Ronaldo (66 in 1996-97), Haaland (64 in 2022-23) and Luis Suarez (64 in 2015-16).
Kane or Spain?
Voters might face a familiar dilemma.
Rodri appears Kane's strongest rival. The former Ballon d'Or winner was arguably Spain's standout performer throughout the tournament, collecting the Golden Ball after helping his country secure a second World Cup title.
Lamine Yamal also added a World Cup winner's medal to a season in which he helped Barcelona reclaim La Liga, although it was teenage team-mate Pau Cubarsi who claimed the Fifa Young Player Award after a series of outstanding performances.
Mbappe and Messi are also expected to feature prominently. Mbappe finished as the World Cup's top scorer with 10 goals, while also claiming the Champions League Golden Boot and La Liga's top scorer trophy, despite France falling short of the final and Real Madrid ending the season without a major honour. Messi, meanwhile, captained Argentina to a second successive World Cup final and at the age of 39 scored eight goals during the tournament.
Should Kane prevail, he would become only the fifth Englishman to win the Ballon d'Or after Matthews, Charlton, Keegan and Michael Owen. He would also become the first player representing a Bundesliga club to lift the trophy since Matthias Sammer in 1996.
History suggests the odds remain stacked against him but few players have entered a Ballon d'Or election with stronger individual credentials.
Voters must now decide if one of the most prolific goalscoring seasons of the modern era outweighs football's biggest prizes, and if Kane can join one of the most exclusive groups in Ballon d'Or history.

Experts say there is no universal clock time that works for everyone. What matters more is when dinner falls in relation to the body’s biological clock and bedtime. An earlier dinner may be beneficial, but there is no fixed 7 p.m. or 8 p.m. cut-off. The gap between dinner and sleep, the quality and composition of the meal, physical activity and individual health needs all play a role.
Insulin sensitivity and glucose tolerance generally decrease as the day progresses, so the body may not handle a heavy meal as well later in the day. However, dinner timing is only one part of the picture. The amount and quality of food, physical activity, sleep and health conditions such as diabetes and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD) also affect how the body responds to a meal.
The gap before sleep
“There is no evidence-based ideal dinner time,” said Aafrin Shabbir, medical director, senior consultant and diabetologist, Tambaram Medical Centre and CODE Clinic. The body’s metabolic efficiency is generally better during the daytime, she said, making a smaller and lighter dinner preferable.
She also cautioned against assuming that eating at 10 p.m. is unhealthy for everyone. Someone who sleeps at 1 a.m. has a different biological rhythm from someone who sleeps at 10 p.m. “One rule doesn’t fit all,” she said.
Saravana Bharathy S. P., internal medicine, Dr Mehta’s Hospitals, recommends leaving about two to three hours between dinner and bedtime. This is particularly relevant for people with reflux or digestive discomfort, as lying down soon after a meal can worsen symptoms.
Swathi Padmanaban, consultant, paediatric & adolescent endocrinologist and diabetologist, Rainbow Children’s Hospital, Chennai, said eating dinner earlier is generally better for metabolic health when practical. She advised against making dinner the largest meal of the day, particularly when it is eaten close to bedtime.
Meal timing is linked to the body’s circadian rhythm. The liver, pancreas and gastrointestinal tract have their own biological clocks that work with the brain’s central body clock. As the biological day progresses, insulin sensitivity and glucose tolerance tend to fall, meaning the same meal may cause a greater rise in blood glucose when eaten later.
Late eating
Studies have found that eating dinner at 10 p.m., compared with 6 p.m., led to higher overnight blood glucose and changes in fat metabolism, despite the meals having the same calories and nutrients.
“Late eating may have greater metabolic implications for people living with diabetes, prediabetes and obesity. A carbohydrate-rich meal late at night can cause a larger rise in blood glucose, particularly when physical activity is low,” Dr. Swathi said.
Late, heavy meals can also cause bloating, indigestion and acid reflux and may affect sleep. However, an occasional late dinner is unlikely to carry the same significance as a regular pattern of late-night eating.
Eating after a particular hour does not, by itself, cause obesity or heart disease. Overall calorie intake, food quality, physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep also play major roles. “People who regularly eat late may also snack more, sleep less or have irregular work schedules. This makes it difficult to separate the effect of dinner timing from other lifestyle factors,” Dr. Bharathy said.
Healthier dinner timing
For children and adolescents, the focus should be on regular meals, adequate nutrition, appropriate portions, physical activity and good sleep rather than restrictive eating windows.
If a late dinner is unavoidable, a moderate and balanced meal is preferable. Vegetables, protein and fibre can be included, while sugary drinks, sweets and fried or fatty foods should be limited. It is also better to avoid coming home extremely hungry and eating a large, carbohydrate-heavy meal just before bed. If possible, part of the meal can be eaten earlier and the later meal kept smaller. A short walk after dinner may also help with post-meal blood glucose control.
For people living with diabetes, meal timing should be planned around their medication, insulin requirements, blood glucose levels and HbA1c rather than a fixed cut-off.
The practical approach is to eat earlier when possible, leave about two to three hours between dinner and bedtime, keep late meals light and balanced, and maintain regular eating and sleep schedules.

US military interests control or have access to more than 100 defence facilities on Australian soil, in what some analysts describe as a “saturation” – even a “colonisation” – of the Australian continent.
New data compiled by the Nautilus Institute and published by Guardian Australia maps the extent of US militarisation. The US military controls 17 facilities on mainland Australia and has access to 75 more Australian-run military installations. US defence corporations have access to an additional 18.
In total, the US military and US defence corporations have control of or access to 110 facilities on Australian territory, well over half of all the military installations in Australia.
“We have been thinking about American influence on Australian defence policy as a matter of penetration,” the database’s author, Prof Richard Tanter, tells the Guardian, “and we’re aware of the closeness of the alliance, the integration of the armed forces …
“But what this database shows is it’s not a matter of penetration, it’s a matter of saturation. Over half of the defence facilities that we have looked at have some level of American access: that means American personnel, it means American corporations, some of the biggest armaments companies in the world.”
| US access to Australian defence facilities |  | 
|---|---|
| Access level | Facilities | 
|---|---|
| United States-controlled facilities with Australian access | 17 | 
| Australian facilities with US military and US corporate access | 24 | 
| Australian facilities with US military access | 51 | 
| Australian facilities with US corporate access | 18 | 
| Australian facilities with no significant US access | 41 | 
| Australian facilities with US access unresolved | 17 | 
‘Aligning ourselves completely’
The US military controls or has access to 92 defence facilities on Australian soil for:
- 
  Gathering intelligence, accessing satellite data for targeting information and communications intercepts.
- 
  Training, including for 2,500 marines on dry-season rotation in the Northern Territory.
- 
  Pre-positioning warfighting assets such as Osprey aircraft.
- 
  Logistics hubs holding weapons, munitions and fuel, stored in case of a war in the Pacific.
Some bases, including Pine Gap, play critical roles in identifying targets for US strikes overseas and are well known by Australians, even if their operations are highly classified.
Others are massive – the Bradshaw field training area in the Northern Territory is the size of Cyprus – but barely known.
Announced in June, Bandiana base in Wodonga will be the site of tens of millions of dollars worth of pre-positioned US weapons, munitions, fuel and vehicles, stationed for rapid deployment in the event of conflict in the Pacific.
Beyond the military’s presence, at least 42 Australian military facilities are accessed by US defence contractors – some of the biggest weapons manufacturers in the world – which use Australian sites for manufacturing, testing and training of weapons systems deployed by militaries across the globe.
Lockheed Martin assembles guided missiles in Port Wakefield, South Australia. Northrop Grumman signed a multimillion-dollar contract this year to build rocket motors for guided weapons at Mulwala in New South Wales. Collaboration with US manufacturers will “promote allied interoperability and provide a second source of supply for critical munitions”, the Australian defence force says.
Of the military bases that operate under US control, with Australian access, Pine Gap is the best known. But its precise role in US warfighting is hidden from public view.
Like several large military bases across Australia, Pine Gap hosts multiple defence facilities, each with distinct functions: a ground-control station for signals intelligence satellites; a relay ground station for early-warning missile launch systems; and a site for intercepting foreign satellite communications.
The Nautilus Institute database counts defence facilities, rather than bases, so Pine Gap consists of three distinct, co-located facilities.
Critical to US operations around the world, including conflicts in the Middle East, it is formally a “joint defence facility” but it is always commanded by an American.
The Force Posture agreement – “with full respect for Australian sovereignty” – gives US forces and contractors “unimpeded access to and use of” agreed Australian facilities, including for deploying forces and materiel, bunkering vessels and refuelling aircraft.
The US military presence will continue to expand. From next year up to 1,200 uniformed military personnel will operate from the HMAS Stirling submarine base just off Fremantle. The government insists that technically this will not be a US base – rather a “rotation” – but there is little contestation of its actual implication.
Arguing in favour of the Aukus nuclear submarine agreement, the former defence minister Christopher Pyne told a public inquiry the multibillion-dollar deal was “a lot more than the submarine procurement”.
“From a strategic point of view, it’s not something that’s ever really discussed in the public, but it’s one of the most important aspects of it: Aukus is also a new United States submarine base in the Indian Ocean.
“For the Americans, being able to have a submarine base in the Indian Ocean is a massive strategic advantage.”
Tanter, a senior research associate at the independent public policy thinktank the Nautilus Institute for Security and Sustainability and an honorary professorial fellow at the University of Melbourne, says the US military’s expanding presence is not in service of its junior alliance partner but rather US interests alone.
“Over more than a decade, the United States has been preparing the capacity for high-tempo warfighting operations with China, springboarding from Australia,” he says. “And that means we are aligning ourselves completely with American strategic planning.
“From a Chinese perspective, Australia is not so much hosting US bases on its territory, it’s a US base in its own right … Australia is a serious piece of real estate in the US warfighting machine.”
There exists no comprehensive public record of foreign military access to bases on Australian territory. This database has been compiled from open-source information, responses provided to parliament, and government and commercial reporting.
Tanter argues that the acceptance of the US military presence has become so ingrained within the government and defence that unwinding Australia’s enmeshment within the world’s most powerful military is increasingly difficult.
“This is a massive institutional failure in Australia, a kind of learned incapacity at a political, parliamentary and bureaucratic level,” he says. “We’ve learned how not to ask those questions.”
‘Waltzing its way into a war’
At a press conference in June, the defence minister, Richard Marles, demonstrated the breadth of the US military presence in Australia.
Speaking in Rockingham, Western Australia – across a narrow bay from HMAS Stirling – Marles was announcing the establishment of a $30m US logistics base in Wodonga, Victoria.
“We are seeing a growing US footprint in Australia that is important in terms of building our own military capability but also it’s very important for Australia’s national security,” Marles said.
Marles said the “hugely significant American presence” in the region was a balance to China’s “very significant military buildup”.
Earlier, the minister told the Defending Australia Summit that US military presence in Australia was indispensable to deter conflict in the region.
“We will see an increasing American military footprint on our continent over the course of the next few years.”
Just last week Marles met the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, at the Pentagon, where both leaders “agreed to accelerate force posture initiatives at Australian bases, bolster cooperation in combined logistics, and build greater interoperability through joint exercises”.
The Guardian put a series of questions to Marles’s office about the implications of an “increasing American military footprint” across Australia. A spokesperson for the defence department said Australia held a fundamental principle of “having no foreign bases on Australian sovereign territory”, and that the Australian government retains sole control over deployment of the ADF and over the use of Australian territory.
But, the spokesperson said, Australia’s 2026 national defence strategy reiterated “Australia’s alliance with the United States remains fundamental to our national security and the Australian Defence Force’s (ADF) capacity to generate, sustain and project credible military capability”.
The alliance with the US allowed Australia to “pursue our national security interests far beyond what we could achieve alone”, they said.
Australians’ fragile faith
Government ministers are fond of the reassuring line that the Australia-US relationship is broader, deeper and more enduring than the tenures of prime ministers and presidents.
But Australians’ faith in the US is fragile and fracturing.
A Lowy Institute poll showed Australians’ “trust in the United States to act responsibly in the world” has fallen to 31%, the lowest level in its polling history.
Just 21% of Australians have confidence in “Donald Trump to do the right thing in world affairs”, the lowest level of confidence in a US president yet.
Just more than half of Australians (55%) said they were either “strongly” or “somewhat” in favour of allowing the US to base military forces in Australia, down eight points from 2022 (63%).
Australians feel the alliance with the US remains important: 73% rate it as either “very important” or “fairly important” to the nation’s security.
Other findings are more damning: a poll for the Australia Institute found more than half (52%) of Australian voters believed Trump was a greater threat to global security than Vladimir Putin (17%) or Xi Jinping (16%).
More than twice as many Australians (59%) now believe Australia’s interests are best served by a more independent foreign policy rather than a closer alliance with the US (23%). Just 13% of Australians believe the US is a “very reliable” security ally.
This represents, Dr Emma Shortis says, a “seismic shift” in Australia’s perception of its once-great and powerful friend.
“After following the US into nearly every war since World War II, Australians have had enough. They see tangible risks in being so close to President Trump’s bleak and violent version of America.”
Shortis, the director of international and security affairs at the Australia Institute, argues that the Trump administration has repeatedly demonstrated that the US is willing to jettison security commitments made to allies. US bases across the Middle East have been repeatedly attacked by Iran.
“Trump has demonstrated that it’s all contingent, it’s all insecure,” she says. “And what he has also highlighted – particularly with his illegal war in Iran – is the way those US bases themselves become targets.
“It doesn’t matter what you do, it doesn’t matter how much you give him, you can literally give him a plane, and it’s not enough, he will not defend those bases.”
Shortis says Australia’s increasing integration with the US military has resulted in “an accelerating erosion of Australia’s independent, sovereign, decision-making power”.
“Instead of having the option of saying ‘no’ to involvement in United States wars, involvement becomes the default position.”
She cites the March attack by a US nuclear-powered submarine on an Iranian frigate, sinking it and killing more than 100 people. Three Australian naval personnel were onboard, part of the submarine’s crew: the US did not forewarn Australia of the attack.
“Australia might maintain the pretence of sovereign decision-making power, but that’s not the reality.”
Dr Albert Palazzo, an adjunct professor at the University of New South Wales Canberra and formerly the director of war studies for the Australian army, tells the Guardian the US military’s accelerating buildup carries danger for Australian security.
“The Australian government seems to be waltzing its way into a war between the United States and China, by allowing this country to become an outpost or bastion of the US military, and as a platform from which they will launch military force against China,” he says.
Dr Vince Scappatura, the author of The US Lobby and Australian Defence Policy, described US base access across Australia as a kind of “second wave of colonisation”.
“Today we are shaping up to be the ‘tip of the spear’ for US power projection into the region – that’s what the sprawling US base access represents,” he says.
“Each one of those dots on the map represents a point of leverage Washington has over Canberra when it comes to matters of defence and foreign policy. Not that they really need to use it.”
Scappatura says the phrase “empire by invitation” was originally coined to describe US hegemony over western Europe “but it is applicable equally here. I sometimes describe it as ‘voluntary subordination’.”

  The Australian bases & US involvement database is coordinated by Prof Richard Tanter at the Nautilus Institute

In Summary
- The Live 780NC are the latest headphones in JBL’s premium mid-segment Live series of wireless ANC headphones.
- Featuring a different design from their predecessors as well as some flashy colors, the JBL Live 780NC boast good mainstream sound as well as a number of smart features.
- Priced officially at Rs 15,999 (but available at lower prices), the JBL Live 780NC are one of the best pairs of headphones one can get for about Rs 15,000 in the Indian market.
They let you not only pump up the bass or turn up the treble of the audio playing on them but can also add bass and treble to your voice and the person you are talking to during phone calls. They come with good ANC that adjusts itself to your surroundings and come with very good battery life. Get them in orange, and you can be assured of being the center of attention in every room. All this at a price of USD 199/Rs 15,999. But can these features (and many others) and that price tag help the JBL Live 780NC become the perfect headphones for those who want a lot of sound and smarts, without parting with a truly premium price?
Table of Contents
JBL Live 780NC Looks: Comfortable and delightfully colorful
The JBL Live 780NC can look smart or spectacular depending on the shade you choose. We got the very elegant Black ones, which are at home everywhere, from cafes to campuses to corporate offices, but the Purple, Green, or Orange will definitely turn heads, thanks to their unusually bright shades. They follow the classic over-ear headphone design, with a band connecting two earcups, but look different from their predecessors, the Live 770NC.
The headband of the Live 770NC was of the same thickness throughout, whereas the band of the Live 780NC becomes thinner as it nears the earcups, giving it a sleeker and more contemporary look. There is plenty of cushioning on the earpads as well as the headband. There’s plenty of JBL branding too, which appears on the earcups and headband, but as the lettering is in the same color as the headphones, it does not get overwhelming. The earcups have left and right printed inside them, which is always better than having tiny letters on the frame.
The right earcup has the sliding on/off and connectivity button, as well as a button for switching between ANC and Ambient Aware mode, as well as a Type-C port. The volume controls are on the left earcup. The outer part of the right earcup is also a touch panel. There is no 3.5 mm audio jack, but a Type-C to 3.5 mm cable in the box lets one use the headphones with a device with a 3.5 mm audio jack.
The headphones are mostly made of plastic but have metal hinges, and best of all, fold all the way inwards, making them very easy to bunch up and carry. There is a rather basic cloth bag in the box, which is not as good as a case but should suffice for most of us. At 260 grams, the JBL Live 780NC are not exactly super light (the Sony WH-CH 720N are the bosses there at 192 grams), but not uncomfortably heavy either. We have worn them for 3-4 hours without ever feeling too burdened. All the padding in the ear cushions and headband makes them very comfortable to wear, and the clamping force is just right – tight enough to let us move our head without making the headphones wobble, and loose enough to never make us feel squeezed in the head.
The JBL 780NC have a very solid and substantial feel to them. But they come with no dust or water resistance, so we would advise due caution while using them in the gym or using them for running sessions.
JBL Live 780NC Specs and Features: An impressive feature list
The JBL Live 780NC come with a very good spec and feature lineup. Sound is handled by 40 mm drivers, which deliver the famous mainstream JBL Signature Sound. Also on board are support for high-quality LDAC, adaptive ANC, six microphones (most headphones in this price have four), spatial audio, and a number of smart features, such as ear detection (audio pauses when you remove the headphones) and an AI-trained algorithm for clearer calls.
On the connectivity front, they come with Bluetooth 6.0, multi-point connectivity, and support for Auracast (so one can listen to public broadcasts and announcements wirelessly). They also boast a battery life of 80 hours (without ANC) and support fast charging. There is no charging cable in the box, though one does get a Type-C to 3.5 mm cable and a basic cloth carry bag. On the software side, the headphones work with the JBL Headphones companion app, which gives one access to a number of features as well as detailed equalizers and regular software updates. For their price, the JBL Live 780NC are pretty well stacked in the spec and feature department.
JBL Live 780NC Controls and Interface: Buttons for some, touch for others
Connecting the JBL 780NC is as simple as putting them in pairing mode (just slide the on/off button towards the Bluetooth icon) and selecting them on the other device’s Bluetooth device list. To experience all their features, however, one should also connect them via the JBL Headphones app, which is available for both iOS and Android. While connecting the headphones is simple, the app takes some time to recognize them every time it connects to them, which can be a little irritating.
The JBL Live 780NC controls are a blend of physical buttons and touch, although the touch works only on the right earcup. A single tap on the earcup pauses audio and also resumes playing it; a double tap takes one to the next track; a triple tap takes one to the previous track, while tapping and holding accesses the voice assistant. A double tap can also enable one to take or end a call, while tapping and holding rejects an incoming call. One can customize the touch controls to an extent, and add options to access equalizer settings and spatial audio, although there is no way to access ANC or volumes through touch – those are accessed through buttons on the earcups.
The combination of touch and buttons controls works well enough, once one gets the hang of them – we kept forgetting that touch worked only on the right earcup, and ended up tapping the left one initially, out of habit.
JBL Live 780NC Performance: Super audio, decent ANC and great smart touches
Most users will love the warm and detailed sound that the JBL Live 780NC deliver. While there is an emphasis on bass, it does not overwhelm the vocals. Those who want a sharper sound can tweak the equalizer in the app (move it to ‘Jazz,’ we suggest) to enhance treble, but most users will love the sound of these headphones right out of the box. Enabling spatial audio makes the sound a little more airy, although the absence of head tracking gives one much more of a “sitting in a room with the music” feels. There are three kinds of spatial audio – Movie, Music and Game – and although there is not much difference between Movie and Game, Music is rather different and seems to add slightly more detail to the sound. One can also use the Person-fi feature to let the app personalize a sound signature for it, although we were not too convinced by it.
The app allows one to tweak the sound significantly. LE Audio makes a huge difference to audio quality whenever supported (although turning it on and off requires restarting the app), adding greater detail and depth to sound. One can also choose from six equalizer settings – a relatively plain Studio, a thump-friendly Bass, a rumbling Club, a boosted bass Extreme Bass, a mids-stressing Vocal, and a treble-oriented Jazz. There is also the option to completely come up with one’s own EQ setting under the My EQ option. Most mainstream users will prefer the Bass setting, while purists will like either Studio or Jazz. One can also adjust the balance of sound between the right and left earcups, although we found no reason to do so.
The JBL Live 780NC are perfect for mainstream audio, whether one wants to listen to pop, trance or rock, or watch a film, play games or just lend an ear to podcasts. At their price, they are perhaps the best-sounding wireless ANC headphones out there.
JBL Live 780NC ANC and calls: Super sound over calls, decent sounds of silence
The JBL Live 780NC come with adaptive ANC. You can either specify the level of ANC you want using a slider, or enable Adaptive ANC and let the headphones decide the level. We suggest simply keeping it at maximum. Noise canceling on the headphones is good for their price. Of course, one does not get the kind of ANC that comes on Sony and Bose flagships; the Live 780NC do enough to dull a lot of the traffic sound, kill the hum of the Metro, and can even make a noisy cafe a little quieter.
Call quality is where the Live 780NC shine. Not only do they handle calls very well, with very good levels of clarity, but the app even lets you adjust the tone of the person you are speaking to and your own voice as well. You can actually add more bass or treble to both sides of the conversation on the JBL Live 780NC. The headphones are also able to keep out a fair bit of the ambient noise – we have used them on auto rickshaw rides, with the person we are speaking to not even realizing that we are in the midst of noisy traffic. That AI algorithm for clear calls definitely helps.
JBL Live 780NC Battery life: Charge them once a week only!
JBL claims that the headphones come with 80 hours of battery life without ANC and 50 hours with ANC. We mostly used them with ANC – it does not affect audio quality, apart from making it a little more bass-y – and got a comfortable 40-45 hours of battery life (we admit to hearing them at slightly higher volumes). In practical terms, charging them once easily got us through close to a week of hectic use, where we used them for everything from making calls to listening to music to watching videos, shorts, and reels to playing games. That makes them great daily drivers.
The headphones charge off their USB Type-C port and take about two hours to charge from empty to full. They also come with a fast-charging function that gave us about four hours of audio listening after being charged for five minutes. One can tweak the power settings for the headphones to switch off automatically after 30 minutes, an hour, or two hours, to further conserve power. There is no charging cable in the box, but any Type-C charging cable should work just fine with it.
JBL Live 780NC Review Verdict: In a zone of their own in the Rs 15,000 segment
The headphones are priced at Rs 15,999, but are often available at lower prices (they are available on Amazon India at Rs 14,999 even as this is being written). Their closest competitors are the Sony ULT Wear, which are now available at close to Rs 15,000 but have a very bass-centric sound. The ULT Wear have better ANC than the Live 780NC, but the Live 780NC beat them easily in terms of call handling. offer almost double the battery life and also have a more elegant and foldable design.
Audio purists might like the sound of the Sennheiser Accentum Plus, which are available for Rs 13,999, but they lose out to the Live 780NC in ANC, call quality, and battery life. Those looking for head-turning headphones might also be tempted by the Nothing Headphone (1), which come with a transparent-ish appearance and very good audio quality (if one is ready to spend time adjusting the equalizer), but are more expensive at Rs 17,999, and again, do not match the Live 780NC in ANC and battery life.
We would say that they are comfortably the best all-round mainstream ANC headphones you can get for around Rs 15,000. They deliver decent ANC, very good audio, and excel in calls and battery life. Get them in orange, purple, or green, and they are a sight for sore eyes too!
