60 years later, 'Star Trek' continues to 'live long and prosper'
60 years ago, NBC aired the first episode of Star Trek, a television show that became a pop culture phenomenon. The original series starred William Shatner as Captain James T. Kirk, who led his diverse crew of humans and at least one alien, on adventures in space.
"Space: The Final Frontier. These are the voyages of the Starship Enterprise," Kirk says, narrating in the title sequence of each episode. "Its five-year mission: to explore strange new worlds, to seek out new life, and new civilizations. To boldly go where no one has gone before."
Over the decades, the original series and its spinoffs earned generations of devoted fans. They're commemorating Star Trek's 60th anniversary with worldwide celebrations, from the Hollywood Walk of Fame to New York Comic-Con to the International Space Station, where one astronaut plans to wear a badge from Star Trek: Strange New Worlds.
At the Science Museum in London, fans hope to set a Guinness World Record for the most people performing the Vulcan Salute — a greeting made famous by Star Trek's beloved half-human, half-alien character Spock.
In Los Angeles recently, the show was honored at a Writers Guild Foundation fundraiser by the cast of the hit TV series The Pitt. Actor Noah Wyle, a Star Trek fan, performed as Captain Kirk. Onstage before an audience at The Lodge Room in Highland Park, Wylie and his castmates read the script of the show's first episode The Man Trap.
NBC aired that first episode on September 8, 1966 (the world premiere was broadcast two days earlier, in Canada). Besides Shatner, the show also featured actors DeForest Kelley as Dr. Leonard "Bones" McCoy, Leonard Nimoy as first officer Spock, whose mother was an Earthling and his father from the planet Vulcan.
"You could characterize Star Trek as being outlined in Greek drama: A hero's got to solve a problem and get back home," says Shatner, now 95, one of the last living main cast members from the original series.
Weeks ago, he told NPR that the show's creator, Gene Roddenberry, had been inspired by a TV show about a wagon train going West — only his show would be set in space…a Wagon Train to the Stars.
"They made a pilot and then NBC saw it and said, 'we don't like the script, we don't like the cast, but we like the idea,'" Shatner recalls.
That's when comedy legend Lucille Ball stepped in. Her production company, Desilu, had produced the pilot. Shatner says she was instrumental in getting it a second pilot. Nimoy was the only actor to return. And Shatner was cast as Kirk.
"I saw this magical world," Shatner recalls. "They took themselves a little seriously, you know, ponderous a little bit here and there. So my contribution may have been: let's add some humor."
Speaking in dramatic pauses and with a twinkle in his eye, Shatner was a charming hero.
But after its third season, the network canceled the series. Shatner says Star Trek fans rallied to return it to the air. In syndication, the show continued its popularity, leading to prequels, sequels on TV and in film, video games, podcasts and fan fiction.
The original series from the '60s had introduced technological concepts such as a handheld communicator — which inspired the invention of the flip phone.
The show also posed sci-fi ideas, such as the potential dilemmas of time travel and encountering new and strange life forms. It also spurred progressive conversations relevant to the 20th century.
One episode in 1968 is credited with showing the first interracial kiss on television, between Captain Kirk and Lieutenant Uhuru, played by Nichelle Nichols.
"It was a thrilling way to make history," chuckles Shatner.
He says he admires all 79 episodes of the original Star Trek, including another one about race that featured two aliens that were mirror images of each other — half-white and half-Black.
"They hated each other. It was great prejudice," Shatner notes. "But looking at two guys, black and white, it seemed idiotic. And so it didn't take any much of a stretch to say how idiotic racism is."
George Takei, now 89, played Sulu, a helmsman of Japanese ancestry. At the San Diego Comic-Con this year, he talked to NPR about the diversity of Star Trek's cast, including a Black woman as the communications officer, a Scottish chief engineer and a Russian navigator... in addition to assorted aliens.
"We have a lot of phrases from Star Trek: Live long and prosper, Boldly go where no one has gone before," Takei said. "But of them all, the one that I think is the most significant is I.D.I.C.: Infinite diversity in infinite combinations."
Takei notes the original series aired at a time when Americans protested the Vietnam War, suffered through political assassinations, and demonstrated for civil rights.
"Gene Roddenberry thought that we would learn from the turbulence of our times back in the 60's and build a better future," says Takei.
60 years later, he says society still has much to learn from the Star Trek philosophy, which Roddenberry often talked about.
"We believe that the often-ridiculed mass audience is sick of this world's petty nationalism and all its old ways and old hatreds. There is an intelligent life form out on the other side of that television tube," Roddenberry said on an album recorded in 1976, "The whole show was an attempt to say that humanity will reach maturity and wisdom on the day that it begins not just to tolerate, but to take a special delight in differences in ideas and differences in life forms."
That philosophy is appreciated by Star Trek fans, a/k/a Trekkies, who've been meeting up in cosplay at conventions for decades.
Among them is Michael Nguyen, a 40-something who's been a Star Trek fan most of his life. He has more than 50 Star Trek costumes and is part of NYC Away Team, a group of Trekkies who do volunteer work in New York City.
"The ethics of Star Trek and that concept of a hopeful future, being respectful of other cultures," he says, "All of those things have stayed constant."
Gene Roddenberry died in 1991. His wife, Majel Barrett, who played Nurse Chappell on the original series, died in 2008. They're survived by a son, Rod, a TV producer and CEO of Rodenberry Entertainment.
NPR asked Rod Roddenberry about his father's legacy. "I think he'd be very proud of the fact that Star Trek has tried new things. Some have been successful, some maybe not," he says. "So I think the only thing I think you could say is thank you to everyone who's worked on it and seriously all the fans."
Captain's log, Stardate 43687.7
There are no new Star Trek TV shows currently in production. But there is another movie in the works.
At Comic-Con in San Diego, writer/director duo Jonathan Goldstein and John Francis Daley talked about how they plan to reboot the franchise.
"The script is in progress and we're very excited about it," Daley said.
Goldstein added, "It won't be the characters that you've seen previously, and I think it will probably be a little further into the future than we've been before. Our hope with this is to satisfy the fans, but also bring people in who may not consider themselves lovers of Star Trek, and surprise them.

Houthis report Saudi reprisals after oil sites set ablaze in wave of strikes
RIYADH: Yemen's Houthis said Saudi Arabia hit back with a series of strikes on Tuesday (Sep 8) after the Iran-backed rebels targeted oil facilities and other sites, wounding dozens, in their heaviest attack in years.
The rapid round of strikes and counter-strikes follows the unravelling of a four-year truce in July, months into the Middle East war between the United States and Iran.
"Saudi aggression" hit Taiz province, where deadly fighting has raged for days, and Marib province, the Houthis' Almasirah TV station said. There was no immediate comment from the Saudis.
Overnight, Houthis attacks caused "temporary" shutdowns at oil sites and left 73 injured, authorities said. Saudi officials had vowed to respond.
The latest strikes add to a rapidly deteriorating situation in Yemen, where hundreds have died in recent days as the Houthis try to capture land at the mouth of the Red Sea.
The Houthis are vying to control the narrow Bab el-Mandeb strait, an increasingly important route for Saudi oil after Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz, slowing Gulf exports to a trickle.
Houthi attacks on oil infrastructure and Saudi tankers are piling pressure on the world's top oil exporter. Oil prices leapt towards US$100 a barrel on Tuesday.
GRIM IMAGES
Saudi Arabia's top diplomat Prince Faisal bin Farhan said the door to diplomacy was still open, but that the kingdom was ready to defend itself.
"The Kingdom will always support peace and diplomatic solutions," he said during a joint press conference in Moscow with his Russian counterpart.
"However, (Saudi Arabia) will not hesitate to defend itself, protect its interests, and support measures that secure the interests, security, and stability of brotherly Yemen."
The Houthi attacks came after the rebels accused Riyadh on Monday of an attack on a prison that killed 11 people and left 20 inmates missing, according to the rebels' Almasirah TV channel.
Grim images from the scene showed rescuers digging in the rubble with their bare hands and carrying bodies wrapped in blankets.
The Houthis said they fired dozens of ballistic missiles, hitting Abha International Airport, King Khalid air base and facilities belonging to state oil giant Aramco in Abha and Jizan.
An energy ministry source told the Saudi Press Agency that "several energy sector facilities and installations" in the south were targeted.
"The attacks caused fires at several locations, leading to a temporary halt in some operations" as well as several injuries, the source was quoted as saying.
Jizan, on the Red Sea coast just north of Saudi's Yemen border, has one of the country's biggest oil refineries with a capacity of 400,000 barrels per day.
According to maritime tracking company Kpler, it was out of action for several weeks until at least Aug 20 following Houthi attacks.
"SPIRAL OF ESCALATION"
The Houthis triggered a return to hostilities in divided Yemen's civil war in July, when they let an Iranian plane land in defiance of Saudi control of Yemeni airspace. The government retaliated by striking the airport.
The Saudi-led coalition, which has been fighting the Houthis on the government's behalf since 2015, said it would "take all necessary measures and actions to respond to the sources of the threat and neutralise its danger".
Andreas Krieg, a Gulf expert from King's College London, said the Houthi attacks create an "extremely uncomfortable dilemma" for Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the de facto Saudi ruler.
After years of trying to withdraw from the Yemen conflict, "restraint now carries the risk of allowing the Houthis to dictate the spiral of escalation", he said.
"Saudi Arabia's immediate response is likely to remain measured, involving airstrikes, intelligence support, and the reinforcement of Yemeni government forces," added Krieg.
"However, should attacks on Saudi cities persist, maintaining this restraint will become increasingly difficult. In effect, the Houthis are testing exactly where Riyadh's true red line now lies."

On the rainy morning of August 26, the front courtyard of District Women Hospital in Maharashtra’s Amravati district was crowded with politicians, reporters and bystanders. Amid them stood 30-year-old Swapnil Borde. His bottle-green shirt hung limp with sweat, while his red-rimmed eyes brimmed with tears.
He is the father of one of the three newborns who died after a fire broke out in the four-storey Special Newborn Care Unit and Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) on the third floor of the maternity hospital around 3.15 a.m. on August 24. Thirty-six babies were rescued and shifted to nearby hospitals, according to Amravati District Collector Ashish Yerekar. Two sustained burn injuries, says Amol Narote, medical superintendent of the government-run super-speciality hospital. Preliminary investigations indicate that a ventilator sparked the fire.
Also Read : Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar fire: 58 rescued, including nine newborns in blaze at hospital
Swapnil’s newborn was of low weight and had breathing issues, so was put on a ventilator two days before the fire.
“Gora bala kala kela. Ek minta pan nahi tambaycha ikde, khup bekar jhala ahe, pan mala ajun majhya mulachi janiv hote (My fair baby was turned black. I don’t want to be here even for a minute, but I still feel the presence of my child here),” says Swapnil, who works as a delivery person.
He adds, “This was the first baby in my family in this generation. It took us four years to conceive him. I took him in my arms only after he died.”
Outside the NICU, the empty fire extinguishers lay on the floor, while the soot-covered room, guarded by the police, continued to be frequented by people. Among them were members of a State-level investigation committee, Amravati MLC Pravin Pote and Achalpur Bharatiya Janata Party MLA Pravin Tayde. Former Leader of the Opposition in the Maharashtra Assembly and Congress leader Vijay Wadettiwar also visited the hospital. The parents of the other two newborns who died in the August 24 fire came from Achalpur and Paratwada, 50 km from the hospital.
Established in 1938, the hospital is one of Amravati’s major government maternity hospitals. It also caters to Wardha, Yavatmal and Washim districts. Primary healthcare centres and sub-district hospitals across Amravati, including Melghat, a tribal-dominated region, refer critical pregnancies here. The hospital was formerly known as Dufferin Hospital, named after Lady Hariot Dufferin, who established the Dufferin Fund in 1884 to provide medical aid to women in India.
Investigation underway
District Civil Surgeon Dr. Vinod Pawar, who is in charge of the maternity hospital, says, “Around 3.15 a.m., my staff in the NICU heard an explosion from the ventilator and saw fire coming out of it. They alerted the fire department and me simultaneously. Our priority was to rescue the babies.”
Dr. Pawar has submitted the fire-audit-related documents to the investigation committee. The police, meanwhile, have registered an accidental death report.
Maharashtra Minister for Public Health and Family Welfare Prakash Abitkar formed a seven-member committee headed by Public Health Commissioner Sanjay Katkar and directed it to submit its report within eight days. He said the committee’s findings would be made public and responsibility fixed.
On August 26, Mr. Katkar and the committee visited the spot and questioned the nurses who were present in the NICU at the time of the incident. The CCTV footage was also handed over to the committee, which comprises officials from the Maharashtra State Electricity Board, AIIMS and the Directorate of Medical Education and Research. It has been tasked with examining ventilator and electrical faults, the fire-audit history and administrative lapses. The report was due on August 31 but has not yet been released.
Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis announced ₹5 lakh in compensation for each family that lost its newborn in the fire and directed that the treatment of injured infants be fully covered by the government.
Of the 36 newborn babies, 11 have been admitted to Dr. Panjabrao Deshmukh Memorial Medical College (PDMMC), 10 to Hope Hospital, eight to Murkey Hospital and two to Parijat Hospital. Five were discharged with their mothers.
Survivors’ accounts
Radhika Yehkade, 19, was the last to deliver her twins before the fire. They were born around 2 a.m. on August 24 and kept in the NICU.
“I had a difficult pregnancy. I was in the hospital the week before my delivery. I am unable to let go of the voices in my head. Nurses shouting, ‘Help,’ people screaming, ‘Fire, fire.’ I am unable to make peace with the fact that my babies’ lives would have lasted only for two hours,” says Radhika, whose twins were admitted to PDMMC.
Radhika’s mother, Phula Shanware, 55, also an eyewitness, adds, “The smoke was dense; the fire brigade reached in time but took almost an hour to take water pipes to the third floor.”
Talking about her daughter, Phula says, “She had a tough pregnancy; we are daily wage earners and have already spent ₹80,000. We have been far from our house in Achalpur for almost 10 days.”
Another woman, Arti Kharale, 27, narrated her story. “When I saw my daughter, she smelt of wet ash. My heart sank when I heard about the fire,” says Arti, who lives in Amravati city. She says this was the second such fire in the hospital. The last, as reported by the media, was in September 2022.
Fifty-three-year-old Asha Dharse’s daughter delivered her baby at PDMMC. Chatting with other women, she says, “In June, I removed my daughter’s name from Dufrin because my cousin said they are negligent. Chutney, bhakri bhetel, pan aulad nahi, navas karava lagto (We will earn food, but not the baby).”
Yogesh Savarkar, 24, is waiting outside the maternity room at PDMMC, where his daughter and wife have been transferred. Recalling the night of the incident, he says he was among the first parents who barged into the room to rescue the infants.
He narrates, “The flames were soaring, wires were sparking, black smoke was coming out of the broken windows, and the equipment was burning. When I entered, I saw three children covered in black powder. One child had burns on his face. We rescued them first.”
Mr. Savarkar is also from Achalpur and came to the maternity hospital on August 17.
Maharashtra’s fire audits
Chief Minister Fadnavis has raised concerns over the hospital’s mandatory fire audit. A fire audit is a systematic inspection of fire safety readiness, assessing electrical load, wiring safety, overloaded circuits, faulty switchboards, and equipment prone to sparking or overheating, such as ventilators, oxygen concentrators and compressors.
According to data from Maharashtra’s Public Health Department, of the 530 government hospitals across the State, 528 have completed fire audits. As many as 442 hospitals have fire safety systems fully installed, while only 372 hospitals hold a fire no-objection certificate (NOC). This means nearly 30% of government hospitals do not have fire NOCs.
In Amravati alone, 18 government hospitals were audited, of which 16 received the NOC. Meanwhile, in Wardha and Gondia districts, 11 hospitals were audited, but none received the NOC. In Beed district in the Marathwada region, 18 hospitals did not receive NOCs.
On August 25, the Public Health Department announced a State-wide fire and electrical safety inspection of all government, private and charitable hospitals. Minister Abitkar had said, “If discrepancies are found in the audit, then they are to be rectified. Every hospital will appoint a nodal officer for fire safety, who will review fire audits, electrical safety, fire-fighting systems, emergency evacuation arrangements, staff training, and mock drills, and submit compliance information to senior levels.”
Initial warning
Records show that the Dufferin Hospital Authority had flagged concerns over the fire safety systems. A letter dated June 29 stated, “The hospital had obtained a fire NOC valid from June 22, 2025, to June 21, 2026. Before this validity period lapses, a registered licensed agency must conduct a fire safety audit, and Form B must be submitted to this office — so the fire NOC renewal proposal can then be forwarded to the Fire Department of Amravati Municipal Corporation.”
A follow-up letter was also written to the Public Works Department on July 17, reminding it to arrange a fire safety audit. “The fire NOC is an essential document for the hospital, and if its validity period lapses, the possibility of legal complications arising during an emergency cannot be ruled out,” the second letter stated, urging immediate action. The letter was marked to Amravati District Collector Ashish Yerekar and health services in the Akola division. Mr. Yerekar has not responded to The Hindu’s query regarding the action taken after receiving this letter.
Meanwhile, hospital staff and patients said this was the second fire incident in the last five years. “We learnt from our mistakes in the 2022 fire. That is why we have been extra careful with fire audits,” says an official from the Amravati maternity hospital. According to hospital authorities, a ventilator in the NICU had also caught fire then, causing minor injuries to two newborns.
The ventilators in both cases were supplied by Schiller Healthcare, which has been called for the investigation. An official said a committee will be set up to create SOPs for the procurement of medical equipment.
Courage under fire
Outside the NICU, the smell of smoke lingered. In the corridor, kaksh-sevikas (nursing attendants) were waiting for their turns to appear before the committee as part of the investigation. Among them was Surekha Dhanvijay, 45, one of the four attendants present in the NICU, who witnessed the fire and called for help. “The moment I heard the explosion, a huge flame burst out. With our bare hands, we tried to douse the fire near the cradle and take a baby out.”
“I have only one regret: that we couldn’t save those three children,” says Kirti Ghanvir, 45, another nursing attendant. Showing her fire burns and blisters, Ms. Ghanvir adds, “I had to feel around in the burning cradles to see if there was a baby. When I found one, I grabbed it.”
In the meantime, they informed others in the hospital, who rushed to help. “Most of us wrapped blankets around ourselves, broke the glass and entered, rescuing babies,” says Lalita Lasbe, 35.
The sevikas say they do not want any appreciation as they consider this part of their jobs, but appeal to the government to increase their salaries. They say they currently get ₹8,000 a month and are hired on contract, so their salaries barely increase.

Ruling BJP expels 42 rebels ahead of first phase of Rajasthan civic polls
Former Ajmer mayor Dharmendra Gehlot whose wife is contesting the polls as an independent is among the 42 expelled
The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has expelled 42 functionaries, including former Ajmer mayor Dharmendra Gehlot, for six years for supporting rebels or standing as independent candidates for the first phase of Rajasthan’s urban local body elections on Wednesday.
BJP state general secretary Shravan Singh Bagdi issued the expulsion orders on Monday night on the instructions of state president Madan Rathore, saying the 42 were found guilty of indiscipline.
Gehlot has been campaigning for his wife, Hemlata Gehlot, who is contesting the polls as an independent, in defiance of the party line. He was also accused of making objectionable remarks on social media and was expelled along with his wife.
Jaipur accounts for the highest number of expulsions (26). Former councillors Harishankar Bohra, Dinesh Kanwat and Raju Agarwal are among those expelled in Jaipur. As many as 13 functionaries were expelled in Jaipur’s Vidyadhar Nagar assembly constituency alone. BJP Scheduled Caste wing state vice-president Mukesh Kirad has also been expelled.
In Pratapgarh, the party expelled seven leaders, including former municipal council chairperson Ramkanya. Leela Devi, wife of former municipal vice-chairperson Tikamchand Soni, is among those expelled in Sirohi.
Rajasthan Congress chief Govind Singh Dotasara warned rebels during the nomination withdrawal period that anyone remaining in the fray against an official candidate would face disciplinary action and be expelled from the party for six years.
Amin Kagzi, who heads Congress’s disciplinary committee for the civic elections, said no candidate had lodged a complaint against any rebel. He promised disciplinary action if a complaint is lodged.
Over 100 Congress rebels are believed to be contesting the elections in Jaipur alone, but no action had been taken against them so far.
Campaigning for the first phase of polling ended on Monday. The 48-hour silence period will precede polling on Wednesday across 5,425 wards and 162 urban local bodies.
The first phase covers municipal corporations, municipal councils and municipalities in cities including Jaipur. Elections to all 309 urban local bodies are being conducted in two phases, with the second phase of polling scheduled for Friday. Results will be announced on September 14.
The Congress last week launched the “Gen-Z for Change” campaign and constituted a state-level Professional Gen-Z Committee ahead of local polls. The move came weeks after student protests over examination irregularities forced the then Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign in July.
Employment, access to opportunities and preparedness for a digital future have emerged as important concerns among young voters.
Rajasthan, where power has alternated between the BJP and the Congress every five years since 1993, is due to go to the assembly polls in 2028.

Tiranga Yatra at 13000 Feet- National Pride Celebrated in Tawang’s Border Villages
The spirit of patriotism reached the high frontiers of Arunachal Pradesh as the Chuna and Mago Sector Vibrant Villages in Tawang district hosted a Tiranga Yatra at an altitude of nearly 13,000 feet. The event brought together local communities, the civil administration, Panchayati Raj representatives, and security forces in a celebration of national unity and pride.
The program was organized as part of the Har Ghar Tiranga campaign and commemorated 150 years of Vande Mataram, connecting the national celebration with the people living in one of India’s most remote border regions.
A Community Celebration at the Frontier
The Tiranga Yatra was organised by the Jang Sub-Divisional Administration in collaboration with the Indian Army, Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), BJP Mandal 3-Mukto, and residents of Chuna and Mago.
The yatra was flagged off by the Zilla Parishad Chairperson, in the presence of the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Assistant Commissioner, Panchayat representatives, Heads of Offices, senior personnel of the Indian Army and ITBP, and local residents.
The participation of people from different sections of the community reflected the spirit of collective responsibility and the strong bond between frontier communities, the administration, and the forces serving in the region.
A 300-Meter Tricolour Across the Mountains
The highlight of the celebration was the carrying of a 300-meter-long National Tricolour from Chuna to Mago village.
Against the backdrop of the Eastern Himalayas, the Tricolour made its way through the high-altitude terrain, turning the yatra into a memorable expression of national pride. The event was further enriched by a band performance by students of Higher Secondary School Jang, whose participation brought the enthusiasm of the younger generation to the celebrations.
Honouring India’s Frontier Communities
Events such as the Tiranga Yatra also highlight the important role of Arunachal Pradesh’s border communities in the country’s frontier landscape. Villages such as Chuna and Mago are located in challenging high-altitude terrain, where communities continue to live, work, and contribute to the social and economic life of the region.
The participation of villagers alongside the Indian Army, ITBP, civil administration, and Panchayati Raj representatives demonstrated the importance of community participation in strengthening the social fabric of the border areas.
The event also complemented the broader objective of the Vibrant Villages Programme, which seeks to improve infrastructure, connectivity, livelihoods, and public services in strategically located border villages while strengthening their connection with the rest of the country.
The Tricolour at the High Frontiers
The Tiranga Yatra at Chuna and Mago was more than a ceremonial event. It brought the national spirit directly to communities living at one of India’s highest and most remote frontiers.
The sight of a 300-meter Tricolour moving through the Himalayan landscape served as a powerful reminder of the unity that connects every part of the country, from its cities and towns to its most distant border villages.
At nearly 13,000 feet, the celebration reflected the resilience of Arunachal Pradesh’s frontier communities and the enduring spirit of national unity.

Spain has seen no evidence “whatsoever” that Morocco planned or facilitated a mass border breach into its north African territory of Ceuta, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has told parliament.
The address on Thursday followed the emergence of a police report, commissioned by a judge and widely quoted in the media, claiming Moroccan border forces had actively aided about 70,000 people to cross the border in late July.
“I can assure you that no institution – not the diplomatic service, nor the European Commission, nor any international body – has provided the Spanish government with any solid evidence that Morocco planned or carried out the incident. None whatsoever,” Sánchez told parliament.
Speaking the morning after about 50,000 people marched in Madrid to protest his handling of the Ceuta crisis, the socialist prime minister also denied the government had received any warning of the mass breach, saying no reports to authorities had anticipated “the scale or probability of what eventually happened”.
Sánchez has repeatedly defended Morocco during the crisis, highlighting Rabat’s cooperation in returning most of the migrants in the days after the surge.
But he said on Thursday that Spain had summoned Morocco’s ambassador on 21 August because of “unacceptable statements” made by two ministers over Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish north African territory. Last month, Morocco’s justice minister, Abdellatif Ouahbi, publicly reiterated Rabat’s sovereignty claims over the cities.
Sánchez said he had “for now” ruled out Moroccan government involvement but conceded that Moroccan forces had allowed crossings to occur during a key 10-hour period on 30 July.
Many of those who crossed said in interviews they had been actively encouraged to do so. Moroccan officials have denied enabling the crossing.
Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party, called on Sánchez to resign for his “incompetence and complicity”.
In response to Sánchez summoning the Moroccan ambassador to discuss the crisis, Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, said: “Morocco doesn’t need an ambassador in Spain – you are its ambassador.”
As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to enter Ceuta at the end of July. The influx unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency and reignited tensions within the EU over immigration.
On Thursday, Sánchez appealed for European solidarity over the crisis. He did not single out any countries by name but, in a pointed passage apparently aimed at Italy and Denmark, the two countries that had led public criticism of Spain, said the principle of solidarity should apply to Ceuta as much as it applies to Greenland and Lampedusa.
Although 90% of the people had returned to Morocco within 24 hours, several thousand, including at least 500 minors, are thought to remain, either living on the street or in makeshift shelters.
Amid calls from Vox to return them to Morocco, Sánchez reminded parliament that under Spanish, European and international law, migrants had a right to be treated as individuals. “You can’t just grab someone by the arm and drag them across the frontier as though they were a sack of dirt,” he told MPs.
In reference to the hundreds of destitute minors, Aina Vidal of the leftwing group Sumar, said: “They’re children, not invaders, not soldiers. They didn’t come carrying bombs, they arrived wearing water wings, in tears.”
It seems likely the government will invest in facilities in Ceuta to accommodate the remaining migrants rather than risk the political backlash both in Spain and across Europe were they to bring them to the mainland.
There is also evidence that, faced with hunger as well as hostility from many local people, some migrants have already begun going back to Morocco.
However, as Sánchez told parliament, the per capita income of Ceuta is eight times that of Morocco and “even if we build a wall 100 metres high there will still be people prepared to throw themselves into the sea to get across”.
“We will not stop working until Ceuta emerges from this difficult situation: stronger, more prosperous, and more integrated with the rest of Spain and the EU,” he added.

While warning that breaching the 1.5°C global warming limit would bring irreversible losses that no adaptation initiatives could undo, the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) on Wednesday (September 2, 2026), for the first time, set out a detailed “overshoot, peak and decline” pathway.
This is a route under which the world overshoots the 2015 Paris Agreement’s central goal — limiting the rise in average global temperatures to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels — which a UNEP report said was now unavoidable, but holds the peak as low as possible and then brings temperatures back down below the limit by the end of the century.
The report, Limiting Overshoot, released in Nairobi, said global warming would cross 1.5°C “in the next few years”. Even a scenario in which every country delivers on its national climate plan and net-zero target puts peak warming at 1.8°C, it said. According to the report, current policies point to a rise of about 2.6°C by 2100, with a range of 1.9–3.6°C. The pathway, the report said, "is by no means an acceptable or preferred pathway; it is simply the best remaining option."
The diplomatic grounds for that framing were laid at the 30th UN Climate Change Conference, COP30, held in 2025 in Brazil’s Belém, where the consensus “Global Mutirão” decision became the first COP text to concede that a temporary overshoot of the 1.5°C limit was likely, given how fast the remaining carbon budget was being spent. At the conference, countries also committed, for the first time, to limiting the size and duration of the overshoot and to closing adaptation gaps, which would require deep, rapid and sustained emission cuts.
Given that cuts alone will no longer suffice, a steep scaling up of nature-based removals such as large reforestation programmes was needed, COP30 CEO Ana Toni said in a statement. UN Secretary-General Antőnio Guterres also released a statement, saying, “This summer’s scorching heat, raging wildfires and deadly floods are a warning of what lies ahead. We must make the overshoot above 1.5 degrees as small and short as possible. That demands an overshoot of ambition."
Compounding costs
The UNEP report suggested that time spent above 1.5°C carries compounding costs such as faster sea-level rise, coral reef collapse, glacier loss exceeding a quarter of global mass by 2100, declines of up to 14% in global food production by 2050 without effective adaptation, and rising odds of irreversible tipping points in the West Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets, the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation and the Amazon.
Moreover, it gets harder to roll back the effects of a tonne of emitted carbon. The report computed that every five years of continued high emissions adds roughly 0.1°C to peak warming. Reversing that same 0.1°C afterwards means pulling about 220 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide back out of the atmosphere over and above whatever is still being emitted. Very broadly, a single large tree growing for about 30 years can cut out only a tonne of carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide removal, the report stresses, is needed in addition to, not instead of, emission cuts, and can credibly cool temperatures back to the 1.5°C limit only if peak warming stays well below 2°C. Even the most optimistic scaling up of emission cuts is unlikely to reverse more than a few tenths of a degree this century, the report underlined.
UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen was explicit that the report is not a concession. “Let’s be very clear, the 1.5 target is still the goal. But now we need to approach it differently from above,” she said.
The report arrives at a moment of uncertainty over whether countries will cut emissions at all. The United States, the world’s largest historical emitter, formally exited the Paris Agreement earlier this year and has also announced its withdrawal from the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change and the Green Climate Fund. Separately, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz following the conflict in West Asia has produced what the International Energy Agency calls the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market, with output from affected countries down more than 14 million barrels a day. Sustained high energy prices could push governments toward coal and other short-term fossil responses.
Methane targets
The report, in a first for the UN, placed significant stress on methane, which currently contributes about 0.5°C of warming. Cutting it is described as the most effective way to slow warming in the near term. Human activity currently puts out roughly 350–400 million tonnes of methane a year, mostly from fossil fuel operations, livestock, rice paddies, landfills and wastewater. When modellers build the pathways that underpin net-zero targets, they typically assume that about half of this gets cut by mid-century through “cheap, technically easy” interventions such as plugging leaks and venting from oil and gas. But the other half, roughly 150–200 million tonnes a year still being emitted in 2050 from agriculture and waste, is harder to cut; though shaving 60–70 million tonnes from it could reduce temperature rise to the same extent as removing 220 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.
Over 155 countries have joined the Global Methane Pledge to cut anthropogenic methane at least 30% below 2020 levels by 2030. India, China, Russia and Iran remain outside it.
The UNEP report co-author Richard Betts of the University of Exeter said, “It is a reality check. We have to live with this warmer world."

Quebec moves to protect supply chains, expand relief to more businesses as trade war intensifies
15% local content requirements on public construction, broader access to trade relief funds
With Canada's new counter-tariffs against the United States set to take effect Tuesday, Quebec's government has announced measures it says will diversify the economy while protecting local businesses and jobs.
"The government aims to be prepared should the situation escalate further," reads a news release issued late Monday evening by the Treasury Board Secretariat and the Ministry of Economy, Innovation and Energy.
Premier Christine Fréchette stepped back from the provincial election campaign Monday to call a special cabinet meeting on the intensifying trade war with the United States.
The move comes as Canada plans to retaliate against the latest U.S. tariffs, slapping new duties ranging from 15 to 50 per cent on hundreds of American products. Those Canadian counter-tariffs are set to take effect Tuesday.
The new Canadian duties are part of the dollar-for-dollar response promised by Prime Minister Mark Carney last August, following the breakdown of negotiations with the U.S. — and the implementation of 50 per cent tariffs on nearly $28 billion worth of Canadian products.
Under the procurement changes outlined in the release, the Centre d'acquisitions gouvernementales can now reserve public contracts for companies with an establishment in Quebec or Canada.
Public tenders can also require goods to be manufactured or processed locally, and bidders can receive a 15 per cent preference margin based on Quebec or Canadian value-added content.
"The government is using its purchasing power to support the local economy — creating more opportunities for businesses, sustaining jobs and reducing reliance on the U.S. market," the release says.
Contracts need Quebec, Canadian sourcing
Additionally, for construction contracts valued under $9.2 million, the Transport Ministry, Santé Québec and the Société québécoise des infrastructures will have to require that at least 15 per cent of the value of materials and equipment be Quebec- or Canadian-sourced.
The release notes that the $9.2-million threshold on construction rules aligns with flexibility allowed under international trade agreements. The 15 per cent local content rule was chosen to boost regional suppliers without causing material shortages or supply-chain overheating.
For projects exceeding $9.2 million, more ambitious requirements could be imposed on a case-by-case basis by decree, the news release says.
The province is also expanding direct financial support. The Fonds offensif pour le renforcement des capacités économiques will be made more flexible to help businesses access needed liquidity, including by allowing available funding to be disbursed more quickly and allowing a company to repay an existing loan.
Emergency assistance for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) is also being expanded, with businesses reporting annual revenue between $200,000 and $2 million now eligible.
To reduce reliance on the U.S. market, the province is deploying a dedicated interprovincial task force led by Investissement Québec International, the release says. The team will help SMEs expand into other provinces by finding buyers, securing contracts and replacing American supplies with Quebec products.
The government is also asking Crown corporations to adopt a Quebec-focused purchasing strategy amid the tariff war. It says they will be allowed to depart from the province's public-contracting law to do so, with administrative discussions already underway.
The news release says the government is not ruling out additional measures.
Party leaders weigh in
The premier held a meeting with party leaders after discussing the matter with her cabinet.
In a news conference following that meeting, Québec Solidaire co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal said Fréchette couldn't specify how severely the counter-tariffs would impact Quebec compared to the rest of Canada.
"Everyone knew very clearly that Quebec is the province most impacted by Trump's tariffs. How come we don't know regarding Carney?"
On X, Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon dismissed the briefing as little more than a "lecture" of decrees and measures already slated for public release.  
St-Pierre Plamondon said opposition leaders still have not received the detailed breakdown of Canada's retaliatory tariff list or recent updates.
In reply to St-Pierre Plamondon's post, Conservative Party of Quebec Leader Éric Duhaime said he felt validated in his decision to not attend Fréchette's meeting, which he called a "great theatrical piece."
Quebec Liberal Party Leader Charles Milliard questioned the premier's readiness.
"I came out of there not at all reassured," he told journalists after the meeting with Fréchette.
He said Fréchette told him she had not yet spoken with other provincial premiers about the tariff crisis. On X, he had accused the Coalition Avenir Québec government of "inaction and improvisation" and waiting until its back was against the wall before acting.

As students head back to school, parents have all the usual worries about their kids, like remembering to pack lunch and making it to the bus stop on time. But parents of immunocompromised kids have a new one: How to deal with the resurgence of measles.
Cases of the highly transmissible disease have reached a 35-year high in the US, with nearly 3,000 confirmed infections in 2026 so far. The first two measles-related deaths of the year were recorded in Pennsylvania, right as the school year is getting going. With vaccination rates dropping across the country, parents of kids who aren’t able to get vaccinated or don’t mount a strong enough immune response due to weakened immune systems are weighing whether it’s safe enough to go to school.
Victoria Schiano, national community engagement coordinator for Little Lobbyists, a nonprofit that advocates for children with complex medical needs and disabilities, says the return of measles is “absolutely terrifying.”
While it’s not known exactly how many US children have compromised immune systems, a study by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimated that 2.6 percent of children are immunocompromised. Immune deficiencies can have genetic causes or secondary reasons, such as chemotherapy for cancer treatment.
Schiano’s kid is among them. Her 10-year-old has mitochondrial disease. The family lives in Chester County, Pennsylvania, which has the second-highest number of measles cases in the state right now. Schiano has been closely monitoring the vaccination rates in her son’s school district, which have dipped below the 95 percent threshold needed for community protection against measles. Measles is breaking through in places where vaccination has dropped below that threshold. In neighboring Lancaster County, for example, just 87.6 percent of kindergartners are fully vaccinated against measles and 83.3 percent of seventh graders are.
Her son can’t be vaccinated, and he receives weekly infusions of immunoglobulin—concentrated antibodies from donated human blood plasma—to help his body fight infections.
“Measles is dangerous for anyone, but for him, this absolutely could be life or death,” she says.
The virus can cause severe, life-threatening complications such as pneumonia and brain swelling. Measles can also wipe out the body’s memory of past infections—a phenomenon known as immune amnesia—leaving people susceptible to other diseases.
Her son already wears a mask and uses a plexiglass screen at school, and the family is diligent about handwashing. Now, Schiano says they’ve had to make the difficult decision to limit her son’s time with friends and after-school activities like karate. She says it’s hard as a parent to balance his quality of life with his safety.
“He just wants to play and to do all the things that he sees other kids doing,” she says.
Her son did online school for a time during Covid-19, and she says she’s prepared to take him out of school if there’s even one confirmed measles case. That comes with a different set of risks, though. During the pandemic, remote learning was associated with an increase in social isolation and behavioral and mental health issues among students.
Amalia, a parent in South Carolina who asked to go by a pseudonym for privacy reasons, has already chosen to keep her 16-year-old son home this year and do online schooling due to concerns about measles. Her son has immunoglobulin A deficiency, in which the body doesn’t produce enough of an antibody found in mucous membranes, body fluids, and digestive tracts that help fend off germs.
“Even if there’s just a flu going around, he gets sicker than the average kid will,” she says.
Her son was able to get the measles vaccine, but doctors monitor his antibody levels regularly to check for waning immunity.
She lives in Spartanburg County, where measles broke out earlier this year and caused nearly 1,000 cases and 21 hospitalizations. About 91 percent of those cases were among children and teens, and most were among those who were not fully vaccinated or had an unknown vaccination status. Even though there was a 94 percent increase in the number of vaccines administered during the outbreak in Spartanburg County compared to the year before, she still wasn’t comfortable sending her son back to school.
“Covid happened, and then measles happened, and we just feel like it's not going to be the last time,” she says. “If it's not measles, it's going to be something else because rates for other vaccines have fallen, too.”
Before this year, her son shared a classroom with other students who have special accommodations. But outside of that setting, Amalia says it has been difficult for him to make friends because of his medical condition. She says it’s hard to talk to other parents about vaccination status because it can be such a hot-button issue. The family is thinking about moving because of what she views as an anti-vaccination sentiment in the community as well as “hostility” toward masking that she’s encountered.
“Some people don't want to take ownership of the responsibility of public health,” she says. “I think it's something we're supposed to share across humanity. It's not supposed to be carried by one person.”
Cortney, another South Carolina parent of an immunocompromised kid, says the state’s measles outbreak was highly concerning because the family needed to travel near the epicenter for medical appointments. Whereas before they might stop in town to eat lunch or do some shopping, they ended any unnecessary stops. “We planned to drive directly into that county, we go only to the doctor, and we leave,” Cortney says.
Her 17-year-old daughter Grace’s condition means that rhinovirus—the cause of the common cold—led to her getting hospitalized. During Covid, Grace and her brother were homeschooled, and that is something mother and daughter considered again for Grace’s senior year.
“At the end of the semester, we're going to reevaluate and see where things are,” Grace says.
Even though she is immunocompromised, Grace doesn’t wear a mask at school because of fear of being bullied. Cortney says her family’s preference would be to mask while in public, but she’s concerned about being ostracized. “You worry that your family could be targeted,” she says. “It’s unfortunate that we have to think about that.”

'The crowd shouted that we'd stolen someone's genitals' - deadly rumours spread on social media
- Published
More than 80 people were killed between October 2025 and July this year following false accusations about what is termed "genital theft", the BBC Global Disinformation Unit has found after gathering data from police forces across six African countries.
The killings are linked to rumours that a simple tap on the shoulder can cause a man's genitals to shrink or disappear. They are being fuelled by widespread misinformation on social media.
"They were shouting that we had stolen someone's genitals and we didn't have any way to escape because there was a huge crowd," Tanzanian mechanic Boniface Mgala told the BBC about his ordeal in April when he was badly beaten by those convinced he was a genital thief.
His experience was similar to those in videos seen by the BBC: men claim that their genital organs - penis and testicles - have vanished or shrivelled after coming into contact with strangers and a mob then demands that alleged perpetrators return what they have supposedly stolen.
Such claims are rooted in longstanding fears and superstitions - and are not new on the continent, particularly in communities where belief in witchcraft remains widespread. Social media has amplified these fears.
The recent wave of rumours appears to have started last year in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where similar claims had surfaced in 2008.
They progressively spread across the region to Burundi, Zambia and Tanzania as well as Mozambique, Angola, Malawi and Kenya.
In Zambia, the hearsay about disappearing genitals first gained traction in March when a woman was lynched, going on to spread panic across the border in Tanzania.
At his home in Mpemba near Tunduma, a busy trading town in Tanzania by the border with Zambia, Mgala traces his fingers along the sickle-shaped scar that runs down the right side of his head as he reflects on his traumatic experience.
"If I had known how close I would have come to death on that day, I wouldn't have gone into that restaurant to eat. Only we don't know how close death is," the mechanic says.
He and his friend had gone into Tunduma on 1 April to meet a client about a car sale and decided to eat lunch beforehand. They had not long sat down in the restaurant when they were dragged outside by a mob.
Two smaller scars on his chin and a missing tooth are other visible marks of his ordeal.
Amid the beating, he lost consciousness. Mgala regained awareness in hospital two days later to news that his friend had been killed.
Back at his house where he lives with his wife and their four children, he now walks with a limp and says he also suffers from constant headaches.
He has not been able to return to work at his mechanic shop but says neighbours and friends have helped cover the cost of some of the medicine he needs.
On the same day that Mgala and his friend were attacked, commercial photographer and businessman Michael Silavwe says he witnessed another similar assault in Tunduma, where he says anxiety had been building after videos about stolen genitalia had begun circulating on TikTok.
Outside his shop he saw people running and says he learned that a man had been accused nearby and was being beaten - and later set on fire.
"After they set him on fire, the police arrived at the scene and everyone scattered and ran away," the 23-year-old told the BBC.
In a video of the attack verified by the BBC Global Disinformation Unit and viewed more than 100,000 times across TikTok and Facebook, a group is seen beating a man while demanding he return the victim's allegedly stolen genitals.
"Those incidents kept escalating and people kept getting beaten," Silavwe said, adding that at the time young people like him did feel scared, but he understands now there is no truth to the rumours.
I came to realise it was not true"
Asha Steven Mwakilasa, a 50-year-old tailor and fashion designer in Tunduma, which is in Momba district, agrees: "I came to realise it was not true."
This does not stop her anxiety - especially if her husband or sons are out, but she says she is grateful that the police are now mounting patrols.
Momba district commissioner Elias Daniel Mwandobo told the BBC local investigations suggested there was deliberate criminal intent behind some of the incidents: "Individuals conspired to commit a crime and incite public panic for their own benefits."
Another video recorded in Tanzania's main city of Dar es Salaam shows a crowd marching a man down a dusty market street, pushing, grabbing and striking him and insisting he returns the genitalia, as the man pleads his innocence.
The BBC Disinformation Unit verified similar videos of attacks in Mozambique and Kenya.
Dozens of these recordings of mob violence, alleged first-person accounts, warnings about alleged incidents, commentary and videos framed as reports of events in particular areas are circulating across TikTok and Facebook.
Many of those analysed by the BBC, including some showing mob violence, remain online.
"We are reviewing the content shared with us and will take action on those that are found to violate our policies," a Meta spokesperson told the BBC.
TikTok has yet to respond to a BBC request for comment.
With some social media creators, who warn viewers to be vigilant, it is often unclear whether they believe the claims or are primarily seeking engagement.
Alongside these posts, some users promote so-called charms said to protect against genital theft, while comedians have parodied the claims through comedy skits.
Smartphones and social media make rumours spread faster, reach larger audiences and become more difficult to control once they begin circulating, says author Julien Bonhomme.
His book, The Sex Thieves: The Anthropology of a Rumor, examines how hearsay about "sex thieves" spread and why people believe them.
People are not simply hearing claims that someone has lost his genitals - they are seeing distressed men say it has happened to them, or watching crowds respond to accusations, he says.
Videos shared on social media can make unverified claims appear more believable, he says, because of their immediacy, describing this as "one of the most significant differences" between the current digital environment and earlier outbreaks.
The worst-hit country has been Mozambique, where the police said in May that 55 people had been killed in six weeks, including a police officer, health workers and civil servants.
Mozambique's President Daniel Chapo publicly condemned widespread rumours and deaths, saying the claims were false and the government had found no medical evidence to suggest anyone had lost a part of their body.
The two healthcare workers were attacked at their home and workplace in April in Cabo Delgado province - a region that borders Tanzania which has been affected by an Islamist insurgency for nearly a decade.
The health facilities in the areas of the attacks had to close for weeks while the authorities launched public awareness campaigns to counter the claims.
As part of the health campaign, the government said some of the fears could be linked to Koro syndrome, a mental illness otherwise known as missing or genital retraction hysteria.
The most recent incidents of violence have occurred in Kenya, where five people were killed by mobs in the coastal counties of Kwale and Mombasa.
After the first incidents were reported in July, Mombasa County Commissioner Mohamed Noor blamed some content creators for spreading the claims to boost engagement "simply to attract views and attention".
"Such misinformation can easily lead to loss of life," Noor told the BBC.
He said police had since contained the violence and made several arrests, including a father and son who were sentenced to a year in prison after pleading guilty to assaulting a woman they accused of causing men's genitals to disappear.
Similar claims also fuelled mob attacks in Malawi, leaving eight people dead.
Back in Tunduma, in neighbouring Tanzania, even as mechanic Mgala recovers from the physical impact of the assault, the emotional pain is still raw.
"It still hurts me deeply when I think back to the senseless manner my friend died because I still don't know what was going on," he said.
"To suddenly find yourself being pelted with stones for no reason, and then end up losing your life?"

In a parallel universe, this week is Harry Brook's first as England's new Test captain.
There are numerous reasons why it will be Joe Root, rather than Brook, leading England into a new era against Pakistan at Headingley: the timing of Ben Stokes' retirement, Brook's workload as white-ball captain and Root's surprise willingness to resume the job among them.
Inescapably, there is also what happened during the winter, when Brook was punched by a nightclub bouncer in Wellington on the eve of a one-day international against New Zealand.
In June, Brook said it would be an "honour" to be asked to succeed Stokes. Almost two months later, he does not know if the Wellington incident has cost him the top job, at least for now.
"I dunno," he tells BBC Sport. "I honestly don't know. I don't really look at it like that.
"The decision to make Rooty captain is the right one. I'm actually really excited to see what he can do. He's definitely the right man to take over that job. I'm really looking forward to working alongside him."
For some, Brook became the poster boy of everything they disliked about the Bazball era, both for what happened off the field and for the way he plays the game on it.
At this point, it's probably worth noting that no man has scored more international runs across formats since Brook made his Test debut in 2022. Of all players to have batted at least 20 times in Test cricket for England in the past 60 years, no one has a higher average than Brook's 53.04.
Brook has occasionally done himself no favours, but there is also something uncomfortable about the narrative that surrounds the 27-year-old, especially in a sport that struggles with elitism.
He often speaks about how he is living his dream - his parents have told him he has been talking about playing for England since he uttered his first words.
But not everything about playing for England is a dream. Scrutiny, criticism and the court of public opinion. Brook had the lot after the Wellington misdemeanour became public knowledge.
"It was a tough period, especially when I was at home, getting ready to face the media," he says.
"I feel like the character that I showed throughout that period to go out there and still perform and lead the white-ball side fairly well - I was proud of myself and the team.
"I don't want to say it's helped me, but it's made me realise how big it is to be England captain. It's not just the leadership on the field. It makes a massive difference if you can lead with responsibility off the field."
Amid the Wellington fallout, Brook led England to important ODI and T20 series wins in Sri Lanka, as well as the semi-finals of the World Cup that followed. His own form was superb. In the maelstrom, he drew on an experience from three years earlier.
In 2023, his only season in the pressure cooker of the Indian Premier League (IPL), Brook struggled. After his one significant score for Sunrisers Hyderabad - admittedly an unbeaten century - he said he was glad to "shut up" supporters that had been "slagging me off".
"I got into a little bit of a rabbit hole with scrutiny and social media when I was at the IPL," says Brook.
"It didn't help me as a person on the field or off the field. I decided to, not stay away from social media, but also not go out of my way to look at it.
"On the other hand, I actually feel it's a little bit of a compliment if people are giving me scrutiny and have an opinion about my game.
"I know it's not a nice thing to see people slagging you off, but it means people care and people think I can put in a better performance than I have done that day."
There are comparisons that can be drawn between Brook and Stokes. Maverick players from working-class backgrounds, often finding themselves outnumbered by the well-to-do members of the dressing room.
But, like Stokes, Brook is authentic in the way he plays and speaks, even if that can get him into trouble. One example would be Brook's "who cares" line about batters being caught in the deep after an ODI against Australia two years ago.
"I would say that I'm an extremely honest person," says Brook. "I'm honest with myself and honest with my game.
"A lot of people say honesty is the best policy. I probably have got into trouble a few times being too honest."
Authenticity bleeds into Brook's batting, for better and worse. He is probably the most thrilling batter to wear an England shirt since Kevin Pietersen and no batter with at least 3,000 Test runs has scored more quickly than Brook, whose strike rate is almost 87 runs per 100 balls.
But Brook can delight and frustrate in equal measure, nowhere more so than on an Ashes tour when an average just under 40 was a disservice to his ability.
Costly crimes included his drive at Scott Boland in the calamitous second-innings collapse in the first Test and trying to hit Mitchell Starc for six over extra cover in the first innings of the second Test. "Shocking shots" were how Brook described them in Australia.
"If supporters get frustrated, imagine how frustrated I get," says Brook.
"It's something I've been really trying to work on, trying to assess conditions quicker, and read the surface better. To go out there knowing what shots are going to be hard and what is going to be easier.
"I practise every single shot and have done since the age of eight. In the nets, I'd do a 360 challenge with my dad. He'd throw balls and I'd have to try to hit it to a certain place: that corner, then that corner.
"I have the ability to hit it everywhere, I just have to figure it out quicker in games."
At the end of that Ashes, Stokes pulled Brook aside to tell him his Test average could be as high as 65 or 70.
Though Brook says it's "not that easy", Stokes' point is only a select few have Brook's talent, and he might not be making the most of it.
"Yeah, maybe," says Brook. "I'm definitely not the finished article and maybe never will be."
And, when Brook says he knows what it is like to be a disappointed supporter, he pulls out his own example from when he was 16 years old, one that goes some way to explaining why he has grown so close to Brendon McCullum.
"I remember as a kid going to watch Baz play at Headingley for Warwickshire and Matthew Fisher got him out in his first over. I was absolutely devastated. I'd only gone to watch him," says Brook.
"After he got out I said to my dad, 'Can we just go home'. I kind of understand it as a fan of cricket."
Brook grew up at Burley-in-Wharfdale Cricket Club, where his entire family is part of the furniture.
Brook's father David recently had his 50th birthday party at the club, while Harry still nets there and gets along to watch while he can.
A scholarship to Sedbergh School - "posh", in Brook's words - was where he honed his game, with 6.20am nets run by former Kent player Martin Speight. Speight remains one of Brook's closest advisors.
Challenged to improve his conditioning as a teenager, Brook has worked hard on his fitness as a professional.
He used the time when he missed England's tour of India in early 2024 - his grandmother Pauline died in March that year - to get back on track after he had "slipped on the wrong path".
"I wasn't as good an athlete as I could have been," says Brook. "I went on meal plans, I went to the gym and ran, with schedules from the strength and conditioning coach.
"When I came back, I felt like I was seeing the ball a hell of a lot easier. The pace of a delivery felt slower. It helped to bat for longer periods of time and run twos better.
"It made a massive difference to my fielding as well. I just think it was a vital area of my career so far that I've improved on and it's made a massive difference."
When he was named as England white-ball captain last year, Brook pulled out of the IPL and remains banned from the competition as a result.
"Not really," says Brook, on suggestions of regrets over his exile from cricket's most lucrative tournament.
Club cricket, school, fitness and no franchise gigs apart from The Hundred are all parts of what Brook has put into his England career.
He may not be Test captain now, though he knows there is a good chance the job will come. When it does, Brook will have a better understanding of what it means to be captain because of his experiences of the past year.
"There are little things you learn throughout your career," he says. "Obviously, the past few months have been on quite a high scale.
"Having that responsibility now has made a massive difference for me. There is the potential I could be captain, but at this moment in time all I'm focusing on is trying to win a few games of cricket. I will be 1,000% behind Rooty and I'm really looking forward to what this Test side can do."
And, in the tough moments, Brook's England career never stopped being his dream.
"I'm an extremely upbeat person. I'm always happy," he says. "Even when things are bad, I think there's no point dwelling on things. You've got to be happy.
"I'm in a very privileged position to be able to say I do something I love as a job. I refuse to call it a job, but I'm doing something I love for work. That is a dream come true.
"Every time I step over the white line, it's always a phenomenal feeling to be able to say, 'This is my life.'"

Chrystia Freeland negotiated with Trump. Now she's watching a trade war unfold
Former Canadian Minister of Finance discusses trade war between the U.S. and Canada
Canada's latest tariffs on American goods took effect Tuesday. It's another escalation in a trade war that is raising costs and testing a relationship that, until recently, was among the closest in the world.
Prime Minister Mark Carney's government imposed tariffs of up to 50% on about $20 billion worth of U.S. goods in response to U.S. tariffs on Canadian products. The latest measures match U.S. tariffs dollar for dollar, though not product for product.
But in Canada, the fight has become about more than tariffs. Many Canadians say they feel betrayed by a longtime ally. President Trump has repeatedly suggested Canada should become the 51st state and has said he would use economic pressure, rather than military force, to make that happen. Canadians have cut back on travel to the United States and boycotted American goods as tensions have grown.
And the economic ties are hard to untangle. U.S. auto exports to Canada have fallen 22% since the trade dispute began. Canada is the largest customer for 26 U.S. states and a top-three customer for 45.
Chrystia Freeland understands the relationship from her time at the negotiating table. The former Canadian deputy prime minister and finance minister helped negotiate the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement during Trump's first term. Trump once called it "the best trade deal ever."
Now, Freeland says, the U.S. risks pushing longtime allies away.
"If Americans are concerned about China in the world, which I am, the best way to act on China is with an alliance with America's traditional allies," Freeland told NPR's Morning Edition. "But it has to start with stopping punching your friends in the face, which is what Washington is doing right now."
Freeland also pushed back on the idea that Canada's much smaller economy means it ultimately has to give in.
She recalled a small meeting during an earlier round of North American trade negotiations when, she said, she was told the United States was 10 times bigger than Canada and therefore "should get our way 10 times more than you."
"That is not a way to have a partnership," Freeland said, "and Canadians simply won't stand for it."

Lonnie Bunch, who has led the Smithsonian as its secretary for the past seven years, said that he will step down at the end of the year.
His departure comes amid repeated criticism from the Trump administration over how the institution depicts and descrives historical events and figures.
In an interview with The New York Times, Bunch said that the pressure from the administration did not lead to his departure, but it “was really just saying, now’s the time.”
In a statement, Bunch said, “There is no place like the Smithsonian—it has been one of the great loves of my life, and I am extraordinarily proud of what we have accomplished together. I leave with pride and sadness, gratitude and joy, and with enormous confidence in the people who will carry this remarkable institution forward.”
The Smithsonian has enjoyed a long history of independence from the executive branch. It was created by Congress and is overseen by a Board of Regents chaired by Chief Justice John Roberts.
Watch on Deadline
In a statement, Roberts said, “From his days as a young curator at the National Air and Space and American History Museums through his tenure as the founding director of the African American History and Culture Museum and culminating in his distinguished service for the past seven years in the Smithsonian’s top job, Secretary Bunch has pursued excellence in the telling of our nation’s story. The Regents, and the Smithsonian, have benefited greatly from his wisdom, vision and leadership.”
In July, the Trump administration released a report on the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History that claimed it was captured by “radical, activist ideology.” That included criticisms of its Entertainment Nation wing. A number of historians’ associations pushed back, with the Organization of American Historians calling the report “part of a broad attempt to return the nation to a vision of America that never actually existed and that serves the ends of superficial patriotism.”

Newcastle were 'preparing for months' for Howe departure
- Published
Newcastle United sporting director Ross Wilson says the club were preparing for former head coach Eddie Howe's departure for up to nine months.
Although Howe had originally intended to carry on this season, the drained manager decided to step down in July because he felt it was in the best interests of all parties for him to take a break.
It was a summer of huge change, as several key players departed, but Newcastle did not envisage Howe leaving when he did following nearly five years in charge.
However, Wilson is adamant the Englishman's exit was not "chaotic" or "painful" because the club had a contingency plan in place, which led to the appointment of Matthias Jaissle.
"We always knew where we were going to go," Wilson said. "That doesn't mean we were always going to Matthias, but he was always part of our planning.
"Part of our responsibility as leaders of the club is to be prepared and Eddie is an exceptionally talented coach.
"That means he was probably going to do something else at some point so we had to be prepared for that."
Newcastle spoke to multiple candidates, but Wilson said Jaissle emerged as their first-choice to replace a "legend of the club".
The Scot, who was appointed in October, said he had "been planning for a managerial change for eight or nine of those months" in the background.
Newcastle's hierarchy always knew they wanted Howe's eventual successor to build on the foundations he put in place with an aggressive, high-pressing playing style.
Jaissle also had a history of developing younger players, particularly during his previous spell at Red Bull Salzburg, which aligned with Newcastle's strategy of targeting signings aged 24 and under.
Following Wilson's first meeting with Jaissle, who joined from Saudi Pro League side Al-Ahli, Newcastle chief executive David Hopkinson told him he sounded "really excited about this one".
"I didn't deliberately go on the phone to do that," Wilson said. "But I remember saying 'you're probably right. I think this is it'."
No public season target for Jaissle
Jaissle remains unbeaten in his first four games in charge of Newcastle in all competitions.
However, only three of the club's eight summer signings - Lukas Hornicek, Amar Dedic and Nico Gonzalez - started in the 2-2 draw against Bournemouth.
It felt like a reminder of the time it will take some of the new arrivals to bed in during what Jaissle has repeatedly called a "transition phase".
Newcastle have forecast a range of financial scenarios, depending on where the club finish this season, but Wilson maintained the German has not been set a specific target for the campaign.
Hopkinson, though, reiterated that Newcastle's ultimate ambition is to "consistently and credibly compete" for the top honours in the long run.
After entering into a Uefa settlement, following a breach of the European football governing body's financial rules, Hopkinson stressed Newcastle needed to be compliant with the game's regulations to do so.
The Magpies have set out to boost revenues by 50% between now and 2030 - mainly through sponsorship deals - but trading players will remain a key part of the club's strategy in order to reinvest.
"We want to have players here who are on a journey with us," Wilson said.
"Equally, if some of those players' journeys go at rapid speed, they might go somewhere else but, of course, that's normal. That's part of football."
Although Newcastle had prepared for the departures of Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali, to Barcelona and Tottenham Hotspur respectively, the club had never planned to lose talisman Bruno Guimaraes.
Newcastle also had to readjust during the window after top targets Victor Munoz and Johan Manzambi joined Liverpool and Aston Villa respectively.
However, aside from Guimaraes going to Arsenal, Wilson claimed "everything else that happened during the window was part of the plan".
"That does not mean that every single player [who signed] was the number one name on our list, but that is never the case in any transfer window," he said.
"Clearly we were disappointed a couple of times but, again, that's normal.
"No club goes into the window and reaches the end getting every target they set out to get. If they say they did, it is a lie."

People taking popular GLP-1 obesity drugs who remain on low starter doses will lose some weight but may still experience side effects, although significantly less nausea than those who graduate to higher manufacturer-recommended doses, a new study suggests.
And they are unlikely to experience the double-digit weight-loss percentages seen with the higher doses, the study found.
The GLP-1 drugs semaglutide, sold as Ozempic and Wegovy by Novo Nordisk, and Eli Lilly's tirzepatide, sold under the brand names Mounjaro and Zepbound, are prescribed initially at a low dose followed by gradual titration to higher doses, to help the body adjust and minimize side effects.
Many patients never achieve the recommended maintenance dose due to tolerability, access, cost, supply or their individual goals.
Researchers analyzed data on 534 patients who continued to take injectable semaglutide at the 0.25-milligram starter dose for at least six months, and the same number of patients who stayed on tirzepatide at the 2.5-mg starter dose for at least that long.
At one year, the percentage of body weight lost on these lowest approved doses averaged 5.5% with tirzepatide and 2.2% with semaglutide, researchers reported on Monday in Biology Methods & Protocols.
By comparison, the average weight loss at one year on recommended higher doses was 20.2% with tirzepatide and 13.7% with semaglutide in an earlier head-to-head trial.
The finding that patients who never escalated past the initiation dose still lost some weight suggests the drugs have a measurable pharmacologic effect well below the maintenance doses that clinical trials have been built around, said study leader Venky Soundararajan of data analytics firm nference.
Semaglutide is currently considered better for kidneys because it has received U.S. approval to reduce the risk of worsening chronic renal disease. Tirzepatide is not yet approved specifically for kidney protection.
Even at the lower doses, kidney outcomes were better with semaglutide, Soundararajan noted.
Low-dose tirzepatide was associated with higher rates of kidney injury after two years in 2.7% of patients versus 0.4% with semaglutide.
The Lilly drug also was associated with more constipation (32.6% vs 22.4%), muscle cramps (8.3% vs 4%), lumbar disc disease (3.3% vs 0.3%), shortness of breath on exertion (9.6% vs 6.8%), and other adverse events.
Patients on sustained low-dose semaglutide had higher rates of ear inflammation (5.6% vs 2.1% with tirzepatide), heavy sweating (5.5% vs 3.2%) and ankle swelling (6.9% vs 3.7%).
Patients who remained on the starter doses did have substantially less nausea and constipation than has been reported for patients taking higher doses, the study found.
Observational studies such as this one cannot prove cause and effect, Soundararajan noted.
Novo Nordisk recently launched a clinical trial to evaluate lower maintenance doses of its Wegovy pill, but results are years away.
"In the meantime, with real-world patients taking lower-than-recommended doses, there's a need for awareness,” Soundararajan said.
“These two medicines are not equivalent,” he continued. “Patients who are not aiming for 20% or 30% weight loss need to know there's a chance they can lose a little weight on these low doses, and they deserve to know the picture around the adverse event profile.”
