The National Investigation Agency (NIA) has not invoked the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA) against six Ukrainian citizens and one U.S. citizen, who were arrested in March for allegedly training anti-India armed groups in Myanmar, in its first charge sheet submitted in a special court on Tuesday.
Instead, the accused were only charged with violations of immigration law, though the agency told the court that a supplementary chargesheet may be filed later if needed.
The development came weeks after U.S. Ambassador to India Sergio Gor raised the arrest of the U.S. national Matthew Aaron Van Dyke with Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri during U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to Delhi in May.
Mr. Van Dyke was arrested by the NIA on March 13, at Kolkata airport. Six Ukrainians — Hurba Petro, Slyviak Taras, Ivan Sukmanovskyi, Stefankiv Marian, Honcharuk Maksim, and Kaminskyi Viktor — were also arrested in connection with the case, at airports in Delhi and Lucknow.
‘Cross-border conspiracy’
According to the Central agency, the accused entered India on tourist visas and travelled to the northeastern region without obtaining the mandatory permits. It was alleged that they subsequently crossed illegally from Mizoram into Myanmar, where they were involved in training ethnic armed organisations.
The NIA had initially invoked provisions of the UAPA, including those relating to conspiracy, as part of its investigation into the alleged cross-border network.
During earlier hearings, the agency told the court that the accused had made significant disclosures about the alleged conspiracy while in custody. The NIA also claimed that they were involved in assembling equipment and had targeted a passenger aircraft in Myanmar.
Only immigration violations
However, in its first chargesheet, the agency has not invoked the stringent UAPA provisions, and only invoked Sections 21 and 23 of the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025. Both offences are compoundable at the level of the Foreigners Regional Registration Office.
Appearing for the agency, Special Public Prosecutor Rahul Tyagi informed the court that the agency had not invoked UAPA sections in this chargesheet, but noted that the investigation is still going on. The agency may file a supplementary chargesheet if an offence under the Act is made out, he added.
Six months behind bars
Advocates Rohit Dandriyal and Rohit Gour, who represented Mr. Van Dyke, told The Hindu that their client had spent more than 180 days in custody before the agency filed the chargesheet without invoking the UAPA.
“On 4 June 2026, when the initial period of 90 days was approaching its end, the NIA sought and obtained an extension of 90 days for completion of the investigation, taking the total period to 180 days. On 8 September 2026, at the end of the extended 180-day period, the NIA has filed a charge-sheet against my client under Sections 21 and 23 of the Foreigners Act, rather than under the serious UAPA allegation with which he was initially arrested,” the advocates said.
Questioning the development, counsel for the U.S. national asked what evidence had ultimately emerged after nearly 180 days of investigation to substantiate the original allegations.
“The State has every right to investigate, but investigation cannot become a substitute for evidence, and incarceration cannot become a punishment before guilt is established. Keeping a person behind bars for 180 days on allegations which, after such an extended investigation, do not culminate in the same serious offences initially alleged raises a serious question concerning personal liberty and the protection guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution,” the counsel added.

This is an edition of The Wonder Reader, a newsletter in which our editors recommend a set of stories to spark your curiosity and fill you with delight. Sign up here to get it every Saturday morning.
A strange thing happens when you see something every day: Eventually, you stop seeing it. A building you once admired becomes part of your commute. The trees on your block become background. Your favorite coffee mug becomes something you reach for without thinking.
This tendency has been compounded by a culture that encourages us to move through life as efficiently as possible: We follow directions instead of wandering, put in headphones instead of listening to the world around us, and fill spare moments by looking at our phone. As Ian Bogost writes in a new article, we’ve become so focused on making life more productive that we risk treating the present as mere preparation for whatever comes next.
Wonder can interrupt that habit, Bogost argues—not just the kind inspired by mountains or sunsets, but the kind available in ordinary things. He describes noticing the warmth of a coffee mug, the crunch of gravel underfoot, and the clever engineering of a toaster. Wonder, in this sense, is less about seeking out extraordinary experiences than it is about paying close attention to the ones already around you.

The driving force behind our universe’s accelerated expansion remains one of the greatest mysteries in astronomy. While this force, which scientists refer to as dark energy, pervades our universe, we know almost nothing about it.
Located on a remote mountain in Arizona’s Sonoran Desert, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) has spent the past five years mapping the cosmos with the goal of unraveling this mystery. The result is the largest three-dimensional map of the universe ever created. And now—with the release of the latest version of the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys, a free online tool for exploring the vast imaging data—you too can poke around the universe.
The new map boasts an overwhelming amount of information: 5.6 trillion pixels containing approximately 4 billion celestial objects including stars, galaxies, black holes, and asteroids. It covers approximately 75 percent of the entire sky, recording both visible light and near-infrared wavelengths.
Those missing pieces include the deeper parts of space blocked by the stars, space dust, and other matter in our own galaxy, which is a major challenge for astronomy surveys, especially ground-based ones. However, since the Milky Way is splayed out like a fried egg—which is why it appears as a dense band of stars in the night sky—the researchers aim DESI’s 5,000 mechanical eyes out of the top or bottom of our galaxy to capture some of the clearest images of distant space yet.
Though this particular survey lasted five years, it built on another 13 years of groundwork. More than 160 scientists were involved in data collection, and over the course of the project, researchers have already published upwards of 1,800 scientific papers referencing the data.
“It’s part of the fabric of astronomy research now,” David Schlegel, a researcher at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and co-lead of the Legacy Surveys, said in a press release. “When you're working with astronomical objects today, you often start by pulling up the Legacy Imaging Viewer to see what you’re looking at.”
Earlier this year, DESI researchers released another map, which projected the distances of 47 million galaxies and quasars. This reconstructed 11 billion years of cosmic history, bringing the effects of dark energy into focus. Dark energy is thought to be responsible for the expansion of our universe, and while the force itself remains ellusive, astronomers can track it by analyzing the rates at which other celestial objects appear to be moving away from us.
Data from the first three years of DESI’s survey—combined with observations of supernovae and the pervasive radiation leftover from the Big Bang—have hinted that dark energy may not be a constant force but is gradually weakening over time. An analysis of the full five years of data is scheduled to be released in 2027, which will scientists believe will paint a picture of the past and present of the universe more vividly than ever before.
Going forward, DESI’s observations will also serve as a reference and comparison point for other cosmic projects, such as NASA’s recently launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. Researchers also plan to train artificial intelligence tools to accelerate analysis of the petabyte-scale astronomical data—within which much remains to be discovered.
“Explorations of our universe always start with images of the night sky,” said Arjun Day, co-director of Legacy Surveys and an astronomer with the National Science Foundation. “These data are fundamental to the investigation of the expansion history of the universe and the formation of our galaxy. But the skies belong to everyone, and this survey gives everyone the chance to marvel at their wonders.”

Taylor's 'dream ending to a dream career'
- Published
"There's nothing like an Irish family."
Katie Taylor addressed the Croke Park crowd as she paid tribute to her mother Bridget, but her extended family of 83,000 inside Croke Park and many more tuning in will have known this one was for them too.
Fairytale endings in boxing are a rarity, but Taylor is no ordinary fighter and her swansong proved as extraordinary as the fighter and person.
After 30 years lacing up the gloves, Taylor, 40, sails off into the sunset after the most perfect of farewells in front of 83,000 adoring fans at Dublin's iconic Croke Park, just three miles from the scene of her first official bout 25 years earlier.
The final act in the ring was to sweep past Flora Pili to cement her legacy in Ireland and beyond, bowing out as a three-time and two-weight undisputed champion.
It was a night of celebration, cheers and plenty of tears as fans and peers turned out for her victory lap, showing love and appreciation for a career which thrilled and inspired in equal measure.
"It was everything I expected and more," Taylor said at her final post-fight news conference.
"Thankfully I was able to hold my emotions together tonight as I was getting emotional all week and the last few months' preparation was so emotional.
"The atmosphere was so special. I was beyond my wildest dreams - what a special night."
- Taylor crowns career in stylish Croke Park triumph 
  - Published9 hours ago
- Tears, blood & triumph - Taylor's iconic career in pictures 
  - Published9 hours ago
Before her hand could be raised in the ring, there were battles to be won outside of it.
Born in 1986 as the youngest of four children to former Irish champion father Peter and mother Bridget - one of Ireland's first female officials - the very notion of women's boxing in Ireland appeared fanciful.
While older brothers Lee and Peter were welcomed into the boxing fold, Katie became K from Bray - a girl hiding her identity to simply compete in an exclusively male environment.
The fighting spirit and determination which characterises her sporting prowess is as much a feature of her personality, and in 2001 as a 15-year-old she took part in the first sanctioned women's bout in Ireland since it was outlawed following future world champion Deirdre Gogarty's 1991 debut in Limerick.
Perhaps fitting, as five years earlier, Taylor wrote to role model Gogarty, expressing frustration at the lack of opportunities to compete and outlining her dreams of one day being allowed to compete at the Olympic Games.
Prophetic words, as it was her exceptional talent on display in front of International Olympic Committee members in 2007 which convinced them to add women's boxing to the programme for London 2012.
All eyes were on her as Katie mania grew throughout the Games - her victory over Sofya Ochigava in the lightweight final a moment of national sporting joy comparable to the heady days of Jack Charlton's Republic of Ireland teams at the 1990 and 1994 World Cups - the Excel arena transformed into a small corner of Ireland on an unforgettable day.
A recognised star in Irish boxing circles was now a household name, her humble and gracious manner winning the hearts of a nation that has remained firmly in her corner.
"The 'ole ole oles' carried me all over the world: to Leeds, to Manchester, Brooklyn, Boston, Dallas, Manhattan," she reflected.
"This night is so special because I wanted to put on a performance for them. I don't think it was a career-best performance, but I got the win for them, just to say 'thank you'."
A seminal night against Serrano
Her star did not dim despite a disappointing Rio Games in 2016, and while Matchroom boss Eddie Hearn took convincing to take a punt on her as a professional, the faith has been repaid in spades.
Within three years, Taylor was undisputed champion at lightweight, rising from undercard to centre stage as she carried out her promise to do for women's professional boxing what she had achieved as an amateur, all to a chorus of the aforementioned 'ole ole oles' from the support which followed her every move.
A seminal night in 2022 saw her defeat Amanda Serrano at a sold-out Madison Square Garden in a fight of the year contender - the first time a women's bout had headlined the famous arena, a major turning point for the female code.
They would trade leather a further two times after Taylor had avenged her sole professional career defeat by Chantelle Cameron to become a two-weight champion.
Perhaps that was the perfect way to sign off, but the Croke Park itch had to be scratched and while those gates seemed destined to remain locked, Taylor's status made it happen.
Could she fill such a vast stadium? Of course. Perhaps the doubters did not grasp the reverence in which the softly spoken yet inspirational woman from Bray is held.
While her trophy cabinet is overflowing with gold medals and world title belts, perhaps her greatest legacy is leaving women's boxing in a vastly better place than she found it - that Serrano trilogy lifting women's boxing to new heights.
Taylor broke through the barriers with a grace which belied the obstacles she faced yet her quiet determination and humble nature will serve as an example of what can be achieved by belief, hard work and a refusal to accept her lot as young girls can now walk the path she laid.
Fierce inside the ring yet unassuming outside of it - even factoring in an impulse-buy speedboat, since sold - superlatives such as trailblazer, icon and Ireland's greatest sportsperson are not hyperbolic, for Taylor's status as a legend is in no way cliched.
She has indicated she will remain in the sport, but for now, there is time to savour an extraordinary career, with her place among boxing's greats set in stone.
Irish boxing is going to be a lesser place.
"I'm retired now so I can eat what I want, but I'm just going to enjoy a nice celebration and look back on a dream ending to a dream career.
"My story is the story of everyone in this room: we all have our ups and downs. I think people resonate with your vulnerabilities and your successes - saw me cope with the heartbreak of Rio, the Chantelle Cameron loss and personal difficulties.
"My story is the story of everyone in this room."

In 1906, in response to public outcry that came after Upton Sinclair’s The Jungle detailed the revolting conditions in Chicago’s meatpacking plants, the US government passed the Federal Meat Inspection Act. The legislation created what would become known as the Food Safety and Inspection Service, a force of federal employees who would spend their days in stockyards and packing plants, checking livestock for disease both before and after their slaughter. They did their work organoleptically—with their eyes, noses, and hands—an approach soon dubbed “poke and sniff.” This 100 percent testing method worked well enough for spotting the lesions that signaled tuberculosis and cysticercosis (a tissue infection caused by tapeworms), and the federal presence discouraged plants from using illegal preservatives and generally unsanitary practices.
But by the end of the 20th century, as American taste for beef mushroomed, the system was clearly and woefully inadequate. The gotta-catch-’em-all approach was no match for plants butchering hundreds of animals an hour. The bigger problem was that testing had once more fallen behind in the arms race. Decades of poking at hearts, bile ducts, spleens, lungs, lymph nodes, livers, and kidneys had effectively rid the country’s meat supply of diseases that could be spotted or sniffed out. But humans can’t see, smell, or feel Escherichia coli.
In 1993, the growing danger of E. coli made itself evident when hamburgers sold by Jack in the Box fast-food restaurants sickened more than 700 people and killed four children. The public outcry rivaled the one sparked by The Jungle and triggered two moves by the Food Safety and Inspection Service. As a short-term fix, it hired 160 extra meat inspectors. More importantly, it accelerated a change in approach that had been bubbling away in the background ever since NASA decided it was time to send astronauts to space for more than a few hours at a time—long enough for them to get hungry.
That happened in the early 1960s, when the Mercury program, which first put Americans into space, gave way to Gemini, which proved out the equipment and procedures necessary for the longer, moon-bound Apollo missions to follow. Sending astronauts into space for multiple days meant dealing with the various elements of sustenance in zero gravity, from swallowing to defecating. But it was the middle step, digesting, that most worried Paul Lachance, the space agency’s lead food scientist. Food poisoning on Earth is terrible. In a spacesuit or space capsule, it could be catastrophic.
The obvious approach would be a 100 percent testing route, screening every morsel for pathogens and taking a zero-tolerance attitude. This was unworkable, because, as with artillery shells, every bite of food that’s tested is one that can’t be eaten. This is known as “destructive testing.” Proving a given batch was absolutely safe would involve eliminating most of it. Private industry was no help; what inspection did take place in the 1960s was far from scientific or suitable for NASA’s needs. Most pathogens were “discovered” by the people who consumed them.
Lachance and his colleagues responded by creating a new way of testing food safety. Where Walter Shewhart’s control chart was a tool for spotting manufacturing issues that could then be resolved, they conceived of an approach that went further, proactively identifying all the points where problems are most likely to start, and focusing inspection there. The core idea was to test food not after it was produced, but to so control its production that such testing was unnecessary. They called it Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point, today better known as HACCP.
To help digest this, think of basic acceptance sampling as the bit of wine the waiter has you taste so you know the bottle hasn’t spoiled before everyone gets a full glass. The basic Shewhart approach, then, is like the “test pancake” you make as you’re starting up breakfast. It tells you whether your production process, which requires a batter of the right consistency and a griddle at the right temperature, is on track. HACCP (pronounced hassip) is more like the way you should make a soup. Each time you add salt or broth or lemon juice or cream, you taste it to see how the flavor, saltiness, and acidity match what you’re aiming for.
For NASA, analyzed hazards could be physical (crystallized Tang powder could break a tooth), chemical (the presence of pesticide residues), or microbiological (the pathogens that posed the most serious threat in space). A critical control point could be any moment or action in the production process, from gathering raw materials to vacuum-sealing a package. “We identified the critical steps that would make the difference between something being safe or not safe,” Lachance said. “The temperature, the pressure, whatever that criteria was, whatever that critical control point was.” A chicken headed into space would be plucked, deboned, cut into pieces small enough to freeze-dry, and cooked, at which point it would be sterile. But as various people handled it, the meat would be checked on its way to the freeze dryer, then on its way into plastic packaging, then again after being vacuum-sealed. To this day, no astronaut has gotten food poisoning while in space.
“HACCP introduced careful design, rigorous standards, and precise measurement into the largely intuitive, loosely organized, hit-or-miss world of industrial food safety prior to the 1970s,” Timothy D. Lytton wrote in his 2019 book about foodborne illness, Outbreak. Pillsbury, which produced crumble-free food for NASA (floating crumbs were also a concern in space) and had a major hand in developing HACCP, implemented the process into its own consumer production lines after 1971, when a Connecticut woman found glass in some of its baby cereal. The approach went national in 1973, when the FDA added HACCP-based rules to its regulation of low-acid canned foods, where botulism was an issue. The European arm of the World Health Organization recommended using HACCP in 1983, and in 1985 the National Academy of Sciences declared it better than “random testing of foods” (aka inspection).
In 1996, three years after Jack in the Box’s E. coli–speckled hamburgers made all those people sick, the Food Safety and Inspection Service demanded that America’s meat processing plants get with the program. By 2004, illness from E. coli had dropped 42 percent, reaching a Centers for Disease Control and Prevention goal six years ahead of schedule. In 2011, the Food Safety Modernization Act required that all US food manufacturers develop and stick to HACCP-based safety plans.
Among experts, this way of thinking about food safety is as established as quality control is in manufacturing. “The testing of finished products for food safety is foolishness,” says Larry Keener, president and CEO of International Product Safety Consultants. He’s looking forward to the potential of new technology, including machine learning and genome sequencing, to make HACCP even more effective. But like all testing, HACCP’s usefulness depends on how it’s used. “Unfortunately, the industry and the regulatory community have, in my estimation, been slow to catch on and pick up and use this powerful strategy to improve the safety of the food supply,” Keener says.
Indeed, every year, foodborne disease sickens 48 million people—that’s one in six Americans—puts 128,000 in the hospital, and kills 3,000. Those numbers are stubborn for a couple of reasons. Food safety is hard to see, so it’s hard for manufacturers to make it a differentiator. And while consumers may say they value safety above all, in reality price and convenience tend to win out, especially when it’s not clear what’s safe and what isn’t. The combined result is that manufacturers have little incentive to make more than the minimum effort. Meanwhile, the FDA (which oversees most food that isn’t meat) isn’t much of a task master. When it does run inspections, it’s focused on verifying that manufacturers can provide the proper documentation of their safety plan.
“They’ll show up maybe once every couple of years. Or if a particular sector starts to cause a lot of foodborne illness, FDA will focus on that more. But usually it’s reactive,” says Denis Stearns, a founding partner at food-safety-focused law firm Marler Clark. “It’s only if you cause a big outbreak, then they also come in and do their own testing … They’re like the fire department. You don’t see them until your house is on fire.”
Yet we have evidence that stricter standards and tighter testing can work. Since the 1960s, the French government has allowed certain manufacturers to slap the “Label Rouge” on their products, signifying that they have gone far beyond the legal minimum for quality and safety. It’s applied to all sorts of products, but is most closely associated with chicken. Its HACCP-like quality control process includes 65 individual tests, strict requirements on how much space and what kind of food the animals get, and—this being France—regular taste tests by experts and consumers to ensure the result is “vividly distinguishable” from the non-label version. Label Rouge chickens tend to cost twice as much as the regular birds, but make up one-third of sales and have a drastically lower salmonella rate than those in conventional flocks.

On September 5, Saurav Das, the co-convener of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP), shared a photo on X that attributed a quote to BJP spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia, under the label of ‘NBT’, which presumably referred to the news outlet, NavBharat Times.
It was claimed that Bhatia had said, “The youth named Swatantra Bhardwaj is a ‘Dimaagi Naxal’, he is filled with casteist venom, and he has nothing to do with the BJP government.”

Several other X users, like Nimo Yadav (@DrNimoYadav), Vaibhav Shukla (@vaibhaw_g), and Gen-Z of India (@GenZ_of_India_) amplified the viral quote. Archives: 1, 2, 3
Bhardwaj, a Hindutva hardliner, recently created an uproar after a clip from a podcast went viral. In it, he boasted about assaulting Sanjay Kumar, father of CJP protester Nishu Azad, during the Jantar Mantar protest, and asserted that he faced no action because of his political connections, naming Kapil Mishra and Chirag Paswan. He now faces criminal charges under Sections 115(2), 126(2) and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, along with provisions of the POCSO Act and SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, with an attempt-to-murder charge also invoked in the case. On September 7, he was sent to 14-day judicial remand.
Fact Check
To verify the authenticity of the viral quote attributed to Gaurav Bhatia, we ran relevant keyword searches to see if any verified news outlet reported on it, but could find none.
However, we found this X post, published by Navbharat Times on September 5, which clarifies that “misleading messages are being spread” through these “fake posts.”
पिछले कुछ दिनों से सोशल मीडिया पर NBT के नाम से कई पोस्ट वायरल हो रही हैं और उन फ़र्ज़ी पोस्ट के जरिये भ्रामक संदेश फैलाए जा रहे हैं। NBT की किसी भी खबर की सत्यता जांचने के लिए केवल NBT के आधिकारिक सोशल मीडिया हैंडल पर ही भरोसा करें। #FactCheck #NBT #FakeNews pic.twitter.com/rA9pC6iHS3
— NBT Hindi News (@NavbharatTimes) September 5, 2026
Thereafter, we found that Gaurav Bhatia had also categorically debunked the viral quote attributed to him by Saurav Das, in an X post. He gave the CJP leader an ultimatum of 24 hours to apologise for spreading the viral misquote, warning that he would file an FIR against him otherwise.
It took only 83 minutes for the post to be deleted. Unqualified apology still remains. Tomorrow will be a day of FIR if no unqualified apology is tendered. Can’t spread propaganda and then just delete and run. https://t.co/oTXLR6ZwKe

After reporting last week that the surveillance company Flock Safety is building an AI search tool for law enforcement, WIRED reconstructed Flock’s latest search tool from code that the company sends to a police officer’s browser and uncovered key details about how the tool works.
OpenAI said this week that its Astra model, which will have a private release soon, is its first model with cybersecurity-related capabilities that the company defines as posing a “critical” risk in public release. Meanwhile, the AI chatbot platforms Claude, ChatGPT, and Grok all suffered outages on Thursday at nearly the exact same time. But while xAI said the Grok outage resulted from issues at a Memphis data center, the causes of OpenAI's and Anthropic’s outages are unclear.
The US has been using a high-energy laser to shoot down drones near the Mexico border as part of an initiative to adopt new-generation directed-energy weapons capable of detecting, tracking, and destroying drones with a concentrated beam of light. And as part of an Immigration and Customs Enforcement inquiry into the identities of protesters who entered a Minnesota church in March, Homeland Security Investigations agents have subpoenaed the outdoor retailer REI for information about every customer who bought a specific green beanie over the past two years.
Plus, research that revealed nine vulnerabilities with impacts on ATM encryption points to broader weaknesses in the software supply chain.
And there’s more. Each week, we round up the security and privacy news we didn’t cover in depth ourselves. Click the headlines to read the full stories. And stay safe out there.
Before Hugging Face, OpenAI Agents Took Over a German Website to Create a Message Board
OpenAI agents on an unauthorized tear hijacked a German website beginning in May to use it as a message board for communicating and collaborating with other agents, according to new research. The incident is reminiscent of the now infamous Hugging Face debacle in which OpenAI agents in a test environment went rogue and developed a vibrant message board for collaborating on attempting to escape their containment, before ultimately breaching the open source AI platform Hugging Face in July. The revelation of the May episode is particularly significant because OpenAI reportedly learned about it weeks ago but did not disclose it. Meanwhile, last week, the company finally released a long-promised postmortem of the Hugging Face incident that raised as many questions as it answered.
More Than 153 Million US and Canadian Driver’s Licenses for Sale Online
This week, a new dark-web service called Nexus started selling around 153 million driver's licenses from the US and Canada, along with 10 million ID cards and millions more travel documents and international IDs, according to Brian Krebs, a longtime independent security reporter. Krebs was first alerted to the service after cybercriminals posted an example of the files and included his license. The tens of millions of records—which reportedly increased by 400,000 over 24 hours—appear to have come from an ID verification service, with the criminals behind the trove saying they have access to a “major” verification company. While it’s unclear which company exactly that may be, according to Kreb’s report, the Nexus service was taken offline shortly after he reported that FBI officials were investigating.
US Military Disables Ad Trackers After Years of Warnings
The US military has begun disabling the advertising identifiers that apps and advertising companies use to track phones and computers in an attempt to make it harder for foreign adversaries to use commercially available location data to track American forces overseas, Reuters reported Friday.
The changes follow years of disclosures that US forces deployed abroad have been targeted using commercially available location data. In 2024, a joint WIRED investigation with Germany’s Bayerischer Rundfunk and Netzpolitik.org obtained an advertising dataset that identified thousands of devices appearing at US military and intelligence sites, including an air base where US nuclear weapons are believed to be stored. At the time, Defense Department spokesperson Javan Rasnake told WIRED that the Pentagon was aware geolocation services could put personnel at risk and said service members in Europe were reminded to follow operational-security practices.
Now, the Air Force, Army, Navy, and US Special Operations Command say they have disabled advertising IDs on at least some military devices, with several of the changes taking effect only this year. It is still unclear exactly how these protections are being enforced. US senator Ron Wyden and Representative Pat Harrigan are now asking the Pentagon to investigate whether its safeguards are adequate.
Mike Yeagley, the technologist who warned Pentagon officials as far back as 2016 that commercially available phone data could expose US troops—at one point demonstrating the risk by tracing devices to a covert US outpost in Syria—says the military’s new fix may already be outdated. “The app is the risk, and there are two and a half million of them in the App Store alone,” Yeagley tells WIRED. “The remedy is architectural: Constrain what an app can extract from the device in the first place.”
Spyware Notifications Make Up “Largest Documented Wave” of Surveillance in Serbia
In August, Apple sent out its latest batch of spyware notifications to people in 110 countries. The alerts, which arrive on people’s phones and in emails, say their owners' iPhones have been targeted by “mercenary” spyware but don’t go as far as naming the software creators. This latest batch of notifications, according to a report by the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab, says 14 members of Serbia’s civil society were targeted with spyware, with at least one of them being infected by the NSO Group’s Pegasus spyware. Among those targeted, according to Serbian rights group the Share Foundation, were members of the country’s student movement, two politicians, and activists. The group called it the “largest documented wave of such surveillance in the country to date.”

How the Government Wastes Our Time
What do we lose in the hours spent filling out paperwork?
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts
Americans are bogged down in paperwork for reasons that are sometimes necessary, sometimes thoughtless—and, at times, nefarious. In her new book, The Time Tax: How the Government Wastes Our Time—And How to Fix It, my colleague Annie Lowrey looks at all those hours spent looking for tax documents or trying to certify income for the Free Application for Federal Student Aid, or the FAFSA and finds that things don’t have to be this way.
A time tax is an infliction of “paperwork, effort, delay, and aggravation” that Americans suffer to get the rights they are guaranteed. We have the right to vote in a democracy; a time tax creates obstacles to those rights and makes realizing them cumbersome: They show up as extra identification requirements, when voter fraud is incredibly rare—or, in Jim Crow, as literacy tests.
So many things are easy now. If I get hungry, I can order food from just about anywhere with just a few swipes of my thumb; one click at midnight, and diapers can be at the door before the sun rises. Why is there still such sludge in our bureaucratic systems? On this episode of Radio Atlantic, Annie joins me to discuss how these time taxes show up in our lives and waste our time, and how to make our government more efficient.
The following is a transcript of the episode:
Annie Lowrey: I think if instead of saying, This is about the poor people getting this program, or This is about making sure that these programs are secure, we could have a politics that says, This is malign; this is bad policy making. We give the government $8 trillion a year, and it passes back this garbage? No! No.
[Music]
Adam Harris: This is Radio Atlantic. I’m Adam Harris, and today we need to think about all of the ways that the government wastes our time.
I’m only half-joking. If you’ve ever thought to yourself while filling out your taxes or trying to cancel a gym membership that This is taking too long! Don’t they already have this information? There has to be a better way!—you’re not alone.
My colleague Annie Lowrey has a name for these cumbersome processes: She calls them “time taxes.” She wrote about the phenomenon for The Atlantic in 2021, and in her new book, The Time Tax: How the Government Wastes Our Time—And How to Fix It, she explores how and why our time is squandered when it does not have to be.
So, what gets lost in the hours spent filling out paperwork? And how do we fix it?
 
 Annie joins me now to discuss. Annie, welcome to the show.
Annie Lowrey: Thank you for having me, Adam.
Harris: So, I wanna start by talking about the DMV.
Lowrey: Yeah.
Harris: Because, right, it’s Labor Day, government offices are closed, but tomorrow across the country, DMVs are gonna be full of people trying to renew their car registrations, get Real IDs, change their addresses, change their names—whatever it might be.
But those long lines at the DMV, I think, are the most trenchant example of what you call a “time tax.” So what are time taxes, and how do they show up in everyday lives, even outside of the DMV?
Lowrey: So time taxes, these show up everywhere you are encountering the government, and really everywhere you’re interacting with businesses, right? It doesn’t necessarily have to be the government. And a time tax—or what’s called in the academic literature “an administrative burden”—is merely the person who is being bureaucratized, their experience of bureaucracy. So how much work they have to do to apply to something; how much work they have to do to research it; the fees that they might have to pay in some cases; and also their psychological or emotional experience, whether that’s DMV-level frustration or emotional anguish in a welfare program, or even a sense of civic pride that you might get when you’re interacting with a service that makes you feel good about yourself.
Harris: So this is how people sort of interact with different things, right? So like you said, it’s not just the government—it can also be canceling a gym membership. In your new book, The Time Tax, you write about the idea that we see some of the most cumbersome examples of these time taxes as they relate to sort of social-safety-net programs. Food stamps, Medicaid, Social Security—things that people in need of help need to survive.
So why is that? Why do we see a structure where the time taxes seem so cumbersome in those social-safety-net programs?
Lowrey: We see time taxes as a general point, I think, being bigger, more onerous, more expensive in a broad sense of the word for programs that are affecting people with less social status, for whatever reason that might be—people with a history of being discriminated against, people viewed with some kind of skepticism by the state. So that could be people who weren’t born here, immigrants. That could be people with a history of interaction or involvement with the criminal-justice system. That could be different racial groups. White Americans are treated very differently than Black Americans. And absolutely, high-income Americans are treated very different than low-income Americans.
And importantly, I don’t think that’s because low-income Americans are the recipients of this generosity that high-income Americans aren’t. So high-income Americans, they absolutely use programs like Social Security retirement benefits. They use tax programs like the 529 college-savings program or the Home Mortgage Interest Deduction. They benefit from the exclusion of employer-sponsored health benefits in some cases. But we don’t think of those as benefits, right? Those are tax policies—that’s not a benefit. It absolutely is. To the government, in accounting terms, it’s the same thing. It’s just that we’re not asking you to pee in a cup for it, which we do for a lot of benefits where you have to apply and reapply and come face-to-face with a social worker and perhaps fill out forms that might be a hundred pages long. And none of those policies interact with each other; they’re really cumbersome.
And I think that’s because we want to dissuade low-income people from using these, because we believe that some share of them are applying fraudulently. And there’s this thought that, you know, Maybe if you’re low income, you need to get a little bit better at paperwork in your life. You need to straighten up and figure yourself out. And this is an imposition of that moral onto you.
Harris: Yeah, and it’s interesting that you mentioned all the paperwork, and that’s even if they know that the programs exist to help them, right?
Lowrey: Absolutely. Yes.
Harris: And that doesn’t—as you write, that’s not by accident, that historically these sort of cumbersome processes have been used as a form of social control that is as old as data itself.
So can you explain that idea a little bit? That these time taxes aren’t something that popped up in the middle of the 1950s and 1960s with an explosion of bureaucracy.
Lowrey: Absolutely not. So a really clear example of these are the voting rules set out in Jim Crow. They are all hypothetically race-neutral. Or perhaps not all, but mostly, right? They are race-neutral.
But, you know, a poll tax is gonna hit lower-income people, namely Black people, way harder than it’s gonna hit higher-income people. Property rules—if you’re a property owner, that isn’t gonna be applied equally. And something like a grandfather clause is instead going to allow white people, white men, to be able to vote, whereas Black men whose ancestors were enslaved are not going to be able to vote.
And so even now, if we scoot forward, look at some of the rules in the SNAP program, which is food stamps. You can’t buy prepared food with your SNAP benefits. So the rotisserie chickens at Costco or at your grocery store? You cannot get those. Right now, there’s a lot of debate over ensuring that SNAP benefits only go to “healthy food.” So we’re saying, This can only be for nutrition as the state sees it, and we’re worried that you’re buying junk food and eating it.
Never mind the fact, I don’t know, maybe somebody is a runner or a diabetic. Maybe they have reasons to access that. Maybe poor kids should be able to have birthday cakes—that seems fine to me. But that is why it’s a tool of social control. We’re making people know that we are skeptical of their spending habits and we’re attempting to control those spending habits through these little time taxes in the program. And I feel like once you see these, you see them everywhere.
Again, I think it’s actually really good to compare it with the home-mortgage interest deduction that, like, if you have a mortgage, you get it. That’s it. They’re not like, Oh, are you living in a floodplain? Are you designing your home in this way? There isn’t that kind of paternalism in there, where there’s a lot of paternalism in a lot of other benefits.
Harris: During COVID, there were so many programs that were intended to simply help people who were struggling, right? Additional tax benefits and things like that. A lot of those programs were very clearly designed so that they reached the most people with the greatest ease, and they worked. Like the children’s tax credit—things like that worked.
Why don’t we do more things like that?
Lowrey: I think often we have multiple goals in mind with a program. So take TANF, which is the cash-welfare program. Its stated goal, or its original goal, is to end child poverty. TANF as it is currently constructed has no effect on the child-poverty rate, which is remarkable to me. That’s in part because it’s a small program. It’s also because the goal of TANF is to control the behavior of the mostly mothers who are using it. There’s very strict work requirements. If you screw up in TANF, you get sanctioned. You are treated as a fraud risk. You are in trouble in some way. Which is not true—even with the IRS, if you screw your taxes up a bit, they’ll ask for the money or they’ll send you the money if you screwed up in the wrong way. But there isn’t this implication that this was a fraudulent act—unless you’re outright committing tax fraud; I’m just saying if you’ve miscalculated something.
And so this is a way that we shrink public programs, where we’re saying, if we’re looking at the example of means-tested programs, the question is not only, Do you have certain characteristics? Do you fall below a certain income line, taking into account the size of your family and some other things? It’s saying, Okay, but we also need you to be good enough at performing for the state, at filling out this paperwork, meeting with this counselor at this given time.
And it’s just, you know, I don’t know that that’s a really legitimate way to go about it, as opposed to simply saying, Yeah, if you meet the income target, you should have this.
Harris: When we come back we talk with Annie about how to address the time tax.
[Music]]
Harris: So there were about 4 million people in the U.S. when the Constitution was signed in 1787. There are about 350 million people in the country now. And so, as the nation has grown, so has its bureaucracy and the systems that it uses. And over time, those systems age.
It makes sense to want to update them, to want to make them better as technology improves. And at the beginning of the second Trump administration, the president established DOGE, the Department of Government Efficiency; appointed Elon Musk to head it up; charged it with cleaning up the government, modernizing old systems, and making it more efficient. You were working on this book when that began. What did you think of that effort at the time?
Lowrey: A few things. So one was that this was presented as a novel thing. And no, no—there’s, like, more than a hundred years of presidents attempting to do this, saying, The systems have gotten too complicated; we’re gonna clean things up; we’re gonna make the entire system more efficient. So it wasn’t new.
I think that the fundamental idea was a good one. I think that the way that they went about it was, like, I would call it clown college if it weren’t so destructive and cruel. They were just firing civil servants at random. They made all of the federal civil servants send a five-point email explaining what they had done every week.
Harris: Wasting their time.
Lowrey: Yeah, exactly—wasting their time. There was no effort to look at the voluminous reports that we have from inspectors general, for instance, or the government’s various accountability offices to say, Okay, can we actually improve procurement contracts? Or, Could we find out the places where we’re really overspending on something, or, you know, We need some deep improvement. There was none of that.
They hurt service delivery by getting rid of some critical people. They created all kinds of busywork. Not just the [five-point] emails. They slowed things down such that some agencies couldn’t get essential components that they would have needed without the approval of a political operative. So for instance, NASA had to get approval for, like, bolts. I’m pretty sure that NASA knows how to buy bolts, right? That is not the problem with an inefficiency in government. And they never considered the citizen experience. Do we really need to wait this long to vote? Do we have to do our own taxes? We don’t, by the way—the IRS would like to do them for us.
And so it was just this all-out assault on the civil service. And it was the second time that we’ve seen it from President Trump, where he just believes that civil servants are a malign politicized force, that they’re there to take sinecures and draw money away from the taxpayer, when many of them, they just love their work—and they’re actually earning less than they would in private industry—because they’re really dedicated to their jobs and they’re very specialized at what they do.
So, yes, DOGE—good idea. And I hope that that idea carries forward, but I hope that they do it much more effectively and efficiently going around the next time. I’d also note that the great sin of DOGE, too, is that it might end up costing the government money because it caused so many lawsuits. They did so many things without the appropriate permissions, without the legal changes that they needed, that they’ve just been mired in lawsuits.
Harris: So when you say we don’t have to do our taxes. The IRS would like to do our taxes for us? What do you mean by that?
Lowrey: Yes, you have to pay your taxes; you have to do your taxes. What I mean is that nine in 10 American households take the standard deduction, which means that they’re not itemizing their taxes. Generally, it’s because their tax situation is pretty straightforward. And so the IRS has all of the information it needs already to do your taxes for you. They have your payroll data from your employer. If you have a retirement account, they’ll have those financial records from the institution, from your bank or your lender. They’ll have local data as well. So they could merely pre-fill your 1040 for you and send it to you to look over, or they could just send you a summary and say, Okay, if you agree with this, just let us know. You don’t really have to do anything. We’ll send you your refund, or there won’t be any money exchanging hands at all.
And so this is the way that taxes work in a lot of our peer countries with high incomes. In Japan, if you’re earning a salary, for the most part you don’t have to do anything. In some countries in Europe, you can do it all by text message. And the IRS is legally prevented from doing this, such that the average American spends 12 hours a year on the 1040 and spends roughly $300 on tax-preparation services. It’s silly. It’s silly. And there’s some people with very complicated tax situations. Fine. The IRS might have some requests for information. Did you have another kid this year? Did you take out another mortgage? Something like that. But they don’t need these endless, endless, endless, endless forms. They don’t need you to do them or hire somebody else to do them. They could do it.
Harris: To that point, are there other ways that we could be doing things? Is there a better way outside of these time taxes? How can the U.S. make government programs more accessible?
Lowrey: There’s a million and one. And it’s almost—there’s so many options out there that I feel like sometimes it’s hard for me to summarize.
So one straightforward thing is that there are different income standards and eligibility standards that target the same group of people using the same programs, many of whom use multiple programs. So for instance, Medicaid and SNAP—they have different income standards. In some cases, they have different standards of qualifying income, and you can’t cross enroll. So you can’t say, Okay, if I’m eligible for this, then I’ll maybe also be eligible for that. Sometimes that’s because of a difficult reason, so consider jobless insurance, which people often use if they’ve lost their job. That goes to the individual, where SNAP is really aimed at households instead. So that’s actually kind of a technical thing. But just unifying these standards and making such that you could cross-enroll in programs would be a wonderful, wonderful thing to do.
Holding states and offices and DMVs and everything else accountable for counting how much paperwork they’re putting on people, how many people they are not serving or are churning off and on programs because the paperwork is too much, and then saying, Okay, we want you to bring these numbers down—that would be really helpful. We don’t do that.
In terms of health care, dealing with hospitals and insurers and doctors is absolute misery. There’s a lot of common-sense regulation that could prevent health-care providers and insurers from denying procedures that should have been approved, or making sure that your medical bill is actually accurate—which half of them aren’t—preventing them from providing you with what you are paying for through simple paperwork and attrition and frustration, as opposed to some other legitimate tool. So those are just some ideas, but there are a lot out there.
Harris: Well, I guess if there are so many ideas out there, why hasn’t the government used some of those ideas, utilized the modern technology in the same way that, if I wanted a burger right now, I could pull my phone forward and just order it from DoorDash and it’s here in 15 minutes. If I needed a car to get somewhere, it’s, like, two clicks and I’ve got it. We have all of this modern technology. Why haven’t they used that modern technology to streamline a lot of this stuff?
Lowrey: Because the government is not really very good at reforming itself.
A lot of these changes would have to be made by Congress, and Congress doesn’t really care; it doesn’t see itself as a benefits administrator. And we’ve screwed up the lines of responsibility here. So if you’re not getting a benefit that you were supposed to be receiving, who’s at fault? Is that the state administrator? Is that the office that you’re working with, where if you complain, you are concerned that you might be retaliated against? Is that the governor? Is that the president? Because he’s the administrator of the programs, right? Is that Congress?
And I also think that there’s these broken feedback loops, by which I mean: If you get Social Security retirement benefits, we have decades of beautiful political-science research showing that it makes you feel like a citizen; it makes you feel like a good person; it makes you more likely to vote; it makes you more likely to be civically engaged in lots of ways. And seniors, when there are threats to Social Security, they come out and they demand that politicians stop it.
But there’s so many other little, tiny problems that relate to other programs that I don’t think that we have a mass politics demanding this. And so that’s why I think it’s hard. Nevertheless, when politicians do this stuff and make things easier, I think often it goes really well. It’s been really popular for, for instance, Zohran Mamdani in New York City. And I think that to a certain extent, we’re still operating under this understanding that these administrative burdens are demanded by the broad public because they’re so afraid of fraud in these programs. But there’s not that much fraud in these programs. We have really good ways to detect it. Giving more money to the civil service such that they could stamp fraud out would be a way to do it. And I just, I don’t know that people are voting on the basis of the way that the IRS is administering audits to other taxpayers. I don’t think that they are.
Harris: I mean, they might be.
Lowrey: Some of it. Everybody’s voting for something.
Harris: About the sort of weaponization of data that we’ve seen over the last year and a half, and the counterargument to The government should do more things to make lives better with our data is that the government can also take our data and do things that are nefarious if they so chose to, right? You can look at the Stasi; you can look at the Pinochet regimes.
How do you balance those concerns? Or does the government just already have so much data that they don’t necessarily factor in?
Lowrey: I think it’s a real concern and a real threat, since we are in an environment of democratic backsliding. This is one of the reasons that mixed-status families with citizen children and perhaps undocumented parents don’t get safety-net benefits that they have every right to get. That kid is a citizen; they’re allowed to get it. It’s because they don’t want to invite this state that could be very threatening to them into their lives.
I think one way to think about this is to give Americans the choice and to give the government permission: Okay, if I want this benefit, I feel comfortable with this office getting my data from the IRS. Something like that, so that it is elective and so that people can decide.
Harris: You point to Estonia in the book as a sort of prime example of a place that’s successfully easing the administrative burden on their citizens. But you also mentioned that they’re a small country. And as you were talking about, the gargantuan task of making the systems talk to each other in the United States, it makes me think that we have a scale problem here, that we might just be too big to eliminate some of the cumbersome bureaucracy. But how do you square the Estonian example with our context in the U.S.?
Lowrey: Yeah, Estonia is something we can aspire to, but I don’t think it’s ever gonna be something that we’re gonna have. So the thing about Estonia is they build a completely new government after they break away from the Soviet Union and regain their independence.
So Estonia regains its independence in the summer of 1991, and they form a government completely de novo, from scratch, at that point. And they do so during a climate where they want Estonians to trust the government because so many didn’t due to the Soviet influence.
And so they create the most elegant system of benefits that are all controlled by an ID number on all of these databases that are designed and updated constantly to talk to each other, such that Estonia has this policy that if you tell the government, any part of the government, a piece of information about yourself once, everything updates.
So for instance, if you tell the voting authority, My address has changed, all of the hospitals know it. All the schools, everything knows it. All of your mail goes to your new address. It’s nothing like that in the United States at all. So I don’t think that we are gonna become that—again, a very small homogenous country that started in the 1990s functionally. But I think that we can become more Estonia-like. And they’ve also had some issues with data security. They take it really seriously. So maybe there’s some lessons from Estonia to us, too, about setting these systems up in a way that is secure.
Harris: What would it take to implement some of those ideas from there? Is this just a political-will question?
Lowrey: Yeah, I do think it is a political-will question. And I think it’s a political-framing question. Because very often, administrative burdens are framed as necessary to prevent fraud. They’re not terribly good at preventing fraud. They’re much better at preventing people from getting needed benefits. But I think if instead of saying, This is about the poor people getting this program, or this is about making sure that these programs are secure, we could have a politics that says, This is malign; this is bad policy making. We give the government $8 trillion a year, and it passes back this garbage? No! No. Right? At least do the obvious stuff here.
And I also think that there’s ways of thinking about new policy changes that could be administratively light. So for instance, there’s always been this idea to put children up to the age of 18 on Medicare, which comes and goes and comes and goes. That’s a nice thing to do because it would mean that just kids are on Medicare. You never have to worry if your kid gets a broken bone or, God forbid, a cancer, that they’re always gonna be able to get treatment. But more than that, it’s just elegant. It’s simple. It’s the government taking work away from you.
I think about this a lot in terms of free school meals as well. That’s not only a benefit for lower-income families that might be having nutritional challenges. It’s also like, If you don’t have food in the house just because you forgot, oh great, the school’s just gonna feed your kid and you don’t have to worry about it. It’s just a nice thing in terms of reducing those burdens.
And so I think that a lot of that could be really popular. One thing I think about a lot is: We focus so much on reducing unnecessary burdens on businesses. Can we think about it in terms of reducing unnecessary burdens on families? Whether that’s these insurers that are not really insuring us, or this tax authority that makes us do our own taxes, or any other program where it’s just hard to grapple with.
Harris: Annie, here is to hoping that that burden is alleviated. Thank you so much for joining.
Lowrey: Thank you. I do hope. Thank you so much, Adam.

Flushing toilets release particles into the “breathing zone” of adults and can remain suspended in the air for at least 20 seconds, a new study has found.
And closing the lid might not be enough to avoid a “plume” of potential pathogens.
Meanwhile, previous research has shown public toilets are an inescapable hotbed of microbes.
Flinders University researchers reviewed 22 studies of toilet-generated aerosols, publishing the results in the Science of the Total Environment journal.
They found microbes from the water used for flushing or from contamination of the bowl ended up as aerosols, with more “turbulent” flushing releasing more particles.
That included bioaerosols – aerosols that contain biological material and can transmit pathogens including legionella, influenza and norovirus. There are differing reports about whether Covid spreads through toilet aerosols.
The researchers found higher levels of aerosols in the water and higher levels of turbulence during the flush increased the volume of particles suspended in the air, but the effects of bathroom ventilation and whether the lid was up or down were unclear.
Despite that, lead author and PhD student Lira Adiyani said she would still recommend putting the lid down after using the toilet.
“Toilet flushing creates turbulence that can release aerosols into the surrounding air,” she said.
“Some studies detected these aerosols at adult breathing height, indicating a potential pathway for inhalation exposure.
“The more microbes present in the toilet, the more bioaerosols may be released. Therefore, larger flush volumes generally produce more aerosols.”
Adiyani said “based on the available evidence” she would still recommend closing the lid as a precautionary measure, “while recognising that it does not completely prevent aerosols from escaping”.
In the report, the researchers wrote that the effects of indoor aerosols had been “understudied” despite the risk of infection. This had “important implications for risk assessment, building design, and infection control in an era of water security pressures and emerging infectious diseases”, they wrote.
“Indoor aerosols influence air quality and human health as their small size allows them to penetrate deep into the respiratory tract when inhaled, providing a direct exposure pathway.”
Co-author, environmental health professor Harriet Whiley, said people didn’t have to be worried in their own homes, unless someone in the house was immunocompromised.
She said the team was working on “protecting the most vulnerable through good design” in places such as hospitals and aged care environments.
They are increasingly concerned about “opportunistic pathogens” that can be present in water, particularly recycled or rainwater. “They don’t affect healthy people,” she said. “But if you’re immunocompromised you can get very sick, and it can be fatal.”
So it’s about getting “an effective flush with less volume and less turbulence”, she said.
Dr Lotti Tajouri, an associate professor in molecular genetics at Bond and Murdoch universities wasn’t involved in the research but warned bathroom dangers go well beyond the toilet.
His own research is particularly focused on public toilets and mobile phone use in toilets.
“As soon as you enter a toilet, consider everything contaminated,” he said.
The door will have microbes on it, as will the floor – so you should never put anything on it, he said. Then you might touch the lid, after which you flush with the lid up or down.
If it’s up, you get the “plume” effect, an “explosion or aerosols … you are literally sprayed [with]”.
Flushing with the lid down might limit your exposure to the plume, but depending on the cleanliness of the toilet, previous users have left microorganisms on every surface anyway. “The roof, the walls, the floor,” he said.
Then, you touch the toilet door again, before (hopefully) washing your hands. But you will probably touch the taps again, blow microorganisms around with the hairdryer, touch the exit door and then touch your phone.
“Studies show between 50% and 80% of people use mobile phones in the toilet. For younger generations it’s almost 100%,” he said. “They will contaminate their phones and fingers with fecal microorganisms – salmonella, campylobacter, all sorts of bacteria and viruses.
“The less contact you have, the better it is.”

Tebogo says late mother 'always there' ahead of emotional return to Budapest
- Published
Olympic 200m champion Letsile Tebogo will return to Budapest for the Ultimate Championships next week, but the Hungarian capital is more than just another stop on the athletics calendar for the Botswana sprinter.
It is the city where the 23-year-old announced himself to the world and where his mother Seratiwa watched him make history for his country by claiming two medals at the 2023 World Championships.
This time Seratiwa will not be cheering on her son from the stands, having passed away in May 2024 after a short illness.
Having shared a close relationship with his mother - one she described as being more like a "brother and sister bond" - Tebogo admits that returning without her is difficult.
"I haven't really looked into the fact that I'm going now to Budapest without my mom," he said.
"It's just been a bumpy ride having to think about it and having to continue with the grind."
Three years ago, Seratiwa surprised her son by travelling to Budapest to watch the then 20-year-old compete in his first senior global championships.
Tebogo won silver in the 100m and bronze in the 200m - the first World Championship medals claimed by a male athlete from Botswana. He also became the first African man to win a World Championship medal in the 100m.
Seratiwa told BBC Sport Africa at the time that she was "proud" of what her son had achieved.
For all the memories the city holds, Tebogo says there is also a source of strength in returning to the place where his mother witnessed one of the defining moments of his career.
"I believe she's always there with me in spirit and in days where giving up is an option," he said.
"She pushes me to give my absolute best and I believe the memories that we had in Budapest, they will still come again."
- African athletes need support and protection - Kebinatshipi 
  - Published29 April
- Botswana welcomes Tebogo home with stadium spectacular 
  - Published13 August 2024
Teaching 'unwavering sportsmanship'
Those memories now sit alongside everything that has happened since for Tebogo.
A year on from his success at the 2023 World Championships, Tebogo scaled greater heights by becoming Botswana's first Olympic champion when he won the 200m at the Paris 2024 Games, carrying his mother's initials on both his shoes and fingernails as a tribute.
He returns to Budapest as one of the faces of a new competition created to bring together the sport's best performers.
The Ultimate Championships is a biennial global event designed to crown the best of the best in a track and field season.
The three-day end-of-season competition includes Olympic champions, world champions, Diamond League winners and the year's other leading performers.
The inaugural edition in Budapest, which runs from 11-13 September, has a $10m (£7.41m) prize pot - the highest in track and field history according to organisers World Athletics - with each gold medallist taking home $150,000 (£111,000).
Tebogo, who helped Botswana to gold in the 4x400m at the World Relays on home soil earlier this year before registering 200m wins at the Diamond League events in Oslo and Lausanne, says the 200m in Budapest will not only be about looking back.
He is one of the team captains for the Kids' Athletics Ultimate Challenge, where young people from across the city will be invited to participate in activities at the Gyula Zsivotzky National Athletics Centre the day before the Ultimate Championships begin.
That will give him the chance to share some of the lessons he has learned since first stepping onto the global stage.
"I believe firstly you should start with accountability," he said.
"Think about your preparation, how you want your journey or your season to be, and then also think of unwavering sportsmanship.
"I would love them to have that unwavering sportsmanship, so that they can share lanes, they can cheer for one another."

The Tesla Cybercab is notable for what it lacks, namely a steering wheel and pedal. By design, there is no way for this vehicle to be manually controlled — or so we thought. Less than a week after the Cybercab was officially launched in Austin, Texas, some riders have discovered the Cybercab’s secret manual controls that appears to be intended only for Tesla employees.
Tesla Cybercab doesn’t have any manual controls — but it does have a virtual joystick
The virtual controls seemingly appeared accidentally to several riders in the first couple weeks of the Cybercab’s public launch.
In at least two videos posted on X, Cybercab riders are encountering a virtual joystick that appears intended to control the vehicle’s movements. A square-shaped screen appears in the lower left corner of the central display, with a toggle in the middle for manual driving. It says “forward” at the top and “reverse” on the bottom. There are also buttons to “stop” the vehicle, sound the horn, and manually open the doors. To the right are views of the live camera displays, though in one rider’s video the image appears to be frozen on a Tesla Supercharger from a previous location.
Clearly these controls are intended for Tesla employees and depot workers who may need to nudge the Cybercab into a tight space at low speeds. Since the Cybercab lacks traditional controls, Tesla needed a work-around for fleet workers who may need to rearrange the vehicles in a parking lot, for example. This display would allow them to do that without having to call in a request to Tesla’s Cybercab control center or use a remote operator.
Theoretically these could also be used by law enforcement or emergency responders who may need to move a Cybercab off the road. Tesla has briefed Austin’s police department on the Cybercab service, though its unclear whether these manual controls were part of the conversation.
The customers who noticed the virtual joysticks tried unsuccessfully to use them to control the vehicle. Thankfully, they didn’t seem to work — or perhaps they weren’t using the controls accurately. Why these controls were on the display during customer rides is anyone’s guess. Chalk it up to an early bug that Tesla can hopefully fix before the Cybercabs gets any wider release.
Tesla built the Cybercab as a fully autonomous vehicle without manual controls. The purpose was to send the message that these controls are relics of the past, and the Cybercab is the vehicle of the future. But even the vehicle of the future may need some manual help every now and then.

For many small-to-medium-sized businesses (SMBs), VMware has become too expensive.
Broadcom’s acquisition of the virtualization firm brought the end of perpetual license sales and the arrival of pricey, stacked, subscription-based bundles that priced out many SMBs.
The most obvious is VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF), VMware’s flagship private cloud bundle that has been Broadcom’s primary focus since taking over VMware. Many SMBs find that VCF is unaffordable and stuffed with unnecessary offerings. However, numerous customers have reported online that VMware sales representatives have still pushed them toward VCF, with some claiming that sales reps have told them that the lower-priced edition of VMware’s virtualization platform, vSphere Standard, was no longer available.
Speaking with The Register this week, Paul Turner, VCF’s chief product officer, said Broadcom’s new sales incentives encouraged the sales team to push VCF.
“We corrected this,” Turner told the publication. He admitted that sometimes VMware had “too big a focus on VCF.”
vSphere Standard update
VMware will release an “updated version” of vSphere Standard “soon,” The Register reported. More information will likely come in October during VMware’s Explore conference in Frankfurt, Ram Velaga, president of Broadcom’s Infrastructure Software Group, told The Register.
VMware hasn’t updated vSphere Standard since 2022 despite an updated version of vSphere arriving with VCF 9 in 2025. This was because, Turner said, VMware was prioritizing improving VCF’s security.
Velaga said that VMware prioritized VCF in an effort to promote private clouds as a more affordable alternative to the public cloud, which are easier to manage. “People could get distracted” if VMware introduced a low-end virtualization product then, the executive said.
Broken trust
Dean Colpitts, CTO of Canadian managed services provider Members IT Group (MITG), which VMware cut from its reseller program after 19 years of partnership last year, told Ars that MITG is not doing any VMware business now and won’t in the future.
I was shocked how unapologetic and straight faced the CEO was when he explained what Broadcom was all about during company wide townhall after acquisition. "We are not in business of developing new technologies. We are in business of acquiring mismanaged great technologies and monetizing them". I think that tells you everything you need to know. I still can't believe regulators let the deal go through.

The lawyer of Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman accused of killing her three young children, has said he hopes Donald Trump will pardon his client after her trial recently ended with a deadlocked jury.
Clancy’s attorney, Kevin Reddington, made the appeal on a televised interview on the ABC show Good Morning America on Tuesday. The plea comes to Trump after a judge on Friday declared a mistrial after the jury in the Clancy case could not reach a unanimous verdict on whether she was guilty or not guilty.
Reddington said he hoped that the president would “consider a pardon” for Clancy given “the type of person she is” and “what she has been through”.
“Mr President, I would hope that you would consider this young lady,” said Reddington, who also alluded to how Trump on Friday called the case a “tragedy”.
Trump’s pardon powers are applicable in the federal justice system in the US, and Clancy was tried in Massachusetts’ state criminal justice system.
But in June in Colorado, Tina Peters – the former clerk convicted in state court of participating in a plot to chase election conspiracy theories boosted by Trump – was released early from a nine-year prison after Democratic governor Jared Polis succumbed to pressure to do so from the Republican president.
Clancy, who is 36, was charged with fatally strangling her three children – Cora, five; Dawson, three; and Callan, eight months old – in their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023. She had also thrown herself out of her bedroom window in an apparent suicide attempt which left her paralyzed.
Prosecutors argued that Clancy was aware of her actions and had “coldly and efficiently executed” the children after planning to do so, including ensuring her husband was out of the house.
But her defense, led by Reddington, claimed that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis which compelled her to carry out the killings and therefore was not legally culpable.
During the trial, Reddington called forensic psychiatrist Dr Phillip Resnick to testify that Clancy had “severe depression” and a history of anxiety, which increased after the birth of her children to the point that she “felt she couldn’t function”.
“At the time of the crime … Ms Clancy was frankly psychotic,” Resnick said. “She was clearly psychotic on that day.”
Jurors in Plymouth state court spent more than 38 hours in deliberations over the charges, which sparked a broader national debate over maternal mental health issues that can occur postpartum.
Ultimately, Reddington has said the 12-person jury, made up of nine women and three men, was split 11 to one in favor of a not guilty verdict. The lack of a unanimous verdict led to the judge declaring a mistrial, opening the way for another trial.
Trump was asked about the trial by reporters on Friday, with the president calling the case “a shame” and a “horrible tragedy”.
“I think the judge has said it’s going to be a mistrial, so there’s going to be another trial,” he said. “It’s a terrible situation. Look, she did a horrible, horrible thing.
“Can’t be worse. But you’ll find out what the price to pay is. There’ll be a price. It’s going to be mental institution or jail or something, but I guess they’re going to go through another trial.”

When Muhammad Shaheem, 17, from Karnataka was diagnosed with severe thalassemia at just five months old, regular blood transfusions became a part of his childhood. Years of transfusions, however, led to severe iron overload that affected his heart and liver, making a stem cell transplant a particularly high-risk procedure.
A possible way out came from within his own family when Shaheem’s younger sister, Zara, 7, was identified as a full Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA)-matched donor. After extensive preparation and counselling at the Sankalp-Bhagwan Mahavir Jain Hospital in Bengaluru, his family decided to proceed with the transplant.
Their mother, Zareena, who lives with thalassemia major, said, “I continue to undergo treatment and regular blood transfusions. Though it was a difficult decision to make in my son’s case, it has ultimately given my son a second chance for better life without being troubled much by the disease.”
Mr. Shaheem is among 1,000 children who have undergone paediatric stem cell transplants with help from Sankalp India Foundation, DKMS, and Cure2Children. The procedure is both risky and expensive, and the treatment cost in India ranges from ₹12 lakh to ₹40 lakh.
On Friday (September 4), Sankalp, along with international nonprofit organisation DKMS and medical partner Cure2Children Foundation, completed 1,000 stem cell transplants for children suffering from thalassemia.
Of these transplants, DKMS has supported the transplantation costs of more than 820 children. On the other hand, Sankalp currently provides care to more than 3,000 children through 30 thalassemia day-care centres and operates paediatric bone marrow transplant centres in Bengaluru and Ahmedabad.
Rajat Kumar Agarwal, president of Sankalp India Foundation, said, “For us, these 1,000 transplants are 1,000 beginnings and proof that cure can be made accessible when organisations combine their strengths with a shared purpose. It shows how centres in resource-constrained settings can still achieve success in medicine and internationally recognised quality while keeping transplantation affordable and accessible.”
