Sharpeville massacre survivors start legal fight for justice in South Africa
- Published
Abraham Mofokeng still carries the wounds of the bloody suppression of a protest in South Africa 66 years ago. In what became known as the Sharpeville massacre, police infamously opened fire on thousands of peaceful demonstrators.
A bullet is still lodged in Mofokeng's spine, and he has a gentle limp from a gunshot to the leg.
"We weren't seen as people," the 86-year-old tells the BBC as he explains the reasons he joined the demonstration on 21 March 1960 against the repressive laws of the white-minority government.
"All you were good for was working. You couldn't question them, you were supposed to just do as you're told."
The massacre at Sharpeville, which he survived, exposed to the world the violence of the racist apartheid system - yet thanks to an indemnity law passed a year after the killings, none of the perpetrators were ever prosecuted.
Mofokeng is now part of a legal case set to be announced on Thursday that will seek to overturn this law.
At least 69 protesters were shot dead by police on that day in 1960, becoming a pivotal event in the history of the anti-apartheid movement.
Though Sharpeville may be a place name rich in historical resonance, it scarcely looks like a site that symbolises the struggle: the township is slowly crumbling.
The once tarred roads of this area south of Johannesburg are returning to dirt. Many of the houses are still the small, brown-faced brick homes built under the apartheid-era government. The earth is dry and barren - heaps of rubbish are piling up throughout the neighbourhood.
While the legalised system of racism was buried in 1994 when the country held its first democratic election and elected Nelson Mandela as president, its scars remain.
There have been attempts at redress - not least through the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) - set up by Mandela's government to investigate crimes committed during the apartheid era.
But the Sharpeville survivors feel they have not seen justice.
Sharpeville's local memorial park, the Human Rights Precinct, tells the story of how the streets of township became the scene of a bloodbath.
Inside the park stand 69 white pillars, one for each life lost.
The victims were killed while demonstrating against the racist pass laws.
At the time, black people were forced to carry a document known as a passbook, known as "dompas" in Afrikaans, which restricted their freedom to move around the country.
A person could be beaten and jailed if found without it - or if found in a "whites-only" area without permission.
Many heeded the call from the leaders of the Pan Africanist Congress in March 1960 to march in protest against the dompas, including then-20-year-old Mofokeng.
"The life we were living under apartheid was a life of oppression. We could not move around freely. We ended up planning to march to the police station against these passbooks that were being used to oppress us," he says.
Thousands turned up to what they thought would be a peaceful protest.
"[The police] had rifles, machetes, even shields. We explained to the police that we didn't want the passes anymore and we were prepared to go to prison. There was a commotion, then all hell broke loose when the police started shooting."
Mofokeng was among the more than 200 people injured and recent estimates by South African researchers have revised upwards the number who died to as many as 91.
Another survivor, Larazus Magotsi - now 90 - walks along the long row of graves in the cemetery where most of those who died are buried. Among them is a headstone marking where a 12-year-old was laid to rest.
Magotsi's eyes are filled with tears as he struggles to compose himself.
"We heard gunshots and ran and hid inside a store, peeping to see what was happening outside," he says.
"People were lying on the ground. When we looked out again, we saw that some were trying to get up, but the police were just shooting at them.
"Others were using machetes to strike the heads of people who were still moving."
It is thought that more than 1,300 bullets were shot into the crowd. Archive photos show policemen walking among the corpses, lying where they fell, in the immediate aftermath of the massacre.
The only legal case that followed the killings was a failed attempt to charge the protesters with affray.
Now, survivors and relatives of those who were killed are hoping to overturn the law they say prevents them from getting justice.
The 1961 Indemnity Act was passed by the apartheid government in the wake of the massacre and protected the police and government from having criminal charges or even civil claims brought against them in relation to what happened at Sharpeville.
Despite more than 30 years of democratic rule, that law remains on the statute books.
But now South African non-governmental organisation Lawyers for Human Rights, together with UK-based law firm Leigh Day, has filed a case at the High Court arguing that the law is unconstitutional under the new constitution that came into effect in 1994.
"Apart from the individual damages, what the community's looking for is basically reparations to enable their healing. They feel as though Sharpeville is a forgotten community," says Charne Tracey, one of the lawyers on the case.
Part of their court application includes getting a class action certified - if approved this would mean that for the first time dozens of victims and relatives of those killed could collectively sue the state. It could also possibly lead to criminal charges being brought against the alleged perpetrators, if any are still alive.
"Nothing has been done that assists with their healing and improvement of their quality of life, or remedy the long-term effects of what they've suffered," Tracey says, adding that 70 people could be involved in the class action.
Constitutional law expert Prof Frans Viljoen believes having the old law repealed is important because it would help to "clean up" the legislation and "close a chapter on the past".
"Although South Africa has a very transformative constitution… The principle of continuity of statehood still applies, which is why the case can be brought against the current state," says Viljoen.
"So if there were laws in our statute book in 1994, the constitution explicitly says they remain in force until parliament repeals them, abolishes them or changes them," he adds.
But he backs attempts to declare the Indemnity Act unconstitutional "to cleanse us of that past".
The TRC, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, was generally praised for bringing together victims and perpetrators who were granted amnesty as long as they, among other conditions, fully disclosed what they had done.
But the greatest criticism of the process was that it did not bring about justice for some as people were not jailed for their acts and no police officers applied for amnesty for the Sharpeville shootings.
The government told the BBC it had supported apartheid victims over the years, and would continue to do so, but did not oppose survivors and families pursuing legal remedies.
When it comes to reparations the justice department said 560 TRC-recognised victims of apartheid-era violence had received individual grants amounting to some $31m (£23m) and though not all Sharpeville survivors and relatives had been identified it encouraged them to come forward.
For many in the community of Sharpeville, there is hope that restitution will help heal decades of lingering trauma.
"Apartheid is dead and buried. A win would bring complete healing, not just for us, but for future generations as well," says Mofokeng.
"Considering how people died, many have not completely healed."

Why Nepal floods should worry India
- Published
Nepal's devastating floods have exposed a risk that does not stop at its borders.
India and Nepal share the rivers that rise in the Himalayas, but the relationship between a flood in Nepal and a disaster in India is more complicated than a simple story of water flowing downstream, say experts.
Some floods can race out of the mountains carrying enormous quantities of mud, rock and debris. Others may lose much of their force as they reach the plains, leaving behind a more conventional flood.
And whether that water becomes a disaster in India depends not only on how much rain has fallen in Nepal, but also on rainfall, river levels, embankments, drainage and development on the Indian side.
Nepal's floods are a warning for India - not simply because water flows south across the border, but because the two countries share a vast and increasingly volatile Himalayan river system.
How many Nepal rivers flow into India?
Nepal has more than 6,000 rivers and streams, most draining south into India and the Ganges.
Three major systems dominate: the Kosi in the east, the Gandaki (Gandak in India) in the centre and the Karnali (Ghaghara in India) in the west, with the Mahakali (Sharda) along the western border.
A dozen smaller rivers rising in the Siwaliks and Chure - including the Bagmati, Kamala, Rapti and Babai - are less famous but can produce faster, more unpredictable floods because their catchments are small and steep.
Seven to nine major rivers flow from Nepal into the Indian plains, and they are responsible for flooding in India, according to Manish Shrestha, a hydrologist at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD).
India's Central Water Commission identifies the Kosi, Gandak, Bagmati and Ghaghara as some of the main transboundary rivers.
Which Indian states are most exposed?
Bihar is by far the most exposed Indian state, with roughly three-quarters of north Bihar officially classified as flood-prone.
Almost all the major rivers that flood the state originate in Nepal, with the Kosi - the "sorrow of Bihar" - the most notorious, followed by the Gandak, Bagmati and Kamala.
But the risk extends beyond Bihar.
Eastern Uttar Pradesh is vulnerable to the Ghaghara, Rapti and Gandak rivers. Districts like Gorakhpur, Bahraich, Lakhimpur Kheri and Shravasti are regularly affected.
Uttarakhand state shares the Mahakali-Sharda rivers. North Bengal receives the Mechi and Mahananda.
"Bihar dominates in scale. Uttar Pradesh is second and often under-reported," says Pradeep Man Dangol, hydrologist at ICIMOD.
Bihar bears the greatest burden, but Uttar Pradesh is a significant and often overlooked part of the risk.
When Nepal floods, what determines India's fate?
Think of it as a three-part chain, say hydrologists.
First, the rain: where it falls and how heavily.
Flood peaks reaching India are often generated not in the high Himalayas but lower down, in the Siwaliks, Chure and Terai, where intense monsoon rain can fall on steep, small catchments.
Second, the river.
Nepal's rivers cross a sharp break in slope at the mountain front, drop their sediment, and spread across the plains as braided, shifting channels.
Third, when the water meets India.
How bad the flooding becomes depends on what the water encounters - the volume of rain on the Indian side, how full the Ganges is, embankments and barrages, and blocked drainage from roads, railways and settlements on the floodplain.
So the peak flow at the border is largely determined by rainfall in Nepal. The severity of flooding depends at least as much on conditions in India.
The 2008 Kosi disaster shows why: the river was carrying far less water than the embankment was designed to handle. The catastrophe was caused by the embankment failing, not by an exceptional flood.
So how much depends on Nepal v India?
"For the peak flow arriving at the border, largely Nepal's rainfall; for the severity of flooding once it arrives, at least as much on Indian conditions," says Saswata Sanyal, ICIMOD's intervention manager for disaster risk reduction.
How Nepal's rain becomes India's flood risk
The 2008 Kosi disaster is a powerful illustration.
Nearly 400 people died in Bihar after the Kosi breached an embankment in Nepal. But, remarkably, it was not an extraordinary high-flow event on the river.
According to Rajiv Sinha, a professor of earth sciences at Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Kanpur, the flow was only about a tenth of the river's carrying capacity. The catastrophe was caused by a breach in an embankment built decades earlier and inadequately maintained.
"The embankments constructed in the 1950s and 1960s had not been properly maintained. They had become eroded and eventually developed a weak point. The river breached its embankment through these vulnerable points and entered parts of India that had not seen flooding for perhaps 100 years," says Sinha.
The failure, in other words, was "structural, not hydrological", adds Sanyal.
How much warning can India get from Nepal?
For ordinary monsoon floods, India may have "roughly 12 hours to two days of warning", according to Sanyal, depending on how quickly the water travels downstream.
Water can take about a day to reach the Bihar plains from the Nepal mountain front along the Kosi and Gandak, and somewhat longer along the Ghaghara.
Flash floods from the Chure rivers can arrive within hours.
A landslide-dam burst or debris flow can be even faster - in the current floods, the peak surge from Rasuwa reached Triveni, near the Indian border, in about seven-and-a-half hours.
India and Nepal do share real-time rainfall and river-level data from a network of stations. Nepal's Department of Hydrology and Meteorology feeds rainfall and river levels to India's Central Water Commission, which uses them for flood forecasts.
But important gaps remain, says Sanyal.
They include too few real-time monitoring stations in the fastest-flowing Chure catchments. There's also no single shared forecasting model between the two countries; and limited routine sharing on embankment conditions, river-channel changes and sediment.
And then there's, crucially, the last mile.
A warning reaching a district office is not the same as reaching a family in danger.
For these transboundary rivers, Sinha says, "cooperation on information sharing and early-warning systems is extremely important. We need rapid continuous monitoring of glacial lakes, their outflows and how they are changing over time".
What is the biggest misconception around Nepal and floods in India?
A common misconception is that Nepal "releases" water into India, say scientists.
Nepal has almost no large reservoirs capable of doing this: its main storage dam, Kulekhani, holds less than a tenth of a cubic kilometre, "so there's nothing to release", says Sanyal.
The Kosi and Gandak barrages are operated by India. When floodwater reaches the border, it is overwhelmingly because rain has fallen upstream - not because Nepal has opened a gate.
But there is an important truth behind the claim: much of the water that floods north Bihar and eastern UP has fallen as rain in Nepal, so Nepal's rainfall largely determines the timing and size of flood peaks reaching India.
Nepal supplies around 40% of the average annual flow of the Ganges - and a much larger share in the dry season - making its hydrology critical to India.
"What is too simplistic is treating that as a story of cause and blame. Rain is not a decision," says Sanyal.
Whether a given flow becomes a disaster depends on conditions in India as much as in Nepal the Ganges' level, Indian rainfall, embankment integrity, drainage and sediment.
"And the effects run both ways: embankments and barrages built for India's protection have raised water levels and caused backwater flooding in Nepal's Terai, which is Nepal's long-standing concern,' says Sanyal.
Nepal and India share one river system, with one country upstream and the other downstream.
The answer is therefore not blame, but better shared data, forecasting and river management.
So what should worry India the most?
"India should be worried. but not necessarily because of the Kosi river in Nepal," says Rajiv Sinha.
In other words, experts say, the real warning is about what is happening in the Himalayas - and what happens when water, rock, ice and enormous quantities of sediment suddenly combine.
Sinha says the latest Nepal disaster resembles a series of catastrophic events that India has experienced in recent years, including the 2021 Chamoli disaster and the 2025 Dharali disaster in Uttarakhand. The Nepal event, he says, was "perhaps five to 10 times larger".
"The fundamental point is that these are not normal hydrological floods," Sinha says.
A conventional flood is largely water. But when water from intense rain, melting ice or a sudden discharge mixes with huge quantities of sediment, the result can become a thick, high-energy slurry capable of destroying almost everything in its path.
That was the lesson of the Chamoli disaster in 2021, when a large chunk of a Himalayan glacier collapsed in the valley of Chamoli in northern India, sending a cascade of debris and water downstream that killed 200 people and damaged hydropower infrastructure.
It was also evident at Dharali in Uttarakhand in 2025, after heavy rains triggered a flash flood and the flow of debris buried parts of a village under metres of material.
And then there's climate change.
Extreme rainfall is intensifying: the region is warming faster than the global average, a warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, and the monsoon is delivering more rain in fewer, heavier bursts, say experts.
High-mountain hazards are also growing. As permafrost degrades, glacial lake outbursts and rock-ice avalanches are expected to increase, producing faster, debris-laden floods that are harder to forecast.
And more extreme events mean more landslides and sediment in rivers, raising riverbeds and reducing channel capacity on both sides of the border.
They are manifestations of the same broad Himalayan hazard system. And India's exposure is considerable.

9-year-old boy killed, toddler injured in leopard attack in Uttar Pradesh
Two leopard attacks in Bahraich left a boy dead and a young girl injured. Officials say flooding is pushing wild animals into villages, intensifying the conflict.
A nine-year-old boy was killed and a three-year-old girl was injured in two separate leopard attacks in Uttar Pradesh's Bahraich district, forest officials said on Tuesday. The officials said cases of wild animals entering populated areas have risen in different parts of the district because of flooding.
In one attack, Rajveer, 9, was mauled by a leopard in Anand Nagar village in the Katarniaghat range at around 9 pm on Monday. In the other, a girl identified as Lado was attacked in Jodwa village under the Nanpara range late on Sunday evening and was later referred to Lucknow for treatment.
Divisional Forest Officer of the Katarniaghat Wildlife Division Apoorva Dixit said Rajveer had gone to fetch water from a handpump near the road when the leopard attacked him.
"The boy had gone to fetch water from a handpump located alongside the road when the leopard attacked him," Dixit said. He added that there are sugarcane fields behind the boy's house and the leopard came out from one of the fields before attacking him.
Rajveer was seriously injured and his family members and villagers were taking him to a community health centre, but he died on the way, Dixit said. The body has been sent for a post-mortem examination.
He said the forest department has given immediate financial assistance of Rs 10,000 to the boy's mother and the process for payment of the remaining compensation under the rules is underway.
Dixit said leopard pugmarks were found near the spot of the attack. Camera traps are being installed to identify the animal and cages are being set up to capture it. "Due to flooding in the area, wild animals are moving towards higher ground and nearby villages," he said.
In the second incident, Divisional Forest Officer of the Bahraich Wildlife Division Sundaresha said the injured girl was first taken to Bahraich Medical College and later referred to Lucknow for better treatment. "According to information received on Tuesday, the girl is safe and her condition is out of danger in Lucknow," he said.
Dixit said a continuous operation is under way to safely remove leopards from populated areas. He said 13 leopards have been rescued since July 21, while 18 leopards have been rescued and shifted to safer locations since the start of the year.
The two attacks came as officials continued efforts to track and capture leopards moving into villages in the flood-hit district.

Tokyo’s Taito Ward, home to popular tourist spots such as Asakusa and Ueno, is moving to ban minpaku in certain parts of the ward beginning next year, as local governments across Japan begin restricting the short-term private-residence lodging system.
An ordinance was submitted to the ward assembly Tuesday that proposes effectively ending the program for new minpaku in residential areas and locations where traditional hotels and inns are restricted. It will do so by limiting the number of days that such minpaku can operate to zero.
The ward cited increasing reports of bad behavior such as improper trash disposal and loud noises as being behind the new ordinance.
Both the number of minpaku in Taito and the number of complaints stemming from them have risen dramatically in recent years. The number of new minpaku applications tripled in 2025 compared with the year prior, hitting nearly 1,400, while the number of complaints accordingly increased fourfold to 257 cases.
In addition to the proposed policy on new minpaku, Taito Ward will begin enforcing fresh restrictions on all minpaku later this year. While the ward currently allows them to operate on any given day up to the nationwide legal limit of 180 days a year, beginning in October they will only be able to accommodate guests on weekends and holidays.
The minpaku program allows approved operators to provide lodging in their private residences. Since starting in June 2018 as a way to meet higher tourist demand and fill houses vacated by Japan’s diminishing population, the system’s popularity has rapidly grown, especially in recent years.
Taito’s potential ban comes as other municipalities around the country are introducing restrictions. Since July, when the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism notified local governments that they had the authority to limit minpaku operations, Tokyo’s Shinjuku Ward as well as the city of Kyoto have moved to implement bans, both referencing an increasing number of local complaints.

Is Russia proving better at protecting friends than fighting enemies in West Africa?
- Published
When mutinous soldiers seized a strategic military base in Niger's capital last Saturday, the country's ruling junta turned to a foreign partner it has increasingly relied on since coming to power: Russia.
Following a night of intense fighting in Niamey, Russia's Africa Corps helped Nigerien loyalist forces to regain control of Air Base 101 at Diori Hamani International Airport.
Africa Corps, unlike its predecessor the Wagner Group, is directly under the control of the defence ministry in Moscow. It provides combat support and military training and is thought to have some 200 to 300 men in Niger.
Russia's ambassador to Niger, Viktor Voropaev, publicly acknowledged the weekend intervention, saying his country's forces had helped "repress a mutiny".
"This is seen as a symbolic victory," according to Beverly Ochieng, senior analyst at Control Risks. "[One] that will continue to put them at the centre of not just the counter-insurgency campaign, but even in the protection and prolongation of military rule."
The attempted coup offers perhaps the clearest evidence yet that Africa Corps' role in three Sahel countries extends beyond its stated mission of helping governments fight jihadist insurgencies.
Russia is increasingly demonstrating that it can provide something perhaps even more valuable to the military rulers of Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso: protection for the governments themselves.
"It was not sufficient to bring stability," said Ochieng, "but it's enough to allow these military governments to have a political lifeline."
The thwarted mutiny also highlights something the ruling junta may not want to admit - just how dependent on Moscow it has become for security.
In January, Africa Corps personnel also played an important role in repelling an attack at the same airport.
"We saw videos of the jihadists walking around the airport basically completely unimpeded," said Jacob Boswall, a security analyst who tracks jihadist activity for the BBC's media monitoring service.
"Probably there is some substance to the claim that Africa Corps was able to restore power in that case [in January]. And I think, again, in this case as well, that intervention was very significant."
One of the Nigerien military's central justifications for the July 2023 coup, which saw Gen Abdourahamane Tiani seize power, was the deteriorating security situation and alleged failure of Niger's civilian authorities, under elected President Mohamed Bazoum, to tackle it.
They also blamed Western partners at the time for their inability to contain jihadist violence.
Yet, three years later, that insurgency remains unresolved.
Militants linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State have continued to launch attacks, including in the Tillabéri and Dosso regions. Some, inflicting heavy casualties on security forces.
Ochieng described this latest mutiny as evidence of longstanding grievances within Niger's own military, compounded by the pressure the soldiers have been facing.
"Counter-insurgency forces do not feel adequately supported by the military government," she said. "There have been challenges in providing equipment and replenishments."
Niger's government is facing threats on two fronts: extremist militant groups attacking the state, and grievances within its armed forces responsible for fighting them. Africa Corps may have helped contain the latter this past weekend, but it has yet to resolve the former.
Unlike Wagner mercenaries, whose status in a private military company allowed Moscow some deniability, Africa Corps is more clearly an instrument of the Russian state.
"The whole point of Africa Corps is that it brings the power back under the control of the Russian Ministry of Defence," said Boswall.
Officially, its forces are deployed to help Sahel governments combat Islamist militant groups.
But dissidents contemplating moves against military governments elsewhere in the Sahel region may now have to factor Russian forces into their calculations.
Despite the struggle to contain the jihadists, no-one anticipates Africa Corps leaving the Sahel any time soon. Keeping those governments in power protects Russia's investment.
"Wagner - and now Africa Corps - have always had a very transactional interest in Africa," Boswall said.
"If they can get mineral resources in exchange for providing protection and defence, then they will. We see that in Mali with gold… and then in Niger, it really is uranium [that] seems to be the main resource that Africa Corps is protecting."
Analysts say Russia also benefits from having friendly governments that could support it in international forums.
"Having that kind of international group of supportive countries, Russia sees as giving Russia credibility - diplomatic credibility," Boswall explained.
Like Mali and Burkina Faso, Tiani's government has built much of its legitimacy using the language of sovereignty, pan-Africanism and liberation from former colonial powers.
All three governments ordered French troops to leave. They also formed the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) and subsequently withdrew from the West African regional bloc Ecowas, presenting the new alliance as an assertion of regional independence.
Some analysts regard this as at odds with its growing reliance on Africa Corps.
"The military governments argue that they have selected Russia on their own terms," said Ochieng.
"Russia is seen as a partner that respects that sovereignty, unlike their previous partnerships with France or even the EU and, to some extent, with the US."
An army captain on Niger state television accused foreign powers, including France and Chad, of being behind last weekend's unrest, while Russia's foreign ministry described the mutineers as "extremists seemingly incited by European former colonial powers".
France has repeatedly rejected accusations that it is attempting to destabilise Niger. Chad's government did not respond to a BBC request for comment.
"[Niger is] underplaying the role that Africa Corps has in these countries, and they're overplaying the resource-nationalism narrative - the idea that the government is in control and fighting back against the jihadists," explained Boswall.
"There is a huge media war going on in the Sahel to control the narrative around that."
Russia's war with Ukraine is another important factor shaping its strategy in the Sahel.
The conflict continues to consume Russian personnel and military equipment, limiting how far Moscow can expand its operations in Africa.
"It's quite a tightrope for Russia because ultimately its priority will always be Ukraine," Ochieng said.
"It will maintain at least enough numbers to allow it to reassure the military governments in the Sahel that it continues to be a reliable partner. They'll continue to deploy just enough weapons and supplies and logistics… to continue supporting Africa Corps."
But there are limits to what that support can achieve. "Russia cannot afford a sustained counter-offensive anywhere in the Sahel," Ochieng said.
This may help explain why protecting allied governments appears to have become such an important part of Russia's regional strategy.
Defending a capital or helping loyalist forces defeat a mutiny requires fewer resources than recapturing and securing vast areas affected by an insurgency.
"These are quite limited interventions, but with an outsized impact," Boswall said.
"I think at that level they'll be able to sustain that over the foreseeable future, even with the war in Ukraine."
Russia may have helped Tiani survive this latest security challenge, but it has not removed the conditions that could produce the next mutiny.

Antonelli 'walks over water' for win that will go down in F1 folklore
- Published
Kimi Antonelli's stunning victory in the Italian Grand Prix from 19th on the grid will go down in Formula 1 folklore - and, remarkably, his team boss Toto Wolff said that he had seen it coming on Saturday.
After Sunday's race, Wolff said that beforehand he thought that one of his two drivers was going to be standing on the top of the podium.
It was an eye-opening statement given they started the race 17 places apart on the grid, George Russell on the front row alongside shock pole winner Pierre Gasly's Alpine; Antonelli on the penultimate row.
"I thought one of the two is going to win," Wolff said. "Either George, because he was on the front row, or Kimi because he's going to walk over water, here at Monza. And I felt that yesterday also."
Wolff was asked to explain why he felt a performance he was comparing to a miracle was on the cards.
"It's been a while that I've seen drivers," he said. "Energy levels, mindset or behavioural pattern. I knew that was his mission today, to win the race. I chatted with his father yesterday. The father also saw that coming.
"These are the moments where you can see how a weekend is panning out through the sessions that a special moment can come."
- Antonelli takes stunning Monza win from 19th on grid 
  - Published49 minutes ago
- Antonelli extraordinary as Gasly has superb weekend - driver ratings 
  - Published2 hours ago
For the Mercedes drivers, this race was all about the context of the weekend.
Antonelli knew coming in that he would be starting at the back because of a grid penalty for using too many engines this year.
Russell knew that he had to make the most of this opportunity and cut as much as he could out of his team-mate's 59-point championship lead.
Fifth or sixth was the general consensus for what might be realistically possible for Antonelli, who himself said after the race that he had "thought a podium was possible".
What changed everything was his remarkable progress in the early laps of the race, which brought to mind another Biblical miracle, the parting of the Red Sea.
Antonelli was 14th after a relatively conservative first lap, then 12th at the end of lap two, when Charles Leclerc crashed his Ferrari to bring the race to a temporary halt.
"With the red flag, I was already P12," Antonelli said. "And then I knew that I could have a shot at it."
A lap after the restart, he was up to eighth, and on the back of the leading group of cars running nose to tail. Seventh a lap later, after dispatching Lando Norris' McLaren.
By now, Russell was in the lead, having wasted little time dispensing with Gasly. But the Briton sensed trouble.
"A great race from the neutral perspective," Russell said. "As soon as I saw Kimi up to P5 after a handful of laps, I knew he was going to be in the fight with us. That was clearly a very impressive opening few laps."
Wolff said: "The differentiator today was the ability to go through the traffic. We've seen it with other great ones in the past. Lewis (Hamilton), who did it in some of the races. That's what he's shown today. When a driver and a car are one, then there's nothing that can stop them."
Antonelli in no mood to obey a computer algorithm
Briefly, for a few laps, Russell and Max Verstappen threatened to break away in the lead while Antonelli was finding a way past Gasly, the two McLarens and Hamilton's Ferrari.
But Russell and Verstappen were fighting at the front, costing each other time, and Antonelli was up to third by lap 13, just 1.8secs off Verstappen in the lead, with Russell between them.
Three laps later, the Mercedes drivers were running one-two, and starting to swap places themselves, until, with Russell leading, it was suggested by that team that they give it a rest and try to break away from Verstappen.
If Russell could not do so, they said, they would "invert the cars" - put Antonelli into the lead to try himself. But slowly they began to inch clear.
At this point, coming up to half-distance, the race victory was still up in the air. There was a virtual safety car (VSC), called when Lance Stroll's Aston Martin broke down at the first corner.
Mercedes called Antonelli for new tyres - a decision they had to make as he had switched to the medium compound at the red flag and that would not make it to the end. Russell continued on his hard tyres.
"It was the right thing to split the strategies," Wolff said, "because we didn't know what the better one would be. In the morning meeting, we said the hard tyre is going to go forever. You can start on it and finish on it. And you can see with George, it was a forever tyre.
"At that stage, the system said that the one-stop comes out ahead, that two-stop was coming close to the end, but didn't catch it. That's what the software said."
Antonelli was in no mood to obey a computer algorithm. Rejoining 14.3secs behind Russell, with 24 laps to go and four cars between them, winning was not an easy task. But he made it look like it.
Antonelli caught Russell with five laps to go and the win now looked inevitable. There was a hiccup when he ran off the track at turn one with four laps to go after Russell blocked his attack on the inside, and Antonelli lost grip on the loose rubber off line and slid into the gravel trap.
That dropped him to 1.7secs off again, but a lap and a half later, he drove past Russell on the straight between the second Lesmo corner and Ascari, and that was that.
The home fans, with split loyalties before the race between Antonelli and Ferrari, screamed with delight as he crossed the line, 60 years since the last time an Italian won his home race.
"It's one that I will remember forever," Antonelli said. "Definitely the fans gave that little bit extra to push more. The support has been great this weekend.
"Definitely seeing the grandstand cheering every lap it gave that little bit of extra to push more and to try and do even better to win it."
- Far too late for title fight priority - Hamilton 
  - Published2 hours ago
'Circle closes' after 'everyone doubted' Antonelli in 2024
The win, Wolff said, was "how the circle closed" after Antonelli's difficult introduction to F1, when he crashed in a one-off outing in free practice at this race two years ago, a moment Wolff said was "probably the toughest moment in his career. For himself and his family. A moment where everyone doubted, including himself.
"Two years later, it's the biggest glory, the biggest moment of his career (so far). That's probably going to be one of his biggest (ever)."
A maiden season in F1 last year followed in which Antonelli showed flashes of promise but little that indicated what has happened this year would follow.
"When you talk about the complete driver, there's the aspect of experience that needs to come," Wolff said.
"There is also that he has this easiness of a young man that helps to overcome difficult moments. That also helps in managing not getting ahead of himself when having these glorious moments.
"There is the fact of is he capable of maturing, of staying the personality that he is, humble, with a lot of introspection, self-criticism, in order to develop. And that only the future is going to show - whether he is like a few drivers before him a complete deal.
"But it is still surprising and amazing to see how quickly he develops. For me, it's like an AI agent that continuously self-improves and learns. That's the speed. And there also, his age is for sure beneficial. The ability, cognitively, intellectually, to constantly become better."
Russell hurts with title almost a lost cause
After the race, Russell tried to put a brave face on it, but it was impossible not to see how much it was hurting him.
Speaking in the news conference, sentences ran out of steam, his voice was on the point of breaking at times.
Russell gently pointed out, in not quite so many words, that without the VSC he probably would have won - "it would have been very interesting to see how the race would have panned out if there was no VSC".
But he was well aware of what Antonelli's stellar performance meant. The strategy, he said, "takes nothing away from Kimi's drive altogether".
And the championship, he now knows, is almost a lost cause. Antonelli's win moves him 66 points clear.
Russell talked about "taking the positives", about how, after a "very tough run" in the early summer, since the season re-started in the Netherlands two weeks ago, "every lap, every session, I've been sort of in the mix of the top three positions, similar to where I was at the start of the year".
That's true. But there has not been a hint all year of Russell being able to put together a run of results where he consistently beats Antonelli, which is now his only hope.
"It's definitely Kimi's in control of it," Russell said. "And, you know, he's deserving to be in control of it.
"For me personally, I'm not even thinking about a fight or a comeback or anything. I'm just focused on taking it race by race and trying to maximise every single weekend.
"He's performing incredibly well. It's going to be exceptionally challenging to overcome that gap. So I'm just sort of accepting that is what it is."

On the intervening night of June 18 and 19, Jalil Akhtar, an elderly Muslim man, from West Bengal’s Bagroi village in Karandighi block of Uttar Dinajpur district, was woken up from sleep and picked up by Dalkhola police from his home, his family alleged. Other members of his household, sleeping in the same home, came to know of his arrest only the next morning.
The 66-year-old man, whose name appeared in both the 2002 and 2026 Special Intensive Revision (SIR) lists, was allegedly arrested on grounds of “being a Bangladeshi”, his family told Alt News. After spending nearly three months in various holding centres and judicial custody, when Akhtar was produced before additional chief judicial magistrate (ACJM) of Islampur court on Wednesday, September 2, the investigating officer of the case gave a written declaration that identity documents submitted by Akhtar were valid. However, Akhtar has not yet been granted bail, the court is expected to hear the matter next on September 10.
During his nearly three-month-long incarceration, Akhtar was kept in two holding centres, and then lodged in Islampur jail, until, his family claimed they were told he would be deported to Bangladesh. They further alleged that during the entire duration, police failed to prove that Akhtar’s citizenship and legal documents were fake, raising questions over why the arrest was made in the first place when his name appeared in the latest SIR list.
“My brother is an Indian, we have all the documents and he has never even seen the Bangladesh border. Yet, he was arrested, kept in holding centres and jailed on a mere suspicion of being a Bangladeshi, which the police could not even prove. Was he held for so long just because we are Muslims and live in a border district with significant Muslim population?” asked Motiur Rahaman, Akhtar’s cousin.
‘Picked up at Night without Family Being Informed’
According to his family and locals, Akhtar slept on a cot in front of his single-room home. His wife, Taufa Bibi, woke at dawn on June 19 to find him gone. She initially assumed that he might have gone to offer ‘Fazr Namaz’, but began to panic when she found his kurta hanging from the family closet.
Motiur was first to launch a hunt for his cousin, a landless villager who was entirely dependent on his two migrant worker sons. Describing the long fight in detail to Alt News, Motiur said he assembled a crew of fellow villagers and they scoured through the entire neighbourhood including forest areas through the day. They were eventually informed by a local that a police vehicle had entered the village the previous night.
Upon calling one of his sources at the recently established Bazargaon police camp, which falls under Dalkhola police station, Motiur learned that the police had picked up a man from his village the previous night, allegedly identifying him as an illegal Bangladeshi immigrant. The group then reached the police outpost, and found Akhtar sitting on the floor of the lock-up, bare bodied, as the police, Motiur claimed, did not even allow him to wear his kurta while nabbing him.
Motiur further alleged that, as per Akhtar’s recollection of the arrest to his family, the police held him at gunpoint, apparently to keep him silent while taking him into custody from the densely populated area.
The Family’s Fight To Prove His Citizenship
“In the police camp we tried to reason with the officer in charge that Jalil Akhtar’s name was not only in the 2026 SIR list, but was also in the 2002 list, so he should be released. The police retorted saying ‘don’t you people dare to threaten me, those days of threatning are over…now the government has changed,” claimed Motiur.
Another officer of the outpost reportedly told Motiur to give them some time to verify the documents and if everything came out clean, his cousin would be released. However, the same morning, Akhtar was moved to a holding centre in Nizampur near Chakulia.
To establish his Indian citizenship, Akhtar’s family began gathering every document they could find. According to his family, they obtained the 1995 voter list and the 2002 SIR list, both of which included Akhtar’s name. They also collected land deeds linking Akhtar to his father, Rousan Ali, as well as a residence certificate issued by the Bazragaon-2 panchayat, stating that Akhtar was a permanent resident of the panchayat area.
On July 9, they visited Dalkhola police station and submitted the documents for verification. Before that, they had also approached the district superintendent of police’s (SP) office. On both occasions, the police asked them to allow time for the documents to be verified and assured them that no harm would come to Akhtar if he was indeed an Indian citizen. According to his family, the police also said they were under “considerable pressure from higher-ups to identify and deport those deemed to be illegal Bangladeshi migrants”, and that they were only acting as per orders.
‘An Attempt To Send Him To Bangladesh’
However, as days went by, Akhtar remained under police custody and shifting between holding centres. Dulal Rajbanshi, organiser of the Votadhikar Surakkha Samanway Samity, an organisation formed to help those whose names were deleted in the 2026 SIR, helped Akhtar’s family. “We were able to prevent the police from sending Jalil Akhtar into Bangladesh twice. When they failed to send him into ‘no man’s land’, the police eventually filed a false FIR and produced him before the court,” Rajbanshi alleged.
According to Rajbanshi, Akhtar was moved to another holding centre near Phulbari border crossing near Siliguri, allegedly to send him to Bangladesh. The state police keeps the detainees at temporary holding centres, before handing them over to the BSF for deportation into Bangladesh, Rajbanshi claimed. He said that in Akhtar’s case, first the police handed him over to the BSF, who took him towards Phulbari to apparently deport him.
“We were informed by local sources that Akhtar was moved from the Nizampur holding centre and taken towards Phulbari on July 6. The next day, we reached Uttar Dinajpur district magistrate’s office in Raiganj, who asked us to immediately contact the SP in Islampur,” he said.
“We travelled a 110-kilometre distance from Raiganj to Islampur, where again, the SP said that he needs time to investigate, as there is “immense pressure from above to deport illegal Bangladeshis”. However, we were later told that Akhtar was brought back to the Chakulia holding centre. It was unclear what happened after this, and which border they took him to in order to attempt deportation the second time.”
However, acting on the SP’s direction, the group then met Dalkhola police station’s inspector-in-charge (IC) in the following days. “The IC asked us whether we could bring any relatives of Akhtar to the police station for verification. By that evening, we had brought even his 90-year-old aunts and all other relatives to the station. But the police did not meet them, instead, they collected the death certificate of one of Akhtar’s brothers,” Rajbanshi alleged.
According to Rajbanshi, the BSF often selects a favourable point along the border to ‘pushback’ alleged Bangladeshis, sometimes at gunpoint. “Currently, the Border Guard Bangladesh and Bangladeshi villagers are on high alert to prevent any pushback from India. As a result, many people are getting stranded in no man’s land, as neither country is willing to take them in. Akhtar’s family was wary of this exact fate,” he claimed.
According to Motiur, the IC also mentioned “immense pressure”, stating that the police were already “holding a list of 500 names whom they have to deport and 50 more were recently added”.
‘It Is Better If They Kill Me’
In the meantime, Akhtar’s family visited him at the detention centre. According to Motiur, Akhtar broke down completely. “My brother kept saying, what will I do if I am sent to Bangladesh? I don’t know anybody there. I have never been to that country. I can’t even beg there. It is better if they kill me than push me into Bangladesh,” Motiur said.
According to the family, a Border Security Force (BSF) team also visited their home to investigate the matter. “The BSF team came and spoke with us. They were infuriated by the state police’s actions — or lack of investigation — and told us that they would not deport an Indian citizen. At least the BSF came to the village to investigate. Nobody from the state police even cared to do that,” Motiur claimed.
On July 20, villagers organised a protest against Akhtar’s arrest in the nearby Rasakhowa Haat. However, before the programme could start, police intervened and dispersed them, they alleged. The next day, Rajbanshi alleged, the administration again attempted to send Akhtar into Bangladesh.
“On July 21, we received information that he had once again been moved from the Nizampur holding centre. We got the news around 2 pm and, by 4 pm, had organised a press conference at the Uttar Dinajpur Press Club in Raiganj. We shared information about the press conference across social media. We were worried that police might announce that he has gone missing. The next day, on July 22, police informed the family that they would produce Akhtar before the Islampur court,” claimed Rajbanshi.
Discrepancies between FIR and Police Submission
As per the FIR lodged against Akhtar by Dalkhola police, he was picked up from Nizampur around 1:05 am on June 20. Nizampur is also where, according to his family, he was subsequently held at a holding centre — the location is around 35 km from Akhtar’s home.
Motiur alleged that upon prodding the police on who lodged a complaint against Akhtar, police refused to reveal the name of the complainant. According to the FIR, Akhtar was detained at the Nizampur centre along with two other “illegal Bangladeshi infiltrators”. The FIR states that all three detainees are from “AndhaRahamatpur village of Thakurgaon district of Bangladesh”. It is claimed that this was revealed by Akhtar himself during interrogation.
The FIR further states that Akhtar crossed the Hili-Malda border and entered India around 24 years ago. However, the documents submitted by his family before the court show that his name appears in both the 1995 voter list and the 2002 SIR list. In both documents, his father’s name is the same. If the police account is accurate and Akhtar entered India only around 23-24 years ago, it would be impossible for his name to have appeared in the 1995 voter list, nearly three decades ago, and subsequently in the 2002 SIR list.
Alt News has seen the case diary submitted by police in court on August 5. It says Akhtar voted in 1982 elections as well, although it does not clarify which elections and where. The submission also mentions that during investigation, police had been told by locals that coming to Uttar Dinajpur in 1982, Akhtar worked as a rikshaw puller in Delhi and does not speak proper Bengali. These statements directly contradict the FIR claim that he entered India around 24 years ago and does not establish any link between Akhtar and Bangladesh.
According to the police’s submission, Akhtar was born in either 1959 or 1960 and first appears in official records in 1982. No records relating to him from before 1982 could be found, the police said. They also claim that he failed to establish a credible link with Raushan Ali, whom he identifies as his father, through land records or other documentary evidence.
However, Rajbanshi claimed that Akhtar was not required to produce his parents’ birth records to establish his Indian citizenship. “Under the Indian Citizenship Act, a person born before 1987 does not need to show the birth records of their parents to prove their Indian citizenship. The 2002 and 2026 SIR exercises were also meant to identify and remove illegal entries from the electoral rolls. Akhtar’s name appears in both lists. Yet he continues to be detained, merely to serve what appears to be the BJP’s political agenda,” he said.
The September 2 Hearing
As per legal records, the police postponed the bail hearing four times stating that they need more time to verify the documents. During the hearing on September 2, the additional chief judicial magistrate and the defence counsel asked the police to testify whether the documents provided by Akhtar were valid. The police ultimately confirmed the documents were legitimate.
According to Akhtar’s lawyer, Firoz Ahmed, the police deliberately avoided telling the court whether the former’s documents were genuine. “The ACJM pressed the investigating to state whether Akhtar’s documents are genuine before carrying on with the investigation. Even then, the IO remained silent,” he said.
Later, however, the police stated in a report submitted in the late afternoon that Akhtar’s voter ID and PAN card were genuine Indian documents, and that his records in the 1995 voter list and 2002 SIR list were also genuine. “They are awaiting an email response to verify the authenticity of his Aadhaar card, so they could not say anything about it,” Ahmed added.
“As his birthplace and his current residence are different, and fall under different police stations, the police are now harping on that, as if relocating to another place is a crime,” Ahmed alleged.
“The police had been given a target to identify and round up Bangladeshis, and they are targeting any vulnerable person they can find. Since Akhtar was born in another village, around four to five kilometres from ours, and is extremely poor and owns barely any land, it is easy for the administration to portray him as a Bangladeshi, citing a lack of evidence,” Motiur alleged.
Dalkhola Police’s Response
Alt News spoke to Sankha Chatterjee, IC of Dalkhola police station. Upon being asked whether Akhtar was arrested at gunpoint as alleged by his family, he said, “A lathi is enough for us to arrest a 66-year old. We don’t need a gun for it. As for the family’s allegation, tell them that we used a Bofors cannon to take Jalil Akhtar in custody.”
He further said that police had submitted their findings before the court. “Now it up to the court to decide whether Jalil Akhtar is an Indian or a Bangladeshi or a Pakistani or a Cuban citizen. According to our investigation, we couldn’t find any documents of Jalil Akhtar till the age of 21. All his documents are from the age of 22 till 66,” said the officer.
Alt News asked about the discrepancies between the FIR and the case diary submitted by the police before the court, however, the officer’s response did not clarify the aforementioned loopholes. Chatterjee simply said: “I don’t want to get political, but if you come to Uttar Dinajpur, I can show you people who have voter cards and other documents of both India and Bangladesh. It’s better not to get into how they were able to cross over to this side.”
Motiur, Rajbanshi and Akhtar’s family claim their efforts have helped prevent Akhtar’s ‘pushback’ till now. But the family’s ordeal is far from over. They still do not know when, or whether, he will be freed from detention and his name will be cleared in this ‘test of citizenship’. For the family, what began as an effort to establish his identity has become a prolonged battle against an administrative process that they believe is inherently designed against them.

Maharashtra Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Bill (CEB) has no provision to regulate treatment rates charged by private hospitals to patients, highlighted Jan Arogya Abhiyan (JAA), a coalition of NGOs and health professionals, on Friday while launching a statewide campaign appealing public to send objections to Joint Legislative Committee (JLC).
JLC is a committee comprising 21 MLAs, who have been reviewing the objections and suggestions on the Bill. The campaign also includes meetings with all 21 MLAs who are members of the JLC, demanding Health Minister convene a statewide consultation with organisations and networks working in the health sector to discuss the Bill.
JAA pointed out that the Bill must include fixed treatment charges for common procedures, different categories of beds, investigations, ICU services and doctors’ consultations; hospitals violating these rates should face penalties, a refund provision, a mandatory estimated bill by hospital detailing the treatment cost to be given to the patient, and the prescribed limit should not exceed estimated limit more than 5–10%.
The other suggested provision includes, ban withholding of patients or dead bodies over payment issues, establish accessible grievance-redressal system, establish an independent, well staffed regulatory authority, and ensure participation of all stakeholders in the State Council.
CEB was introduced in state Assembly on July 3, advocating compulsory registration of hospitals, clinics, and diagnostic centres transparency in treatment prices, and no deposit mandate for emergency cases. The new bill replaces the 77-years-old Maharashtra Nursing Homes Registration Act, 1949.
According to Arogya Abhiyan representatives, the analysis of hospital data from five major private hospitals in Mumbai, Pune and Nagpur shows that the average treatment charges faced by patients in these hospitals range from ₹24,000 to ₹62,000 per day. “This means just one day’s treatment in a large private hospital can cost as much as the average monthly per-capita income of a person in state,” said Abhay Shukla, the public health expert.
The latest NSS 80th Round data for Maharashtra shows as many as 77% of all hospitalisations in Maharashtra take place in private hospitals, highest among all states in India, average out-of-pocket expenditure on hospitalisation is ₹40,500, and on average rural hospitalisation costs have increased by 87%. 40 lakh people in Maharashtra are estimated to be pushed into poverty because of healthcare expenses.
Jan Arogya Abhiyan appealed to the Joint Legislative Committee to substantially strengthen this Bill in public interest as Section 11-Q of the Maharashtra Nursing Home Registration Act Rules, 2021 states that treatments rates should not exceed rates determined by the government.

When Gloria Steinem’s plane touched down in Bombay in 1957, she could not have known that her stay in India would become what she later called a “pivotal, life-dividing event [that] made me who I am”.
She was 22, with a degree in government from Smith college and was travelling on a Chester Bowles fellowship.
India was “not only a place I’d always wanted to go, but (also) an escape from a very kind and tempting man to whom I was engaged and knew I shouldn’t marry,” Steinem later wrote. The prospect of marrying Blair Chotzinoff, a pilot from a well-connected New York family, depressed her “enormously because marriage meant the end of life to me”.
Funds were short, so she wangled a free airline ticket in exchange for an article “that I still feel guilty to this day because I never wrote”.
While in London waiting for her Indian visa, she discovered she was pregnant and obtained an illegal abortion – an experience that underpinned her conviction that, without control over reproduction, women could not control their own lives.
Steinem, who died this week at the age of 92, arrived in Delhi with romantic expectations of “ageless beauty and jewelled elephants”. They were quickly displaced. Driving from the airport, she had what she called her “first glimpse of Asian poverty”, seeing people sleeping on pavements and doorsteps.
She lived at Miranda House, one of Delhi University’s leading women’s colleges, immersing herself in student life.
“At night in our rooms we have long sessions and are asked everything: the Christians’ conception of God, the intricacies of western lingerie, the dating system, how much milk the American cow gives,” Steinem wrote.
Steinem’s Indian years have been extensively documented by Rashida Shafiq of Southern Methodist University, who drew on her fellowship reports and other archival material for a recently published PhD thesis.
She adopted the sari as everyday dress, writing: “Saris make one stand straighter and walk more slowly and worry less about time and efficiency.”
India was not entirely unfamiliar territory. Her mother and paternal grandmother had been Theosophists, part of a spiritual movement that drew heavily on Hindu and Buddhist ideas such as karma and reincarnation, and at college Steinem had written a paper on the Communist party of India.
When her fellowship money ran out, she supported herself by writing for Indian newspapers, doing advertising work and taking occasional modelling jobs – including posing in saris.
Wider travel in the country brought some of her most important encounters.
She met Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, the former princess and follower of Mahatma Gandhi who became independent India’s first health minister, and spent two hours with Indira Gandhi, whom she described as “shy to uncertainty, gentle and a little whimsical”.
At a Radical Humanist study camp in Mussoorie, followers of the former communist MN Roy debated democracy, individual freedom and political organisation. Steinem later said she learned there that “radical” need not mean violent or extremist, but could mean “going to the root,” and that “the means we choose dictate the ends we achieve”.
But some of her most lasting political education happened on the road.
On a journey from Calcutta to Kerala, Steinem travelled third class in a railway carriage reserved for women, which she later described as “a dormitory on wheels”.
Women settled in with children and food, nursing babies, sharing tiffins and talking. They wanted to know everything about her and conversations ranged across marriage, childbirth, contraception and family life. “Had I been isolated in a car, this talking circle could never have happened,” Steinem wrote later.
Years before American feminist “consciousness-raising” groups brought women together to discover that supposedly private problems were widely shared, Steinem had watched women in India exchange intimate experiences among themselves.
But the experience she regarded as most important came after caste violence erupted in what was then Madras state in 1957.
Steinem joined workers associated with the movement of Vinoba Bhave, a leading disciple of Gandhi, who were walking from village to village trying to counter rumours, discourage revenge and bring people together to talk.
She travelled with little more than “a cup, a comb and the sari I wore”.
In settlements scarred by violence, meetings were held beneath trees and in village courtyards.
“I listened as villagers narrated burnings, murders, thefts and rapes, with fear and trauma needing no translation,” she wrote.
The lesson was to listen before offering solutions. “Ask the people what they want, don’t tell them what they need,” was how Steinem later described it.
She remembered “the ancient and modern magic of groups in which anyone may speak in turn, everyone must listen and consensus is more important than time”.
“If you want to know how people live, you have to go where they live; if you want people to listen to you, you have to listen to them,” she later said. “I believe I learned that in India.”
Steinem returned to the United States in 1958, more than a decade before she became one of the leading figures in the women’s movement.
“I couldn’t integrate into the rest of my life these two very, very crucial years,” she recalled. “It was only after the women’s movement started that links began to be forged.”
She repeatedly connected her later organising methods with India. “The first organising I did was in India, though I didn’t realise it then,” she said.
Her years travelling across America as a feminist activist, she later wrote, were “just a western version of walking in villages”.
And when Ms. magazine, which Steinem co-founded, produced its spring 1972 preview issue, its cover featured an American housewife depicted as the many-armed Hindu goddess Kali, pregnant with her hands clutching a frying pan, duster, telephone, iron and other symbols of the domestic demands placed on women.
Steinem said the image “had come out of my Indian past”.

In Summary
- As concerns around smart glasses and privacy grow, Meta has ensured that users cannot use the cameras on its smart glasses if they cover or tamper with the LED that lights up during recording.
- While Meta’s move is a step in the right direction, it still does not go far enough to address the privacy issues posed by smart glasses.
- Smart glasses brands need to do more to prevent misuse. This includes informing and educating not just users, but also the public, who could unknowingly end up in footage shot on these devices.
Smart glasses have existed for a while but have attained a whole new dimension of popularity since Meta invested in them. For those of you who might not be aware (welcome to high-tech planet, folks), smart glasses look like regular glasses but come with a number of tech add-ons, such as displays, speakers, and most notably, cameras. These smart glasses can take photos, record videos, handle phone calls, play music, let you speak to an AI assistant, figure out your way around town, get recommendations, and more.
Table of Contents
Smart glasses? Pervert glasses, more like!
Sound uber cool, cutting-edge and futuristic, don’t they? Unfortunately, this tech rose comes with a stack of thorns that would make a cactus turn even more green with envy. While the tech world and content creators may be going gaga over all these smart glasses can do, more and more people are beginning to refer to them as “pervert glasses.” There is a sound reason for this – these glasses are increasingly being used to record people (often women) without their consent and knowledge, resulting in a massive breach of a person’s privacy. There have been a number of incidents in which people have been recorded without their knowledge and the footage shared in public or private groups, causing severe trauma to those who appeared unknowingly in the footage.
What’s worse, the onus of figuring out that they are being recorded fell on the person being recorded. Being vigilant, actively looking for signs of someone wearing smart glasses, and catching up on tech cues were all part of the package – we also did a story on ways one could find out if they are being recorded as smart glasses moved from being content creators to destroyers of privacy. As incidents of “secret recordings” through these glasses increase, pressure has finally started building on the brands making these devices to make them safer not just for their users, but also for those in their vicinity.
Meta finally moves, but is it enough?
Recently, Meta finally fixed a flaw that was making it easier for users to covertly record others. In a post made on Threads (https://www.threads.com/@ahimel/post/DcjTatTGyn-), Alex Himel, Vice President of Wearables and Vice President of Augmented Reality at Meta, said that the camera on the glasses would stop working if the LED on the glasses was covered.
He was referring to a small LED indicator on the glasses that lights up when the glasses are recording. While the cameras on the glasses would not allow users to record if the LED was covered, many users found ways around this. One method was as simple as covering the LED light after starting to record the video. Following Himel’s announcement, an update will ensure that if the LED is covered at any stage (before or after starting a video recording), the glasses will automatically stop recording the video or taking photos. What’s more, if users tamper with the LED light and destroy or disable it, the glasses will now disable the camera feature permanently.
While this is definitely a step in the right direction, it does not really solve the biggest issue around these glasses. We have seen Meta’s glasses in public, and it is very difficult to spot when they are recording, especially in daylight or if the person is some distance away. The LED light is bright, but can easily be missed if one is not looking for it. What’s more, one can place a hand in front of it to stop others from seeing it, without actually covering it. We really think more needs to be done to safeguard the privacy of users in the vicinity of these devices. Brands need to come up with stronger measures that can help people spot those who may be wearing smart glasses and steer clear of their line of vision, if they so wish.
Making smart glasses safer: five more things brands can do
Given how limited the LED indicator can be, here are five measures that tech brands can take to make smart glasses safer for those in front of them:
Just make them look different…VERY different
One of the reasons why it is extremely difficult to find out if a person is wearing smart glasses is because they look exactly like usual glasses. Clear, tinted, or even running smart glasses all come with designs/frames that make them look like “normal” glasses. This makes them difficult to spot and enables users to record footage without being noticed.
We think that, given the privacy nightmares they can potentially pose, smart glasses need to look fundamentally different from everyday glasses. Visible badging, colors, even frame size or design should make them easy to spot. Who knows, this might even catch on as a style statement, but at least it will alert those in the vicinity that the person is walking around with a camera literally on their eyes!
Better, brighter (and maybe even more) LED lights
An LED light blinking while recording or taking photos is currently the only way to find out if someone is recording video or taking photographs from their smart glasses. As we have said before, a single light can be missed or even discreetly covered. The solution? Brands could perhaps use multiple LEDs of different colors, and which are of larger size, to pretty much advertise that a smart glasses’ camera is in use. Something like Nothing’s Glyph UI would be very handy!
Pump up the volume
Smart glasses should also give clear audio signals when their cameras are functioning. It should not be possible to take photographs without a loud camera shutter sound, and adding low but constant beep sounds when video is being recorded would also alert people to the presence of a camera in their vicinity.
Mandatory identifying apps
There are already apps like Zuckoff in the market that notify users if they are around someone wearing smart glasses. But these are unofficial and a little hit and miss. We think it would be wonderful if smart glass manufacturers took the initiative to come up with an app that can alert people in a small radius (say, 10 meters if based on Bluetooth), letting them know that they are in the presence of someone wearing smart glasses. Yes, it does violate the privacy of the person wearing smart glasses, as it is likely to make people in their vicinity notice them, but then that’s the price one pays for wearing such a device.
Better marketing and awareness
Brands have been pouring sackfuls of money into normalizing and promoting smart glasses. It would be great if they could allocate some of these funds to also highlight the dangers they can pose, and how they can be misused. Some might think this is counterproductive, but we feel this is the socially responsible thing to do – to make people aware that the device has its dark side too. And it is best that the brands do it themselves before they are forced to do it by Governments around the world.
The Government needs to step in as well. While new tech does make lives easier, there are always people who can find ways to misuse it. It happened with the Internet, it happened with smartphones, it is happening with AI, and it is happening with smart glasses too. To make sure that technology is not misused, there need to be strict privacy laws that are implemented effectively and come with stringent punishments. Perhaps statutory warnings on devices, advising consumers not to misuse them, might be an option worth considering. People need to realize that with great tech comes great responsibility.
Smart glasses need a Meta-morphosis, pun intended. They do not need to blend in, but to stand out and make people realize that they are present in a room. People need to know that they could be on camera. And the onus for this lies not just on those doing the recording, but on the brands who facilitate this.

Since the dawn of Silicon Valley, there’s been a widespread perception that San Francisco is, put gently, not exactly a dating mecca.
The city famously has a skewed male-to-female ratio (per census data, there are about 105 men for every 100 women), and there’s a perception among many women that men who work in tech tend to have poor social and emotional skills and a lack of style—opting for Patagonia vests and Meta glasses rather than putting substantive effort into their appearance.
On August 31, however, Celeste Amadon, the founder of the AI-powered dating app Known, valiantly attempted to reverse that stereotype. In an X thread accompanied by a moody, upward-angled selfie, she announced that she and her team were compiling a list of “SF’s most dateable people,” titled “San Francisco’s Hot List.” She attached a link for people to nominate their single friends according to criteria like “ambition,” “accomplishment,” “reputation,” and “aura.”
The post was skewered online by many in and outside of the tech scene, with some referring to it as “cringe” or mocking the lack of eligible singles in San Francisco: “The solution to dating in SF is to leave SF,” posted one female founder. But it was an extremely effective bit of marketing for Known, garnering more than 15,000 submissions 24 hours after the tweet was posted, according to Amadon. It was also an effective piece of counter-propaganda to the stereotype of San Franciscans, officially heralding that San Francisco Is Hot.
“Not to be cheesy, but I think the SF dating scene deserves some defending,” Amadon tells WIRED. “It gets so much flak for being a place where it’s hard to meet people, but there are many people who are super eligible in not just their physical attractiveness but in their holistic dateability.”
Known’s Hot List is part of a broader conversation focused on the general attractiveness of the San Francisco populace—and why some locals seem to be placing more importance on being perceived as hot.
Last summer, two women who work in tech—Madison Kanna (who is on the Hot List) and Cat Orman—threw an “enforced ratio” party at a Tesla showroom in the city, ensuring that there were as many women as men. The invite stipulated that the vibe would be “unapologetically feminine and fun” and that “Patagonia vests will be turned away at the door.” On August 28, Mantis Biotech startup founder Georgia Witchel posted an X thread titled “Tech Is Having a Hot Girl Renaissance.” In the thread, Witchel describes how social media has been deluged with “young, attractive women taking tastefully slutty duck-faced mirror selfies” to promote their startups, citing Known and the insurance company Corgi as examples.
Witchel says her argument is not so much that she objects to young women using their attractiveness as a marketing strategy—it's more to explain how and why it has emerged as a marketing strategy to begin with, telling WIRED the trend is a result of “a renaissance of sales culture in SF.”
Throughout much of Silicon Valley, software marketing was “nerds selling to other nerds,” she says—but with the emergence of vibe coding, the barrier to entry for the industry has gotten lower, and the standards for marketing a product higher. “The fact that you are able to build a complicated product is not enough to give you the leeway of not being charismatic,” says Witchel. “People are recognizing that.”
When reached for comment, Brooke LeBlanc, head of community at Corgi, who Witchel cites in her thread, referred WIRED to an X post. “My mom just heard about the hot girl in tech renaissance and she’s absolutely thrilled by the news,” she wrote. “No one in my family from Georgia can believe that it’s breaking news for a woman to care about how she looks.”
Amadon says the Hot List has “minimal” connection to Witchel’s thread, but she understands why Known’s marketing “draws interest” (though she notes that X specifically is “not a primary marketing channel” for the app). She concedes that the list was intended to capitalize on the discussion and create “positive discourse” around dating in San Francisco.
And it’s working: On September 1, Known posted the first round of Hot Listers, including LeBlanc and startup founders like Jasper Carmichael-Jack, the CEO of the AI-driven company Artisan. There was nary a Patagonia vest in the bunch.
