Did a goat herder's lucky $200 nugget spark a gold rush in western Kenya?
- Published
A goat herder from a remote area of western Kenya has told the BBC his discovery of a golden nugget has sparked a gold rush, overwhelming his small village over the last few weeks.
When people found out that 33-year-old Manasse Lomachar had sold his three grams of gold for 36,000 Kenyan shillings ($280; £205) several weeks ago, he believes this led to thousands of prospectors arrived in Cheporor.
And it is true that what last month was just bushland and rough grazing ground near the village is now scarred by pits, mounds of earth and makeshift mining camps.
It is not clear if was Lomachar's lucky find or other recent discoveries that sparked the excitement. But local authorities estimate that about 10,000 people arrived at the height of the rush.
Even a small amount of the precious metal can transform the futures of these men and women - from Kenya and neighbouring Uganda - many of whose precarious lives rest on an unreliable farming income.
People do sometimes pan for gold in these parts - but rarely find anything significant.
Lomachar's says his discovery came about purely by chance. While he was searching for a missing goat he encountered a group of women panning along a riverbed.
"I joined them, and that's how [the village] realised there was gold in this area," he says.
Farmer and herder Patrick Lokolia, from neighbouring Napawoi village, joined the gold rush hoping to earn some extra money to support his family.
"I have children in school, and paying school fees has been a big problem for me," he tells the BBC wearing an old Chelsea football top and standing amid the mining activity.
Eighteen-year-old Abigael Chelengat says she had never mined before coming to Cheporor from a nearby district, but arrived hoping to find enough gold to pay her school fees and help keep her younger siblings in school.
Behind her hundreds of people work side by side, hacking into the rocky ground with hoes and shovels.
Others carry the earth to a nearby seasonal river, where mostly women crouch in the murky water, washing and sifting mud and sand hoping to detect a tiny trace of the element.
Some of the more experienced miners are deep in holes excavating the earth and drilling at rocks with the same goal.
Hope is kept alive by stories of those for whom the effort has paid off - like Lomachar.
Samuel Kiarie, the deputy commissioner of West Pokot county, says he thinks the rush began after two notable discoveries.
"Young men found what appeared to be a substantial amount of gold. The following day, women made another significant find in the same area," he tells the BBC.
Kiarie explains that women have been finding small quantities of alluvial gold along the same seasonal riverbed for years, typically earning $8-$23 a week.
But the uncovering of larger quantities at the beginning of August is what caught the attention of many people.
Kiarie reckons as rumours spread, the number and size of the discoveries were exaggerated - drawing in ever larger groups of people with little or no mining experience who hoped to replicate the reported early successes.
Since the initial rush, the number of prospectors has gone down to around 2,500 as some have given up the search.
While there is little doubt that some gold has been found in the area, questions remain about the size of the deposit in the earth and its commercial potential.
"I can confirm that small-scale gold traders told us they received an average of about 100 people every day," the deputy commissioner says - though whether the finds were actually gold is not known.
Individual discoveries reportedly range from amounts worth a few hundred Kenyan shillings to one find valued at approximately 78,000 shillings ($600).
West Pokot county borders Uganda, and communities on both sides have long-standing social and family ties.
Mugisha Godfrey, an artisanal miner from Busia in eastern Uganda, travelled to Cheporor after hearing about the discovery from a friend.
He immediately set out for the village spending about 100,000 Ugandan shillings ($27) to get there.
However, the living conditions in Cheporor are not favourable, he says.
"We sleep under the trees, and when morning comes, we continue working. Sometimes we work both day and night," Godfrey tells the BBC.
So far, he has found nothing. But he is not discouraged.
"We can't return unless we find something. Only when we have found what we need can we go back home," he says.
For others, the gold rush has created opportunities without requiring them to dig.
More than 200 businesses have emerged around the site, according to local officials, selling food, water and other essentials to the village's new population.
Irene Ameja travelled from neighbouring Baringo county to cater to the crowds. She sells bottled water, soft drinks, bread, milk and other foodstuffs.
"I am hoping that when I leave, I will have made enough money to continue with my business and expand it," she says.
But the rapid growth of the settlement has also exposed the area's lack of basic services.
"This is a forest and we are in the middle of the mountains," she says. "We don't have clean water to drink or even to bathe."
For women, she adds, the challenges become greater after dark: "You have to find somewhere safe to stay because most of the people sleeping here are men."
Local officials admit the influx has placed enormous pressure on an area with little infrastructure, no piped water and limited sanitation.
Public health officials have been deployed to monitor conditions and help prevent disease outbreaks.
The authorities say they have also increased security patrols amid concerns over sexual violence and the vulnerability of women and girls at the site.
Officials are also worried that children could be drawn into mining activities as schools prepare to reopen in September.
Measures are being put in place to discourage young people from remaining at the site once the new school term begins.
Those still searching are increasingly turning to deeper excavation.
Several truckloads of material have already been transported to nearby Ortum town for processing, with the authorities awaiting the results.
Until then, the size and commercial viability of any mining remain uncertain.
For Lomachar, the answer is not to stop the mining, but to make it more organised.
He wants the government to help local miners establish safer and more effective ways of finding and extracting the gold.
"We would ask the government to help us with things like metal detectors, which could help us find out whether there are other minerals here, so that our community can develop," he says.
He points to the homes nearby as evidence of the area's poverty.
"If you look around, there are hardly any houses with iron-sheet roofs; most are just thatched houses."

There isn’t much that we Indians agree on these days. GDP numbers are no exception. Last week, India released glowing GDP numbers for the latest quarter – 7.8% growth – higher than the forecast 7%. It sparked a furore.
Subhash Garg, a former finance secretary under Narendra Modi’s government and now a critic, reframed what Modi called a “herculean feat” as mere smoke and mirrors. According to Garg, the government revised last year’s current-price GDP downwards to inflate this year’s number – he believes the real growth is only 2.6%.
The assertion, made on a television channel, immediately went viral. A flurry of op-eds and hot takes have been published since. Supporters of the government, predictably, rejected the claims. Those who have questions agree on a more fundamental problem: a lack of transparency and statistical credibility in India’s economic data. So why is there no consensus?
Over the past decade, critics say, the government has systematically hollowed out the integrity of its own data infrastructure, weaponising economic data for political gain and creating a trust deficit. Methodologies have been changed, crucial surveys have faced long delays and there have been attempts to suppress inconvenient findings.
In November, the International Monetary Fund rated India’s national accounts data a ‘C’ on a four-point scale, the second-lowest grade. In its report, the IMF said some of the methodologies are outdated, including relying on an old base year, unexplained discrepancies between GDP calculated from the production and expenditure side, as well as a lack of seasonal data.
India’s statistical system once commanded respect, and its data on economic and social indicators was considered rigorous. There might have been disagreements on the quality of estimates but their independence was widely accepted. That trust appears to have eroded in recent years.
“There seems to be a systematic effort by the government to hide the truth,” said R Nagaraj, an economist who taught at the Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, adding that some of the other contested datasets include employment numbers, poverty numbers, health data and consumption data. “Over the last 10 years, the government has changed the methodology for many of these, raising questions. They have apparently also removed critical officials who headed some surveys. All of this adds to the scepticism.”
In one of the most prominent examples, from 2019, a Business Standard journalist revealed that the government had not published an official report showing unemployment at a 45-year high of 6.1%. Two expert members of the National Statistical Commission resigned in protest. The government initially denied it, calling it a draft. The figures were only released months later.
Then there is the census, which for the first time since independence, was delayed in 2021. Economists say relying on outdated demographic data means, among other things, inequitable allocation of welfare entitlements. (The first phase of the latest census finally began in April 2026.)
Nagaraj has witnessed some of this first-hand. He served on a subcommittee in 2014 whose report forms a part of the GDP. “The [numbers] we had discussed in the committee and what came out in the final report were different. So, I had to raise a red flag,” he said. The difference was notable: one figure in the published report had been inflated by 108%.
But government economists reject the ongoing criticism of the GDP numbers. Shamika Ravi, a member of the Economic Advisory Council to the prime minister, described it as a “noisy and very ill-informed debate” arguing that political leanings, not data, are behind the criticism.
The IMF rating was expected, she said. “The IMF rating of ‘C’ is the same rating that China has for its statistics. Several large developing or just developed economies have data issues.” Revisions to its calculations that the government was accused of having manipulated, she added, were precisely the sorts of changes the IMF had recommended.
The sticking point, as some including India’s former chief statistician Pronab Sen have pointed out, is the trustworthiness of the underlying data used.
Complicating this debate is the reality for many Indians. This year, young people have taken to the streets in frustration. Protests, which first began over leaked examination papers, have crystallised into a broader reckoning over systemic failures in education, jobs and the promise of a better future.
Almost 40% of graduates under 25 are unemployed, a recent report by Azim Premji University concluded. An estimated 87 million (8.7 crore) Indians between 15 and 29 are neither working, studying, nor doing skill training, a government thinktank reported last month.
That is why we should care about data quality, economists say. Incorrect data means bad policy. As economist Reetika Khera wrote in her recent book, Freebies or Rights: “Data shines the light to guide policymaking and is important for informed public debates.” As evidence, she points to gaps in basic statistics such as urbanisation and literacy numbers due to the delayed census. The consequences, she argues, are not abstract. Because the government still relies on outdated population numbers to decide who gets food subsidies, she estimates approximately 100 million (10 crore) people who should be covered are being deprived.
The controversy is making waves further ashore. In Sri Lanka, where second-quarter GDP figures are expected, the Daily FT newspaper wrote: “One hopes Sri Lankan policymakers and experts are not watching the theatrics in India with watering mouths and dreaming up smart arguments. Spare us such theatre!”
What else we’re reading about
Lollapalooza | British pop star Olivia Dean is to perform in India for the first time in January when she headlines Lollapalooza 2027 in Mumbai. Limp Bizkit is another headline act at the two-day event. Indian artists on the lineup include Ricky Kej (performing with Stewart Copeland) and Aditya Gadhvi.
The price of gold | Prime Minister Narendra Modi asked Indians once again to refrain from buying gold and travelling abroad. He had first made an appeal to self-reliance in May, in part to conserve India’s declining foreign exchange reserves amid a rise in import prices and global energy shocks.
Census 2027 | The new and expanded questionnaire for the 2027 census is raising concerns, reports Scroll’s Anant Gupta. The questionnaire asks respondents for details about their identity documents, as well as their parents’ religion and place of birth. Several of these questions were part of the controversial National Population Register that has remained in abeyance since 2020 and was controversial due to fears that the data might be used to target minorities through a citizenship registry.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Singer Prateek Kuhad (@prateekkuhad), whose latest album, Full Moon Chamber, was released in July, shares an indulgent treat: “I’m a big fan of artisanal Indian chocolate makers. I really like Manam, Carra and Naviluna, and there are many others. Although India has been growing cacao [commercially] since the 1960s, its craft bean-to-bar movement is more recent. Even a plain chocolate bar from one of these makers can be remarkably complex and delicious. More people outside India should know about it and try it.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
4,756,000
One-third of the electorate in Delhi, about 4.76 million voters, have been deleted from the draft voting list as the Election Commission carries out a contentious revision of its rolls across states. So far, about 130 million names have been dropped from draft rolls in 30 states and union territories, the Indian Express reported.
Vibe check
Earlier this year, Shakira’s concerts in India was postponed. But Rajasthani folk musicians the Ismail Langa Group (@ismaillanga_official) decided the music had to go on, in their own way. Their mashup of the Colombian star’s Hips Don’t Lie with the traditional folk song called Moruda has got everyone grooving (42m views and counting).
It took two months to pull off, says creative director Jagirdar RV. Most artists in the group, aged between 23 and 60, don’t speak or read English and learned the lyrics by rote. The song choice was simple, he said, because it “has a very nice vibe which matched our vibe”.
It’s been a breakout year for the group, which had a semi-final run on India’s Got Talent and are becoming known for taking folk songs to gen Z audiences on Instagram. They are working on their next English mashup – just not spilling which song, yet.

Tanzanian President Samia's husband dies in hospital
- Published
The husband of Tanzania's President Samia Suluhu Hassan, Hafidh Ameir Hassan, has died while receiving treatment at a hospital in Zanzibar.
Vice-president Deogratius Ndejembi - who made the official announcement of Ameir's death - said he had been suffering from a heart condition.
He was buried at his family's residence in Kizimkazi, a village on the country's semi-autonomous island of Zanzibar, on Monday evening.
Ameir was an agricultural academic who largely kept a low public profile. He became Tanzania's first First Gentleman after President Samia took office in 2021.
In his announcement, Ndejembi said Ameir died at 08:00 local time (06:00 GMT) on Monday at the Emilio Mzena Memorial Hospital.
The vice-president led tributes as he conveyed his condolences to Samia, as well as Ameir's family and friends.
Kenyan President William Ruto said he received the news of his passing with "deep sorrow".
"President Samia has lost a lifelong companion, her children a beloved father, and Tanzania a distinguished son," he wrote on social media.
Zambia's President Hakainde Hichilema also shared his condolences, saying that they "stand side by side" with the first family, and all of Tanzania during "this difficult time".
Similarly, Burundi's President Évariste Ndayishimiye paid his respects and prayed for Samia and her family to have "comfort and strength in this difficult moment".
"May he [God] grant eternal rest to the soul of Hafidh Ameir Hassan," he added.
The First Gentleman rarely appeared in public alongside the president. He was only occasionally seen with her at official events.
He married Samia in 1978, before she entered national politics. The couple had four children - three sons and a daughter - together.
Their daughter, Wanu Hafidh Ameir, is also a politician who currently serves in Zanzibar's House of Representatives in the National Assembly.

A food safety officer has become a social media star in India - why?
- Published
The images are hard to ignore.
Cockroaches scurry across kitchen floors. Spider webs cling to walls. Spoiled vegetables rot in corners, while food counters show signs of pest infestation.
One might assume these scenes belong to a struggling restaurant. But the photos are from a members-only club in Mumbai - India's financial capital and the capital of its richest state Maharashtra.
They are among dozens of photos and videos that have gone viral since May, after Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration (FDA) began a series of inspections at restaurants, cafes and other food businesses across the state.
At the centre of the crackdown is 51-year-old civil servant Tukaram Mundhe, the state's new food commissioner.
Since taking charge in May, Mundhe has overseen thousands of inspections and says food safety laws must be enforced regardless of a business's size, influence or reputation.
His department has suspended the licences of several quick-commerce warehouses and sent notices to Bollywood celebrities for doing advertisements suspected of indirectly promoting restricted products.
"These actions are taken in public health interest. We will continue to take them against violations," Mundhe told the BBC.
The campaign has made Mundhe a recognisable face across India, rare for a civil servant.
Videos of his inspections and press briefings circulate widely on social media, where reels and podcasts have turned him into an unlikely celebrity.
But the spotlight - and the controversy that often comes with it - is nothing new to him.
An officer in the Indian Administrative Service, Mundhe has more than two decades of experience and has been transferred so often that reports say the number exceeds his years in service, though he declines to confirm it.
"I have stopped counting my transfers," he told the BBC.
Admirers see the transfers as evidence of his uncompromising style. Critics argue that this confrontational approach has put him at odds with colleagues and elected representatives.
In the past decade, Mundhe has won praise for his handling of the Covid pandemic outbreak during his time as Nagpur city's municipal commissioner and earlier for his work on water conservation in Maharashtra's drought-prone regions.
"When he was transferred out of Nagpur during the pandemic, thousands showed up outside his home to bid him farewell. It took him an hour just to reach his car," says Shafi Pathan, a journalist who's written Mundhe's biography in the local Marathi language.
But his food-safety crackdown has brought him the most attention yet.
The scale of India's food-safety problem is serious and numbers presented to the parliament in July offer a glimpse of just how widespread the issue is.
Of 223,808 food samples tested across India in 2025 and 2026, nearly one in five, external were found to be "non-conforming" - which means the samples were either unsafe, substandard or mislabelled.
And Mundhe has responded with an unusually aggressive enforcement drive.
By the end of July, his department had carried out more than 3,100 inspections across the state - a number he expects has since crossed 4,000.
Around 300 licences had been suspended and more than 1,000 improvement notices issued. A new complaints portal had also received more than 16,000 complaints in its first three months, Mundhe said.
"Hygiene has always been a problem here," Pawan Agarwal, former chief of India's food regulator, told the BBC. "What Mundhe has done differently is make it visible".
Consumers have responded positively to that visibility, Agarwal says. Unlike in India's conventional system, where food safety cases and consumer complaints can take years to move through regulators and courts, enforcement actions are now playing out in public.
The campaign has also made Mundhe a social media star - he now has more than 3.8 million followers on Instagram.
However, even as consumers welcome the speed and visibility of his actions, many in the food industry are less enthusiastic.
Restaurant associations allege the official has been bypassing a statutory process, while courts have termed some of his actions "high-handed".
Under India's food safety laws, businesses are usually given time to fix violations before regulators suspend or cancel their licences. Regulators can suspend licences immediately only in urgent public health situations but must record their reasons.
"While compliance is non-negotiable, high-handed approaches - like public naming-and-shaming, instant suspensions over minor procedural or rectifiable issues and treating administrative oversights with harsh penal measures - create panic rather than reform," said Niranjan Laxman Shetty, legal chairman of hospitality association Indian Hotel and Restaurant Association.
Responding to the criticism, Mundhe said his raids are lawful and that suspensions are only for extreme cases. However, some businesses have publicly claimed that they've been shut over minor violations, without warning or a chance to improve first.
His actions have also faced legal challenges. In some cases, courts have overturned licence suspensions, ordered compensation for affected businesses and criticised the regulator's approach.
In August, for instance, the Bombay high court ordered, external Mundhe's department to pay 500,000 rupees ($5,291; £3,893) in compensation to a sweets shop whose licence remained suspended even after a reinspection found it 98% compliant with the law.
The court said the regulator's intentions were "laudable" but that it had "gone overboard".
The judges also raised a question - was the regulator applying the same scrutiny to government establishments as it was to private businesses?
Within a day of that criticism, Mundhe's team inspected canteens in the state's high court complex and flagged violations.
For Mundhe, it is proof that the rules apply equally to everyone.
"Had the food business operators or establishment complied with existing regulations, I would not be needed to take those actions," Mundhe told the BBC.
He also insists that they are not trying to shut down businesses but only ensure safety.
"We are not here to close down or suspend every licensee," he said at an event last week. "We are here to ensure food is safe, food is not substandard, it is not misbranded and it is good for consumption."
The restaurant inspections - which dominate social media - are only a part of his work.
Mundhe has enforced bans on using newspapers to wrap food, synthetic dyes and banned analogue paneer - non-dairy cottage cheese substitutes.
Its focus has now shifted to schools. The department has ordered canteens, hostel kitchens and midday meal suppliers to obtain proper licences, and banned the sale of food high in fat, sugar or salt within 50m of schools.
But the bigger question is what happens once Mundhe moves on to his next post.
"The efforts of Mundhe have created a nationwide awareness about food safety, both amongst businesses and consumers, which is desirable - but not sustainable," says Agarwal.
The challenge is to build systems that outlast an individual officer, he adds.
For now, however, the effects are being felt even on the streets.
Yuvraj Yadav, who sells sandwiches in a Mumbai suburb, says he used to wrap them in discarded newspapers, despite concerns that chemicals in the printing ink can leach into food. He recently switched to greaseproof paper after hearing about the ban.
"We started this a few months ago after newspapers were not allowed for packing as it's bad for health," he says.

England different from when Pietersen left - Root
- Published
Joe Root said the England team is "very different" to the one Kevin Pietersen was sacked from in 2014 after the former batter joined the coaching staff of the white-ball side.
Captain Root is the only remaining England Test player to have been in the same team as Pietersen and was on the Ashes tour of 2013-14 that signalled the end of the 46-year-old's international career.
On Monday it was announced that Pietersen will join the white-ball team as a mentor in the build-up to the 2027 World Cup in South Africa, the country of his birth.
"I'm fortunate enough to be in that position where I did play alongside him," Root told BBC Sport.
"A lot of the guys will have watched him and got into the game because of him. It will be great for those guys to have the opportunity to work alongside him."
Pietersen is one of the finest batters to ever play for England, known for his innovative strokeplay and ability to dismantle opposition bowling attacks.
His style of play across a 10-year international career was ahead of its time, much more in keeping with the batting now commonplace in modern white-ball cricket.
But 'KP' could often be a divisive figure. In 2012, he was dropped by England over allegations he sent derogatory text messages about then captain Andrew Strauss to the South Africa team.
Pietersen was reintegrated into the England team under Strauss' successor Alastair Cook. Cook's England fell apart during the 5-0 Ashes humiliation in 2013-14, after which Pietersen was dropped.
In 2015, Strauss, in his role as England director of cricket, said Pietersen would not be recalled because of a "trust issue".
Root, who played 12 Tests and nine one-day internationals alongside Pietersen, said the former Nottinghamshire, Hampshire and Surrey batter is not afraid to speak his mind.
"That's him as a person," said Root. "When you get someone involved you want them to be themselves and you want them to come into an environment for a reason.
"With his experience and knowledge about the game, and all that he can offer, I think he's going to be great.
"You're looking at so many hypothetical things that could go wrong, when there are so many amazing things he will bring to that environment. The world is a very different place to what it was in 2014, and the England team is in a very different place to that as well."
Only Root and Cook have scored more than Pietersen's 13,779 international runs for England.
Pietersen will join Brendon McCullum's staff for the white-ball series against Sri Lanka next week, and Root highlighted the work the pair did together when the Yorkshireman was a young player.
"He was always someone who gave me a huge amount, to be honest," said Root, who made his England debut as a 21-year-old in 2012.
"He didn't need to offer as much as he did to me, but he would sit there and work tirelessly, making sure I felt comfortable with my own game. He listened to all my questions and helped as much as he could. As a senior player, he was outstanding."
Root will lead England in the third and final Test against Pakistan on Wednesday, with the home side looking for a 3-0 clean sweep in the 35-year-old's first series since returning as captain.
As with the previous two Tests, Root declined to confirm his XI ahead of the toss, though the home side are expected to be unchanged.
Since England won the second Test at Lord's, a debate has arisen about ticket prices for the home Ashes next summer.
At Edgbaston, the venue for this week's Test, Ashes tickets for the famous Hollies Stand are priced at £165 up from £125 in the same stand for the series against Australia in 2023.
"I don't know what it takes to run a county or run a venue, I don't know what goes into that," said Root. "From a playing point of view and as a captain, you want the grounds to be full, and you want them to be full of every demographic of person.
"You want the game to feel like it is for everyone, that they can come to support you and enjoy that. I don't really know what more to say on it, to be honest. It would be great to see this place full and thriving, and for everyone to have the opportunity to come to watch Test cricket."
Under Root's predecessor Ben Stokes, England developed a habit of starting Test series well but ending them poorly. England have lost the final Test in their past six consecutive multi-match series.
Root admitted only a win in Birmingham changes that record, and also had a strong defence of Stokes and former Test coach McCullum.
"We wouldn't have been able to play these last two games without all of the work those two did," he said. "I think it's undervalued the impact what those two guys had on English cricket.
"You look at where we were and how we played our cricket, you look at how we've been able to perform in the last two games, a lot of that is down to the hard work and the way they changed the mentality within English cricket and this team.
"I'm not going to sit here and have comparisons thrown against those two, I don't think that's fair whatsoever. They deserve a lot of credit for the last two performances."

In September 2026, many people online claimed the White House had created its own arcade games and made them available to play on its website, including a game that involved catching migrants.
Screenshots of the alleged online game spread on Instagram (archived), Facebook and X (archived). Snopes readers asked us to verify the claim.
The White House has launched an official government arcade featuring games designed to promote Trump administration policies. One has you play as a Border Patrol agent rounding up migrants. Another, called "Build the Wall," asks players to defend the border from what the game literally calls the "coming horde." This is not some random MAGA website or parody. It is official White House messaging on a .gov website, turning immigration enforcement and the detention of human beings into a game. We have officially entered the dystopian arcade portion of the timeline.
An X post shared footage from the alleged game:
The claim is true. The White House published a series of arcade-style games on its website on or about Sept. 3, including ones in which players are tasked with building a border wall and deporting unauthorized migrants. We found the games at the URLs whitehouse.gov/arcade (archived) and arcade.gov.
The White House advertised the games in a social media post (archived) with the caption: "CAN'T STOP WINNING. 🎮 Build the wall. Deport. Fill a Trump Account." A promotional graphic shared by the account appears to copy the logo font of Sega, a video game company, but replaces the company's name with "MAGA," referring to President Donald Trump's campaign slogan, "Make America Great Again":
There are several games available in the White House arcade as of this writing, including one called "Flappy Bill" that tells players to keep a piece of legislation in the air as a bald eagle flies past national monuments.
Another game, called "Build the Wall" (archived), is captioned "Protect the border from the coming horde" and encourages players to stack falling bricks against green zombies running toward a wall. It also has an arrow with a sign saying "Southern Border."
The above game's similarities to Tetris, a video game involving falling blocks, prompted a response from that company. Tetris posted on X: "The Tetris Company was not involved in the creation of 'Build the Wall'. P.P.S. We take copyright infringement very seriously."
A third game, "Rio Run" (archived), tells players to "Patrol the line along the river. Pick up every crosser in the lot. Never double back over the line." When we clicked on the game and lost, a label came up saying "0 deported."
(arcade.gov)
Other games make players "sort the school lunch to Make America Healthy Again" or fill fake Trump savings accounts with money.
As of this writing, the games are still available on the White House website.
For further reading, Snopes has previously reported on other online PR campaigns from Trump's White House, including when it posted Spider-Man-inspired graphics of immigrants trapped in webs next to an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent.

Flights in and out of the UK have been significantly disrupted due to an air traffic control issue affecting airports including Heathrow and Gatwick, with cancellations and delays continuing into Tuesday evening.
About 300 flights have been cancelled so far, flight monitoring website Flightradar24 said.
Departures from London airports were most severely affected, with few take-offs since a fault was reported early on Tuesday afternoon.
Air traffic control service provider Nats said shortly before 5pm that it had fixed the problem in its system. Airlines renewed calls for the agency to be overhauled after the third major incident in just over three years.
Most flights due to depart Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester, Stansted and London City airports since 2pm appeared to have been delayed or are yet to take off.
About 90 flights in and out of Heathrow and Gatwick had been cancelled by 4.15pm, according to data by analytics company Cirium.
Flights from other airports around the UK, including Edinburgh, Birmingham, Bristol and Belfast airports, were also affected.
Ryanair said more than 65,000 passengers had been delayed with 50 flights cancelled. The knock-on effects hit flights around Europe, according to easyJet. Eurocontrol said some inbound flights were being held at airports abroad, with disruption likely until the evening.
The air traffic control service Nats said at 1.46pm that it was “investigating a technical issue which is causing some disruption to flight departures”. Nats later identified the problem in its flight processing system, and at 4.40pm announced it had implemented a fix.
However, it said the system was only “starting to recover”, adding: “We are continuing to work closely with our airline and airport customers on recovery. We apologise sincerely for the disruption to people’s journeys today and they should continue to check with their airline.”
Heathrow originally said only departures were affected but a later statement confirmed that the Nats issue was “impacting arriving and departing flights across UK airports”.
It added: “We are supporting our local Nats team in their efforts to resolve the issue as quickly as possible. We apologise to those affected by the disruption and advise passengers to check with their airline for the latest flight information and only travel to the airport if their flight is confirmed.”
British Airways said it was experiencing some disruption and was in touch with its customers.
Belfast City airport warned of “some disruption” to flights after the technical issue affecting Nats. “Due to the technical issue referenced below, there may be some disruption to flights due to arrive in and depart from Belfast City airport,” they said in a statement.”
A Birmingham airport spokesperson apologised to customers and advised them to “arrive at Birmingham airport (BHX) in line with their airline’s check-in requirements and to contact their airline directly for the latest flight information and updates”.
Edinburgh airport said it was aware of the issue which “may impact operations”.
The air traffic control problems follow an “isolated event” a year ago which caused widespread disruption, although it so far appears less severe than the full grounding of flights in August 2023, which prompted a parliamentary inquiry.
Airlines have been increasingly critical of Nats after the outages.
Ryanair repeated its calls for Nats chief executive, Martin Rolfe, to resign. The Irish airline’s chief operating officer, Neal McMahon, said: “Families travelling on holiday, people travelling for work and thousands of visitors to the UK have once again paid the price for Nats’ abhorrent failure.
He said the government should “stop making excuses for repeated Nats failures and appoint a new leader capable of running the UK ATC system”.
Wizz Air said: “A critical national infrastructure provider should not repeatedly bring the aviation system to a standstill. Nats is simply not fit for purpose in its current form.”
The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, said: “I’m aware of a technical issue impacting flights at airports including Heathrow and Gatwick. Technicians have identified the issue and are fixing it as we speak. I know this will be frustrating for passengers and I’m sorry.”

Editor’s note, September 6, 8 am ET: We’re bringing you some of our best-loved Your Mileage May Vary columns while Sigal Samuel is on parental leave. The one below was originally published last year.
My students think it’s fine to cheat with AI. Maybe they’re onto something.
To save the humanities, we need to rethink our assumptions about AI — and education.
This unconventional advice column offers you a unique framework for thinking through moral dilemmas. It’s based on value pluralism: the idea that each of us has multiple values that are equally valid but that often conflict with each other. Submit your own question here.
I am a university teaching assistant, leading discussion sections for large humanities lecture classes. This also means I grade a lot of student writing — and, inevitably, see a lot of AI writing too.
Of course, many of us are working on developing assignments and pedagogies to make that less tempting. But as a TA, I only have limited ability to implement these policies. And in the meantime, AI-generated writing is so ubiquitous that to take course policy on it seriously, or even to escalate every suspected instance to the professor who runs the course, would be to make dozens of accusations, some of them false positives, for basically every assignment.
I believe in the numinous, ineffable value of a humanities education, but I’m also not going to convince stressed 19-year-olds of that value by cracking down hard on something everyone does. How do I think about the ethics of enforcing the rules of an institution that they don’t take seriously, or letting things slide in the name of building a classroom that feels less like an obstacle to circumvent?
Dear Troubled Teacher,
I know you said you believe in the “ineffable value of a humanities education,” but if we want to actually get clear on your dilemma, that ineffable value must be effed!
So: What is the real value of a humanities education?
Looking at the modern university, one might think the humanities aren’t so different from the STEM fields. Just as the engineering department or the math department justifies its existence by pointing to the products it creates — bridge designs, weather forecasts — humanities departments nowadays justify their existence by noting that their students create products, too: literary interpretations, cultural criticism, short films.
But let’s be real: It’s the neoliberalization of the university that has forced the humanities into that weird contortion. That’s never what they were supposed to be. Their real aim, as the philosopher Megan Fritts writes, is “the formation of human persons.”
In other words, while the purpose of other departments is ultimately to create a product, a humanities education is meant to be different, because the student herself is the product. She is what’s getting created and recreated by the learning process.
Have a question you want answered in the next Your Mileage May Vary column?
Fill out this anonymous form! Newsletter subscribers will get my column before anyone else does and their questions will be prioritized for future editions. Sign up here!
This vision of education — as a pursuit that’s supposed to be personally transformative — is what Aristotle proposed back in ancient Greece. He believed the real goal was not to impart knowledge, but to cultivate the virtues: honesty, justice, courage, and all the other character traits that make for a flourishing life.
But because flourishing is devalued in our hypercapitalist society, you find yourself caught between that original vision and today’s product-based, utilitarian vision. And students sense — rightly! — that generative AI proves the utilitarian vision for the humanities is a sham.
As one student said to his professor at New York University, in an effort to justify using AI to do his work for him, “You’re asking me to go from point A to point B, why wouldn’t I use a car to get there?” It’s a completely logical argument — as long as you accept the utilitarian vision.
The real solution, then, is to be honest about what the humanities are for: You’re in the business of helping students with the cultivation of their character.
I know, I know: Lots of students will say, “I don’t have time to work on cultivating my character! I just need to be able to get a job!”
It’s totally fair for them to be focusing on their job prospects. But your job is to focus on something else — something that will help them flourish in the long run, even if they don’t fully see the value in it now.
Your job is to be their Aristotle.
For the ancient Greek philosopher, the mother of all virtues was phronesis, or practical wisdom. And I’d argue there’s nothing more useful you can do for your students than help them cultivate this virtue, which is made more, not less, relevant by the advent of AI.
Practical wisdom goes beyond just knowing general rules — “don’t lie,” for example — and applying them mechanically like some sort of moral robot. It’s about knowing how to make good judgments when faced with the complex, dynamic situations life throws at you. Sometimes that’ll actually mean violating a classic rule (in certain cases, you should lie!). If you’ve honed your practical wisdom, you’ll be able to discern the morally salient features of a particular situation and come up with a response that’s well-attuned to that context.
This is exactly the sort of deliberation that students will need to be good at as they step into the wider world. The breakneck pace of technological innovation means they’re going to have to choose, again and again and again, how to make use of emerging technologies — and how not to. The best training they can get now is training in how to wisely make this type of choice.
Unfortunately, that’s exactly what using generative AI in the classroom threatens to short-circuit, because it removes something incredibly valuable: friction.
AI is removing cognitive friction from education. We need to add it back in.
Encountering friction is how we give our cognitive muscles a workout. Taking it out of the picture makes things easier in the short term, but in the long term, it can lead to intellectual deskilling, where our cognitive muscles gradually become weaker for lack of use.
“Practical wisdom is built up by practice just like all the other virtues, so if you don’t have the opportunity to reason and don’t have practice in deliberating about certain things, you won’t be able to deliberate well later,” philosopher of technology Shannon Vallor told me last year. “We need a lot of cognitive exercise in order to develop practical wisdom and retain it. And there is reason to worry about cognitive automation depriving us of the opportunity to build and retain those cognitive muscles.”
So, how do you help your students retain and build their phronesis? You add friction back in, by giving them as many opportunities as possible to practice deliberating and choosing.
If I were designing the curriculum, I wouldn’t do that by adopting a strict “no AI” policy. Instead, I’d be honest with students about the real benefit of the humanities and about why mindless AI cheating would be cheating themselves out of that benefit. Then, I’d offer them two choices when it comes time to write an essay: They can either write it with help from AI, or without. Both are totally fine.
But if they do get help from AI, they have to also write an in-class reflection piece, explaining why they chose to use a chatbot and how they think it changed their thinking and learning process. I’d make it shorter than the original assignment but longer than a paragraph, so it forces them to develop the very reasoning skills they were trying to avoid using.
As a TA, you could suggest this to professors, but they may not go for it. Unfortunately, you’ve got limited agency here (unless you’re willing to risk your job or walk away from it). All you can do in such a situation is exercise the agency you do have. So use every bit of it.
Since you lead discussion sections, you’re well-placed to prompt your students to work their cognitive muscles in conversation. You could even stage a debate about AI: Assign half of them to argue the case for using chatbots to write papers and half of them to argue the opposite.
If a professor insists on a strict “no AI” policy, and you encounter essays that seem clearly AI-written, you may have little choice but to report them. But if there’s room for doubt about a given essay, you might err on the side of leniency if the student has engaged very thoughtfully in the discussion. At least then you know they’ve achieved the most important aim.
None of this is easy. I feel for you and all other educators who are struggling in this confusing environment. In fact, I wouldn’t be surprised if some educators are suffering from moral injury, a psychological condition that arises when you feel you’ve been forced to violate your own values.
But maybe it can comfort you to remember that this is much bigger than you. Generative AI is an existential threat to a humanities education as currently constituted. Over the next few years, humanities departments will have to paradigm-shift or perish. If they want to survive, they’ll need to get brutally honest about their true mission. For now, from your pre-paradigm-shift perch, all you can do is make the choices that are left for you to make.
Bonus: What I’m reading
- I went back to Shannon Vallor’s first book, Technology and the Virtues: A Philosophical Guide to a Future Worth Wanting. If there’s one book I could get everyone in the AI world to read, it would be this one. And I think it can be useful to everyone else, too, because we all need to cultivate what Vallor calls the “technomoral virtues” — the traits that will allow us to adapt well to emerging technologies.
- A New Yorker piece about AI and cognitive atrophy led me to a 2024 psychology paper titled “The Unpleasantness of Thinking: A Meta-Analytic Review of the Association Between Mental Effort and Negative Affect.” The authors’ conclusion: “We suggest that mental effort is inherently aversive.” Come again? Yes, sometimes I just want to turn off my brain and watch Netflix, but sometimes thinking about a challenging topic is so pleasurable! To me, it feels like running or weightlifting: Too much is exhausting, but the right amount is exhilarating. And what feels like “the right amount” can go up or down depending on how much I practice.
- Astrobiologist Sara Imari Walker published an essay in Noema provocatively titled “AI Is Life.” She reminds us that evolution produced us and we produced AI. “It is therefore part of the same ancient lineage of information that emerged with the origin of life,” she writes. “Technology is not artificially replacing life — it is life.” To be clear, she’s not arguing that tech is alive; she’s saying it’s an outgrowth of human life, an extension of our own species.

Since May 2025, the Delhi government has been setting up Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (AAMs), which serve as primary healthcare centres, across the Capital. In phases, they replaced the Aam Aadmi Party government’s Mohalla Clinics, which are no longer operational. While many staff members were absorbed into the AAMs, some say they have not received their final salary dues and have been told that the budget for the payments is “under consideration”.
There were 553 Mohalla Clinics. So far, the Delhi government has set up 415 AAMs and aims to establish 1,100 in all. The centres were envisaged to provide additional services such as maternal and child healthcare, routine immunisation, free screening for non-communicable diseases and nearly 80 types of free diagnostic tests.
However, some former mohalla clinic staff who were not absorbed into the AAMs are still awaiting their dues. Dr. Amit Gupta, who worked at a mohalla clinic near Mandawali metro station, said he is owed ₹78,000. He said interviews for AAM posts were open to all staff and some were selected. He is currently practising at his own clinic.
‘Budget under consideration’
In an email to an east district health official, Dr. Gupta wrote, “It is very unfortunate that our salaries for January and February are still pending”.
He received a response from an official on August 27, seen by The Hindu, stating that the file had been transferred to the respective cell and that “the approval of budget is under consideration”.
Another senior Health Department official said, “Many of them have been retained by AAMs and have received their salaries till date. If there has been any negligence, we will look into the matter”.
Two staff members retained at AAMs told The Hindu that they had been receiving their salaries. Those who spoke of pending dues were among the staff not retained.
Pending dues
Mohalla Clinics employed four staff members each: a doctor, a pharmacist, a multi-task worker and a lab technician. AAMs have a similar staffing structure, though the number of personnel varies with the size of the centre.
A former multi-task worker at a mohalla clinic in the east district said, “I am trying to get a job in the AAM but the vacancy has not risen yet. We have been told by supervisors that the funds have not been released for our last salaries. I have been without a job since March, when the Mohalla Clinic shut.”
Another doctor said that, besides salaries, which were linked to the number of patients seen, staff had not received other dues, including cleaning and costs incurred in transporting medicines for the final month. “Authorities have said that they are doubtful that it will come through but we are still waiting.” The doctor said she was ineligible to apply to the AAMs because the age limit was 55.
Last year, Mohalla Clinic staff protested outside the Secretariat, demanding that they be retained at AAMs. Selection tests have since been conducted and several former staff members have been appointed. Some have approached the Delhi High Court over the matter, which is to be heard on September 8.

Following the devasting flash floods in Nepal on August 26, which claimed over 1,200 lives and caused massive destruction, a video has gone viral on social media, purporting to show the Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) phenomenon. It displays footage from a search helicopter, ostensibly showing the breach of a glacial lake in China. Users on social media have widely shared the clip, claiming that this was the immediate trigger to the Nepal floods.
X user Bhavesh Mane (@iambmane) posted the clip on August 27, with the hashtag #NepalFloods. At the time of this article being written, the post garnered 2 million views, and was reshared close to 2,000 times. (Archive)
A Glacial Lake Outburst Flood #GLOF can happen when a glacier-dammed lake suddenly breaches. 🌊🧊
Pressure and fractures create a pathway for the trapped water to escape, sending a massive surge of water and debris downhill at terrifying speed#GlacialFlood #NepalFloods #Nepal pic.twitter.com/0zrw0SIEqO
— Bhavesh Mane (@iambmane) August 26, 2026
Also Read: Nepal floods: Unrelated videos of past disasters, AI visuals falsely viral
A journalist with Dainik Bhaskar, Ashish Rai (@journorai) also posted the clip on X, which received 2 million views and close to 4,000 reshares. (Archive)
Several other X users, like former MLA Rajpal Singh Sekhawat (@Rajpal_BJP), Dr. Kiran J Patel (@kiranpatel1977), Pradhyumn Sharma (@pradhyu78651514), AH Siddiqui (@anwar0262) and (@greatandhranews) posted the clip with the same claim. (Archives: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
Fact Check
To check whether the claims surrounding this viral clip are authentic, we broke it down into keyframes, then ran reverse image searches on the keyframes. This led us to an Instagram reel, uploaded by an user with the handle (@helipilotleigh), on August 22. It contains the exact same footage as the viral clip.
View this post on Instagram
In the caption, the user, whose name is Leigh Coates, explains what a Glacial Lake Outburst Flood, or GLOF is, and mentions that the video shows one happening over the Columbia Glacier in Alaska.
The description on her YouTube channel states that she is a helicopter pilot based in the United States, who specialises in ferry flights and advanced training for mountain flying, as well as airport landings.
We noticed that she had uploaded similar videos of glacial outbursts on her Instagram profile, and her YouTube channel.
In conclusion, the video that went viral recently in the context of the Nepal flash flood, showing a glacial outburst — purportedly in China — is actually from the Columbia Glacier in Alaska. It was uploaded by a helicopter pilot named Leigh Coates on her Instagram handle, a few days before the flash flood in Nepal. Thus, the claim that the phenomenon shown in this video was a direct trigger for the August 26 Nepal floods is false and misleading.

In a quiet summer garden, a caterpillar perches on a branch, munching serenely on leaves. A moment later it freezes. It senses danger—and just in time. From behind, a wasp approaches, sizing up its prey.
Tobacco hornworm caterpillars don’t look like they have ears, and yet they’re able to sense predators such as wasps. How does the caterpillar know a wasp is approaching?
Scientists do not fully understand how this caterpillar’s senses work, but we are part of a team of biologists and engineers who want to figure it out. Our ongoing research suggests that tobacco hornworms can hear using tiny, supersensitive hairs on their body.
Understanding the intricate biological mechanisms that allow this organism to perceive and interact with its environment would help solve a mystery of the natural world. It could also help scientists design new, cheaper microphone technology.
Because the hornworms’ hairs are so sensitive, we have to study them in complete silence. And where better to study hearing than in the complete silence of an anechoic chamber?
What Happens in the Anechoic Chamber
What happens outside the anechoic chamber stays outside the anechoic chamber, because it is meticulously built that way. Anechoic chambers are some of the quietest places in the world. They are engineered specifically to block the entry of any undesired sounds. Heavy-duty steel springs support the “floating” chamber and keep it from touching the ground. This detachment isolates the space from outside vibrations or noise.
In such a chamber, we studied the caterpillars’ responses to vibrations. Every day for a year, we set up a caterpillar on a platform and sent vibrations toward the platform at a variety of intensities.
To measure the movement and precise vibrations that traveled through the platform the caterpillar sat on, we used a device called an accelerometer. In response to vibrations, we sometimes saw the caterpillars jump; at other times they twitched or even shuddered from the sheer physical force.
Through our observations, we pinned down the specific threshold where the caterpillars stopped reacting to vibrations. Any vibration weaker than that magnitude, and the caterpillar wouldn’t visibly react at all.
After noticing this consistent pattern, we decided to test more caterpillars inside the anechoic chamber, but this time using airborne sound as the stimulus. The idea here was that if the caterpillars are more sensitive to sound than they are to vibrations, they are probably hearing airborne sounds independent of any vibrations.
Sound is broadly defined as a form of vibration or energy that becomes audible, meaning you can hear it with your ears. But here’s the catch: Sound also causes objects to vibrate. To make sure the caterpillar wasn’t just sensing the sound’s vibrations through the platform, we also used the accelerometer to measure the vibrations that the platform experienced from the sound. Our goal was to compare the platform vibrations produced in two distinct scenarios: when sound through the air was used as the stimulus versus when just direct vibrations were used as the stimulus.
We noticed that this time the caterpillars continued reacting to the sound even beneath their threshold of response to the direct vibrations. This finding suggested that they were hearing the airborne sounds.
Finding the Caterpillars’ “Ears”
So, where are their “ears?” Or rather, what are their “ears?”
There are two ways of hearing sound: from the sound waves’ pressure and from the velocity of the particles making up the sound waves.
For the longest time, scientists have associated hearing with tympanal organs. A tympanal organ in most mammals is a membrane that vibrates in response to pressure from sound waves. Its vibration moves the bone structures adjacent to it as well.
In most insects that respond to sound pressure, the structure analogous to the tympanal organ is a sac filled with air. They perceive any vibrations to this sac as sound.
But caterpillars pose a challenge to this typical hearing system, because they can hear but do not have obvious tympanal membranes. After digging into some past research and examining the caterpillars under the microscope, we spotted the distinctive hairs on their bodies.
Thus, our next project began. We removed their hairs and compared their responses to sound before and after the hair removal. Sometimes we surgically removed all the hairs by plucking them with tweezers under the microscope, and sometimes we strategically targeted a few.
The result was striking: The caterpillars’ defensive reactions decreased dramatically across various sound frequencies depending on which specific hairs were removed. While our research continues, and we haven’t yet published our results in a journal, this work is allowing us to piece together the caterpillar hearing puzzle and investigate which of these hairs are tuned to register different sound frequencies.
This line of research into how insects hear sounds using specialized, microscopic hairs could inspire a new generation of acoustic tools. Standard microphones are devices that contain membranes within them that can detect sound pressure levels. By mimicking these biological systems, such as using structures like these hairs in place of membranes, future microphones could be designed to instead measure the air particle velocity caused by sound, alongside the sound pressure levels.
Microphones that can detect air particle velocity would also be able to determine the direction of origin of the sound wave. In the case of microphone designs for hearing aids, a microphone that is able to track both sound pressure and air particle velocity could provide the user with information on both volume and direction of the sound wave. And studying caterpillars’ hearing systems and imitating how their “hearing hairs” work could inspire such directional microphones.

Before the chicken tender became the hottest fast-food must-have, there was the humble and hearty chicken nugget.
Its small size made it the perfect side dish, post-work snack, or, as millennials will recall, the perfect drunchie (drunk munchie).
One way fast-food brands are attempting to capitalize on chicken's popularity, especially among Gen Z diners, is by adding — or upgrading — chicken nuggets on their menus.
Most recently, on September 1, Burger King released an updated version of its classic chicken nugget in response to customer feedback that its originals were "rubbery," "dry," and "disappointing." The same day also saw the return of McDonald's Spicy Chicken McNuggets, which will be available for a limited time.
Here's how six fast-food chain chicken nuggets ranked, from worst to best.
My least favorite nuggets came from Wendy's.
Cost: $7.49 — excluding tax and tip — for a 10-piece serving at a Wendy's in New York City.
All prices listed here may vary in different markets.
The chicken nugget was crispy, but instead of being juicy, the chicken tasted a little chewy.
Like Burger King and McDonald's, Wendy's is primarily a burger chain. So, it should come as no surprise that its chicken nuggets are pretty unremarkable, in my opinion.
They were decently seasoned, and the breading had a lot of flavor, but they were also pretty small. Wendy's nuggets definitely act more as a side dish than a reason to go to the chain.
KFC's nuggets were a little bare-bones.
Cost: $7.31 — excluding tax and tip — for a 10-piece serving at a KFC in New York City.
KFC's nuggets were the least breaded out of the ones I tried.
They were a little bland, but I thought the chicken itself tasted higher quality than the nuggets from Wendy's, Burger King, and McDonald's. It was more shreddable and paired well with the chain's comeback sauce, but I would have liked more breading to give it that crunch.
I'd probably recommend the chain's chicken tenders or fried chicken over its nuggets.
McDonald's nuggets were a classic.
Cost: $2.39 — excluding tax and tip — for a four-piece serving at a McDonald's in New York City, or $5.79 for a 10-piece serving.
The nuggets from McDonald's were predictably good.
McDonald's chicken nuggets are the stuff of legend. They've been around since the early '80s, and there's something about the tempura-style fried chicken nuggets that keeps me coming back for more.
They're always crispy, always salty, and always consistent — I know what to expect with a McDonald's nugget. That being said, I thought they were a touch too salty.
Burger King recently upgraded its chicken nuggets.
Cost: $5.19 — excluding tax and tip — for a 10-piece at a Burger King in New York City.
The nuggets were crispy and paired well with the chain's sauces.
Released September 1, the new chicken nuggets are crispier than the original nuggets, and were updated to include a more flavorful marinade and new packaging, Burger King said.
I thought the nuggets had just the right amount of crunch and flavor, and held their own as a stand-alone entrée on the Burger King menu.
While they were very similar to McDonald's nuggets, they were slightly cheaper, giving them the edge.
Chick-fil-A
Cost: $9.19 — excluding tax and tip — for an eight-piece serving at a local Chick-fil-A in New York City.
The nuggets were flavorful and juicy, with just the right amount of seasoning in the breading.
While some of the other nuggets leaned on the drier side, these nuggets were moist and would likely pair well with practically any dipping sauce.
Each nugget was on the smaller side — despite being the most expensive of the ones I tried — but packed a lot of flavor into a small bite.
Taco Bell's nuggets may not be on menus right now, but they were my favorite.
Cost: $3.99 — excluding tax and tip — for a five-piece order and one dipping sauce. However, I was invited to taste the chicken nuggets at an early preview hosted by Taco Bell in New York City in December 2025, and I received complimentary samples.
The exterior felt hard. However, when I bit in, the chicken was extremely juicy and flavorful.
These chicken nuggets, coated in a blend of breadcrumbs and crunchy tortilla chips, stood out from the competition with their well-balanced flavor.
They were salty, with a subtle corn taste from the tortilla-chip breading. They reminded me more of a boneless wing than a chicken nugget.
Paired with the chain's Hidden Valley fire ranch sauce, a standard creamy ranch sauce with a slight hint of heat, and jalapeño honey mustard, an unusual combination of tangy mustard and strong yet balanced jalapeño flavor, these nuggets blew me away.
The nuggets were initially rolled out as a limited-time offering, but Taco Bell continued to bring them back in 2025 and 2026 as it expanded its crispy-chicken menu.
Here's hoping they'll be back again soon.

On 26 August 2026, massive flash floods hit parts of Nepal and Tibet, causing widespread destruction (here, here, and here). In this context, a video showing an avalanche is being widely shared on social media (here, here, here) with the claim that it depicts the first visuals of the floods in Nepal. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: The video depicts the first visuals of the floods in Nepal.
Fact: The viral video does not show floods in Nepal. The visuals actually show an avalanche at Lake Humantay in Cusco, Peru, from July 2026. This was available online before the Nepal floods. Hence, the claim made in the post is MISLEADING.
On conducting a reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video, we first found the same video uploaded on the Facebook account of a Mexican user on 27 July 2026. The post contained hashtags including Peru.
Further, we found a video featuring the same visuals on the Instagram account of a Spanish media page, uploaded on 30 July 2026. The accompanying caption stated that the video showed an avalanche captured by tourists at Lake Humantay in Cusco, Peru, and credited Instagram user @memomtz88. We noticed that the credited user was the same Mexican user whose Facebook account had uploaded the video on 27 July 2026. We then found the same video uploaded on @memomtz88’s Instagram account on the same day.
Several Spanish media outlets reported this incident with the same visuals (here, here). We also compared the scenes in the viral video with photographs of Lake Humantay in the Cusco region of Peru available on Google Maps and found that the surroundings in the footage match those of the lake. A comparison of the viral visuals and the Google Maps images can be seen below.
To sum up, an old Avalanche Video from Peru is being falsely shared as Nepal flood visuals.

The Pet Zone Smart Scoop for $166: This is probably the least “smart” automatic litter box we've tested—it's a typical rectangular plastic box with an automatic arm that acts as a rake and scoops the clumped (soiled) litter into a small bin on the other side. Once the cat leaves, it begins a 15-minute countdown and the rake slides over the length of the box, (ideally) scooping up the waste and lifting it into the receptacle. You’re only allowed to fill the device with about an inch and a half of litter, which my cats didn’t like (they prefer a few inches to really bury it). My cats tend to pee on the side of the litter box, which, because of the rake’s placement, means it misses an inch on either side—I still had to scrape the caked-on litter from the edges. The cycle timing can’t be adjusted, so the litter didn’t have time to clump completely, and the rake would immediately break it down into smaller clumps that would then be missed because they were too small. For me, the hassle's not worth it, and I’d rather just scoop it myself.
How Do Automatic Litter Boxes Work?
Automatic litter boxes vary depending on the brand and litter type. Generally, they have sensors, either by motion or weight, to tell when a cat has entered or exited the device. Usually customizable and controlled via app on your phone, or on a more rudimentary timer system, the cleaning cycle will begin a short time after the cat has used the box. With dome-shaped litter boxes, the cleaning will happen via a cycle where the litter spins and rotates around the spherical interior; the bigger soiled clumps will be deposited into the waste basket while the clean granules pass through the grates and get recycled back into the box.
The Petkit PuraMax 2, for example, rotates backward and then forward (rather than a clock-wise/counter-clockwise spin cycle) to sift the clumps from the clean litter, depositing the larger clumps into the waste basket. The Pet Zone Smart Scoop is the most rudimentary design we tested, simply using a rake attachment to scoop the bigger clumps into a waste receptacle in the back.
Are Automatic Litter Boxes Safe?
Pet owners should always do research and make an informed decision regarding which box is best for them and their cat. We only tested automatic litter boxes that remain open during cycling to ensure that if for some reason the weight sensors didn't pick up on a cat being inside, the cat could jump out. We don’t recommend devices that close completely because of the potential that the machine could not sense the cat and kill it during its automatic cycle.
These automatic boxes use sensors—some only needing 1 pound of weight to detect your cat—where the cycle will automatically stop no matter where it is in the cleaning process. Many also have anti-pinch sensors. For added security, the devices on this list have customizable schedules, including “do not disturb” modes. If you're a neurotic helicopter cat mom like me, you could only run the clean cycles when you choose, like when you're in the room to observe the cycle (although if you do that, the box won't stay clean for as long).
Where Should I Put the Automatic Litter Box?
All of these automatic litter boxes require electricity, so they will need to be near an outlet. Since cats will generally take a little while to get comfortable with their new potty, I recommend that you keep your old litter box until they use the device regularly. It helps to put the new automatic litter box near the old boxes to familiarize your cat with it. Adding in litter attractant and using old litter from the previous box also encourages your cat to use the new model.
As a general rule, for old-school litter boxes, you should have one box for each cat, plus one. With automatic models constantly cleaning, there is less need for multiple options, but we recommend leaving your old litter box out for an extended period to ensure the cat has acclimated to the new automatic box.
What Should You Look for When Shopping?
After testing around a dozen automatic litter boxes, I look for several things that make day-to-day life with the device easier for you and your pet. First, the connected app. This is what you'll be checking daily, so it's important that it works well. This is one of the reasons the Litter-Robot 4 was our top pick for a long time: its connected app is intuitive, simple to use, and reliable. I absolutely love the Petkit models we've tested, but the app is subpar, overcrowded with ads for other products and poorly translated. I also look for anything that makes filling litter easier: I love the Litter-Hopper attachment, which refills litter for you on Litter-Robot models, the self-filling litter reservoir on Homerunpet, and the self-sealing waste bags of the newest Petkit models. You'll also want to keep the cat's size in mind. My two cats are large, so I tend to opt for something with an extra-large, front-facing hole. Which box you choose depends on litter type and compatibility—if you're using tofu litter, make sure you get a model that is compatible with your preferred type. Budget is also a factor, with some models as low as $150 or as high as nearly a grand.
How Does WIRED Select Models to Be Reviewed?
I do a lot of research, looking up other reviews online, including our competitors, to see which are getting buzz. Since I'm the pet tech writer here at WIRED, I also have knowledge from other pet tech brands I love for things like automatic feeders and pet water fountains. Most of these brands also have automatic litter boxes, which I always try to test among their lineup of new pet tech. I also talk to other cat-parents to see what they're using (and liking). I aim to test a wide range of styles and price points for every type of budget and cat.
How Does WIRED Acquire the Boxes?
Sometimes we reach out to brands we're excited about and receive samples for potential review; other times we will buy a model we're interested in and expense it.
What Does WIRED Do With Them After Testing?
We keep some models on hand for long-term testing to see if they hold up over time. This is especially useful for our former top pick, the Litter-Robot 4, whose Litter-Hopper attachment eventually stopped working, or the Petkit models, whose AI starts falling flat without a Care+ subscription. Keeping some devices for longer-term testing helps ensure that we are giving our readers a comprehensive review. Most boxes we test for several weeks and donate locally upon completion.
History of the Automatic Litter Box
Rudimentary automatic litter boxes have been around since the late ’80s. These early models featured an automatic rake attachment (much like the Pet Zone Smart Scoop box) but had problems with reliability and loudness. It wasn’t until the 2010s that the devices started incorporating advanced tech like Wi-Fi and app control. In the decade since, that technology has continuously grown and improved, with most devices providing insight into your cats’ habits and health—truly becoming an asset in understanding your feline friends even better.
What I'm Testing Next
My cats are currently testing the Petkit Purobot Max 3, the newest model in beloved brand Petkit's automatic litter box lineup; and the Bissell CleanWell Self Cleaning Litter Box, the first automatic litter box model in the cleaning titan's new pet tech category.

U.K. accuses Israeli settlers of 'ethnic cleansing' in West Bank and bans their goods
LONDON — British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced a ban on imports of goods produced in Jewish settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on Tuesday. He called Israeli settlers "terrorists" and accused them of carrying out "ethnic cleansing" against Palestinians, in a strong escalation of British rhetoric.
The measures are intended to put pressure on Israel over settlement expansion, which the U.K. says is undermining prospects for establishing a Palestinian state alongside Israel, known as the two-state solution to the conflict.
In a joint statement Canada and France announced similar bans on goods from Israeli settlements, with France also pushing for a European Union-wide ban.
They added their names to Ireland, Spain, Norway, Belgium and the Netherlands who have already taken steps to restrict trade in settlement goods, or are in the process of doing so.
Speaking in the House of Commons Miliband said, "Our argument is not with the people of Israel, with whom the U.K. has unshakeable bonds, our argument is with the conduct of its government."
"The British government agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank, perpetrated by settler terrorists," Miliband told members of Parliament. He said there had been "houses bulldozed, roads and public infrastructure destroyed, families displaced from their homes."
The U.S. ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, warned of possible repercussions for British businesses in the U.S., while describing the U.K.'s move as "irrational."
"I don't understand what it's supposed to achieve," Huckabee told the BBC's Today programme. "If the U.K. is really interested in dealing with issues they feel like are wrong, where are the sanctions against North Korea, China, Russia?"
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham spoke to President Trump on Monday ahead of today's statement. In a readout of the wide-ranging call, Downing Street said Burnham stressed the UK's commitment to peace and security in the region, as well as the importance of a two-state solution.
The measures announced today are understood to be limited but symbolically significant, and will not come into force immediately. The government is expected to target goods originating specifically from settlements, rather than imposing a wider ban on Israeli products.
Opponents warn that, if not tightly defined, the sanctions could evolve into broader restrictions on Israeli goods, services and companies.
The move marks a significant deterioration in U.K.-Israel relations and is likely to increase pressure on the government over how far it is prepared to go.
Israel has warned it will respond. Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar has threatened consequences, while far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich has called for the British ambassador to Israel to be expelled.
Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has also called on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to "close the British consulate in East Jerusalem", accusing it of operating "openly on behalf of the Palestinian Authority" and calling for a "resolute response" to what he described as British "audacity."
