For a diehard fan of Donnie Darko, meeting director and screenwriter Richard Kelly is a thrill in itself. But to first encounter him as a silhouette in a darkened movie theater is to feel almost like a character in one of his films—unmoored by indefinite space and physics, questioning your altered perception.
It’s a hot Friday in mid-August when I sit down with Kelly, 51, at Santa Monica’s Aero Theatre, a beloved repertory venue that makes a key appearance in Donnie Darko, his remarkable debut feature. Released in October 2001 with virtually no marketing due to the tragic events of 9/11 weeks prior (the plot hinges on a plane accident), it couldn’t get a toehold at the box office. But in the months and years that followed, the film became a hit on the home video market and gained a fervent cult fandom thanks to its unique supernatural mystery.
To mark its 25th anniversary, the movie will enjoy another limited theatrical run, beginning on October 2, the date that launches mentally disturbed suburban teenager Donnie Darko (Jake Gyllenhaal) on a surreal journey that may or may not lead to the end of the world. Kelly has just finished recording an intro for the new 4K restoration, and snippets of it play without sound on the big screen as we talk.
“My memories of this film run the entire spectrum from fear to love,” Kelly jokes, alluding to the corny pop psychology peddled by Patrick Swayze’s self-help guru in the film. This occasion, Kelly says, is all about the “love,” as he couldn’t be more grateful to “all the people who have continued to support” his work.
That camp should be pleased to hear that on December 15, Kelly will publish his mammoth first novel, The Philosophy of Time Travel, available for preorder now. The 800-page volume picks up right where the movie left off and is intended to set the stage for a film sequel as well. “It’s been very inspiring for me to remain focused on continuing the journey that began 25 years ago, on my own creative terms,” Kelly says. “This film has defined my entire career, but at the same time, it's set a benchmark in the sense of the movies that I want to continue to make.”
Here, the auteur revisits the unforgettable dreamscape that put him on the map, and considers the artistic possibilities still ahead.
On when he realized Donnie Darko was becoming a cult hit:
There was one specific moment, I think in March of 2002, when I was in New York City. I was walking through the East Village, and I walked past a pizza restaurant called Two Boots, and my poster for Donnie Darko was hanging in their window. I saw the poster and I was like, “What's going on? This is bizarre. Why does a pizza restaurant have a movie poster?” I went inside and I asked the manager, and he said, “Well, we have a little theater in the back, the Pioneer, and we're playing your movie every Saturday night at midnight—and it's selling out.”
I showed up the next Saturday night at about two in the morning, when the movie was finishing. I expected there’d be maybe 10 people there, and he wasn't joking, it was sold out, and there were people with camcorders and lights in my face, and Michael Musto from the Village Voice was there. I was just completely bowled over by the fact that there were people who cared, who were really, really connecting with the movie. That was the moment I knew that it wasn't over, that the movie was going to have a second wind.
On how Drew Barrymore and Jason Schwartzman saved the screenplay from Hollywood purgatory:
It all started with Jason Schwartzman. He attached to play Donnie, and by virtue of his attachment, the script got sent around to a whole new round of people. It had been circulating for about a year, and the story was, “Oh, the writer won't sell it. He wants to direct. It's his first movie, it's too ambitious. It's just a writing sample, he's never gonna get that movie made. He won't let anyone else take it away from him.”
Then the script got sent to Nancy Juvonen, who’s partners with Drew Barrymore [at Flower Films]. She read it and flipped out and wanted to meet me, so we went down to the set of Charlie's Angels. We went into Drew Barrymore's trailer, and she was finishing the script, and we just immediately hit it off. I'm like, “Drew, would you like to play the English teacher, Mrs. Pomeroy?” And she's like, “Will you let my company, Flower Films, produce the movie with you? And I'm like, “Of course.” She had a one week window in August of 2000 before she was going to do a Penny Marshall film called Riding in Cars with Boys. We had to meet that deadline and get Drew to shoot her out in one week.
Jason Schwartzman had a scheduling conflict, and then in walks Jake Gyllenhaal. So it all happened really quickly. Nancy and Drew really deserve an enormous share of the credit in getting this whole thing off the ground—and Jason Schwartzman, too. Had he not attached, I would not have a career.
On having real-life siblings Jake and Maggie Gyllenhaal anchor a fictional on-screen family.
I heard from Joseph Middleton and Michelle Morris Gertz, our wonderful casting directors—they told me that Jake has an older sister, her name is Maggie Gyllenhaal, and she's a brilliant actress. She had only appeared in one movie thus far, Cecil B. Demented, a John Waters film. I think she had a tiny cameo, but she had done a lot of theater and was obviously an enormous talent, like her brother, and once I realized there was a possibility of getting her, I was just like, “We have to get Maggie. It will anchor the family with real siblings, and Maggie will be this great foundation for Jake, and for the whole cast, and she was just so essential.” Sometimes the cards are dealt in your favor in terms of who's available, who is interested, and so much of filmmaking is just the timing. It’s a miracle that any movie gets made.
On giving Seth Rogen his first film role (as a high school bully):
He had done Freaks and Geeks, and he was a standup comedian, performing in comedy clubs. Seth was one of these prodigy kids, really wise beyond his years and ahead of the game. He was maybe 19 years old when we shot the movie, the same age as Jake—incredibly observant, very articulate and funny young actor and writer and comedian, he was already pursuing all these different avenues. I felt like we had access to all the cool LA kid actors, because we shot in Los Angeles, it was the summer of 2000, and there was a commercial [actors] strike where all of the commercials were dark.
On creating the 1980s setting of Donnie Darko.
When we were doing the ‘80s, it was the year 2000, and we were capturing 1988, which is completely insane. That's 12 years. So you subtract 12 years from 2026 and we are in 2014, which seems completely insane to do a period piece about 2014, because things don't look that different than they did in 2014—but the disparity between 2000 and 1988 aesthetically was pretty significant. The cars looked completely different, the TVs looked different, the clothing looked different.
In terms of the ’80s aesthetic, we wanted it to feel subtle, we didn't want a lot of big ’80s hair, and we didn't want someone wearing a “Beat It” Michael Jackson jacket. We didn't want it to be kitschy. April Ferry, our incredible, Oscar-nominated costume designer, who we lost a few years ago, was so wonderful in bringing the ’80s fashion for Mary McDonnell and Beth Grant—you see them with the shoulder pads and the different ’80s suburban costuming.
On the movie reference from his original script that didn’t make it to the screen:
In the original script, Donnie and Gretchen went to go see C.H.U.D., just because I thought it was a funny ’80s horror movie. Linda McDonough, who was an executive at Flower Films, was trying to track down the licensing permission for the movie C.H.U.D. as we were approaching the shoot date here at the Aero Theatre, and she was getting nowhere. It was one of the big studios, and there was some woman in charge of licensing at that studio who was just like, “You're never getting this.”
You would think we were trying to license Lawrence of Arabia or Citizen Kane. They wanted so much money, and we were three days from shooting the scene, and we didn't have a movie to show. Linda, to her enormous credit, said, “Richard, I am friends with the producers at the studio that owns The Evil Dead, they own the negative. Sam Raimi is a great guy, and they will let us have the poster to show at the front in the lobby of the theater. They'll let you show any clip from The Evil Dead you want, the music, you can have it basically for free.” It was like a deus ex machina in the form of Sam Raimi. That led to the whole Evil Dead sequence in the movie, that was so perfect. Then we were able to do the marquee with The Last Temptation of Christ—we weren't showing a clip from the Scorsese film or the poster, just showing the title. That's an easier ask.
On the influential soundtrack of post-punk and new wave music:
I wasn't thinking that deep. I was just like, “I love this song.” Like, “Head Over Heels” [by Tears for Fears] was written into the script because I knew that when Donnie and his friends jump out of the school bus, when Donnie's feet hit the pavement, that first big piano note of “Head Over Heels” starts. When the camera flies through the window and you see all the kids sitting down and Drew Barrymore gathering the class together … “Time flies.” I had to get from the feet hitting the pavement to when they said, “Time flies,” and I had to edit the song down. It was just me doing a music video and loving that song and the vibe and the energy of it.
I have to give an enormous amount of credit to Manish Raval and Tom Wolfe, my music supervisors, who really expanded the canvas of the music in the movie to include Joy Division and Echo and the Bunnymen. It really did form a cohesive musical narrative. We were very fortunate, because no one was really trying to license a lot of that music in the year 2000.
The one song that we could not get—if you go back and watch the dailies, the Sparkle Motion dance scene was choreographed to Pet Shop Boys, but that was a no-go, we could not afford it, so we replaced it with Duran Duran.
On the dialogue that has had a surprising impact—such as the line “Sometimes I doubt your commitment to Sparkle Motion,” as delivered by actor Beth Grant:
It's so ridiculous. You never know it's gonna connect. Literally that's gonna be in my obituary, that line of dialogue, the only thing people remember that I wrote. Beth Grant is the best.
On what the social media reaction would be like if Donnie Darko came out today:
I can't even wrap my head around it. Online discourse is terrifying, and you kind of try to stay away from it. Any filmmaker that gets too caught up in online discourse, that can only have a negative impact on one's art. You have to be cognizant of what's going on in the world, but I think you need to curate your own art as the artist. We need more of that, art that is purely what the artist wants to say.
But I'm emboldened and excited about the younger generation going back to the theaters and reading books. Launching a book, the enormous amount of work that's gone into writing a novel—it's very gratifying to get to the finish line on something like that because you realize how a novel can help be the engine for something that is very difficult to get made because of the budget.
On the newer films and filmmakers to catch his eye:
Like everyone else, I saw Obsession. I thought it was terrific. Incredibly well done for such a small budget. The performances were great. I love Ari Aster's work. I love Jane Schoenbrun's work. I've not seen [Sex and Death at] Camp Miasma, that's next on my list.
On the movie he most wants to make (besides a sequel to Donnie Darko):
There are so many scripts I've written and projects that have hit roadblocks for various reasons. I would love to get my Rod Serling biopic made. That is a very ambitious project that tells the life story of Rod Serling using a fantasy and science-fiction language, in conjunction with his daughter Anne Serling and her memoir about her father. It's an expensive movie to make, given the fantasy elements and the period elements and the scope. If there are big influences, they would be Defending Your Life, the Albert Brooks film, A Matter of Life and Death by Powell and Pressberger, and All That Jazz by Bob Fosse.

As Maharashtra gears up to celebrate Ganesh Chaturthi, mandals in Mumbai have now sought clarification from Maharashtra's Food and Drugs Administration (FDA) regarding standard operating procedures (SOPs) for serving ‘mahaprasad’ during the upcoming festival. The move comes at a time when Tukaram Mundhe, Maharashtra FDA Commissioner, is cracking down on eateries and restaurants selling adulterated and expired food. On Monday, the Brihanmumbai Sarvajanik Ganeshotsav Samanvay Samiti (BSGSS), which coordinates Sarvajanik Ganapati mandals across Mumbai, sought clarity from the authorities on the rules governing the distribution of prasad, PTI reported. Speaking at an interaction at the Mumbai Press Club, BSGSS president Naresh Dahibavkar said the committee was prepared to support measures aimed at ensuring food safety. However, he urged the authorities to take into account the financial limitations of smaller mandals and clearly communicate the norms that would apply to them. The committee chief said that representatives of mandals had reached out to them and flagged concerns over applicable norms and SOPs, following which a letter was sent to officials. Dahibavkar said, "If the mahaprasad has to be stopped altogether, then tell us that. But, as far as I know, we have not received any answer yet." A committee representative said, "I agree 100 per cent that action being taken by the department is correct. But our difficulty is we cannot appoint contractors because we do not have that much money. If a reputed contractor is mandatory, please tell us what we should do." Last week, the Mundhe-led FDA announced a year-round SOP to strengthen food safety monitoring across the state. Under the new guidelines, enforcement activities for festivals will begin 21 days before the event, with a standardised schedule covering all major festivals. In the past, authorities issued separate orders for individual festivals at short notice, often forcing food safety officers to carry out inspections at the last minute while food businesses faced unexpected enforcement action. The decision to announce a year-long SOP came amid intense pushback over the FDA's recent crackdown across the state, which resulted in the seizure of unsafe food items and widespread licence suspensions. Additionally, FDA officials will identify areas and food products considered particularly susceptible to adulteration and conduct inspections at manufacturing units, mills, wholesale markets, storage facilities, and other establishments. In late summer 2026, a rumor circulated that U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. once sought to avoid paying alimony by claiming during divorce proceedings that severe brain damage prevented him from holding a job.
The claim appeared on Threads and Facebook. One post on X said Kennedy had asserted he "was too brain damaged to work so therefore couldn't pay alimony." (archived):
Snopes readers also searched the website and emailed us to confirm the veracity of the rumor.
The claim stemmed from a 2024 New York Times report that cites a 2012 deposition Kennedy reportedly gave in the context of divorce proceedings from his second wife, Mary Richardson Kennedy, who died by suicide that year.
According to the newspaper, Kennedy said in his deposition that his brain damage "was caused by a worm that got into my brain and ate a portion of it and then died."
We found one document that appeared to be part of these divorce proceedings, but we could not find the deposition the New York Times referenced in its 2024 story. While we have no reason to doubt the veracity of the Times' reporting, Snopes relies on primary evidence, including documentation, to rate claims. For this reason, we've left the claim unrated until we learn more.
We reached out to the Department of Health and Human Services for comment and await a response. We also asked the Times to direct us to the deposition and will update this story if we hear back.
The Times' story said Kennedy argued in his deposition that his cognitive issues impaired his ability to make a living. It's worth noting that the report did not state that Kennedy specifically claimed he could not hold a job. The report stated:
Some of Mr. Kennedy's health issues were revealed in the 2012 deposition, which he gave during divorce proceedings from his second wife, Mary Richardson Kennedy. At the time, Mr. Kennedy was arguing that his earning power had been diminished by his cognitive struggles.
Kennedy appeared to confirm there was a worm in his brain in an X post (archived) he shared during his 2024 presidential campaign. However, his post boasted that his cognitive state was still superior to that of his competitors — then-former President Donald Trump and then-President Joe Biden.
"I offer to eat 5 more brain worms and still beat President Trump and President Biden in a debate," he wrote.
Further, his campaign reportedly said he had a dead worm in his brain but had made a full recovery.
The document we found was a 2011 affidavit by Kennedy in which he alleged his second wife had physically abused him, stolen from him, abused his children from a previous marriage and threatened to commit suicide. However, this document, which was published by Newsweek, did not include any information about Kennedy's alleged brain damage affecting his earning power.
For further reading, Snopes has investigated numerous quotes attributed to Kennedy, including the claim that he once said infertility was genetic.

Every year around this time, Apple announces new iPhones. The products go on sale soon after, usually ranging from a base model to more premium and more expensive Pro models. But this year will likely be different—not just because the company has a brand-new CEO.
Apple’s iPhone event will be held on September 9 at 10 am Pacific (1 pm Eastern), announced last week with the title “Surprise and Shine!” If you tune into the livestream, expect the announcement of an iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max, and, if all the rumors and widely held analyst expectations are true, the first look at an Apple foldable device.
Based on leaks and the ongoing tech rumor mill and its decent track record for figuring these things out, Apple is expected to prioritize its more expensive, premium devices this year and hold off on announcing its base model iPhone 18. That cheaper model is rumored to launch in the spring of 2027, potentially alongside an iPhone 18e and maybe a second-generation iPhone Air.
Why the drastic change in strategy? It may be due to the ongoing memory shortage, which has made just about everything more expensive. Apple hasn’t been spared. In June, former Apple CEO Tim Cook acknowledged that Apple would raise product prices to keep up with manufacturing costs.
“Our assumption is that they're going to be launching three models in the fall, the premium side of the models of the 18 series,” says Nabila Popal, a senior director of data and analytics at IDC. “Then the mid/budget devices will be launched in the spring.”
Popal says it's a smart strategic move because Apple is aiming to spread out its revenue between a usually very strong fourth quarter and a typically much weaker spring quarter the following year. Apple’s portfolio has also expanded, and the iPhone Pro and Pro Max lineup are more enticing for people already prepared to spend the money on a new iPhone.
When components become more expensive, companies have three real options: Eat the costs, raise prices, or, as Apple seems to be doing, lean into it. By moving its cheaper options to a later date, Apple can drum up excitement for its bigger, better, pricier offerings. When it charges more for those, it is likely to be less off-putting than making a cheap phone even more expensive. It’s part of a “premiumization” of devices, as Popal calls it, that Apple hopes to leverage and build hype for its pricier options.
Shawn DuBravac, chief economist at the Global Electronics Association, tells WIRED he is optimistic about what these kinds of rising prices ultimately mean for customers.
“Throughout the history of time, the deflationary pressures of technology have always flowed to the consumer,” DuBravac says. “I'm confident that will be the case again. It just will take some time for the markets to solidify.” In other words, new technologies launch with a high price, but manufacturing efficiencies and competition inevitably drive costs down for consumers.
That may not be the case anytime soon for folding phones, which are seeing higher prices than ever. Samsung’s entire 2026 Galaxy Z folding smartphone range saw price increases, as did Google’s new Pixel 11 Pro Fold, and Motorola’s Razr 2026 models. Apple’s folding iPhone is rumored to cost around $2,000.
To help mitigate those high costs, Apple is turning to financing options and trade-in programs. In July, the company launched an iPhone leasing program that lets people pay a monthly fee to rent the newest iPhones, then swap them out when a new device releases. The program will undoubtedly help more people afford the newest devices, but ownership advocates have criticized it, saying it keeps you from truly owning and managing your device. It also fits Apple’s broader effort to turn all of its products into a subscription service.
“The way most consumers buy Apple phones is through financing or trade-in programs,” Popal says. “We can expect a lot more aggressive trade-ins to help cushion that.”
Thanks to the memory crisis and price increases, all smartphones are getting more costly to make. Less expensive phones become less appealing for manufacturers to prioritize, and leading smartphone brands have started to see them as far less economical to produce.
On the flip side, demand for refurbished devices has been climbing for a while now, with sales of used devices growing even as new phone sales slow down. More people are looking to save money or purchase more eco-friendly products.
“The days of the cheap smartphone are over,” Popal says.

Nepal cracks down on online abuse against flood survivors
- Published
Nepal is cracking down on online abuse directed at survivors of last month's deadly floods, with Prime Minister Balendra Shah warning that authorities will "show no leniency" to people who "belittle" those who are suffering.
Some have taken to social media to appeal for information about their loved ones and to urge officials to step up search efforts, only to be hit by hostile comments.
"People who make unnecessary remarks, belittle those in pain or seek to cause them further suffering at this sensitive time are criminals," Shah wrote in a Facebook post.
Nepali police say they are looking into where these comments have originated from to identify addresses and phone numbers.
A woman, whose brother has been missing since the floods hit two weeks ago, had earlier told the BBC that search and rescue operations were too slow.
"If the government had mobilised experts and equipment for rescue in time, would we have known the condition of our family members sooner?
"We still hope we can find him alive."
Days later, she wrote back saying she had "received many nasty comments" in response to her criticism of the search efforts.
"We are already suffering so much and this has only added to our pain," she said.
In a separate case, a young woman had expressed her anger at what she perceived as authorities' "lack of urgency" in searching for her husband.
"My husband is missing now, if the government cannot find him, can it at least show me his body?" she said in a video clip that has gone viral online – and attracted its fair share of insults.
One comment, for instance, urged her to "jump into the river" and help with the search, while another read, "not everything happens just by you putting the blame on the government".
But others have called out the insensitive remarks. "The victim should be consoled at this time, not cursed," one of them read.
Nepali police say they have convened a 10-member committee to look into these online comments.
Under the country's Electronic Transactions Act, those who use social media to defame or harass others could be jailed for up to five years and fined up to 100,000 rupees ($662; £490), or both.
Dovan Rai, the executive director of Body & Data, a Nepal-based non-profit organisation that advocates for a safe digital space, says some of the insensitive comments could have come from social media users who engage in "rage baiting" – that is, those who produce negative content as a "bait" to trigger outrage, or force people to click on or share their posts.
They could also have come from "staunch supporters of the government".
"There is also extremism that is very sympathetic to the government and condemns those who question it. That has further polarized the dialogue on social media," she told the BBC.

Smaller ball for women makes it 'harder to do my job'
- Published
England will play Australia, Canada and New Zealand in the next three weeks and, like all the world's top women's players, they have some new equipment: a smaller ball.
During September and October's WXV Global Series, World Rugby is trialling a size 4.5 ball - about 3% smaller than the size five used in the men's game, but the same weight.
Their introduction has not been without controversy and for England hooker May Campbell, responsible for throwing the ball in at the line-out, told BBC Sport it can go "a bit skew-whiff".
One of England's kickers, Helena Rowland, has found a much bigger margin for error with the smaller ball, saying: "If you get it slightly wrong, the difference is massive."
The fly-half says England players have noticed passes "dying", falling to the floor earlier than expected, "which they wouldn't have done previously".
Not all feedback has been negative. Wales wing Lisa Neumann is a fan, saying "it's changed the game" for her passing because of improved grip on the ball.
The thinking behind the trial is that the smaller ball will suit women's physiology and improve their skillset. In other sports, like basketball, women use a smaller ball, and in athletics sprint hurdles are lower for females.
But Rowland says she has never felt "hindered" by playing with the same size ball as in men's rugby.
'Harder to do my job'
Players with a specific skillset may find the change harder than others. Hookers must throw in at a line-out, scrum-halves are the most frequent passers and fly-halves the most regular kickers.
Rowland explained: "We've learned for however long how to kick with a size five.
"So I've had 13-odd years of doing that and training my routine and trying to nail that and get as much consistency as I can.
"So it's about, I suppose, trying to pack all those years of training and all those kicks into a four- or five-week block to get used to it, to then go out on to the world stage."
Rowland added that she has not "necessarily seen any positives", saying: "I know some of the girls have said that from an offload perspective, it's maybe made them more confident.
"But for me, it hasn't. I don't think there's enough of a change in the ball for me to be able to be running around with it in one hand and offloading left, right and centre.
"I haven't necessarily found any of the positive impacts. I've just found it a bit harder to do my job."
A World Rugby spokesperson said everyone involved in the WXV Global Series, including players, coaches and match officials, would have their views taken into account "with equal value" through surveys.

  - Published6 May
John Mitchell, England's head coach, has said "it's too early" to judge the impact of the smaller ball, and conclusions would have to be drawn after the world champions' opening three Tests in September.
Some England players were given a size 4.5 ball to practise with in the off-season and Campbell says "there's no point in complaining about it", given every side in the WXV Global Series will be in the same position.
But she adds: "I feel like a lot of us don't know how it's going to change the game, and kind of the reason behind it changing and the data behind it.
"It's just this decision has kind of just happened that we're now trialling it at the top level."
Inconsistency in shape
One area of concern for the England players is the ball changing shape.
Campbell says they "played around" with how much the ball was blown up, adding: "In previous weeks it was actually a bit fatter, and then this week it definitely feels smaller."
Rowland agrees, saying: "There needs to be a bit more done in terms of how the balls are made. We had some new balls today versus the ones we've had for the last three weeks [and the difference] is massive.
"If you've been training with an old ball that's fat to then go into a game and it's a completely different shape, actually that makes a massive difference as well, which I think is something that you don't necessarily find so much in the size five."
The ball has already been trialled in the Under-18s and Under-20s Women's Six Nations as well as the HSBC Sevens Series.
Rowland says she would "love to see the data on if it actually has made a difference".
It seems a fair request, and is one that BBC Sport put to World Rugby, but we did not receive any data.
A spokesperson said: "The balls haven't been used in the international XVs environment yet so there isn't directly comparable data to share with players either directly or via their unions.
"Once we've built up a large enough data set of player responses, match official responses and game data, we'll publish the results, so it'll be available to players, unions, the International Rugby Players Association, coaches, match officials, the media and everyone else."
Some players are frustrated as they feel they have become guinea pigs on the global stage. To compound that frustration, they will then return to their clubs where the league season will be played with a size five ball once again.
BBC Sport asked World Rugby when the trial period is likely to conclude, and were told: "We'll be able to assess our position on women's 15s once the international window has started.
"This will allow for completion of the WXV tournaments and full analysis in early 2027. The evidence to date suggests that further exposure produces greater results."
While it looks like players and coaches will get to see the data in early 2027, any wider outcomes or decisions might take longer.

On the eve of Apple's highly anticipated folding iPhone, Samsung isn't feeling threatened. Instead, the folding smartphone pioneer says the competition is “absolutely welcome.”
That's according to Hee-Cheul Moon, head of Samsung's Advanced Mechanical R&D Group, who sat with WIRED on a virtual Zoom call with Seungki Choi, head of Samsung's Smartphone R&D Group. Before the talk veered toward Apple, the pair spoke about how the company managed to shave 75 grams off the weight of its latest Galaxy Z Fold8 in the 7 years since it debuted the original.
Weight is integral to a folding phone's success. If the device is too chunky and heavy, you're less likely to want to use it. Over the past two years, folding devices from Honor, Google, and Samsung have rapidly gotten lighter, which each iteration featuring thinner designs. It may be why Samsung saw preorders for its latest folding handsets increase 30 percent globally versus last year's models, with the Fold8—the device with a new smaller shape that’s easier to hold—accounting for nearly half.
“Seeing these other brands entering the market, we feel very proud of ourselves that the value that we pioneered with this new category of foldables is being acknowledged and recognized,” Moon says through a translator.
When I asked what advice the company had for Apple ahead of its folding debut, Moon says, “The key to providing the highest customer value in this market is all about the weight of the device. As you know, it's not easy." Apple's folding iPhone, rumored to be called the iPhone Ultra, is expected to weigh between 230 and 241 grams (the iPhone 17 Pro Max weighs 233 grams), heftier than Samsung's latest.
Samsung has made notable strides this year in making its main Galaxy Z Fold8 smartphone lighter than top-end candybar-shaped smartphones. The single-screen Galaxy S26 Ultra weighs 214 grams, but the Fold8 is merely 201 grams, thanks to its smaller, passport-style shape. The company says its own customer data and YouGov survey data from 2024 show that bulky designs were a chief concern for people uninterested in folding phones.
The company says it analyzed every single component in the latest Fold8 and Fold8 Ultra—approximately 270 components and more than 180 auxiliary parts—from circuit boards and antennas to tapes and fastening components.
The team looked everywhere to cut weight. For example, it redesigned the printed circuit board to remove unnecessary circuits and improve component layout, reducing the space requirement. Samsung says it even eliminated 15 auxiliary parts and machined the internal display support plate down to roughly 0.2 millimeters. To keep that thinner panel durable, Samsung developed its “Flex Titanium” screen—a titanium alloy film roughly one-third the width of a human hair designed to maintain surface flatness and keep the crease from worsening over years of folding.
You'll also notice Samsung's primary folding phone no longer has three cameras on the back. Instead, it's powered by a dual-camera system, a main camera and an ultrawide—there's no more telephoto. For those who still demand high-end zoom and a 200-megapixel primary shooter, Samsung points to the larger Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra, framing the Fold8's camera cutback as an intentional concession to deliver that lightweight, passport-style design.
Apple's folding iPhone is also expected to have a wider and shorter passport-style shape, and it's likely to have a similar camera setup. Both Apple and Samsung made similar concessions last year chasing ultra-thin-and-light smartphones.
Choi says this came down to user feedback as Samsung's customers wanted a folding device that was “effortlessly portable” yet could be unfolded for an immersive multimedia experience. “We continue to always monitor the voice from the market, and we are open to any possibilities,” he says. We spend most of our time consuming multimedia with our smartphones, and the Fold8's new shape is specifically tailored for media, with less obvious letterboxing than previous Folds.
Yet chasing that slim, lightweight profile leaves foldables exposed where traditional flagships excel: durability and ingress protection. Most candybar smartphones sport an IP68 rating for dust and water resistance, meaning they'll be fine even after spending some time at the bottom of a pool, but the Galaxy Z Fold8 series is still stuck at IP48—it can get wet, but dust will cause problems. Dust notoriously forced Samsung to delay the launch of the first Galaxy Fold in 2019, as little specks could get through the hinge and damage the screen.
Google's folding Pixels are the only models with an IP68 rating. Still, even with the higher rating, dust can pose a problem, according to Elizabeth Chamberlain, iFixit's director of Sustainability. The repair company's teardowns show that dust can get inside the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, making the hinge sound “crunchy” and causing what could be a serious liability over time.
“We still haven't seen a solution for that,” Chamberlain tells WIRED. “Repair is still a problem for foldables.” iFixit's recent teardown of the Galaxy Z Fold8 gave it a 4/10 for repairability. “The hinge is buried under all the other components, and the hinge is the thing most likely to get damaged,” Chamberlain says. She did give Samsung props for its new adhesive system that makes battery removal easier.
Moon reiterated that Samsung's Folds have the “best-in-class” dustproof and waterproof performance in the industry, and that the company isn't just “chasing the numbers for the sake of it.” He also emphasized that despite the Fold8's slim profile, internal components are far easier to detach and service than earlier iterations.
That tension between engineering finesse and long-term durability is what Apple is stepping into. While Samsung enjoys a boost in Fold8 preorders, the broader foldable category was staring down a double-digit decline after five consecutive quarters of losing steam.
Nabila Popal, senior research director at the International Data Corporation, says this niche market is stabilizing, and the upcoming iPhone is expected to help the category grow nearly 13 percent year over year—the only bit of growth in the smartphone market right now. Drew Blackard, Samsung's senior vice president of Mobile Product Management, previously told WIRED that more competition will help bring visibility to the category.
Popal says foldables are more durable and dependable now, arguing Apple is entering just as hardware anxieties have eased.
Chamberlain isn't convinced the category is truly mature. “I want a phone that is durable and repairable, and I think it's highly unlikely that Apple will have solved the hinge problem,” she says.
Even with the durability question unanswered, Samsung's engineers believe they've finally landed on the right formula. When I asked what device everyone in the room was using, a sea of Galaxy Z Fold8 models appeared in the air. Moon held up both the Z Fold8 and the Fold8 Ultra, smiling and saying, “We use the Fold8 Ultra also.”

Six Movies to Get You in the Fall Mood
From cozy classics to unlikely favorites, The Atlantic’s writers and editors share their seasonal picks.
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.
September has arrived, bringing the first hints of fall: cooler days, changing leaves, and the urge to revisit comfort watches. Below, The Atlantic’s writers and editors recommend six films that put them in an autumn spirit.
When Harry Met Sally (streaming on Prime Video and Apple TV)
There’s the cornucopia of cable-knit sweaters, a chocolate-brown velvet bowler hat, the fog of bright-orange leaves streaming through the glass wall at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Autumn in New York is the backdrop of When Harry Met Sally, but that doesn’t fully account for the place that Nora Ephron and Rob Reiner’s classic occupies in my life: For me, it’s the chicken noodle soup of movies. I have my personal reasons for considering it the ultimate comfort watch. Maybe it’s my affinity with Sally (played by Meg Ryan), the curly-haired journalist determined to have life happen to her, though her job is to “write about things that happen to other people.” Or the movie’s love for my hometown, which forms the bedrock of so many of Ephron’s films. Or the weirdly specific fantasy of having your date unwittingly quote to you something you wrote in a magazine.
This time of year, I’m far from the only person who considers a When Harry Met Sally rewatch as inevitable as digging my denim jacket out of the back of my closet. If there’s a universal magic to the movie, maybe some of it comes from magic in real life. The original script saw Sally and Harry’s (Billy Crystal) story ending bittersweetly, with the two apart. But midway through making the film, Reiner fell in love with his wife, Michele Singer. This fall—our first without Reiner and Singer—I’ll be revisiting the movie in large part for the ending he decided on instead: perhaps the most memorable, and certainly my favorite, in the romantic-comedy genre.
— Marie-Rose Sheinerman, assistant editor
Michael Clayton (streaming on Prime Video and Apple TV)
Fall is not really about melancholy and the inner life, as the poets would have you believe. It’s that period, after summer’s frivolities, when things get serious again. Michael Clayton, a film I first saw at the urging of my friend and colleague James Parker—and which we both regularly rewatch—is charged with that urban, autumnal, overcoated feeling of things getting serious.
The people in it are grown-ups. If they’re not, as with Timmy—Michael Clayton’s brother, whose feckless behavior leaves Michael exposed to loan sharks—they’re basically ignored. Sydney Pollack? What a performance! What an impeccably serious guy! Tom Wilkinson, Tilda Swinton—they’re brilliant in this. And George Clooney, playing the titular character, is haunted by his own rotting, inky-eyed charm and stymied at every turn, despite his good intentions. He’s at his best in the scene where Michael, working as his law firm’s fixer, advises an affluent, arrogant client who has just committed a hit-and-run. The client, thinking it’s still unfettered summer, throws a childish tantrum. Michael, in his best autumnal mode, sets him straight: “There’s no play here. There’s no angle. There’s no champagne room. And I’m not a miracle worker; I’m a janitor.”
— Sebastian Smee, staff writer
Little Women (streaming on Prime Video and Apple TV)
Fall is a happy-sad season: The sunlight is golden (but that’s a sign that the days are getting shorter), the leaves are ochre and maroon (a sign that they’re dying), and the air is crisp (a sign of impending winter). And to me, Greta Gerwig’s 2019 adaptation of Little Women perfectly embodies this feeling. The story follows the four March sisters through the different seasons of their life. Their childhood flashbacks are scenes captured in warm, autumnal tones, and adulthood flash-forwards are shot in cooler, harsher light, to reflect the girls’ feelings about the passage of time.
Jo March wants to grow up, and yet she clings to girlhood, panicking as those around her—such as her sister Meg, who gets married—seem content to let the past go. In one pivotal scene, Jo tells her mother that she wishes she could still want what she wanted as a child, when simply being with her family was enough. Now her aspirations for a career and romantic love seem at odds, and her sense of independence has become inextricable from an acute sense of loneliness. For those of us who also cling to the past (even if that past is just “summer”), this film will comfort you and remind you that change is inevitable.
— Nancy Walecki, staff writer
You’ve Got Mail (streaming on Prime Video and Apple TV)
The first 30 minutes of You’ve Got Mail are an unabashed ode to autumn. “Don’t you love New York in the fall?” the film’s romantic hero, Joe (Tom Hanks), writes in an email to the heroine, Kathleen (Meg Ryan). When Kathleen arrives at work a few minutes later with a perfect orange pumpkin under her arm, she breathlessly repeats the question: “Don’t you just love New York in the fall?” And how could you not? The film shows children bobbing for apples at a street fair, a tree with copper leaves set against a row of brownstones, and characters walking around the Upper West Side in good knits, blazers, and fleeces.
Even when the movie shifts to winter and then spring, You’ve Got Mail still feels autumnal. That feeling goes beyond the scenery: It’s a wistful movie, and at times a sad one. Characters major and minor express regret over lost loves, broken family relationships, and unrealized dreams. Kathleen and Joe spend most of the film in relationships with people they clearly do not love. These notes of melancholy make it a perfect romantic comedy to turn to as the days get shorter.
— Eleanor Barkhorn, senior editor
Point Break (streaming on Peacock)
I grew up in Los Angeles, and as a result, I do not really understand seasons, weather, or people’s fear of being seen perspiring. Since I moved to the East Coast eight years ago, I have found autumn to be a cute but unwelcome reminder that winter is real and, even worse, that I will soon be forced to experience it.
The 1991 action thriller Point Break is also about Angeleno men who do not condone the end of summer. In the movie, they take this aversion one step further, robbing banks to fund the travel necessary to never stop surfing under the hot sun. The dialogue is clunky, albeit quotable, and almost nothing about the plot is believable. And yet, it’s so fun to watch these guys, and the FBI agent who tails them, try to make one summer weekend last forever. That is how I will be spending the fall: in denial, doing as much hiking, paddleboarding, and swimming as possible, until I am forced to stop.
— Marc Novicoff, staff writer
Silent Friend (streaming on Prime Video and Apple TV)
Silent Friend is a meandering film that has nudged me toward accepting slowness and inevitable change. The historical drama follows three environmentalists at a German university across three epochs as each tries to uncover the secret life of plants: In 1908, Grete navigates sexism and her own position as one of the first female students in the university’s botany department; in 1972, a young man named Hannes, immersed in his college campus’s Cold War–era counterculture, develops sensors to understand how a potted geranium perceives him; and in 2020, a neuroscientist runs an experiment connecting a tree’s electrical activity with his own after the COVID lockdown cuts off his access to human subjects.
At the center of it all is a nearly 200-year-old ginkgo tree that provides quiet solace to the three characters. The tree becomes a central figure in the story, observing, listening, and breathing alongside its subjects. Its presence embodies the spirit of the film, which is more sensory-driven than narrative-driven and makes it easy to lose yourself in the foliage. Now every time I see a leaf change color, I’m reminded to pay closer attention to the natural world around me and all of the life that brims within it.
— Kim Jao, assistant editor

The Measles-Stricken Mother Who Lost Her Newborn Son
By Tom Bartlett
When the Amish man emerged from his barn to greet me, he had no idea that his newborn son’s death had become national news. The man wore a straw hat, black trousers, and suspenders over a long-sleeved blue shirt; one of his similarly dressed sons was guiding a horse-drawn plow in a nearby field.
The man told me that, like most Amish people, he and his family don’t watch TV or use the internet. They don’t read the newspaper either. So they didn’t know until I told them that last Tuesday, Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, held a press conference to announce the first two “measles-associated” deaths in the state in 35 years.

Healthtech-focused VC firm W Health Ventures has closed its second fund at ₹700 Cr (about $84 Mn), sailing past its original target corpus of ₹630 Cr. A combination of family offices and institutional investors from India and the US were the limited partners (LPs) that backed the fund. Launched in July 2025, the fund marked its first close in February at ₹550 Cr ($60.6 Mn), it targeted to back eight to ten early stage healthtech startups over the next four years, from pre-idea stage to growth stages startups in India and the US. W Health Ventures’ managing partner Pankaj Jethwani told Inc42 that the firm looks to identify concepts at a very early age and then spends a fairly large amount of time pressure-testing these ideas. “Once we pick the area we're most excited about, we build a founding team around it and surround that team with resources. We have about a 50-person in-house team of technologists, entrepreneurs, and clinicians. From there, it's a collaborative build to bring these companies to scale — we act as co-founders of the business," he added. Via the second fund, the firm has established two startups and has poured in capital so far. Firstly, it partnered with Narayana Health to set up Everhope Oncology, a cancer care platform and infused $10 Mn (about ₹86 Cr) in March 2025. It launched Everbright Health in the US and infused $7 Mn, along with Sanos Capital, in October 2025. Founded in 2020 by Sunil Wadhwani and headquartered in Mumbai, W Health Ventures builds healthcare companies from pre-idea to category leader across India and the US-India corridor. The fund typically writes cheques in the range of ₹30 Cr to ₹50 Cr, and has backed 12 startups in India and the US via its first fund, including Wysa, BeatO, Mylo, Reveal, and BabyMD. W Health’s fund close comes at a time when India's healthtech funding market is undergoing a reset, with investors becoming more selective about digital-health business models. The firm is also part of a broader shift among venture investors towards company creation, as funds increasingly look to participate earlier than the traditional pre-seed or seed stage. Instead of waiting for founders to build businesses around identified opportunities, these firms are identifying problems themselves, validating the opportunity and assembling founding teams.

'Nothing good was supposed to come out of me'
- Published
A Nigerian man has shared the story of how he rose up out of "abject poverty" as a child, to become one of the leading UK academics in his field.
David Etor, 43, who grew up in Nigeria, only learned to read and write aged 12 and was told as a child that "nothing good will come out of you", but is now a lecturer in electrical and mechanical engineering at the University of Bristol.
He told the BBC how his family was so poor growing up that his mum would pretend to cook food in a kitchen they shared with others, "to protect our integrity" in front of neighbours.
"I didn't see a way out," he said.
'The poor called us poor'
Speaking to John Darvall on BBC Radio Bristol about the publication of his first book, Etor described growing up in a "compound" with several other families, all sharing a single kitchen, toilet and bathroom.
"It was a very poor neighbourhood. We were particularly very poor that the poor neighbours would refer to us as poor," he said.
"I do remember that there was a time where my mum would boil water.
"[She would] go back in and out, lift the lid, stir the water, go back into the room [and] come back as though she was preparing food...
"She would come back in with that pot of water after a couple of hours and it will be as though she's just finished cooking a meal, but it was just water.
"She was trying to protect our integrity."

Etor's first break came whilst doing a kind of national service in Nigeria, when he realised lots of locals were being hospitalised with food poisoning, because they were trying to preserve things by drying them in fields.
To solve the problem, he designed and built a kind of "solar oven".
"It worked incredibly well," he said, which led to an award from the state government and a job.
He then completed an undergraduate degree at Newcastle University and a PhD at the University of Durham, before securing his current job in Bristol.
Sir Steve Webb, the former MP and Pensions Minister, who got to know Etor through the church in Bristol, called his achievements "remarkable".
"David's message is very much that people shouldn't be defined by their upbringing or their background," he said. "They shouldn't be written off."
"I was pinching myself on my way here this morning," Etor added.
"Nothing good was supposed to come out of me."

Indian Embassy in China asks families for DNA samples to identify victims
The Embassy will forward the data to the concerned Chinese authorities for comparison.
The Indian Embassy in China on Monday urged families of Indians missing since the August 26 flash flood in the Tibet-Nepal border region to provide DNA samples to help identify them.
The Indian mission made the request after Chinese authorities confirmed that they were now able to receive DNA samples from families of Indian nationals listed as missing in the disaster, an Embassy press release said.
Families willing to provide DNA information have been asked to submit the relevant data in the internationally recognised CODIS format, it said.
The Embassy will forward the data to the concerned Chinese authorities for comparison.
"The Embassy will be notified, and will in turn inform the family, should a match be confirmed", it said.
"Blood samples can be collected from the parents of the missing foreign national or the spouse and children (samples from multiple children should be collected wherever possible)," the Indian mission said.
"If the missing person has no living parents or children, kindly collect blood samples from siblings (collecting samples from all siblings is preferred)," it said.
The Indian mission said that if necessary, samples can be collected from other maternal relatives (e.g., cousins on the maternal side) and paternal relatives (e.g., cousins on the paternal side) with specified details of the relationship.
"DNA STR data for the aforementioned samples is required; for males, Y-STR data must also be included. Data should be stored in the internationally recognised CODIS format", it said.
The embassy said that the samples should be well labelled with the nationality, name and passport number of the missing person, name and passport number of the family member and sample ID number.
"Families may contact the Embassy of India at the following for further guidance: Telephone: 86 18514284905 Email: cons1.beijing@mea.gov.in", it said.
The disaster was triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, sending a massive surge of water and debris downstream through the Bhotekoshi River and devastating settlements in northern and central Nepal.
On Sunday, Chinese officials updated the death toll to 43, with 519 others remaining missing.
The missing include 261 foreigners, of whom 49 are from India.
Most of the dead and missing foreigners were on both sides of the ill-fated immigration building when it was devoured by the flood.

India stands at a defining moment in its journey towards the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047. Under the Healthcare for All pillar, the government has rightly prioritised strengthening Ayushman Bharat, expanding primary healthcare, reducing out-of-pocket expenditure, and promoting preventive care. Yet there is one element that cuts across all these ambitions and determines their success: mental health.
Mental health is not a niche concern. It influences educational attainment, workforce participation, social cohesion, and physical health outcomes. A healthier and more productive India cannot be built without placing mental well-being at the centre of public health.
Major implications
The scale of the challenge is substantial. Mental illness affects one in seven Indians, with nearly 200 million people living with a diagnosable mental health condition. The contribution of mental disorders to India’s total disease burden has doubled over the past three decades. Yet the national treatment gap remains 84.5%, meaning that more than four out of five people who need care do not receive it. The reasons are well known. India has only 0.3 psychiatrists per 1,00,000 population, alongside significant shortages in clinical psychologists, psychiatric social workers, and psychiatric nurses. These shortages are the result of decades during which mental health received insufficient attention, both in India and globally.
Mental disorders significantly increase the risk of chronic diseases, while chronic diseases in turn increase the risk of mental illness. More than 60% of people attending primary care facilities have a diagnosable mental disorder. Rates of anxiety and depression are substantially higher among people living with diabetes, hypertension, tuberculosis, and HIV/AIDS. Ignoring mental health, therefore, undermines efforts to control non-communicable diseases and reduce healthcare expenditure.
The economic implications are equally compelling. A 2025 modelling study by researchers from PGIMER and NIMHANS estimated that integrating universal depression screening into India’s primary healthcare system could generate net savings of ₹291 billion to ₹482 billion annually, equivalent to as much as 0.32% of GDP. Mental health is not a social welfare issue alone — it is also a human capital investment and an economic growth strategy.
The encouraging news is that India has already built many of the foundations required for transformation. More than 1.73 lakh sub-centres and primary health centres have been converted into Ayushman Bharat Arogya Mandirs, with mental healthcare included among the essential service packages. The District Mental Health Programme now covers more than 90% of districts. Tele-MANAS, launched in 2022, has expanded across all States and Union Territories.
Three main priorities
The task now is not to start from scratch. It is to build on this foundation at scale.
First, one must empower frontline health workers to become the backbone of community mental healthcare. India’s one million ASHA workers represent the world’s largest community health workforce. Evidence from Madhya Pradesh and other States demonstrates that, with appropriate training and supervision, ASHAs can successfully identify, support, and refer individuals with common mental disorders. Expanding this model through validated screening tools, digital learning platforms, and performance-linked incentives could expand access to care.
Second, India must invest more systematically in community-based care. Models such as Zimbabwe’s Friendship Bench, Atmiyata in India, and programmes implemented by The Live Love Laugh Foundation demonstrate that trained community workers can bridge the gap between awareness and treatment, particularly in rural and underserved populations. These approaches improve access and reduce costs, and deserve wider adoption and funding. Third, the country must fully realise the promise of financial protection. Extending outpatient mental health benefits under the Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana and strengthening the implementation of insurance parity as per the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017, would make mental healthcare affordable for millions who currently go without care.
If India is to become a truly developed nation by 2047, mental health must move from the margins of public policy to its centre.
Indu Bhushan is the founding CEO of India’s National Health Authority and Ayushman Bharat; Anisha Padukone is the CEO of The Live Love Laugh Foundation

Football administrator and entrepreneur Ranjit Bajaj has moved the court seeking directions to the All India Football Federation (AIFF) to immediately notify the schedule for elections to its Executive Committee and complete the process within a time-bound period.
In his writ petition, Bajaj has sought a writ of mandamus or any other appropriate direction requiring the AIFF to conduct its elections strictly in accordance with its Constitution and the National Sports Governance Act, 2025.
Bajaj has also sought directions for completion of the entire electoral process, including declaration of results, within a timeframe to be fixed by the court.

The petitioner has further sought an interim restraint on the present AIFF Executive Committee from taking policy decisions or decisions having long-term, financial or otherwise irreversible consequences in relation to the federation’s affairs until the elections are completed.
The petition also seeks any other order that the court may deem fit in the interest of justice.
Bajaj’s plea comes against the backdrop of the AIFF’s decision to defer its elections as it transitions to the new electoral framework under the National Sports Governance Act, 2025.
In his petition, Bajaj has contended that the AIFF has already adopted an NSGA-compliant Constitution and completed its constitutional alignment, and therefore there is no justification for any further deferment of its elections.
He has also relied on the court’s July 17, 2026 order in the All India Tennis Association case, arguing that compliance by state associations cannot be treated as a pre-condition for holding elections to the national federation.
According to Bajaj’s plea, the alignment of state associations should be undertaken by the newly elected Executive Committee after the national federation’s elections, rather than being used as a reason to postpone the electoral process.
The petitioner has accordingly urged the court to direct the AIFF to initiate and complete the election process at the earliest.

Flight recorders recovered from 'devastating' Amazon cargo plane crash
- Published
Investigators have recovered the flight recorders from the Amazon cargo plane that crashed at Miami International Airport, but the priority remains the recovery of victims, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) has said.
Five people were killed and five others seriously injured when the Boeing 767-300, operated by 21 Air, overshot the runway shortly before 14:00 local time (19:00 BST) on Sunday.
The plane hit two vehicles, including a white van carrying seven people within the airport perimeter, and a Toyota with three passengers.
NTSB chairwoman Jennifer Homendy said it was too early to draw conclusions about what caused the crash, with investigators still in the "fact finding stage".
Speaking at a press conference at Miami International Airport on Monday, Homendy said the aircraft had two crew members on board and was arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, on its third flight of the day.
The plane struck navigational aids and equipment after overrunning the runway, before hitting a white Ford van owned by a contract cleaning company.
It then travelled through a perimeter fence and collided with a Toyota Corolla, coming to rest about 1,300ft (394m) beyond the runway.
Homendy described the crash scene as "devastating", with debris from the aircraft, vehicles and airport fencing scattered across the area.
"It's hard to see, and I'm sure very difficult for the first responders as well," she said.
She said recovering victims' bodies was the current priority, adding: "The investigation and access to the aircraft, as well as evidence, can wait."
The flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder have been recovered and are being sent to NTSB headquarters for evaluation.
Homendy said investigators could not yet say anything substantive about the cause of the crash as they were still collecting evidence at the scene.
Investigators will examine the flight history, crew experience and training, radar data, and aircraft performance. Separate teams will look at the plane's systems and engines, while a meteorologist will assess the weather conditions at the time of landing.
The NTSB will also examine whether the runway should have had an engineered materials arresting system (EMAS), which is designed to slow and stop aircraft that overrun a runway. Homendy said this would be a "key" part of the investigation.
Earlier analysis by BBC Verify found there was an active thunderstorm near the airport shortly before the crash, with winds gusting up to 26 knots.
The NTSB has appealed for members of the public to share photographs or videos that could aid the investigation.
Homendy said the agency would make safety recommendations at the end of its investigation. "That's why we're here - to prevent the next tragedy," she said.
"Our recommendations must be implemented, or we'll be here again."
Two of the four runways at the airport remained closed following the crash. Passengers have been warned to expect further disruption after Sunday's cancellations affected the arrival of aircraft and flight crews.
The crash happened during the Labor Day holiday weekend, one of the busiest travel periods in the US.
Amazon said it was "heartbroken" by the loss of life and that it was working closely with authorities.
21 Air, the company operating the aircraft, expressed its condolences and said it was co-operating with the investigation.

In NIA charge sheet, no terror charges against US national VanDyke, 6 Ukrainians
VanDyke was arrested from Kolkata airport by NIA on March 13 under UAPA, which punishes conspiracy, advocacy, abetment, or incitement to commit a terrorist act.
The National Investigation Agency (NIA) on Tuesday charged US national Mathew Aaron VanDyke and six Ukrainians, arrested in March this year, under the Immigration and Foreigners Act, and not the Unlawful Activities Prevention Act (UAPA).
VanDyke was arrested from Kolkata airport by NIA on March 13 under Section 18 of UAPA, which punishes conspiracy, advocacy, abetment, or incitement to commit a terrorist act. His six Ukrainian associates - Hurba Petro, Taras Slyviak, Ivan Sukmanovskyi, Marian Stefankiv, Maksim Honcharuk and Viktor Kaminskyi - were arrested from Delhi and Lucknow airports on the same day.
But in the charge sheet filed in the court of special judge Prashant Sharma at Rouse Avenue Courts, NIA only charged them under sections 21 and 23 of the Immigration and Foreigners Act, which cover illegal entry and violations of visa conditions.
NIA said the accused violated the conditions of their Indian visas by entering the notified Protected Area without the requisite permit and subsequently crossing the India-Myanmar border through unauthorised points. The two offences carry a punishment of up to five and three years in prison, respectively.
“We have filed a charge sheet against seven accused under the Immigration and Foreigners Act. The probe has been kept open in all other aspects, including the UAPA charges,” Rahul Tyagi, NIA’s special public prosecutor told HT.
VanDyke, according to his website, is from Baltimore and has worked as a soldier, international businessman, war correspondent, columnist and international businessman. He claims to be a veteran of the Libyan revolution, a former prisoner of war there and the founder of a military contracting firm — SOLI (Sons of Liberty International).
In the charge sheet, NIA said it had completed a substantial part of its investigation into the offences committed under the UAPA but needed more time. Already, NIA, which was to file the charges within 90 days, was granted an additional 90 days to file the charge sheet.
“Further investigation is under-going and more time is required in order to ascertain and verify the true and complete facts about the commission of offences under UAPA,” the agency said in the charge sheet, seeking permission to continue investigating the alleged conspiracy.
NIA claimed it needed to further probe the import and recovery of a large quantity of drones and accessories through India and the seizure of several digital devices, “which may indicate their possible involvement in acts affecting/threatening the unity, integrity, security and sovereignty of India”.
An NIA spokesperson didn’t comment on the developments.
Advocate Rohit Dandriyal, who is representing Van Dyke, said the NIA was investigating fake terror charges.
“NIA did not find any evidence against the accused even after being granted an additional 90 days for investigation, during which time the accused remained incarcerated on fictitious UAPA charges,” Dandriyal told HT.
Myanmar training mission
According to NIA, the seven entered India on valid travel documents in December 2025 but later travelled to Guwahati and Mizoram without obtaining the mandatory Protected Area Permit (PAP) or Restricted Area Permit (RAP).
The agency alleged that they illegally crossed into Myanmar to reach Victoria Camp, where they were allegedly to conduct pre-scheduled training for Myanmar-based Ethnic Armed Groups in drone warfare, drone operations, assembly and jamming technology.The agency said the accused returned to India from Myanmar around March 5, 2026.
NIA claimed that some of these groups had links with insurgent organisations in India.
Six taxis, Tiau river route
According to the charge sheet, six taxis were hired through a car rental company catering to foreigners to transport the accused from Guwahati into Mizoram’s Protected Area. They allegedly halted for several hours before crossing into Myanmar through the Tiau river route and reached Victoria Camp on December 29, 2025.
NIA said two persons, Abika and Viktor/Kima, allegedly arranged the logistics for the border crossing.
NIA claimed that the alleged trip was not merely an immigration violation but formed part of “a larger conspiracy involving Indian insurgent groups, particularly those active in the northeastern states”.

Whatever happened to the Taliban threat: 'We will flog the women'?
We have previously reported on the Taliban's position that public flogging (as well as stoning) are appropriate corporal punishment if they believe a citizen has violated certain precepts –- enabling girls to be educated despite the ban on secondary education for females, for example, or engaging in an adulterous relationship. Have Taliban authorities been employing these methods?
We're revisiting some of our past global health and development stories to see "Whatever happened to ..."
In March 2024, NPR reported on a statement issued by the Taliban's usually elusive supreme leader Hibatullah Akhundzada announcing a return to a type of punishment in its justice system. "We will flog the women ... we will stone them to death in public [for crimes]," he said in an audio message.
True to his words, the Taliban have gradually increased public and violent punishments. According to an April 2026 report by the Afghanistan Human Rights and Democracy Organization (AHRDO), an nongovernmental organization that investigates human rights violations in Afghanistan. Between February 2022 and April 2026, AHRDO documented 2,745 individuals who had been subjected to corporal punishment drawn from the Taliban's own public records.
The U.N. has documented similar figures, in a report in March 2026. Citing at least 1,110 flogging cases last year, the U.N. states: "in 2025 alone, more men and women were subjected to public flogging than in all previous years combined."
These counts are based on cases published by the Taliban's Supreme Court on their website and social media channels and in over 500 press releases. Advocates believe that there may be cases that are not documented in court records — instances when Taliban authorities confront and flog the accused on the spot, such as women violating the Taliban's strict dress code.
MA is an activist in Afghanistan who shared a video with NPR that shows the public flogging of a woman, reportedly in Kandahar province. She asked to be identified only by her initials, fearing repercussions from the Taliban for calling attention to flogging.
MA also pointed to several similar videos on social media. The Taliban bans filming in public areas where flogging as well as stoning takes place, but MA says that individuals who oppose the practice have been discretely filming these events, then posting the video.
NPR was not able to independently verify the content of the videos. A request for comment from the Taliban was not answered.
'A very important element of how they see justice'
Why has the Taliban embraced flogging?
"The floggings are an important aspect of administration of justice in the Taliban's eyes," says Shaharzad Akbar, executive director of the Afghan human rights group Rawadari. "It's a very important element of how they see justice, the rule of law and how they use it to control and repress the population," says Akhar, who is based in Europe.
Samira Hamidi, South Asia regional campaigner at Amnesty International, says she agrees. "The increased use of public floggings and other corporal punishments serves not only as a form of punishment but also as a tool of intimidation and social control."
Beyond the brutality of these punishments, legal experts say they violate the country's commitment to international law.
"Afghanistan is a party to several human rights instruments, and even after the Taliban took over, it has remained a member of these international human rights treaties, which therefore carry obligations on the government to protect these rights for all individuals in Afghanistan," explains Haydee Dijkstal, a U.K.-based lawyer specializing in international human rights who provided legal analysis for the AHRDO report. These treaties include the Convention against Torture, the Convention on Civil and Political Rights, and the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination.
"These obligations prohibit treatment that amounts to cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or torture," she says.
"When something is called a punishment but itself constitutes a human rights violation, it cannot be considered a lawful punishment or justice," she says.
Who gets flogged? Women and marginalized groups
The AHRDO report noted that women and marginalized groups such as Afghanistan's LGBT community remain most disproportionately impacted by the rise in such punishments.
One reason, the report notes, is that the Taliban officials are flogging individuals based on discriminatory and illegal charges. The crimes of the accused, such as women appearing in public without a mahram (a male guardian), same-sex relations, extramarital relations or women "running away" from homes, are protected fundamental human rights under international law.
"Women face a heightened risk because they are subject to a range of discriminatory restrictions that regulate their movement, dress, behaviour, and participation in public life," Hamidi says.
Since taking over, the Taliban have issued dozens of decrees that prohibit women from higher education, most forms of employment and political and even public participation.
"In this context, corporal punishment becomes another mechanism for enforcing gender-based discrimination and maintaining the Taliban's systematic repression of women and girls," she adds.
The Taliban commitment to these punishments is part of its dismantling of the Afghan legal system since taking power.
"The rise of corporal punishment aligns with that lack of an independent and impartial judiciary in Afghanistan and is a way of imposing fear and control over the population," Dijkstal says.
"The cases lacked due process and violated the right to a fair trial," she says, adding that in cases documented by AHRDO, not one person was allowed proper legal representation or allowed to present a defense or even speak in court. "It was a gross violation of what is considered under international law to be a minimum standard to be considered a fair trial."
At the same time, women have been shut out of the justice system, says Akbar. Since taking power in 2021, the Taliban has dismissed approximately 270 women judges as well as roughly 1,500 women registered as lawyers with the Afghanistan Independent Bar Association. Today, there are no women judges, prosecutors or officially registered female lawyers in the country.
"So for women, when they are accused of something, there's no way that they can pursue a defense. It's much harder to negotiate a way out of that punishment, because they simply can't," she says.
In one case documented by AHRDO, identified as PF003, the victim was detained from the public bazaar for wearing a long coat instead of the burqa. "They were settling the bill with the shopkeeper when several Taliban members entered the shop and questioned the shopkeeper about why he had allowed an "unveiled" woman into his premises," the report noted. The woman was arrested and beaten, causing a bleeding head wound, and then sentenced to 15 lashes.
"This is not a system meant to serve the population," Akbar says. "It's not meant to keep anyone safe. It's certainly not meant to keep women and children safe. In fact, it exposes women and children to more violence and abuse and trauma," she added.
In several case studies documented by AHRDO, women who approached the Taliban courts to complain about domestic abuse, violence and even rape were arrested and charged with moral crimes and sentenced to public lashing.
In one case, documented as PF006, the report noted that the victim, who had an intellectual disability, was detained by the Taliban in her garden and taken to a security checkpoint where she was raped. These details were provided when AHRDO interviewed a family member.
When the family tried to register a complaint against the Taliban member, the authorities instead imprisoned the victim and sentenced her on a charge of "having a relationship outside of marriage."
She was convicted and sentenced to twenty lashes and two months' imprisonment, during which she suffered life-threatening injuries, as her family shared with AHRDO.
Flogging in public has many consequences
The public nature of these punishments is also a reason for concern among activists. Several victims interviewed for the AHRDO report talked of the social ostracization that followed the sentencing.
"In cases of women being whipped or jailed, there's additional damage to her reputation which, in a place like Afghanistan, impacts her ability to reintegrate into her family and community," Akbar points out, noting that many women victims have struggled to find medical help for injuries suffered during the floggings.
"They are completely isolated and stigmatized as well, in addition to having experienced that trauma," she says.
Akbar worried about the impact of these public punishments on another group: the spectators. "I wonder about the people who are invited to watch these; what does it say about someone who would line up to see another human being beaten up?" she says.
Hamidi raises similar concerns. "It normalizes violence, fosters fear and self-censorship, and weakens trust in justice systems and public institutions," she says.
The psychological impact on the population, not just the survivors but also the community, "the people watching," is worrisome.
"The Taliban will not last forever," Akbar says, "but what if we can't break out of this chain of trauma, anger and resentment they are inculcating within the communities.
