No new striker, no worries - Havertz and Odegaard torment Chelsea
- Published
Arsenal shelled out close to £200m on new signings during the summer transfer window but fell short of landing the elite forward they craved.
Former Manchester City goalscorer Julian Alvarez was on their radar but remains at Atletico Madrid, while the Gunners were also interested in Aston Villa's Morgan Rogers, Paris St-Germain's Bradley Barcola and Vinicius Jr.
While Rogers opted for London rivals Chelsea, Barcola moved to Liverpool and Vinicius Jr has stayed at Real Madrid.
Yet reigning champions Arsenal have started this season as strongly as they finished 2025-26, when they celebrated their first Premier League title for 22 years.
After wins over Coventry City and Aston Villa, they came from behind to beat big-spending Chelsea 2-1 in a thrilling derby on Sunday - thanks to goals from two familiar faces.
Kai Havertz, an Arsenal player since 2023, and Martin Odegaard, who joined in 2021, scored as they passed their first big test of the campaign against opponents who have spent close to £350m since the end of last season.
A maximum nine points from three games, one goal conceded and big players stepping up.
"I can't see anyone stopping Arsenal," former Premier League winner Chris Sutton told BBC Sport.
'Our mentality is to keep fighting'
It is surely too early in the season to get carried away, and there are likely to be bigger tests ahead for Mikel Arteta's side.
But Arsenal have set down an early marker as they chase back-to-back Premier League crowns.
Along with Manchester City, they are one of only two clubs with a maximum nine points from three games.
After sweeping aside Coventry on the opening day of the season, they produced a mature performance to come away with all three points at Villa.
Against Chelsea, they had to find a different way to win after £117m signing Rogers fired Chelsea into a second-minute lead.
"Our mentality is to keep fighting. We have shown that many times," said captain Odegaard, who scored the 50th-minute winner after Havertz had equalised before half-time.
"We never want to concede early, but the reaction is top. We got our reward in the end and the response was brilliant.
"We showed our quality with and without the ball and the result reflects that."
Odegaard has scored three goals in four appearances in all competitions this season, after netting only once in 36 last term.
"It was a big game, massive game, tough opponent, and we got there in the end, so brilliant," he said.
Former Manchester United and England player Ashley Young said Odegaard's form will be key for Arsenal this season.
"He's just a joy to watch," Young told BBC Sport.
"He's exciting when he gets on the ball, he's allowing other players to get on the ball.
"The connection down the right side between him, Bukayo Saka and Havertz - it's just good to see when you've got players that know each other and build relationships in that way.
"Riccardo Calafiori has been brilliant from last season. He seems to me like he's the one that's got a free role in the team.
"It was his run, and he played it precisely, for the winning goal. He goes quickly, takes people out of the way. It's just clever. Arsenal deserved all three points."
Havertz said Odegaard was back to his "very best".
"He's an unbelievable player - we have seen that over the last years," said the Germany forward.
"He's going to help us a lot this season."
'Arsenal are a powerhouse'
Sutton said Arsenal are still ahead of the rest, despite their rivals spending hundreds of millions of pounds during the transfer window.
"They're such a powerhouse," said the former Blackburn and England striker.
"Chelsea are a good team, but Arsenal always find a way to win. Can you stop Arsenal? I don't think they [other Premier League teams] can."
Arsenal have won their opening three games of a top-flight campaign while conceding fewer than two goals (1) for the third time - after 1924-25, when they finished 20th, and 2003-04, when they went the season unbeaten.
They have also won eight league games in a row stretching back to last season.
Having seen off big-spending Chelsea, their next league match is at Sunderland on Saturday.
Before that Arsenal launch their Champions League campaign at Napoli on Wednesday.
Havertz said Arsenal will head to Italy with confidence high with after seeing off his former club Chelsea.
"Chelsea have an amazing squad, but so do we," said Havertz, who scored the winning goal for the Blues against Manchester City in the 2021 Champions League final.
"We knew it was going to be tough. They scored early, so it's not easy for us, but we believed in ourselves and changed the game around."

Australia will allow social media account holders to opt out of the powerful algorithms pushing dangerous and divisive content into users’ feeds, part of new laws designed to boost online safety.
Users over 16 years of age will be given new tools to turn off algorithm-driven content, with platforms facing fines of more than A$100m for non-compliance.
Under the plan – dubbed “my feed, my way” – users opting out of the algorithm will see content only from individuals and groups they have actively chosen to follow.
Users would be asked what they want their default feed to be through a pop-up message provided on their platform of choice.
New laws designed to provide a digital duty of care for social media users under 18 will also require services such as online games, apps and AI chatbots to protect children from specific harms.
They will include pornography; content that promotes, encourages or accelerates eating disorders; misogynistic content; content that glorifies crime or life-endangering stunts; and content that causes serious mental health distress, including abuse and bullying.
The regulator, the eSafety commissioner, will have the power to issue removal notices to social media companies, with platform operators required to document measures taken to address online harms.
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, is expected to highlight the plans at the United Nations general assembly in New York later this month.
“This is not about giving government control, it is about giving people control,” he said.
Albanese dismissed concerns of possible retaliation by big tech platforms, and their owners, many of whom have close relationships with the US president, Donald Trump.
The Labor government will require the support of the Greens to advance the laws through parliament. The opposition Liberals and Nationals have flagged opposition, warning the government against efforts to censor the internet.
“Of course there will be opponents, because what this is about is changing the power relationship,” Albanese said.
“We’re taking power from big global tech companies and giving it to ordinary Australians. That is what we are doing. It’s the right thing to do.”
The communications minister, Anika Wells, said tech companies had for too long been allowed to run real-time, unregulated product testing on Australian users.
“There is a global reckoning coming for big tech,” she said. “And it started here in Australia, with the introduction of our world-leading social media minimum age laws.”
The legislation is expected to be introduced to parliament before Christmas, but will likely face a lengthy public inquiry and negotiations.
The Greens communications spokesperson, Sarah Hanson-Young, warned the draft legislation should have a lower threshold for harm, and penalties for platforms should be a percentage of their global revenue.
“Opt out is not acceptable,” she said.
“Opt out is a recipe for big tech to manipulate and to get around it. They’ve got a lot of money, and we know that big tech will be looking for every crack, every possible workaround. So we need to tighten this up and make sure it is watertight.”
The Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, said Labor could not be trusted with “censorship powers”.
“Rather than trying to rig the algorithm, the government should focus on fixing the problems of too high prices, too much tax and too much migration.”
A spokesperson for DIGI, the lobby group representing tech companies including Meta, Snapchat and Google, defended algorithms as helpful to users seeking diverse content.
“We also recognise there is community concern about how these systems work and DIGI welcomes the discussion on the role of recommender systems in online safety,” they said.
“We support an approach that gives people meaningful choice and control over the content they see, while managing safety risks.”
Campaigner Chanel Contos, founder of Teach Us Consent, called the draft laws a good first step by the government.
“This reform sends the right message to Big Tech,” she said. “You cannot introduce harmful features into our digital lives without asking for our consent first.”
Tom Mooney, campaign director for Democracy Counts, an alliance of organisations concerned about the function of democratic institutions in Australia, said common facts and diversity of opinion was essential.
“Social media is where the majority of Australians get their news, where many people spend hours each day,” he said. “It is common sense to require platforms to give users choice over those experiences.”
Countries including France, Britain and New Zealand are following Australia in implementing social media bans for children, even as expert research showed the systems put in place in Australia in December is only partly effective.

The days when almost every other fast-growing startup could attract large investor cheques are over. However, this heightened caution has not diminished investor interest across the board. Sectors such as quick commerce, AI, deeptech, and robotics have come to the forefront. Since several businesses in these sectors are capital-intensive and require longer gestation periods, patient capital has also emerged as a key theme in the ecosystem this year. India’s startup ecosystem, which now commands a combined valuation of more than $700 Bn, is therefore entering a phase in which investor caution is coexisting with the emergence of new billion-dollar companies. Edu leaves Nottingham Forest after turbulent spell
- Published
Global head of football Edu has left Nottingham Forest after just over a year at the City Ground.
The former Arsenal midfielder has not attended a game since February and his exit, with his contract believed to have been terminated, has been expected.
His position came under the spotlight after a falling-out with Nuno Espirito Santo, who was sacked last September, the first of four managers at Forest last season.
Nuno hinted at internal tensions and said at the time his relationship with owner Evangelos Marinakis had changed.
Edu is not expected to be replaced, with Forest's chief football officer George Syrianos assuming his responsibilities.
Appointed in July 2025, Edu's remit included Greek side Olympiacos and Portuguese club Rio Ave, who are also owned by Marinakis.
He arrived after six years at Arsenal, where he became the club's first sporting director in 2022, having won two Premier League titles and two FA Cups as a player with the Gunners.
He brought Mikel Arteta to Emirates Stadium, who delivered the club's first Premier League title in 22 years last season.
Edu's departure comes after former Olympiacos vice-president Theodore Giannikos was appointed chief executive last week.
He replaced Lina Souloukou, who stepped down from the role at the City Ground at the end of last season.

A pair of heels, a saree or a kurta bought for Diwali could easily be worn again at a wedding or a family function. Similarly, a skin or haircare product picked up during a festive sale may end up becoming part of the shopper’s daily routine. But there is no guarantee that the shopper that stumbled upon new brands during the festive season sale will return to that same brand again and again. So brands often find themselves back at day zero, fighting for attention all over again and spending money to reacquire users after the festive season bows out. This raises a simple question: how can brands retain users beyond the festive season? Making Customers Reopen Their Wallets Inc42’s conversations with D2C brands around this year’s festive marketing playbook point to a broader shift in how companies are thinking about growth beyond the festive season. Retention and remarketing are emerging as critical levers for brands looking to turn festive shoppers into repeat customers. Brands need to track what the shopper bought and what they might need next. Most brands we spoke with see smart product recommendations and discovery as a key way to drive repeat purchases and build. The first step is communication and messaging. Having scaled up to ₹270 Cr in operating revenue over the past nine years, Bengaluru-based The Bear House is now seeking a larger contribution from denim, trousers and complete outfits. The brand’s scale thus far has come from building a business weighted towards topwear or shirts. Cofounder Harsh Somaiya said this journey to selling more jeans starts as a communication challenge. “For example, if someone comes to us for shirts, the next conversation shouldn't be, ‘Here is another shirt.’ It could be, ‘If you liked this, here's how you can complete the look,’” he told Inc42. Libas founder and CEO Sidhant Keshwani takes this one step further and added that personalisation in communication greatly improves the chances of getting the second purchase. According to him, customer segmentation is vital to enable personalisation at scale. The brand separates customers by product interests, age, location and season, which allows the marketing team to tailor WhatsApp messages and other communication accordingly. Escaping The Discount Trap Personalisation allows brands to retain new customers at higher margins rather than a discount-driven play. This is also why most brands are constantly experimenting with low discount phases even during peak season. The real test of festive retention is not whether customers buy again but whether they come back without another discount. A customer who returns only when the brand cuts prices is boosting repeat orders but doing little for profitability. Higher purchase frequency may therefore conceal a risk in which the brand keeps surrendering margin to secure the next order. Women’s occasion wear brand Koskii encountered that pressure while expanding online. Cofounder Umar Akhtar recalled that its stores had largely sold at full price, but last year’s online push involved more discounting than the company wanted. “You have some brands where they launch at a 70% discount. Nobody will buy them at 50% because 70% is a standard discount,” said Akhtar. In 2026, the startup plans to control incentives more closely and focus on sharper product pricing, rather than become associated with a permanent sale. The risk also extends to how customers perceive the original price. Speaking to Inc42 earlier, Aukera founder Lisa Mukhedkar highlighted how large markdowns can raise doubts about pricing and quality. This is why separating repeat demand from festive purchases requires a clear starting point. Segmentation has to cover each stage of the customer journey from registering interest to placing the first order to finally returning for another purchase. Each of these has to be treated as a different stage and requires specific processes to help grow retention. Akhtar recalled that Koskii’s September 2025 bridal campaign attracted approximately 10,000 registrations, of which 864 participants subsequently bought. At an average order value of about ₹17,000, the campaign generated roughly ₹1.5 Cr in directly attributable revenue, with purchases continuing into August 2026. But this success only captures prospective customers becoming buyers, not buyers returning for repeat purchases. Assessing the campaign immediately after the festive season would have missed revenue arriving later through repeat purchases, and there is the risk that some of the delayed conversions would be treated as retention and this would overstate repeat customer data and behaviour. This is why a 90-day repeat-purchase assessment should trigger after the customer places their first order. Each category’s buying cycle can then inform how such an assessment should be interpreted. Don’t Bet Before You Test But simply following customers throughout this phase is not for every brand. Only brands that can afford a large campaign to stay visible through this 90-day assessment period should look to formalise such a process. The choice entirely depends on how much capital is available to stay on the customer’s radar and how quickly the business needs evidence that its retention strategy is working. Koskii’s Akhtar highlighted this distinction when discussing the limits of broad offline advertising. He recalled that roughly 60% of Koskii’s media budget once went towards non-digital channels, even though an overwhelming majority of customers identified online channels as a discovery source. This feedback gave the company a reason to reconsider its allocation. That does not mean low-cost experiments will not work. They offer a different proposition. Akhtar added that Koskii is testing pop-up shops in apartments and corporate parks to improve visibility. While these experiments are early, their appeal is partly rooted in the limited budgets required to execute this given the high visibility the brand will get in return. The same test-before-expansion approach worked for cosmetics brand RENEE. Cofounder Ashutosh Valani recalled that a television campaign targeting selected regions and programmes last year did not deliver the expected results. But since it was a pilot, the company could reevaluate its approach after the initial response and avoided committing to a larger campaign. A message, an ad or a reminder can bring a shopper back, but it cannot fix the reason they left your shop without buying in the first place, said Valani. Product performance, education and satisfaction are foundations of retention and RENEE’s subsequent campaigns introduced related products. All this comes to nought if the product experience is poor. Brands can identify where that experience falls short by integrating data from various channels (online and offline) as well as customer touchpoints. Having spent the first few years of their lifetimes trying to bring in new users, mature D2C brands are today putting more money into keeping customers beyond the temporary peak and bringing them back to their storefronts multiple times. Shoppers are easy to win over during the festive season but retention is a tough nut. So, who’s up for the challenge? When is the Ballon d'Or ceremony?
The 70th Ballon d'Or ceremony will take place on October 26, 2026 in London.
How are the Ballon d'Or winners decided?
The shortlist was compiled by a group of journalists from France Football working alongside French sports publication L'Equipe.
For the men's Ballon d'Or prize, winners are decided by a voting system involving one journalist from each of the top 100 FIFA-ranked nations.
Each journalist casts votes for their top 10 players from the 30-player shortlist. The 10 players are awarded 15, 12, 10, seven, five, four, three, two and one point based on where they rank.
If players are tied on points, then whoever has the most first-place rankings from the 100 journalists finishes ahead on points. If that is tied, then it's the most second-places and so on.
Journalists are encouraged to consider three factors when deciding their vote:
- Individual performances, decisive and impressive character
- Team performances and achievements
- Class and fair play
For the women's Ballon d'Or, the same process applies but only journalists from the top-50 ranked nations are invited to vote.

After 52 patients from Andhra Pradesh were rushed to Bhadrachalam Area Hospital in Telangana’s Bhadradri Kothagudem district during an overnight medical emergency, the Polavaram district administration offered to support the Telangana hospital with medicines and drugs, recognising that nearly 40% of its patient load comes from Andhra Pradesh.
The 52 patients, including 47 children and five adults, were brought to the hospital from Gollaguppa village in Polavaram district, Andhra Pradesh, after reportedly falling ill post taking chloroquine tablets distributed during a health camp. One child was brought dead, while 12 patients tested positive for malaria.
A large number of children and adults arrived at the facility within a short period, but the hospital did not turn away patients from across the border. Despite having limited staff initially available, Bhadradri Kothagudem District Coordinator of Hospital Services (DCHS) G. Ravi Babu and Area Hospital Superintendent Rajasekhar Reddy and the hospital team immediately mobilised additional doctors and support staff who worked through the night, initiating treatment and closely monitoring the children and adults.
Polavaram District Collector K. Dinesh Kumar appreciated the Bhadrachalam Area Hospital team for extending immediate, compassionate and professional care to patients from Andhra Pradesh.
But the response from Andhra Pradesh went beyond appreciation. The Polavaram district administration assured that medicines required by Bhadrachalam Area Hospital would be extended to the facility. Nearly 40% of its patient load comes from Andhra Pradesh, making the Bhadrachalam facility an important healthcare centre for people living in neighbouring areas of the State.
Dr. G. Ravi Babu said the incident demonstrated the strength and responsiveness of a well-coordinated public healthcare system. “For a healthcare professional, a patient’s identity is never defined by State boundaries,” he said.

It's festive season again and in Bengaluru's upscale neighbourhoods, the sight of women in colourful uniforms — black, purple, pink or green — is becoming too commonplace to ignore. Most of these women, gig workers for the likes of Urban Company, Snabbit or Pronto, are stationed just outside the gates of the large community that they visit routinely. Many of them spend hours waiting for the next order or a ride back home. In inclement weather, there’s no shelter or cover. Some sit on the back of a parked motorbike or perch themselves at a bus stop if there’s one nearby. Many often mill at roadside tea stalls, if they find a safe space. That last part is key. A few have taken to the steps of a nearby temple, phone in hand, scrolling, waiting for the next booking to land so that they are finally able to earn their dues of the day. “Typically, the waiting can stretch for hours and even though we are out of our homes for a living, we don’t earn anything unless an order is placed. When someone books the service it is assigned to the nearest professional or the one who can reach you within 10 minutes,” said Jhanki Devi (name changed on request) who works with Urban Company’s InstaHelp vertical. On a good day, she completes 4-5 hours of household work within a single gated community but on most days, this is not enough to meet her app commitments. She then has to continue being logged in to go to the home where the next order comes from. Gig workers along the way keep the chain going, because if she can’t find the right bus, she has to book an auto or a bike taxi using Namma Yatri, Uber or Rapido. While the scene of gig workers outside prominent gated communities has become ubiquitous in dense residential neighbourhoods in Bengaluru, Mumbai and Delhi NCR, not much focus has landed on the plight of the gig workers fuelling this boom. With another festive season upon us, it’s pertinent to see where things are headed. Because just under a year ago, Inc42 wrote about the festive season rush that created the instant help category. Now the rush in 2026 is taking Snabbit, Urban Company and Pronto to expand, grow more profitable and extract more from its gig worker base. In Diwali 2025, when the category was still finding its feet, the focus was on bringing in more workers. Now this Diwali, the category doesn't need a festive season to prove itself; the focus is on maximisation. Order volumes touched record highs in August, weeks before the festive season began. A nearly 6x rise in consolidated order volumes has been seen since October 2025, i.e. from 8 Lakh monthly bookings to more than 50 Lakh bookings in July 2026. The upcoming festive season will further lead to a spike in bookings and the need for the overall industry to meet the demand, but it’s not just about adding more workers, there’s also some focus on maximising revenue. And in this churn, gig workers are getting squeezed even further.. A New Growth Era For Instant Help Speaking to Inc42, Bengaluru-based Pronto’s spokesperson said the company’s professionals served more than 1.5 Mn bookings in August alone across 10 cities — up from 1.25 Mn, 950,000 and roughly 837,000 in the three months before that. One year ago, Pronto had operations in two cities and about 20 micromarkets, serving a few thousand bookings a day. But this 5x growth in terms of city presence was expensive. Pronto closed its Series B funding round at $45 Mn (₹425.3 Cr) in May 2026, led by Physical Intelligence founder Lachy Groom. The startup raised the round at a valuation of $200 Mn (₹1,890 Cr), double compared to $100 Mn at which it reportedly raised funds just a few months prior in March 2026. Similarly, Snabbit raised $56 Mn (about ₹527 Cr) in its Series D round co-led by Susquehanna Venture Capital, Mirae Asset Venture Investments and Bertelsmann India Investments. These big deals have fuelled the latest round of growth, but will this growth last or will these startups turn profitable? Even Urban Company, which has well over a decade of operational experience in home services, has not managed to turn profitable when it comes to instant services. All three platforms are still in the red, competing on discounts to hold onto share, and all three depend on the same scarce resource to keep it going:women willing to do this work, at the pay and on the terms currently on offer. Founders and investors believe the boom isn’t because of discounts alone or funding-fuelled customer acquisition, but in fact is possible due to a consistent supply of gig workers. This in turn allows companies to expand into new cities without spending too heavily. So, a year on since the advent of instant help services, it’s pertinent to see how satisfied the workers are when it comes to earnings, social security benefits and working conditions. Inc42 has sent a detailed questionnaire to Snabbit and Urban Company on the payment structures, leave policies and other welfare initiatives for its partners. We will update the story as and when these companies respond, but based on our interviews with workers and some insiders in the companies, here’s where things stand. Urban Company’s Tier-Based Payouts When Insta Help launched in March 2025, the pitch to workers was straightforward: a promised, largely assured monthly income for showing up. Urban Company assured a minimum of ₹20,000 per month, contingent on a worker logging 132 hours in that month. That's not how it works today. Partners are now grouped into tiers described to us as diamond, gold and silver, based on customer ratings and the number of hours logged on the app. “I working as a diamond tier professional, hence some of the benefits like access to more orders, salary cuts if we take more leaves than sanction within 15 days or a month period and earnings are better than those who are in the other tiers,” one professional, working in a North Bengaluru locality, said. She said that the volume of orders for any worker is tied to ratings within that tier and this can translate into better pay if the worker consistently gets high ratings . Meanwhile, Urban Company’s claims of assured salary were disputed by a majority of the workers who told us that the company follows the broader industry wage structure now. This means tying payments to logged-in hours and customer ratings. Notably, InstaHelp currently advertises an assured income of ₹20,000–25,000 a month at an hourly rate of ₹150–180, with the company's own claim that its top 5% of workers earn more than ₹50,000 a month. Inc42 could not independently verify whether any workers in Bengaluru earn that high an amount every month. Meanwhile, an independent survey of workers from March 2026 put InstaHelp’s average monthly pay at roughly ₹21,000 for an eight-hour day. This is in the same range the company cites — and separately the survey found that a worker who logs out mid-shift for an emergency can be docked a full day's pay, not just for the hours missed. The payout, according to the UC InstaHelp workers we spoke to, comes every 15 days or every 30 days, depending on the tier. Plus. earnings are strictly tied to being logged in 6 to 8 hours each day of the month. The company permits workers only two days of paid leaves a month, and these days are not accounted for when payouts are calculated. Inside A 12-Hour Snabbit Day Snabbit is not publicly listed and as such the company is not obligated to disclose how many workers it currently engages for instant help services. The company's public numbers have stayed in a fairly narrow band over the past year, even as its order volumes multiplied more than tenfold. After its Series B round in May 2025, Snabbit said workers on a 12-hour shift earned "upward of ₹40,000" a month, with four hours a day translating to just over ₹10,000. By its Series C round that October, the figure being quoted had shifted to a ₹25,000–30,000 every month. However, this pay was still hour-linked, and most certainly not fixed. Snabbit’s annual revenue rate is said to have been around $11 Mn at its peak in 2025 (FY26) and as per media reports, it’s currently on track to achieve close to $40 Mn in revenue by the end of the ongoing FY27 fiscal year. But Snabbit has not disclosed its audited financials for the past fiscal year (FY26) and without this, it’s hard to verify these numbers. Earlier this year, Snabbit’s CEO Aayush Agarwal claimed that time spent on the app has increased by 50%, and the company is said to have displaced Urban Company in terms of monthly order volume with 1.5 Mn orders in the month of June 2026 Snabbit has onboarded more than 15,000 workers just this year, according to numbers reviewed by Inc42. But the pay structure, according to four Snabbit workers we spoke to, has remained unchanged since last year. Social media posts have alleged that Snabbit workers lose an average of ₹1000 for every day of missed work. This repeatedly came up during our conversations with workers, but Agarwal had denied that any such policy exists in previous statements. Is Pronto Any Different Than The Others? The youngest company of the trio told Inc42 that its professionals earn a fixed component every month, which is linked to the hours they work and a variable component tied to completed bookings, with a 12-hour day resulting in an average ₹1,000 payout for workers. “There is no promised fixed minimum monthly salary. Earnings depend on the availability and how much work a professional takes on,” the company said in an emailed statement to Inc42. The worker-side app breaks down each day's earnings and any deductions in real time. Separately, Pronto's own in-app pricing has been reported to be as low as ₹1 an hour for first-time bookings and around ₹50 an hour for utensil-cleaning bookings. This pricing floor raises its own questions about how this claimed fixed-plus-variable structure would hold up, when the customer-side pricing is so aggressive. Pronto is one of the most aggressive when it comes to discounts in the space. Its discounts are primarily funded from the company’s balance sheet, not impacting the worker wage structures, the company claimed. But again, this is not a company that has disclosed its financials in the past fiscal year i.e FY26. These claims will only be tested and the company’s confidence in its business model can only be justified when the numbers are out in the open. The Unpaid Hours In Between Beyond work hours, what becomes even more challenging for a worker on the field is the waiting time between jobs. This part of the job is not paid. Pronto founder and CEO Anjali Sardana had earlier stated that the waiting period roughly constitutes 13-20% of the working day on average. But our conversations with instant help workers revealed going to and fro bookings is largely left to the worker themselves. Most rely on public transport, or simply walk, because the cost of an auto ride might be too high. Pronto, responding to our questions, said the vast majority of its workers get to their next job on foot, with a smaller share covered on Yulu bikes that the company provides in certain localities. Workers are urged to wait close to the neighbourhoods where they get bookings from, which the company says, helps reduce travel time. Yulu CEO Amit Gupta told Inc42 earlier that the company has partnered with instant help apps in some areas and he expects the demand to increase because workers can afford the daily rental cost of ₹200 for bikes. Another issue plaguing gig workers currently is unavailability of waiting spots or restrooms in high demand areas, where usually access to facilities is not available. “We use public washrooms, wherever possible. It is a hindrance because we cannot directly ask just any customer to allow us access to their washrooms,” 28-year-old Anisa (name changed), who works with Pronto in Bengaluru, told us Waiting outside large gated societies is not always safe and some workers have complained about safety and security risks too. Pronto had reportedly started setting up local waiting centres or hubs in some areas of Bengaluru, however it is not clear whether these facilities are adequately distributed or have the amenities that gig workers might need. On the safety side, each of the platforms claim to have introduced some sort of feature within the app for workers to reach out when in distress. However, when we asked how many such SOS complaints or queries have been fielded by these companies in the past year, we did not get a specific answer from either Pronto, Urban Company or Snabbit. Shaik Salauddin, the national general secretary of the Indian Federation Of App Based Transport Workers (IFAT) which also looks at the welfare of other gig workers, told us that the union has received complaints from women workers related to harassment, including alleged sexual harassment by customers. The pressure of poor ratings, complaints or account suspension can force women workers to tolerate unacceptable behaviour, he added. “The algorithmic allocation of orders, that could also lead to pressure on women workers to accept jobs even when a location or customers feel unsafe has also been reported to us,” Salauddin added. New Festive Season, Same Old Math Now with another peak demand season here, instant help apps are expecting major growth numbers this year. They are working on top of a bigger base as compared to 2025, catering to millions of customers who had never heard of the app one year ago. But for the all-women workforce of these instant help apps, working conditions are yet to change for the better and for others, the situation is getting worse. The real question is whether the companies will invest in infrastructure and higher incentives for workers when they see the outcome after this boom. While platforms have invested heavily in the consumer side of the business by waging a discounts war, the companies cannot retain the workers under existing conditions and that is probably why even the instant help segment has worker supply and retention problems. Jhanki Devi, who was quoted earlier in the story, said candidly that the instant help industry which is entirely driven by women workers is yet to realise the challenges that women face while going about their daily work and responsibilities. She brought it back to one simple thing: menstruation leave. “In physically demanding jobs like this, we aren’t even entitled to one day of period leave. And that should tell you why many of us cannot see ourselves doing this kind of gig work for long.” For instant help platforms like Snabbit, Urban Company and Pronto who often pat themselves on the back for providing a platform for unemployed women, fixing these arcane practices should be the biggest priority this festive season.

Fiorentina brought back Paolo Vanoli as coach on Monday, a day after showing former World Cup winner Fabio Grosso the door following a nightmare start three games into the new Serie A season.
Grosso was dismissed after three successive defeats left Fiorentina bottom of the league standings, with the team scoring only one goal while conceding nine.
The appointment marks a swift return for Vanoli, who previously rescued the club from relegation trouble last season after replacing Stefano Pioli in November following a winless 10-game start.
He eventually guided them clear of the drop zone to a 15th-place finish while also steering the club to the Conference League quarterfinals where they were knocked out by eventual winners Crystal Palace.
“ACF Fiorentina  announces that Coach Paolo Vanoli has been appointed as the new technical director of the Viola first team,” the club said in a statement.
“A huge thank you goes to the coach for his enthusiastic acceptance of returning to lead the first team.”
Vanoli will get his first chance to turn things around on Friday when Fiorentina travel to face promoted Venezia, who are also winless after three games with no points.

Hungary expels 10 Russian diplomats, Moscow vows ‘painful’ response
Budapest says the envoys had acted in ways incompatible with their status, but stresses the decision does not mean cutting ties with Russia
Hungary expelled 10 Russian diplomats on Tuesday, saying they had acted in ways incompatible with their diplomatic status, in a stark reminder that the pro-Russian years of former prime minister Viktor Orban are over.
Russia’s foreign ministry said it would retaliate and its response would be painful for Hungary, local media reported.
“The response to the Russophobic lobby in Budapest will be harsh and painful,” said foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova.
Orban, swept from power in Hungary in April after 16 years in office, had kept close ties with Russian President Vladimir Putin even after Moscow invaded Ukraine in February 2022.
Under him, Hungary continued buying Russian oil and gas, held up European Union sanctions on Russia and blocked a €90 billion (US$97 billion) EU loan to Ukraine.
After Russia invaded Ukraine, many European countries expelled dozens of Russian diplomats, while Hungary expelled none. Until Tuesday, it had not sent any home publicly since 2018.

A school aged child has died and six others have been taken to hospital with injuries after a single vehicle crash in Parwan, west of Melbourne, this afternoon.
Emergency services received reports of a crash near the Nerowie and Parwan-Exford road intersections just before 4pm.
Victorian Police said one child died at the scene while six others were injured.
"Despite CPR being performed, one school-aged child died at the scene," a spokesperson said.
"A second child was airlifted with critical injuries. Five more children were taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.
"One woman was taken to hospital for observation."
Ambulance Victoria said its specialist crews were responding to the incident.
"Two specialist Air Ambulance Victoria helicopter crews, two Mobile Intensive Care Ambulance paramedic crews and five Advanced Life Support paramedic crews are currently on scene," a spokesperson said.
"Their priority is with their patients."
An investigation into the crash is ongoing.

The world is bracing for a “super” El Niño, and its effects are already being felt in India, where the monsoon has brought less rain than average but more intense downpours.
Meteorologists predict that the current El Niño, which is developing over the Pacific, could be one of the strongest in living memory. India is likely to be heavily affected, particularly later in the monsoon, when El Niño’s influence tends to strengthen.
But, as Ligin Joseph of the University of Southampton explains in The Conversation, its effects on India’s monsoon are not straightforward. A previous study in Science found that El Niño tends to bring more extreme summer monsoon rainfall to India.
This year, the southern state of Kerala has felt the brunt of the building super El Niño, with about a fifth less rain than normal. Yet intense downpours in the first week of August triggered flash flooding and landslides, killing 26 people.
The super El Niño is expected to peak after India’s monsoon season, but Indians are already keeping an anxious eye on the skies, wondering where and when the next deluge may come.

In India, newborns are dying. Earlier, they used to die at home without medical care. Now, they are dying in hospitals. On August 24, 2026, three newborns lost their lives in an accidental fire at the government women’s hospital in Amravati, Maharashtra. This was not the first such episode in government newborn care units, and it will not be the last — unless we view it not as an isolated event, but as a trend.
These are episodes of clustered newborn deaths in the government institutions (that were identified by ChatGPT)/in the format of Year/Government hospital/Newborn deaths — 2017 BRD Medical College, Gorakhpur 17; 2017 Government hospital, Ahmedabad 18; 2019 JK Lon Hospital, Kota 10; 2020 JK Lon Hospital, Kota 9; 2020 Government hospital, Shahdol 8; 2021 District Hospital, Bhandara One fire 10; 2021 Kamla Nehru Children’s Hospital, Bhopal One fire 4; 2021 Government Medical College, Ambikapur 4; 2022 Medical College, Ambikapur 4; 2023 Government Medical College, Nanded 12; 2024 Maharani Laxmi Bai Medical College, Jhansi One fire 10; 2025 District Women’s Hospital, Budaun 4; 2026 District Women’s Hospital, Amravati One fire 3
This is not a comprehensive national registry, but only a partial list. The pattern, however, is recurring and therefore demands a systemic response.
The problems and challenges
What is going wrong? The first reason is overcrowding. India has achieved remarkable success in ensuring that women increasingly deliver in health institutions — from 39% in 2005-06 to 90% in 2023-24 (National Family Health Survey-6). But this success has created a new challenge. The absolute number of women delivering in institutions has risen from 109 lakh in 2005 to 194 lakh in 2024-25 (Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), Government of India). The total number of sick newborns hospitalised in public Special Newborn Care Units (SNCUs) has also risen rapidly, from 11.3 lakh in 2021-22 to 14.45 lakh in 2023-24 — a 28% increase in two years (Health Management Information System, MoHFW). Hence, newborn-care units everywhere are becoming overloaded.
The second reason is the changing case mix. As institutional deliveries have expanded, government hospitals have become the destination not only for normal deliveries but also for large numbers of high-risk births, including premature, low-birth-weight and sick newborns referred from peripheral facilities.
Infrastructure failures are the third reason. The Gorakhpur episode of August 2017 was attributed by a district-level inquiry to oxygen deprivation following an interruption in oxygen supply. The fires at Bhandara in January 2021, Bhopal in November 2021 and Jhansi in November 2024, as well as the more recent incident in Amravati, demonstrate the risks posed by fire and electrical hazards in neonatal units. Sick newborns need warmers, incubators and ventilators. Overcrowding can increase the electrical load on these units.
Infection and staffing problems would be the fourth reason. Overcrowding, inadequate nurse-to-baby ratios, equipment shortages and poor infection-prevention practices can turn a neonatal unit into a setting where hospital-acquired infections can spread rapidly.
The Gadchiroli model
This diagnosis leads to some obvious solutions. But there is an additional way.
India already has another solution. More than two decades ago, the Gadchiroli field trial conducted by the Society for Education, Action and Research in Community Health (SEARCH) demonstrated that trained community health workers (CHWs) could provide effective home-based neonatal care (HBNC), resulting in a 62.2% reduction in neonatal mortality in the rural area (The Lancet, 1999). The trained CHWs identified and managed neonatal infections at home, supported breastfeeding and warmth, and managed low-birth-weight and preterm babies. Subsequent data from Gadchiroli, published in the Journal of Perinatology in 2005, showed that between 1996 and 2003, 97% of low-birth-weight and preterm babies — including those with birth weights above 1,800 g and gestational ages of more than 34 weeks — were managed at home, with a very low case-fatality rate.
The principles of the Gadchiroli model have already become a part of India’s public health system (MoHFW, 2011). Around 8,00,000 Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs) have been trained to provide HBNC, using training modules developed from the Gadchiroli experience. Therefore, India does not have to invent a new system. ASHAs, if adequately trained, supervised and supported, can provide many components of newborn care. This could take a considerable load off SNCUs and help reduce overcrowding.
Of course, a baby with severe prematurity, respiratory distress, shock, severe sepsis, serious birth asphyxia or another danger sign needs immediate facility-based treatment. HBNC is not a substitute for neonatal intensive care. But not every newborn who needs care requires a hospital bed.
The optimum strategy
India should therefore adopt a three-part strategy. First, decongest neonatal units. Strengthen HBNC by ASHAs so that appropriate, stable newborns can safely receive care at home rather than occupying scarce SNCU beds.
Second, strengthen neonatal care units. Ensure adequate numbers of doctors and nurses, appropriate nurse-to-baby ratios, functioning equipment, reliable oxygen and electricity supplies with backup systems, along with rigorous infection-prevention measures.
Third, make neonatal units intrinsically safe. Fire detection and suppression systems, electrical and oxygen-system safety measures, emergency evacuation drills and independent safety audits should become mandatory.
The success of the Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY) is unquestionable. Institutional delivery can help save mothers and babies. But the next phase of India’s newborn-health strategy must recognise that getting mothers into hospitals is only the first step. Every mother will give birth to a baby who needs care. But not every newborn who needs care requires a hospital bed. The future of newborn care should not be hospital versus home; it should be hospital plus home.
That would reduce overcrowding and, most importantly, ensure that each newborn receives the right care, at the right place, at the right time.
Abhay Bang is a physician and the founder of Society for Education, Action and Research in Community Health (SEARCH), a community health research organisation

It's back to school season. Here's why there's a push to get rid of cars at dropoff and pickup
Scientists say car-free zones boost safety but making them last has been challenging
As Lily Dejnicki prepares to get back to the classroom, she hopes to see fewer cars during the morning and afternoon rush hours outside her school.
The 13-year-old would like to see the return of a pilot project to get cars out of the regular dropoff zone at her school, Sts. Peter and Paul Catholic Elementary in Mississauga, Ont.
As part of the School Streets project promoted by a non-profit environmental association, volunteers directed cars away during dropoff and pickup times by using barricades and signs. Kids and parents were encouraged to cycle and walk to and from school, as opposed to driving.
"It was lots of fun," said Lily, who is going into Grade 8.
"Kids … wouldn't rush home," she said. "Instead, they would … take a couple minutes to play and stuff outside."
Anita Dejnicki, Lily’s mom, sits on the school’s parental advisory council and said more parents were talking to each other and more kids were active and playing compared to before.
"Once it ended, it just seemed like it was quiet again."
As the school year starts, environmental association Green Communities Canada is continuing its efforts to implement School Streets across the country.
The pilot at Sts. Peter and Paul Catholic Elementary, which ran for a month, is part of a bigger push led by the organization called the National Active School Streets Initiative. It received $3 million in funding from the Public Health Agency of Canada in 2024.
At least 20 School Streets are planned for the 2026-2027 academic year. Over the past few years, they have been piloted in six provinces: British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec and Nova Scotia.
Nicole Roach, sustainable mobility director at Green Communities Canada, said School Streets usually take the form of a temporary barrier installed on both ends of one street next to a school.
The street is typically one that is not on a major thoroughfare or one that is going to cause issues for buses or students with disabilities, she said.
For those who need to drive, one alternative is to drive to a nearby parking area and walk together the rest of the way, Roach said.
Roach points to safety and air pollution from cars as among the reasons to implement School Streets.
"Many schools at pickup and dropoff are just absolute chaos," she said. "We see a lot of dangerous driving behaviour, really unsafe environments for the children walking or wheeling or even just getting to their vehicle for pickup."
Lily, who walks to and from school, said the usual lines of cars at dropoff and pickup can be bothersome.
"It would kind of be not … too safe because it would be really, really crowded," she said.
"Most of my friends … liked [the School Street]. But some people didn't really like it. They would … say that there's no point in doing it."
A bumpy road
Although it's estimated that at least 36 schools across Canada have tested School Streets, implementing them long-term has proven challenging.
Just two permanent, year-round School Streets exist, and at least one pilot ground to a halt after pushback.
Last year, a School Street project at Corliss Public School in Mississauga was cancelled after a parent started a petition, raising concerns about safety and disruption.
"Every day, children and parents are forced to navigate confusing road closures and restricted areas, which not only causes delays but also increases the risk of accidents," the petition, which collected nearly 200 signatures, said.
"The setup leads to congestion in nearby areas, forcing parents to opt for potentially unsafe detours or parking in locations that are less supervised."
Kerstyn Lutz, who studied four School Street pilots in the Greater Toronto Area in 2022, recalls witnessing disruption first-hand.
"At least at the beginning, [it] felt like chaos. You have cars driving up to these barriers, they don't know what to do," said Lutz, a PhD candidate at the University of Toronto at the time of her research. "We have to have vehicle diversion plans…. The reality is not everyone is going to walk."
What do the experts say?
But Raktim Mitra, an urban planning professor at Toronto Metropolitan University who studies sustainable transportation behaviour, said there’s no evidence to suggest School Streets push congestion onto nearby roads or lead to more unsafe driving.
Over the past year, Mitra collected data on travel patterns close to two School Streets pilots in Mississauga.
More cars drove below the designated speed on the street, and a "significantly" higher number of cars were yielding to pedestrians in nearby streets, he said.
As for clogging up nearby streets, Mitra said none of the data suggests that to be a likely problem.
"None of the nearby roads … reached a congested condition."
While children who travel to school by themselves may encounter more people, there's no evidence that more walking as a result of such an initiative would lead to more potentially problematic interactions with strangers, said Lewis Smith, spokesperson for the Canada Safety Council.
"We believe that the bigger concern is teaching children to recognize unsafe situations, to recognize unsafe behaviors and be able to respond to them accordingly."
As for benefits, Mitra and Lutz noted more kids cycled or walked to school.
The absence of cars outside the school also led to a reduction in air pollution in the immediate area, Lutz said.
Canada's 'culture of mobility'
School Streets began in Italy in the 1990s and has spread to other countries.
Mitra said Canada's "culture of mobility" is a factor that can make School Streets face opposition, particularly in suburbs where car travel is the dominant mode of transportation.
He said many parents are used to driving and that "asking them to change that culture … is always difficult."
Resources to enforce School Streets programs have posed another challenge.
In 2023, a year-round program at Lord Roberts Elementary School in Vancouver ended because there weren’t enough volunteers to supervise the School Street.
The volunteer burden is the reason why many School Streets only run as short pilots, said Lucy Maloney, a Vancouver city councillor who was president of the parental advisory committee at Lord Roberts at the time.
"Trying to run a School Street all year round where parents are required to set it up and dismantle it and supervise it is just too much for people to manage."

Maloney, who plans to push for more School Streets as a councillor, said there are measures that could reduce reliance on volunteers such as retractable bollards or camera enforcement.
Lutz is skeptical whether School Streets with permanent, physical infrastructure would work for Canada’s suburban streets.
"Is it going to work the same way it works in a country like Italy? Probably not, because they're already better built for walkability than we are."
For urban areas, Mitra sees School Streets as a possibility.
"About half of our children who attend elementary school … live within half a mile [0.8 kilometres] from their schools, which technically is a 10- to 12-minute walking distance," he said.

While he doesn’t foresee every child walking to school, he said the program can help those who live close by convert short car and bus trips.
"I think that would have significant impact in reducing localized congestion and improving the health and well-being and safety of children."
Lily, for one, sees many positives.
"When I come to school … I'm actually looking forward to doing something … rather than just, like, going straight home."

Saudi Arabia vows to respond after Houthis attack cities and energy facilities
- Published
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement has attacked energy facilities and other civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia with dozens of drones and missiles, injuring 73 people, Saudi authorities say.
Tuesday's attacks hit four south-western cities, causing fires at oil facilities and installations that led to a temporary halt in operations, according to Saudi Arabia's military and energy ministry.
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said that its forces would respond to the "dangerous escalation".
The Houthis said the attacks were retaliation for dozens of recent Saudi strikes on areas of north-western Yemen that they control.
On Monday, they accused Saudi Arabia of bombing a prison in the city of al-Hazm and killing at least 11 people. Twenty inmates are reportedly missing under the rubble.
The spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, said the Houthi drone and missile attacks targeted civilian and economic sites in the cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran, and that women and children were among the injured.
An energy ministry statement cited an official source as saying that injuries were also reported after "several energy sector facilities and installations" were targeted.
The attacks "caused fires at several locations, leading to a temporary halt in some operations," they added.
Maliki described Houthi attacks as a "dangerous escalation that confirms the hostile and irresponsible approach of this terrorist militia" and said the Saudi-led coalition would "take all necessary operational measures to deter" the group.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea accused the Saudi military of carrying out more than 120 air strikes on the Yemeni provinces of Marib, al-Bayda, Hudaydah, Taiz and Jawf over the past three days, and of committing "grave crimes".
He said the Houthis had responded to this "brutal aggression" with "dozens of ballistic missiles and drones", which he claimed caused "significant damage".
A Saudi-led coalition of Arab states has backed Yemen's government against the Houthis in the country's devastating civil war for more than a decade.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.
There has been heavy fighting on Yemen's south-western coast since Thursday, when the Houthis launched an offensive against Yemeni pro-government forces in a bid to take control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
The fighting has reportedly left more than 300 people dead and displaced 18,500.
The Red Sea has become crucial for oil shipments from Saudi Arabia during the US and Israel's war with Iran, which has led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

An experimental Novartis drug for a rare neuromuscular condition failed to improve muscle function in a pivotal study, its second major trial collapse in a matter of days, STAT writes. The two study flops will likely stoke concerns about its pipeline and acquisition strategy as it navigates a major patent cliff, though the company did see a victory with a multiple sclerosis drug last week. The stock was down by as much as 10% in early trading in Switzerland. The Phase 3 HARBOR trial was testing the drug del-desiran in a condition called myotonic dystrophy type 1, known as DM1, which causes progressive muscle stiffness and weakness.
Novo Nordisk stopped two trials of a drug that aims to tame inflammation as a way to improve cardiovascular health, another blow for the approach, STAT notes. The company said it had halted the HERMES and ATHENA trials of its drug, ziltivekimab, after a data monitoring committee found they were unlikely to succeed. Novo informed trial investigators on Friday. The move follows the earlier failure of the drug in the ZEUS trial, which showed that the medicine, despite lowering markers of inflammation, did not reduce the risk of major clinical complications, including deaths and heart attacks.

The Victorian One Nation leader, Warren Pickering, has admitted he “made mistakes” in his 20s, including using ecstasy, methamphetamines and marijuana, losing his licence multiple times for drink driving and hurting people he loved.
But he has denied claims by his ex-partner, published by The Australian, that he smoked ice – also known as crystal meth – in front of children and said he was considering legal action against the publication at a press conference on Tuesday. Guardian Australia and the ABC were barred from attending the press conference.
Accompanied by James Ashby, One Nation’s national director, and his daughter and stepson, Pickering said he was “no angel” as a young man and used illegal drugs in his 20s.
“Never would I have ever said that I was somebody who was a drug addict. I did use them … as a young man and I’m not proud of that,” Pickering said.
He listed ecstasy, methamphetamine, speed and marijuana, but denied using ice or smoking it while his children were home.
“No, I did not,” Pickering said, when asked directly.
Pressed by a reporter about whether he had used ice, Pickering said “ice is not on that list.”
When the reporter said methamphetamines are ice, Pickering replied: “Well, speed”.
“Look, guys, I’m clearly not as familiar with the terms … as you would like me to be,” he said.
“I wasn’t an experienced drug taker.”
Pickering also confirmed he lost his driver’s licence three times for drink driving.
“I believe I lost my licence for drink driving as an 18-year-old, and again as a 20-year-old, and then probably a decade later, I believe they were low-level drink driving,” he said.
Pickering said his actions “hurt people I loved, and I will live with that forever”. But he said he had “changed his life dramatically” for the sake of his daughter and three stepsons, stopped using drugs and joined the Australian Defence Force, which he said gave him a sense of purpose.
“That’s what inspired me to engage in the political sphere to provide service to community in a different way, post-service,” he said.
Ashby also spoke, telling reporters a handwritten note from Pickering published by The Australian, which references “sexual deviance”, was in relation to “behaviour that involved the couple’s open relationship”.
“They opened that relationship to a third person, and at the same time, Mr Pickering was exploring his own sexuality,” Ashby said.
Pickering said he was “working with the lawyers” to get the stories taken down and was receiving advice about possible defamation action.
Reporters from The Australian were able to attend the press conference at Crown Casino. However, reporters from both Guardian Australia and the ABC were asked by Ashby to leave after identifying the media outlet they worked for.

It was at the 1992 Olympics in Barcelona when the mutterings about a new "secret weapon" started.
Dozens of Great Britain athletes had been taking a new product that increased muscle mass and improved athletic performance – a "wonder pill" that didn't fall foul of any doping rules.
They were talking about creatine.
Now found in tubs and bags on many supermarket shelves and tagged in your social feeds, it is the supplement of choice for millions of people and one of the most scientifically researched.
But back then, when it came on the scene at the very top of British elite sport, there were suspicions and stigma around the use of any substance described as 'performance enhancing' – even if it was legal.
From the minute an athlete wakes, to the moment they go to bed, they are thinking about how they can optimise their performance and recovery.
Today, creatine is just one of a long list of supplements taken by elite athletes in this pursuit of marginal gains. Some help with muscle size and strength, while others correct deficiencies in the diet.
"There are various reports in the literature of some studies that say maybe up to 90% of athletes take supplements. I often jokingly say that means 10% are lying," says Prof Graeme Close, professor of human physiology at Liverpool John Moores University.
"The sports teams that I've worked in, I think that's probably closer to 100% of athletes will be taking some form of supplementation."
So, what do supplements actually do and why do athletes take them? And in the world of strict liability, where elite athletes are solely responsible for what they put in their bodies, how do they make sure they stay clean?
While experts like Close advocate for seeking to meet nutritional needs through food in the first instance, it may not always be possible or practical to do this - and that is where supplements come in.
Take, for example, creatine, which is found naturally in meat and fish.
"You would need the best part of a kilogram of raw chicken a day to get the amount of creatine you need," says Close. But it is unsafe to eat raw poultry because of the food poisoning risk from harmful bacteria.
Creatine is a natural compound in the body produced in the kidneys, liver and pancreas. It is a quick source of energy for muscles, which is especially important for short-duration, high intensity activities such as sprinting.
Its big break as a supplement came in the 1990s when two scientists who had been researching it for two decades shared their findings with Steve Jennings, whose Maxim sports nutrition company supplied products to the British Olympic team.
During the 1992 Barcelona Games, investigative reporter Doug Gillon had learned of a 'secret trial' involving British athletes and seen a box of their Ergomax C150 – effervescent creatine tablets. He wrote that if the scientists' claims - that creatine could improve explosive athletic performance by 1-3% - were true, then "sport may never be the same again".
In terms of sport supplements and nutrition, he was right. By the time of the next Olympics in 1996, an estimated 80% of athletes were taking creatine, and since then it has become mainstream, with research suggesting there may be cognitive benefits as well as physical.
According to the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, the creatine breakthrough of the 1990s had "launched a new era in sports nutrition" and "sparked exploration into other supplements".
The global dietary supplements market size was valued at $209.5bn (£154bn) in 2025 and is projected to grow to $431.7bn (£317.4bn) by 2033, according to Grand View Research., external
Close, who oversaw nutrition for last year's British and Irish Lions rugby union tour, sees supplements as the "final piece of the jigsaw" rather than a starting point.
"What we're talking about is small margins of benefit, where actually these athletes who focus on the food, I think what you often find is that they've got the big-ticket items right," he says.
"So they're seeing great performance benefits because their overall diet is immaculate.
"They might be missing out on the one per-centers, but they've really nailed the 99 per-centers. And they often do better than those who chase the one per-centers but have not given enough attention to the 99 per-centers."
Australian cyclist Nicole Frain agrees, adding: "I'm a pretty big believer that they are called sport supplements. They are there to supplement the things you already do right.
"I don't think supplements are the answer to fix my problems.
"You need to be eating a balanced diet, training well, sleeping right, recovering well, hydrating – all of those things – before we add in all of the extras."
Close puts protein powders top of the list of supplements taken by athletes he works with, followed by creatine and vitamin D.
Protein powders maximise muscle repair and contribute to muscle growth, while creatine is a quick source of energy for muscles and important in short-duration, high-intensity activities like sprinting. Vitamin D, meanwhile, is essential for bone health and supports muscle function.
Other popular supplements include carbohydrate gels, which Close says were key in the first sub-two hour marathon run earlier this year by Kenyan long-distance runner Sabastian Sawe.
"As sport nutritionists we were all fascinated at what the fuelling programme was, and it was the sports drinks and gels that played a huge part of that fuelling," Close says.
"There was a calculation done of what it would take to break the two-hour marathon, and that did involve making sure that over 100 grams of supplemental carbohydrate were ingested per hour.
"And the reports coming out of the recent sub-two-hour marathon was that it was 110 grams of carbohydrate per hour that was achieved."
Supplements can improve performance, but there is an uneasy ring to describing them as 'performance enhancing' because of the association with banned substances and anti-doping rule violations.
So what determines whether something is on the World Anti-Doping Agency's (Wada) banned list?
"For Wada to put anything on the list, it's got to hit two out of three criteria: dangerous to health, performance enhancing, and against the spirit of sport," Close explains.
"So just because something enhances performance, if it's not dangerous to health and not against the spirit of sport, Wada will not touch it.
"So creatine is a good example.
"Though something like an anabolic steroid, where it's against the spirit of sport to be injecting yourself for a performance benefit, it's dangerous to health and it's performance enhancing - that hits all three."
But taking a supplement still carries anti-doping risks.
"No guarantee can be given that any particular supplement is free from prohibited substances," UK Anti-Doping advice states, urging athletes to "be vigilant" in using them.
And if you test positive for a prohibited substance, consuming it unintentionally can result in the same four-year ban as if you deliberately took it.
There are supplement-testing programmes which batch test products before they are sold to make sure they do not contain any Wada-prohibited substances.
One of those is Informed Sport, which says as many as one in 10 supplements is contaminated with ingredients and compounds prohibited in sport and points to a study carried out by the Anti-Doping Knowledge Centre that showed product contamination was responsible for 8% of all anti-doping violations between 2005 and 2022.
While Informed Sport is a very well used system among athletes, Wada makes it clear that quality assurance schemes can reduce but do not eliminate the risk of an anti-doping infringement.
If you do accept the risk, you need to be organised to keep track.
In the case of Great Britain rower Heidi Long, it takes a spreadsheet.
"I've recorded the batch number of every product that I've taken and its expiry date because if you take it after the expiry date the Informed Sport [certification] is no longer viable," she says.
Close says he has also done site visits to factories to see where the supplements are made to check the manufacturing processes because "the risk of failing a drugs test is huge".
There are risks to the general population too, he adds, saying: "You can be buying supplements off the internet that are made in somebody's garage and you've got no idea of the manufacturing processes."
He points to studies on creatine products which have found there is no creatine in them and so "you're completely wasting your money" and that in the worst case scenario it may contain substances that are dangerous to your health.
"So it is really important that the message is that while they can play a small role, the safety considerations are the key factor," he says.
There is, however, more than one way for an elite athlete to chase a competitive edge – and some are going back to basics.
For every trending supplement, there is an unprocessed, wholefood alternative – from the anti-inflammatory benefits of turmeric, staving off cramp with pickle juice or consumption of high-nitrate foods like beetroot before competition.
It is what Close calls a "food-first" or "food-only" approach and something he says every athlete should use as a starting point.
The latest to have its moment in the spotlight is an ancient Ethiopian grain called teff.
Used for thousands of years in traditional east African diets, teff is now making its mark globally in performance nutrition.
In comparison to other popular grains like wheat, rice and quinoa, teff has a high mineral content and is rich in calcium, iron and vitamin C. Naturally gluten-free and good for the gut, it is also unique for being a 'complete' protein, meaning it provides all nine essential amino acids required for human nutrition.
These superfood credentials have caught the attention of some of the world's best athletes over the years, from Olympic champion marathon runner Haile Gebrselassie to seven-time Grand Slam singles champion Venus Williams, and it is now becoming a more common sight on UK supermarket shelves.
British boxer Fran Hennessy was introduced to teff by her nutritionist and it is now part of her daily routine.
"I've never looked back," she says. "What I'm putting in my body is good fuel and energy and teff has so much. It energises you so much before a workout and it gives you the fibre you need."
As well as boosting her performances, Hennessy credits teff with being key to recovery.
She says: "Each meal I'm having there's a reason behind and everything that's in it there's a reason behind... I know what I'm putting in my body is fuelling me, recovering me, energising me."
Cost is another consideration when athletes are deciding on supplements.
"The supplement industry is really expensive," says Long. "And we're definitely not made of money. So I think it's really picking and choosing when you want to put that investment in."
She says it makes sense to have more supplements around racing time "when the performance is super critical and very time dependent".
"[But] on a daily basis if I can get the protein intake from my dinner and a glass of milk or yoghurt and breakfast then actually I was going to be eating that food anyway so it's not as expensive."
And then there is taste.
"I would much rather enjoy a coffee in the morning with friends or while I'm working rather than have one of the gels," she says. "Some of the gels ... you'll end up holding your nose when you take it.
"I guess it's just like the enjoyment of what you're taking, you know, it's nicer to eat food than it is to take supplements."

Labor Day sales are the last gasp of summer DIY season, and it almost always means steep discounts on tools and batteries—especially as retailers clear inventory space for the holidays. The Home Depot Labor Day sale goes pretty hard this year, bolstering the usual battery of BOGO deals, as well as end-of-season grill discounts.
Alas, not everything is a winner. The smart home and home-security deals I've seen for Home Depot are either not great deals—or they're on older models or services like Ring that WIRED doesn't recommend for privacy reasons. Check out WIRED's Best Tech Labor Day Deals of 2026, or the Best Amazon Labor Day Deals, if this is what you're after.
But here are the best deals on tools and grills that I've found for 2026's Home Depot Labor Day sale, or check out my colleague Kat Merck's Labor Day deals guide to getting an excellent tool starter kit for less than $400. You can also browse Home Depot's Labor Day deals by category, but fair warning: There's a lot to sift through.
Home Depot Labor Day Grill and Griddle Deals
The steepest Labor Day price cuts are often on grills and griddles. At Home Depot, the best deals are on Traeger's stock of pellet smokers that offer easy temperature control, but maybe a little less smoke than charcoal or wood cookers. These have the side benefit of maintaining utility through the cool months. In the temperate, four-season Pacific Northwest, I actually far prefer fall to summer as a grill and smoker season.
Discounts include a cool hundo off the basic model of Traeger's Woodridge smart pellet grill, whose bigger, upgraded version, the Woodridge Pro (8/10, WIRED Recommends), was WIRED's previous top-pick pellet smoker. Its no-fuss operation and cleaning, sophisticated temperature control, and absolute beastly capacity set it apart. But Home Depot's steepest discount is on Traeger's standby, entry-level Pro 22 smoker. We have not tested this recently, but after a dozen years it's a near-classic, and $390 is the lowest price it's seen all year.
Other deals among WIRED-recommended grills include $50 off a couple of Weber's durable, last-you-forever standbys—the Weber Kettle and the Weber Spirit E-210. I and fellow WIRED reviewer Scott Gilbertson tend to love these two models precisely because they are basic, durable, reliable, and low-cost. The Weber Kettle, especially, can be upgraded with smart features into a temp-controlled, smart-charcoal beast.
This $50 off deal tends to be the standard Weber deal. But the price already starts out affordable, and so the sale price amounts to an excellent value on a grill that's likely to be with you a while. If you'd like your kettle in green, you can get it for half off, a mere $100.
Home Depot Milwaukee Tool Deals
Buying power tools is all about picking an ecosystem (and a battery pack). WIRED reviewer Scott Gilbertson favors Milwaukee for its intersection between reliability and value, and for tentpole sales Home Depot usually offers free battery packs or buy-one-get one deals.
One of the best and most versatile tools Gilbertson recommends is Milwaukee's excellent impact driver ($179). Lucky you: During the Labor Day sale, this comes free with the purchase of the portable M18 battery you'll need to operate it wirelessly. If you've already got a Milwaukee battery, the BOGO still holds for an assortment of tools including an oscillating multi-tool that's also one of the more underrated tools in the DIYer home kit.
Home Depot Ryobi Landscaping and Tool Deals
Ryobi is the brand that former WIRED reviewer Parker Hall has consistently recommended for yard and landscaping tools, in large part because of their service philosophy. In many regions including mine (the Pacific Northwest), Ryobi keeps a local repair technician on retainer to come and fix your mower or blower, instead of making you ship your machine to a repair center somewhere. This is clutch, even if you won't have to use the service often.
Home Depot is offering its usual BOGO battery deals on Ryobi's landscaping tools, including the heavy-duty leaf blower ($159) you're going to need sooner than you expect.
For entry-level tool kits, my colleague Kat Merck also recommends this shockingly low-cost starter power tool kit from Ryobi—which is not going to make you the envy of any job site, but offers great value and torque for the money. This set offers a ½-inch drill/driver, an impact driver, a circular saw, and an LED light. There's also another discount kit with a sander, drill/driver, and circular saw.
Home Depot DeWalt Tool BOGO
My editor, Kat Merck, is a DeWalt devotee. But the DeWalt Deals are a bit more specialized this season. There's still a few good BOGO offers, though, especially if you're in the market for a circular saw or angle grinder, or a hammer drill kit to carve holes into masonry.
