Dronetech startup AVPL International parent AITMC Ventures reported a net profit of ₹14.2 Cr in the fiscal year FY26, a meager 1% increase from last fiscal’s profit of ₹14.1 Cr. However, AVPL's operating revenue jumped 26.3% to ₹106.8 Cr in FY26 from ₹84.5 Cr in the previous financial year, according to its annual report. Breaking down its top line, the dronetech startup generated ₹70.48 Cr from sale of services, while product sales contributed ₹36.28 Cr, comprising ₹3.40 Cr from drones and drone parts and ₹32.88 Cr from other IT equipment. Including other income of ₹51 Lakh, total income rose 23.8% to ₹107.27 in the year under review. The startup's net profit margin fell to around 13.3% in FY26 from 16.7% in FY25, as total expenditure grew 34.7% during the year, outpacing the 26.3% growth in operating revenue. The startup’s EBITDA for the year under review stood at ₹29.01 Cr, compared to ₹29.07 Cr in FY25. Its EBITDA margin consequently fell from 34.4% in FY25 to 27.2% in FY26. Founded in 2016 by Preet Sandhuu and Deep Sisai, AVPL International offers drone training and other skill development programmes for the agriculture sector. As per its website, the company operates over 70 drone training centres across 16 states. It also offers drones, drone-as-a-service, and other agri solutions. Last year, AVPL International signed a term sheet for a “strategic company merger” with listed rival DroneAcharaya. However, the deal did not go through. Months later, AVPL International pre-filed DRHP for ₹200 Cr IPO in October last year. Although the SEBI gave its nod to the public listing in January, AVPL is yet to file its updated IPO papers. Inc42 has reached out to the company to discern the timeline of the public offering. The story will be updated based on their response. To note, this marks the dronetech company’s second stab at a public listing. In December 2023, the startup filed its DRHP with SEBI for a listing on NSE Emerge. At the time, the startup was eyeing a fresh issue of up to 2.1 Cr shares, with no offer-for-sale component. However, its IPO didn’t materialise Zooming Into AVPL International’s Expenses Total expenditure increased 34.7% to ₹88.3 Cr in FY26 from ₹65.6 Cr in the last fiscal year. Here’s where AVPL International spent most of its costs: Cost Of Services: Including centre food expense, centre running expense, infra partner expense, fee and lease rent, the spending under this head stood at ₹27.5 Cr in the year under review, marking a 15.1% fall from ₹32.4 Cr in FY25. Purchases Of Stock-In-Trade: The overall expenditure was partly driven by the company's purchases of IT equipment, which stood at ₹27.2 Cr in FY26, compared with no corresponding expense reported under this head in FY25. Employee Benefit Expenses: The company spent ₹8.6 Cr towards employee costs, which includes salary, wages, bonus, allowances and such, marking a 1.9% rise from ₹8.5 Cr in FY25.

The suspected murderers of two Australian surfers and an American at a Mexican surfing hotspot have gone on trial, two years after the killings in a suspected robbery.
Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33, respectively, and 30-year-old American friend Jack Carter Rhoad were on a surfing trip to Mexico’s Pacific coast when they were shot dead in Baja California state.
They had been camping in a remote beachside area when they were allegedly attacked in April 2024.
Their bodies were found dumped in a cliff-top shaft several days after they went missing.
They bore gunshot wounds to their heads. Three men are on trial over their killings.
The Robinsons’ parents traveled to the port city of Ensenada for the start of the proceedings on Monday.
Bereaved mother Debra Robinson stared at the accused before bursting into tears in the courtroom.
“It’s about representing our sons, being here for them. I know they want us to be here,” her partner, Martin Robinson, had earlier told reporters.
“We want to find out what happened. We want to find out why.”
Authorities allege the men were murdered during an attempt to steal their pickup truck, which was found burned near their bodies.
Three witnesses appeared before the court on Monday, including the stepson of one of the defendants, who described his stepfather as violent.
Testifying from an adjoining room with his face concealed, he said he accompanied the accused to the crime scene, waiting nearby when the “commotion” began.
“I heard a lot of noise,” he said, explaining that he had run away but rejoined the group after they called him.
He said they warned him that “the same thing that happened to the gringos would happen to him” if he said anything.
The crime sparked outrage and grief in Australia and the US, where the surfers’ friends and families galvanized a major search on social media for their bodies.
Callum Robinson played professional lacrosse in the US. His brother Jake was pursuing a career in medicine.
Rhoad was killed a few months before he was set to marry.
Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organized crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity doesn’t usually affect tourists.
Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast.
Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were murdered in 2015 while traveling through the northwestern state of Sinaloa in the north-west. Their bodies were later burned.

Vasseur: Ferrari missing pure power despite engine upgrade
Ferrari introduced their second and final engine upgrade of the season but were still slower than the Mercedes-powered cars on the straights.
Straight-line speed has been Ferrari's biggest weakness, something which will not be an issue around the new twisty Madrid circuit, and Vasseur says he was "not expecting" to make up the power-unit deficit to Mercedes.
"When you have a lack of pure power, then you start to play with deployment, to try to compensate in the straight line," he said.
"But if you deploy more somewhere, for sure you will deploy less somewhere else. Then you are going in the wrong spiral to try to play with this when you are fighting.
"Honestly, it's not about deployment. Even McLaren, they were playing a little bit Friday and Saturday morning. In the end, we are missing pure power."
After the first Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities (ADUO) review earlier this year, Ferrari were deemed to be more than four per cent behind benchmark engine manufacturer Red Bull.
It meant Ferrari could make two engine upgrades this year, and also for 2027, when the Scuderia will have a new engine.
"The process of the engine is mega long. The chassis you can make an upgrade from one day to the other very quickly and come back into the pace," said Vasseur.
"On the engine, the process is mega long because the lead time of the parts is long and the cost cap is not easy - you have to produce the engine for the season.
"And if you want to start to do the development, you have to produce a new batch of engines. We are not expecting to recover with ADUO 1 or ADUO 2. We are doing small steps.
"If you make a small step on the engine, keep in mind that behind us, it was hundredths of a second. In terms of position, even if you make a couple of horsepower, it's a good step on the grid. Now we will have a new engine next year. For sure, the target is to catch up as soon as possible."

Gurugram-based ecommerce enablement platform Shiprocket is starting to reap the benefits of business bets it began placing well before its stock market listing earlier this year. Its core business has traditionally involved helping online merchants ship orders by connecting them with multiple logistics providers. Over the years, however, Shiprocket has added checkout, omnichannel commerce, cross-border logistics, and marketing technology (martech) offerings to generate revenue from more stages of every order. The early results are beginning to show in its financials. Shiprocket’s revenue from operations rose 34% YoY to ₹592.1 Cr in Q1 FY27 from ₹442 Cr in the year-ago quarter. While its core shipping business grew 22% YoY to ₹411.7 Cr, its emerging business, comprising omnichannel, cross-border, and martech offerings, grew 70% to ₹180.4 Cr. Consequently, its contribution to overall revenue increased to 30% from 24% a year earlier. Within this portfolio, martech emerged as the fastest-growing business, with revenue surging 193% YoY. Omnichannel revenue jumped 92%, while cross-border revenue declined marginally amid global volatility. However, the rising share of emerging offerings has lowered Shiprocket’s overall revenue per transaction because these businesses currently generate lower realisation than core shipping. The company is initially focusing on increasing transaction volumes and subsequently monetising them through its broader product stack. Monetising The Entire Order Journey Shiprocket is betting that a single ecommerce order creates monetisation opportunities across customer acquisition, checkout, fulfilment, shipping, returns, and repeat purchases. Martech, including checkout and advertising tools, has emerged as a key part of this strategy. During its Q1 post-earnings call, Shiprocket’s management said the company can use data on purchases, customer behaviour, product catalogues, locations, and repurchase patterns to help merchants improve their marketing outcomes. Instead of relying entirely on external sources, Shiprocket can use commerce data from its shipping operations and monetise it through a separate product. It claims to have more than a decade of consumer behaviour data covering 15 Cr consumers, while 93% of checkout addresses are auto-filled through its platform. At its core, Shiprocket is trying to monetise the same transaction across multiple touchpoints. A merchant that initially comes to the platform for shipping could eventually also spend on checkout, advertising, omnichannel, and other tools for the same order. The strategy is part of a broader trend among digital platforms to monetise data generated through their core businesses. IPO-bound PhonePe, for instance, recently launched PulsePro, an enterprise intelligence platform built using aggregated and anonymised transaction data from its payments network. Existing Merchant Opportunity Shiprocket’s martech play also allows it to extract more business from its existing merchant network instead of relying primarily on new customer acquisition to grow its top line. This has become more important as CAC for its core shipping business increased 13.5% YoY to ₹3,560 in Q1 FY27, while overall CAC rose 9.2% to ₹6,429. The management attributed the increase to experiments across acquisition channels. Shiprocket’s merchant network stood at around 2.22 Lakh in Q1 FY27, including 10,170 “power merchants”, or higher-value sellers, compared with 10,282 a year earlier. However, average revenue per power merchant increased to ₹18.7 Lakh from ₹15 Lakh, underscoring the opportunity to generate more from existing sellers. The proportion of core merchants using Shiprocket’s emerging products increased to 8.8% from 7.3% in a year. Meanwhile, the number of merchants served by the emerging business jumped 57% YoY to 48,406. These numbers indicate that more merchants are moving beyond Shiprocket’s core shipping offering. However, adoption among core merchants remains relatively limited, while the emerging business is yet to demonstrate that rapid revenue growth can translate into profitability. Will Merchants Pay More? Despite growing 70% YoY, Shiprocket’s emerging segment remains loss-making. Its adjusted EBITDA margin improved to negative 24.3% in Q1 FY27 from negative 38.1% a year earlier, while its contribution margin expanded to 15.3% from 9.3%. Shiprocket attributed the improvement to operating leverage and a better product mix, with martech growing considerably faster than the rest of the emerging portfolio. It is also investing in product and technology as it looks to increase the share of relatively higher-margin martech offerings. Shiprocket’s stable core business gives it room to continue these investments. The segment’s adjusted EBITDA rose 50% YoY to ₹52.7 Cr, while its margin improved to 12.8%. At the consolidated level, adjusted EBITDA increased more than ninefold to ₹8.9 Cr, while net loss narrowed 24% to ₹13.7 Cr from ₹18 Cr in the year-ago quarter. The company will now have to get more merchants to use its checkout, advertising, omnichannel, and cross-border offerings. In doing so, it will compete not only with logistics platforms but also with a wider universe of ecommerce, advertising, and SaaS players. Other listed logistics companies are also widening their revenue pools, albeit through different routes. Shadowfax, for instance, is expanding across D2C, hyperlocal, and quick commerce while building higher-value offerings such as Prime Large for shipments weighing more than 15 kg. Its D2C business grew around 2.7X in Q1 FY27. Unlike Shadowfax’s expansion into adjacent delivery categories, Shiprocket is betting on selling a wider set of commerce tools to the same merchant base. Its emerging business is already growing much faster than its core operations, with martech becoming its most aggressive bet. However, the next phase of Shiprocket’s growth will depend on whether more merchants follow it beyond shipping and whether the company can turn its commerce data into products they are willing to pay for.

“I could not breathe. We were brutally dragged up the stairs. I kept saying, ‘Please stop, let me breathe. Tell me where you are taking me.’ But they did not tell us anything.”
This is how journalist Shaheen Khan described the ordeal she and her sister and colleague Nafisa Khan allegedly endured inside Saket police station on September 3, after they were detained while covering the inauguration of Max Smart Super Speciality Hospital in Delhi attended by Union home minister Amit Shah and Delhi chief minister Rekha Gupta.
According to Shaheen, what began as a detention soon turned into an assault. She alleged that their phones were snatched, they were dragged upstairs into a room, slapped, kicked and hit with a baton. She further alleged that the assault intensified after a policewoman saw the name of an incoming caller on her phone and said, “Oh, you are a Muslim. Then I will hit you with four more baton blows and slap you four more times.”
Speaking to Alt News, Shaheen gave a detailed account of what happened at the venue and later at the police station.
The two women journalists work for digital news platform 4PM News Network. The outlet posted a video in which Shaheen appeared visibly distressed and in tears, alleging that she and Nafisa had been assaulted by police officers. The report asked whether asking questions to the chief minister had “become a grave crime” for which journalists could be beaten up, and called for an impartial investigation. It also demanded that all available CCTV footage from the site be preserved.

According to an Indian Express report, police denied the allegations of assault, and said that “the journalists were detained after they allegedly blocked the exit and parked their scooty on the VVIP movement route, and had an altercation with police personnel deployed there”. Multiple calls from Alt News to Saket Police went answered.
In an X post, DCP South Delhi called the allegations ‘factually incorrect and misleading’. However, the post was deleted shortly after being shared.
‘Illegally Detained’
Speaking to Alt News, Shaheen alleged that she and Nafisa had been detained around 11 am and taken to Saket police station. “The SHO threatened us with an FIR and spoke about putting us in the lock-up,” she added.
“We kept asking them to tell us what our crime was, what we had done wrong, why they wanted to keep us in the lock-up and why they wanted to file an FIR against us. We told them that we were educated people, that we were journalists, and that we would cooperate with the police. But we were given no answers. Instead, they said, ‘Put them in the lock-up’.”
“We had been told that they were taking us home. But when we were brought to the police station, some police officers began threatening us. At that point, I felt that the police could do something to us, either legally or otherwise, and I thought I should inform my family. Until then, I believed this was simply a routine detention. I thought the police would question us and let us go.”
Shaheen said that after the SHO had threatened them, she tried to call her family and was scrolling through her phone when a woman in civilian clothes, wearing a pink suit, approached her.
“Her name is Sonam Solanki. She told me, ‘Give me your phone.’ I asked her, ‘Why are you asking me for my phone, and under which law? Tell me what my crime is, and I will give you the phone.’ She then told me to go upstairs because she wanted to talk to me.”
‘Phones Snatched, We were Repeatedly Slapped’
Shaheen said she asked why they had to go upstairs and told Solanki that whatever she wanted to say could be said in the main area of the police station.
“Solanki told me, ‘I have to talk to you. My way of talking is very different.’ I later understood what she meant by that,” Shaheen said.
The sisters then asked to be allowed to call their families. At that point, their phones were taken away, Shaheen alleged.
“The moment they snatched our phone, she began slapping us repeatedly. This happened in the reception area. If the CCTV footage has not been tampered with, all of this should be recorded.”
“We kept asking, ‘Why are you hitting us? What have we done? You cannot hit us. We have committed no crime, and even if you believe we have committed a crime, you do not have the right to beat us’.”
Solanki then allegedly began dragging them towards another room upstairs.
“We did not know where she was taking us. She dragged us through the area where the SHO’s room is located. She pulled our hair and clothes,” Shaheen alleged.

‘Teach them a lesson’: Dragged, slapped, kicked
Shaheen said she managed to break free and rushed into the SHO’s room, seeking his intervention.
“I asked the SHO what we had done wrong. I told him, ‘Under what authority is she beating us? Please intervene.’ But instead of listening to me or helping me, the SHO told the police constable who had followed me into the room to take me upstairs and ‘teach them a lesson.’”
Shaheen alleged that she was then forcibly dragged upstairs.
“They beat us and dragged us by whatever they could grab — our hair, our clothes. We were brutally dragged up the stairs. I could not walk; I could not breathe properly. I kept saying, ‘Please stop, let me breathe. Tell me where you are taking me.’ But they did not tell us anything.”
The room where the women were taken did not have CCTV cameras, Shaheen said, although there was a camera in the corridor leading to it.

Shaheen alleged that the assault escalated inside the room.
“They threw me to the floor. They kicked me, punched me and slapped me repeatedly. They slapped me continuously. Then they picked me up and threw me onto a sofa. They began pulling my hair and scratching my face. My head was banged against the wall.”
She alleged that a baton was then brought into the room.
“She told me, ‘I will show you. You ask too many questions.’ She hit both me and Nafisa with the baton. At one point, when she became tired, she sat down at a table. The phone they had taken from me rang at that moment.”
‘Oh, you are a Muslim!’
Shaheen said the officer’s demeanour changed after she saw the name of the incoming caller on her phone.
“When she looked at my phone, there was an incoming call from someone named Mohammad Khan. The moment she saw the name, there was a complete change in her demeanour. “She then began hitting me again. She also told the constable accompanying her to hit us. All of them then started beating us, including people who had stood still until then. They beat us so badly that I could not breathe. I needed water and told them, ‘At least give me some water’.”
Shaheen broke into tears while recounting the incident.
MLC ‘Delayed’, Police Sought Compromise
Neetu, another colleague of Shaheen and Nafisa, told Alt News that the police did not arrange a medico-legal examination (MLC) after the alleged assault and instead sought a compromise.
“After the assault, they did not arrange an MLC. They wanted us to compromise and suppress the entire matter. We then called the police ourselves on 100 and went for the MLC on our own.”
Neetu alleged that the MLC was deliberately delayed and took five hours to be conducted. After the medical examination, the journalists returned to Saket police station around 9 pm.
“After that, they made us wait there until around 4 am without registering an FIR. Three SHOs came to the police station and eventually left. We were then told to remove two names from the complaint and that ‘whatever happens will happen’. But the FIR was not registered,” Neetu said.

Shaheen disputed the police’s version of the incident.
“The DCP posted a tweet and then deleted it. If what he said was true, why did he delete it? The DCP should be ashamed of making such a statement. Under what law are they trying to justify this heinous act?” she said.
“Even if we assume that I had committed a crime, under which provision of law and under what procedure were we detained, assaulted, locked inside a room and had our phones snatched? We were literally kidnapped. On what legal basis was all of this done?”
“Whatever I may have done, you could have registered an FIR against me and taken legal action. You could have prosecuted me according to the law. I would have cooperated with you,” Shaheen said.
What was Shaheen Reporting on when She was Detained?
Shaheen claims she was detained for asking questions to the chief minister.
“I did not question anybody there directly. I was simply shooting my segment, in which I raised a few basic questions. The government has a responsibility towards its citizens, right? But instead, it appears to be devoting so much attention to private hospitals.”
In the roughly two-minute segment, Shaheen questioned why elected leaders were giving so much time and attention to a private hospital while public hospitals, women’s safety and law and order remained issues.
“This was a barely two-minute video. In it, I raised these questions and showed the venue and the surrounding area, which had been transformed and decorated for the event yesterday, even though it is usually littered with waste,” Shaheen said.
Several journalists’ associations, including the Press Club of India, “strongly condemned” the incident and called for “punitive action against Delhi Police officials posted at the Saket Police Station, including the Station House Officer (SHO), for brutally assaulting freelance journalists Shaheen Khan and Nafisa Khan while they were reporting…”

Electric vehicle batteries are lasting longer than previously feared by drivers, with most used EVs able to retain about 90 percent of their original usable battery capacity after 150,000 kilometers, a new study has shown.
Despite a surge in global EV sales on the back of rising fuel prices, long-term battery durability continues to be one of the key concerns for drivers when they consider switching from a petrol model to an electric car.
EV battery warranties typically cover eight years or 100,000 miles (160,000km) with car manufacturers required under the warranty to provide a replacement battery if capacity falls below 70 per cent.
According to the latest study published by Aviloo, an Austria-based group that analyzes battery health, the median state of health (SoH)—which represents the remaining percentage of a battery’s original usable capacity—for 20 popular EV models stood between 87 percent and 94 percent after 150,000 km.
The median SoH was between 91 and 97 percent after 50,000 km, and 88 and 95 percent after 100,000 km. The study was based on more than 500,000 tests Aviloo carried out globally on the 20 EV models including Tesla’s Model Y and Volkswagen’s ID.4 between 2022 and 2026.
The Aviloo study, which did not include Chinese models due to lack of data, also showed that the speed of battery degradation varied significantly even within the same EV model depending on climate conditions, battery size, and driver habits, such as parking.
“In contrast to a combustion engine car, where age and mileage would more or less carry the value of the car and technical condition, that’s not the case for an EV,” said Marcus Berger, chief executive of Aviloo. “The car might look the same—same age, same mileage—and you don’t know how it has been treated.”

Two held from Chennai for sending bomb threats to Gujarat HC, Surat court: Cop
Two emails were sent on September 5 at 11.57am and 11.59am from a new email ID created under a false name
Ahmedabad Cyber Crime Branch and Surat Crime Branch arrested two men from Chennai for allegedly sending hoax emails threatening to blow up the Gujarat high court and Surat sessions court, police said on Monday.
The accused, Mahammad Asfaq, 28, and Rajesh alias Raj, 33, are both from Surat, police said.
According to police, the threat was sent to evade legal proceedings against Asfaq, who had a trial hearing at the Surat sessions court on September 5 but did not appear. The email was sent on the same day to disrupt the proceedings and avoid his appearance, police said.
The two were arrested in Chennai within 48 hours after the emails were sent. Police traced them through technical analysis, surveillance and human intelligence.
Two emails were sent on September 5 at 11.57am and 11.59am from a new email ID created under a false name. The mails threatened bomb attacks on the Gujarat high court and Surat sessions court.
Asfaq had earlier been jailed in an Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) case and was released on parole. He allegedly failed to return to jail after his parole ended and was absconding for about nine months. Rajesh had earlier been lodged with him in Lajpore Jail, police said.
The two travelled to Chennai in search of a cannabis supplier and allegedly planned the threat the said courts, police said.
Asfaq created the email ID while travelling by train from Mumbai to Chennai. In Chennai, they changed hotels and locations before the email was sent, police said.
Investigators said the accused used different email IDs, SIM cards registered in other persons’ names, multiple Wi-Fi networks and proxy or other technical means to conceal their identities and location. They also sent the email while travelling on a moving train.
A case has been registered under provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), including section 351(3) (criminal intimidation involving threat to cause death or grievous hurt) and section 351(4) (criminal intimidation through anonymous communication), and section 66-C (identity theft) of the Information Technology Act.
Police records show Asfaq was earlier arrested in an NDPS case involving 512 grams of hybrid cannabis, while Rajesh was arrested in a case involving 100.260 grams of mephedrone.

How to update your GPU drivers in Windows 11
Graphics card driver updates are important, but finding them can be confusing.
Software updates for apps, operating systems and services primarily serve two benefits — they deliver new features and fix known issues. Hardware driver updates largely fall into the latter category, so don't offer as much excitement, but keeping them up-to-date is a good way to ensure your computer's internals perform optimally.
Graphics cards (GPUs) often receive the most updates, with new game releases often requiring a driver update to yield the best possible performance. But knowing the best place to get them on your Windows PC can often be confusing.
If you haven't updated your GPU drivers in a hot minute, navigating to Settings > Windows Update and clicking on Check for updates will fetch available updates and install them. However, you can also check for new graphics card drivers through another built-in utility.
Open the Start Menu and search for Device Manager. Here, you'll find a list of all the hardware connected to your computer. Expand the Display adapters section and double-click on your GPU's name. It's likely one made by AMD, NVIDIA or Intel. Navigate to the Driver tab, click on Update Driver and select Search automatically for drivers.
Though this is a handy way to deal with outdated drivers, Windows Update doesn't have the best reputation with how it handles GPU drivers. If it finds and installs a version that's several releases behind what's available directly from the manufacturer, you could be missing out on the latest performance improvements and bug fixes. If you have a little more time on your hands, it's recommended that you grab the latest drivers directly from your graphics card maker.
Using your GPU's companion software
You'll first need to determine which company made your GPU. Looking inside the Device Manager app is a quick way to find out. Next, launch the Start Menu and check if you have your GPU's companion software already installed. Just type in "AMD," "Intel" or "NVIDIA" and see if any results pop up.
If nothing shows up, head to the manufacturer's website and download the latest version of the companion software. It's either going to be the NVIDIA App, AMD Software: Adrenalin Edition or Intel Graphics Software. Upon installation, the app should automatically detect your graphics card and let you know if newer drivers are available to install.
To manually check for updates in the NVIDIA App, launch it and navigate to the Drivers tab on the left and click on Download if there's a newer version available. If you have an AMD GPU, launch the Adrenalin companion app, click on the settings cog icon located in the top-right corner and click on Manage Updates. This will open the AMD Install Manager, which is yet another utility (yeah, we know it's annoying) that handles driver updates. Click on Install if you spot any pending GPU driver updates here. If you're using an Intel GPU, the Intel Graphics Software utility places an Install All button front and center for any pending driver updates.
During installation, it's normal for your display to flicker a few times. Once done, you should see a confirmation popup saying the latest drivers have been installed. You don't always have to restart your computer, but it wouldn't hurt to do so anyway.
Manually installing GPU drivers
Though relying on your GPU's companion software for driver updates is usually the easiest option, you can also install drivers manually if you need a specific version or simply don't want to keep another piece of software running on your computer. The quickest way to find drivers for your GPU is to search on Google for its exact model name followed by "drivers." Then, follow the link that takes you to the manufacturer's official website. This works great for both AMD and Intel GPU drivers.
If you have a GPU from NVIDIA, head to the company's Driver Updates page. Search for your GPU by its product name and series, or by using the drop-down menus. Download the latest available Game Ready Driver. Open the executable file and you should see an option to install just the driver or pair it with the GPU's companion app. Select your preference and click on Install.
In most cases, staying up-to-date with the latest available driver for your GPU is what's recommended. However, there are instances where a new release may cause game crashes or performance issues. Windows Update has already begun reverting problematic drivers automatically, but being able to find and install an older version of your GPU's driver can come in extremely handy.

Several videos have gone viral on social media following the devastating flash floods in Nepal on August 26, 2026. Some users shared a video claiming that after the disaster, the world’s largest Shaligram, said to be more than 170 million years old and weighing 30 tonnes, was found in Muktinath.
In this context, Zee News put out a report with a screenshot from the viral video and, along with the hashtags #Nepal, #Flood and #Shaligram, wrote: “Viral Video: Floods have revealed a secret, a 170-million-year-old Shaligram has been found.”
Shaligrams are naturally formed stones traditionally found in Nepal’s Kali Gandaki River, and revered by Hindus as representations of the deity, Vishnu.
Right-wing X user Amitabh Choudhary (@MithilaWaaala), who has been found spreading misinformation and comminal propaganda several times in the past, shared a video and wrote: “Stone older than dinosaurs. Worlds largest Shaligram weighing 31 tonnes is revered as Form of Bhagwan Vishnu has been found in Nepal.”
Kisi ne sahi hi kaha hai, “शुरुआत भी वही, सफ़र भी वही, और अंत भी वही।”
Stone older than dinosaurs !!
Worlds largest Shaligram weighing 31 tonnes is revered as Form of Bhagwan Vishnu has been found in Nepal 🇳🇵 pic.twitter.com/GIv851LJbV
— Amitabh Chaudhary (@MithilaWaaala) August 29, 2026
X user Shashank Shekhar Jha, who claims to be a Supreme Court lawyer, and others such as @Nalanda_index, @CodexZeroTR, @Krishnavallabhi, @bhaktSenapati, along with several Facebook and Instagram users, too, shared videos and photos with similar claims.
Fact Check
To find out the truth behind the viral claim, we performed a relevant keyword search. This led us to reports published on June 30, 2026, by Himalaya Times and Online Khabar featuring images of the giant sculpture seen in the viral video.
The reports stated that a 22-foot-tall Shaligram sculpture in Nepal’s Mustang district was gradually becoming a centre of religious faith. According to the reports, sculptors from the Nepal Academy of Fine Arts carved a huge rock on the banks of the Kali Gandaki River in Jomsom in Gharpajhong rural municipality area and created the 22-foot-tall Shaligram replica between April 20 and May 4, 2026.
During our investigation, we found a report by a website called Desh Sanchar. According to the report, the 22-foot-tall sculpture had been unveiled on the evening of May 28, 2026, after religious rituals on the banks of the Kali Gandaki River.
We also located a video uploaded on April 23, 2026 on the Facebook page, Nepal Raibar, in which artists could be seen carving a rock to create a Shaligram statue.
We also geolocated the Shaligram statue shown in the viral video. It’s located on the Kali Gandaki River, opposite ‘Thakkhola Lodge & Jimihendrix Restaurant in Jomsom. When we compared Google Street View images from 2025 with the viral video, we found that the 2025 image only showed a large rock.
This makes it clear that the Shaligram statue shown in the viral video is not a natural or ancient stone. Rather, it is a statue created by carving a rock.
We also tried to look for the sources of all the variants of the now-viral visuals. We found the original version of the video and the screenshots shared by Zee News on the Instagram account of a user named Durga Prasad Poudel. It was posted on June 2, 2026.
View this post on Instagram
Similarly, we found the second viral video uploaded on June 30, 2026, on the Instagram account of a user named Rijan Dongol.
View this post on Instagram
The third viral video was shared on June 8, 2026, on the Facebook account of a user named Arjun Singh. Its caption reads: “A huge 22-foot-tall Shaligram statue is located on the banks of the Kali Gandaki River in Jomsom, Mustang. This monumental work, inaugurated by Jagadguru Shankaracharya Mahaswami Vidushekara Bharati, attracts a large number of pilgrims and stands as a major spiritual and cultural site in Nepal.”
Thus, all three viral videos featuring the Shaligram statue have been available on social media since June 2026. They have absolutely no connection with the recent disaster in Nepal in August.
Overall, the claim by Zee News and other users that after the recent disaster in Nepal, the world’s largest Shaligram, more than 170 million years old and weighing 30 tonnes, was found in Muktinath is completely misleading. In reality, the 22-foot-tall Shaligram statue seen in the viral video was created by carving a rock on the banks of the Kali Gandaki River in Mustang district, during April–May 2026. The videos of the Shaligram statue circulating on social media are also from June 2026 and have no connection with the recent disaster in Nepal.

New prize named for late author Andrew Pyper will recognize horror and thriller writers
Announcement of $20,000 award coincides with release of Pyper's final novel
Heidi Pyper says her late husband, Andrew, wasn't just a bestselling author. He was also generous, curious and truly cared about people.
Affectionately known as "Canada's Stephen King," Andrew died in January 2025 of complications from cancer at the age of 56.
He was a prolific and acclaimed writer of horror, thrillers and other types of speculative fiction, including The Killing Circle and The Demonologist, and Pyper said her husband wrote characters who had great depth.
But she said she's frustrated that writers like Andrew don't get the recognition they deserve, noting there aren't many genre-specific awards available for horror or thriller writing.
That's why Andrew's friend and fellow author, Craig Davidson, helped create the Andrew Pyper Prize for Genre Fiction.
The $20,000 prize will be administered through the Writers’ Trust of Canada. To be eligible to win, writers must have published at least three books in the horror, thriller or speculative fiction genre. Thanks to a massive campaign, enough money has been raised to support the prize for seven years.
The announcement for the award coincides with the release of Andrew's final novel, Driven.
As a reader and writer of horror, he believed that the genre could expand people’s understanding of the human condition.
Pyper said she hopes the prize will help support and encourage authors like Andrew. She spoke to Matt Galloway, host of The Current, about the prize and legacy she wants it to leave.
When you listen to Andrew talk about horror and the human condition, what's going through your mind?
It brings such a smile to my face hearing Andrew talk about horror, thriller and genre writing in a way that's deep and meaningful because he brought a lot of depth to his writing. Particularly with the characters that he put under great duress. I remember my dad reading The Wildfire Season and saying, "Why does he keep putting these people I care about in such jeopardy?" And I was like, "That's the trick."
When he died, there was this huge outpouring of sadness from this country and beyond. There are people who perhaps only know him from his books. Tell us a little bit more about Andrew.
It's hard to talk about Andrew without sounding hyperbolic, but he really was a lovely man. He was smart, funny and talented. I would be remiss if I didn't mention how good-looking he was. People really loved him.
Many writers told stories of him and his generosity towards them, encouraging them to write, agreeing to come into classrooms to talk to students. The other thing that people kept saying was how he made them feel, he made them feel important. I think that stems from his curiosity. So when you were talking to Andrew, he didn't want to talk about himself, he wanted to hear about you and what was going on in your life.
This idea for this writing prize, in many ways, speaks to the generosity that he had. I'm sure he’d love this idea.
I think he'd be quite chuffed.
Tell me more about this prize and how the idea for this sparked.
Andrew played poker with a group of guys – writers, bookish-professor types – and he was no gambler, but he was dedicated to this group. About six months after Andrew died, Craig Davidson came to me and floated the idea, asked me what I thought and if it was OK if they tried to pursue this. Of course, I thought it was a wonderful idea.
Then he made the mistake of asking if I wanted to help. I'm sure he regretted that because I'd show up with my to-do list and a work-back schedule. But it came out of love and friendship amongst these men who played cards together.
But also from the fact that Andrew, despite the fact that he was a bestseller and wrote great books, didn't get the nod from some of those "literary prizes in Canada."
Yes, I think that was a frustration for him that he was disqualified before even being considered.
It wasn't like he was nominated and didn't win. It feels like there's a gap. Genre props up the publishing industry, people gobble it up. Movies and television are made from our writing, and it feels like a missing piece in the awards landscape. They recognized that, and the Pyper Prize began in that spirit.
It'll be $20,000.
It's a good chunk of change.
I think that's the distinction. There are awards for thriller writers and horror writers that exist. There's the [Bram Stoker Award], the Shirley Jackson [Award], I think there's the International Thriller Writers Awards but none of them come with a prize purse. So this really is a one-of-a-kind prize, not just in Canada, but we have yet to find one that is the equivalent.
The prize arrives at the same time as his new book comes out.
Yes. So Andrew left us with a few final words. Driven is the third and final book under his pseudonym Mason Coile. So the confluence of these two things happening at the same time is really meaningful.
How are you doing in all of this?
It's a lot, I'm not going to lie. I say it's very weird to have someone who has left us be so top of mind and such an ongoing concern, I kind of live with him in my head. I've elected to keep his social media active. His publisher offered to do it, but I just felt like I wanted to keep control of that.
In some ways, the book and the prize mean that the legacy lives on, there's a voice that’s still there.
I just reread Driven a couple of weeks ago. I read it when he finished it, but he was so sick when he was writing, it was right at the end of his life. He had said to me, "Should I write another book?" And I said, "Yeah, what else are you going to do? It's the thing that's going to get you up in the morning.” I started to read it then, but it was too dark. I said, “Our life is too scary for me to read this.” So I just read it again and you can really hear his voice. The sound of it is very clear in my mind.
Interview produced by Enza Uda

Shares of Pernia’s Pop-Up Shop parent Purple Style Labs made a weak stock market debut, listing at a discount of nearly 7% to their issue price. The stock opened at ₹535 on the NSE, 6.96% lower than the issue price of ₹575. On the BSE, the shares listed at ₹539, representing a discount of 6.26%. The company’s market capitalisation stood at ₹4,315.29 Cr (about $456.7 Mn) at the BSE’s opening price. The muted debut came after the company’s ₹680 Cr IPO closed with an overall subscription of 1.29X. Investors placed bids for 88.54 Lakh shares against 68.49 Lakh shares on offer. The company had fixed the price band for the IPO at ₹546-₹575 per share. The IPO comprised entirely a fresh issue of shares, with no OFS component. Ahead of the public issue, Purple Style Labs raised ₹306 Cr from anchor investors, allotting 53.2 Lakh shares at ₹575 apiece. Morgan Stanley and BofA Securities were among the investors participating in the anchor book. Founded in 2015 by Abhishek Agarwal, Purple Style Labs operates luxury fashion platform Pernia’s Pop-Up Shop and owns designer brands such as Wendell Rodricks and Hemant Trivedi. It acquired Pernia’s Pop-Up Shop in 2018 and subsequently expanded the primarily online business into an omnichannel platform. The company operates an omnichannel model spanning its online platform and physical experience centres, offering products across womenswear, menswear, jewellery, accessories and kidswear. It works with more than 1,100 active designer brands, according to its IPO documents. Of the IPO proceeds, Purple Style Labs plans to deploy ₹371.1 Cr towards meeting lease liabilities associated with its experience centre network. Another ₹138.9 Cr has been earmarked for sales and marketing expenses, while the remaining capital will be used for general corporate purposes. On the financial front, Purple Style Labs’ consolidated net loss widened 51.5% to ₹285.4 Cr in FY26 compared to ₹188.4 Cr incurred in the previous fiscal year. Operating revenue for the fiscal rose nearly 14% to ₹557.8 Cr from ₹489.9 Cr in FY25.

Canada is set to impose retaliatory tariffs on billions of dollars’ worth of American imports early on Tuesday, escalating a trade fight with its largest trading partner as tensions between US president Donald Trump and Canadian prime minister Mark Carney intensify.
The tariffs, which take effect at 12.01am on Tuesday, will range from 15% to 50% and apply to products covering C$27.6bn in imports from the US. The measures will target sectors including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics – industries that have been most affected by US tariffs.
The retaliatory tariffs come “as a result of the United States’ decision to impose a 50% tariff on $27.6bn of Canadian goods effective August 22”, the Canadian government said.
“Canada’s counter-measures do not apply to US goods that are in transit to Canada on the day on which they come into force,” it added.
Tensions between Canada and the US have intensified in recent weeks, with Carney last week urging the Trump administration to “start being serious” as the trade dispute has increasingly spilled into broader diplomatic tensions.
Trump and senior US officials have repeatedly criticized Canada and its leadership, while Trump has taken a series of symbolic digs at Canada including signing an executive order renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America” – which Canadians have rejected.
US vice-president JD Vance has also reportedly mocked Carney, apparently saying the Canadian prime minister “comes in and puffs his chest out and says: ‘I’m going to, like, out-tough Donald Trump.’”
Last month, Trump announced a new 50% tariff on cars and raw materials from Canada. He accused the country of “ripping off” the US “for years”, adding: “We don’t need Canada, they need us!”
Carney said last month Canada would not accept a US trade deal that weakened French-language protections, saying American negotiators viewed the measures as an “irritant”, while “in Quebec, these are rights”.
Quebec has long maintained laws aimed at protecting French and preserving its distinct cultural identity. Those measures have become a sticking point in the trade talks between the two countries, with American negotiators raising concerns about rules they say can disadvantage US businesses.

A magical spell by Nashru Sandhu- a six-wicket haul while giving away just seven runs helped Pakistan trounce Hong Kong by 72 runs and make the semifinals of the Women’s Asia Cup.
With the win, Pakistan finished second in Group A behind India with two wins and one defeat, and will face Sri Lanka in the second semifinal on September 11.
Having won the toss and decided to bat first, Pakistan managed to score 143/8 in the first innings. Shawal Zulfiqar top scored for Pakistan with 47 while Joyleen Kaur shone with the ball for Indonesia (4/19).
In the second innings, Hong Kong trudged along painfully slowly, its approach resembling that of a team that had mentally given up on winning the match even before the chase got underway.
The Pakistani bowling attack, led by captain Fatima Sana, kept things tight, offering no scoring opportunities to the Hong Kong batters.
Nashra was brought on after the first six and it didn’t take her long to put the game to rest. The 28-year-old first broke the partnership Yasmin Daswani and Kary Chan and two overs later, prised two more batters in the space of four balls.
Nashra completed her six-wicket haul off the final delivery of her spell as Hong Kong was bowled out for 71 in 19 overs.
The left-arm spinner also broke multiple records in her match-winning performance. She became the first Pakistani bowler to take six wickets in a T20I, while her figures of 6/7 are also the best by a Pakistani bowler in the shortest format.
Nashra also became just the third Pakistani bowler to take a fifer in women’s T20Is after Nida Dar and Omaima Sohail.

Russia announces the closure of the German consulate in St. Petersburg
Russia’s Foreign Ministry has announced the closure of the German consulate in St. Petersburg
MOSCOW -- Russia’s Foreign Ministry on Monday announced the closure of the German consulate in St. Petersburg, a tit-for-tat move that reflected the simmering tensions between the two countries.
Russia’s Foreign Ministry said the German consulate must stop operations and its workers must leave Russia by Sept. 18. It reaffirmed the previously announced decision to shut German cultural centers in the country and said their employees must leave no later than Sunday.
The ministry said the moves were retaliation for Germany’s “unfriendly” decision Wednesday to close both the Russian consulate in Bonn and the Russian House cultural center in the German capital, Berlin.
Germany blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport on Aug. 4, when an explosives-laden drone was found near a Ukrainian plane.
The airport is a major international freight hub used for providing support to Ukraine. The drone was later defused.
Moscow has denied involvement.

In the latest episode of Bigg Boss 20, Mary Kom opened up about her children and admitted that she has not been very supportive of their interest in gaming. During a conversation with Tanmay Singh aka ScoutOp, Mary revealed that her children often play games throughout the night. She confessed that she does not want them to spend so much time gaming, to which ScoutOp, who earns his living through esports, suggested that she give them six months to a year to explore their potential and see if they can make a career out of it.
While discussing her children’s gaming habits, Mary told ScoutOp, “Isme zindagi kya karega. Kabhi maine support nahi kiya.” Hearing this, ScoutOp encouraged the Olympic medallist to support her children and give them some time to determine whether they are genuinely good at gaming.

Mary Kom has four children with her former husband, K Onler Kom (Karung Onkholer). In 2018, Mary and Onler adopted a daughter, Merilyn. As of 2026, the twins are around 19, Prince is around 13, and Merilyn is around 8. Reports state that Mary and Onler separated in December 2023.
In the latest episode, three contestants became the contenders for first captaincy. The new episodes of Bigg Boss 20 air every day at 9 pm on Jio Hotstar and at 10.30 pm on Colors TV.

Bajaj Finance, the NBFC arm of Bajaj Finserv, has acquired a 5% stake in Delhi NCR-based AI video generation platform TrueFan AI. The company didn’t disclose the investment it made to purchase the stake. The investment is part of Bajaj Finserv’s strategic applied research and innovation initiative, Finserv Intelligence. The initiative aims to develop and support high-tech, scalable solutions built in India for domestic and global markets. Bajaj Finance has been a customer of TrueFan for a while, having deployed the startup’s platform at scale to generate millions of personalised videos for customer engagement and dealer enablement initiatives. The partnership also aligns with Bajaj Finance’s broader strategy of deploying AI-led automation and personalisation across its digital ecosystem, it said in a statement. “As a FINAI company, we are deploying AI at scale across the company. Our investment in TrueFan AI follows sustained, production-scale use of its technology, giving us first-hand experience of the platform’s capabilities and its execution,” said Rajeev Jain, vice chairman and managing director of Bajaj Finance. With the investment, Bajaj Finance will gain TrueFan AI’s AI video skills to augment its marketing, videos, multilingual communication, employee training as well as their onboarding. The investment comes months after TrueFan AI raised $10 Mn in a Series A round led by Baring Private Equity Partners India and Z3Partners, with participation from IAN Alpha Fund and 3Lines Venture Capital. Overall, the startup had raised close to $15 Mn prior to this investment. he fresh capital will allow TrueFan to expand its enterprise customer base, enter markets across Southeast Asia and the Middle East, and scale its presence in the US, the startup said in June. Founded by Nimish Goel and Devender Bindal in 2020, TrueFan AI started as a celebrity engagement platform before shifting its focus to enterprise AI in 2024. It now helps companies create personalised videos using celebrities and AI avatars. The startup claims to serve more than 100 enterprise clients operating across sectors including finance, healthcare, consumer goods and media. Its clients include HDFC Bank, Cipla, BharatPe and Goibibo. TrueFan AI is also developing real-time AI video agents for tasks such as customer support, sales, onboarding and product discovery. It has more than 110 employees and says its infrastructure can generate up to 5 Lakh videos a minute. Bajaj Finserv’s Startup Push The investment also marks an expansion of Bajaj Finserv’s efforts to back technology startups through Finserv Intelligence. In March, It plans to invest up to ₹2,000 Cr over five years in startups and early-stage companies through the initiative. The focus areas include AI, cybersecurity, quantum technologies, fintech and consumer technology. Finserv Intelligence operates via making investments, academic partnerships and in-house research, with plans for R&D labs, centres of excellence, venture-led models and a Scholars-in-Residence programme. Bajaj Finserv has also partnered with IIT Bombay to establish a joint research centre focused on AI, cybersecurity and quantum technologies. The company said the initiative would focus on building high tech, low cost and scalable solutions from India for domestic and global markets. The latest investment comes as Bajaj Finserv looks to deepen its presence in India’s technology ecosystem. Earlier this year, chairman Sanjiv Bajaj said the group planned to invest ₹400 Cr to ₹450 Cr in AI-focused ventures in FY27 through a combination of its AI-focused fund and balance sheet. The company is increasing its focus on AI as India’s artificial intelligence sector expands. At the heart of this push is India’s rapidly growing AI market, which is projected to reach $126 Bn by 2030 as the country moves from AI pilots to production-first, workflow-native systems.

After nearly three decades, Practical Magic 2 had a tall order to fill in conjuring the same magic as the original 1998 adaptation of the Alice Hoffman book.
While the sequel is sure to serve as an entertaining day at the movies with mom, it reads a bit more Harry Potter than Witches of Eastwick in this long overdue reunion between Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman as witchy Massachusetts sisters Sally and Gillian Owens.
Based on Hoffman’s 2021 novel The Book of Magic, the Susanne Bier-helmed followup picks up shortly after the original, with Sally’s soulmate Gary (portrayed by Aidan Quinn in the first movie) succumbing to the curse that kills anyone who falls in love with an Owens woman. In order to spare her daughters Kylie and Antonia (originally portrayed by Evan Rachel Wood and Alexandra Artrip, but recast with Joey King and Maisie Williams for the sequel) the pain of the curse in their own lives, she casts a spell to erase all their memories of magic.
Cut to 25 years later, Kylie begins to uncover the family secret when her own love Gideon (Xolo Maridueña) gets injured in a life-threatening accident. Setting off to break the curse, she follows an ancient book and mysterious visions to the U.K., where her ancestor Maria Owens was born before moving to Massachusetts. Sally and Gillian go after her, teaming up with their aunts’ academic colleague Ian Wright (Lee Pace) to take on a dark force that threatens their family.
Watch on Deadline
Whereas the original Griffin Dunne-directed film was a romantic slow burn, rich with emotion and passion, the sequel wastes no time getting into the action of the plot. That might fit a modern streaming formula of capturing an audience’s attention before they can pick up their phone, but the second chapter lacks a unique character-driven flow that made the first such a timelessly enjoyable watch.
King doesn’t quite get the chance to build the necessary chemistry with her soulmate before Maridueña slips into an onscreen coma for the majority of the film, depriving them the childhood sweetheart backstory of the book. So… why should we care if the curse takes him too?
Meanwhile, Nicole Kidman and Maisie Williams are relegated to side roles with no apparent lives of their own, unlike the book that gives Gillian and Antonia each their own love story. As for the aunts Franny (Stockard Channing) and Jet (Dianne Weist), they seemingly only exist to [SPOILER ALERT] die in sacrifice to their younger counterparts.
Another character that was reprised for the sequel was the Owens family seaside house, originally built as an architectural shell on San Juan Island for the first movie, but recreated this time in the U.K. Unfortunately, the house only gets about 15 minutes of screen time as the Owens women swap the cozy setting for the beautiful England countryside.
Although Bullock has teased she wants to “pass the torch” to the next generation of witches with a potential trilogy-concluding installment, I’d be more intrigued to see the franchise go in the opposite direction. With two prequel books in Hoffman’s series, The Rules of Magic (2017) follows the magical coming-of-age of Franny, Jet and their brother—Sally and Gillian’s grandfather—Vincent in 1960s New York City, and Magic Lessons (2020) goes back to 1600s, tracing Maria’s journey from learning magic as an orphan in England to following her lover to Salem, Massachusetts, where her heartbreak ultimately sets the family curse.
So, while Practical Magic 2 is not quite as satisfying as the original, failing to capture what made it so magical in favor of a nostalgia-driven IP grab, it lays the groundwork for a franchise that could take the opportunity to redeem itself.
	Title: Practical Magic 2
Distributor: Warner Bros.
Release date: September 10, 2026 
Director: Susanne Bier
Screenwriters: Akiva Goldsman, Georgia Pritchett and Kelly Marcel
Cast: Sandra Bullock, Nicole Kidman, Lee Pace, Joey King, Maisie Williams, Stockard Channing, Dianne Wiest, Xolo Maridueña and Solly McLeod
Rating: PG-13
Running time: 2 hrs 10 mins

After 12 years of dominating American politics — either as president, as a candidate, or from the sidelines — Donald Trump will finally exit the stage in 2028, and it’s anybody’s guess what will come next. But one thing we do know is that Gen Z, many of whom were children during Trump’s first campaign, will play a large role in shaping that future.
Gen Z’s politics aren’t what people think
Is it time to update our understanding of Gen Z?
What’s less clear is what direction they might choose or what their politics are in the first place.
We do know a few things, thanks to a Vox collaboration with the polling firm Murmuration. For one, they’re highly independent: Almost 30 percent answered “none of the above” when they were asked to choose their political label in Murmuration’s survey. They’re an economically insecure cohort, at least for now; Murmuration found that only 28 percent of respondents between the ages of 18 and 30 said they could cover an unexpected expense of $500. And they had the largest gender gap of any age group when it came to supporting the Democratic presidential nominee in 2024 — women preferred Kamala Harris by 17 percentage points over men.
To find out more, Vox’s Astead Herndon spoke with Gen Z researcher Rachel Janfaza for a recent episode of America, Actually. They discussed the group’s political identities, preferences, and top issues, and what that all could mean for politics going forward. They discussed an important distinction between two versions of Gen Z, and whether its infamous gender gap is shifting. They also touched on how, contrary to seemingly everyone else, Gen Z is hope-maxxing.
Below is an excerpt of Astead’s conversation with Janfaza, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel.
You’ve done a lot of work around the different Gen Zs. I’ve heard you talk about Gen Z 1 versus Gen Z 2. How would we describe those differences?
I call this the theory of the two Gen Zs. I really started to cultivate it doing focus groups with young people in 2022, hearing the way that high school students at the time and college students at the time just had a different outlook, and I realized that those who had graduated high school before the start of the pandemic, those Gen Z-ers, just had a different worldview than the younger half of Gen Z, who were still in high school at the time that the pandemic hit.
And that is because of the taste of independence that people on the older cusp of Gen Z had prior to the lockdown situation. Anyone who is between roughly 29 and 22, I would say, is Gen Z 1.0, and anyone younger than that would be Gen Z 2.0.
And there’s no official end date to Gen Z right now. Like, it’s sort of 1997 to 2012, so it’s not very clear yet.
Can you just name for me what the difference was between the generations? How did that shape a different form of politics?
Gen Z 1.0 really came of age during Trump’s first term in office. This was a new phenomenon. He was breaking down past barriers, and we saw a lot of youth-led activism in response to actions or inaction from the first Trump administration.
You saw things like the March for Our Lives and climate strikes and the Black Lives Matter movement. And there was this very real sense that, you know, if we protest and demand change, perhaps there could be a difference.
Whereas Gen Z 2.0 came of age during the Biden era. This was a post-Covid sort of upbringing. And they really grew resistant to authority because they saw Democrats in charge during the time when kids went back to school and when there were things like mask mandates and vaccine mandates, especially in blue areas across the country where Democrats were handling the way that schools were reopening.
Young people whose lives and childhoods were on the line felt like they were guinea pigs in an experiment that they didn’t sign up for, and I think this is when we saw a movement away from Democrats. I don’t necessarily think that was toward Republicans.
Trump capitalized on this in 2024. Broadly speaking, Gen Z 2.0 is far less trusting of authority and institutions, far more independent. They hate labels, and this isn’t just political. They hate labels when it comes to gender, their relationships. No one wants to be boxed in. I hear this all the time in my focus groups, and so they just moved away from both parties writ large.
I also want to ask a couple of questions specifically about the gender divide, because that was such a big topic in the 2024 election.
We heard at that time, and I reported on, the change among young men that we saw manifested in that race. There was a 17-point gap between the votes of Gen Z men and Gen Z women. Before we get to where we are now, what do you think drove that gap?
No. The easy thing to say is it’s the algorithm, but that’s not the whole picture. I think a lot of young women felt like their bodily autonomy, freedom, rights were on the line. And a lot of young men care about that, but when I asked them, “What’s the top issue in the 2024 election?” few said abortion. They were like, “I care about that, but that’s not an issue that personally affects me.” And so I think that’s sort of what it came down to.
Women literally felt like it was their futures that were in question. And when you talk about the gender gap, you noted that young men shifted to the right, and that’s of course true.
Young women, since 2017, have remarkably moved to the left. And there have been a number of different causes to that, but every time there’s been a social wedge issue, whether it was early with immigration during Trump’s first term, the MeToo movement, the conversation about reproductive healthcare access and the fall of Roe v. Wade and the Dobbs decision … there have been so many examples of things that have pushed women further to the left, and then also a frustration with the way that Trump talks about women or accusations that have been made against him.
This is part of what I think makes this political period for Gen Z so fascinating. The Trump era will shape history across every generation, but Gen Z are the ones whose ideology was forming. And so there was this real sisterhood that emerged between young women during this time, where both on social media and in person, they were finding camaraderie around this shared fear for their future, but also appreciation of their individual rights and freedoms.
And young men didn’t see that same sort of bonding happening. And we talked a lot in 2024 about how Democrats had a problem with young men because they weren’t actively reaching out to young men. I’m the first person to say that Democrats really screwed that up, and that was a problem. But I think that there were not shared spaces for young men to come together in that way as there were for young women. I think that was part of what has driven this gap as well.
Should we update our thinking, though, of that gender divide from then to now? Like, are we still seeing the same big gaps between voting and political behavior from Gen Z men and women?
No. So largely, when I ask young people about the gender gap, they acknowledge that it exists, but they don’t like it. They don’t want to be stuck in this divide. Gen Z wants out of the gender war. They do.
We’re also now seeing a generation unite around a new set of issues that are pretty communal, that everyone can kind of agree upon. There’s a new shared set of issues that are less gendered and more affecting everybody.
AI? What are you talking about?
AI and the economy. Gen Z now agrees that the two main issues are AI and the economy. And obviously those are related.
I see this. You’re saying the gender gap among young people was at its peak because the parties were positioning themselves on gendered lines as well. And now, because of the consensus about issues that touch everyone, mainly the economy and AI, it’s a little bit of a permission structure to put the knives down in the gender fight because everyone’s lives are affected by this.
I think a lot of the gender war in the first place was kind of manufactured by people who were talking about Gen Z and not to them. You had the main candidates for president playing into that, too, and it was a man versus a woman, and it was kind of like, “These are your two options.” And we’re far past that.
I’ve talked about how Gen Z is hope-maxxing. You can say, “Oh, like it’s giving Obama,” but they really are looking for something to feel excited about. It’s enough of the doom and gloom. Growing up in this era has been exhausting.
The division and the vitriol isn’t fun for anyone. And maybe it’s the hopeless optimist in me, but I think that there is a real appetite for a post-Trumpian era of politics that is just less toxic. And that feels more hopeful and gives you something to rally around and unite around, rather than to be divided.

Kenya's chai lovers are not happy as the nation's cows run dry
- Published
Kenyans love their milky tea, or chai, but some are facing the worrying possibility of doing without as the country has been hit by a milk shortage.
A breakfast here is often incomplete without a cup of chai, made by boiling tea in generous amounts of milk, sometimes flavoured with ginger and spices. It is often served at meetings and during social visits, with many people taking the hot brew several times a day.
But now some may have to do without as supermarket chilled sections are nearly empty. Retailers have upped the price and are limiting how much shoppers can take home.
The government has put the dearth of milk in recent months down to drought, which has significantly reduced pasture and hampered production.
But the recent shortages are unusual, with the country's industry regulator itself admitting to "supply constraints" and "low stock levels" across the country.
Muthoni Macharia, who runs a restaurant in the capital, Nairobi, usually buys more than 70 packets of fresh milk - and is desperate and puzzled by the scarcity.
"Where has the milk gone?" she asked when the BBC spoke to her as she was out searching for at least a few packets to quench her customers thirst for chai.
Macharia says there have been shortages for about a week - and it was especially affecting her morning rush hour. Her regulars are not happy: some opting to take their tea black - but many will not.
"If they come in groups, and there's no milk tea, you see that's a loss for me," she said.
Kenya is one of the leading milk producers on the continent.
A long-established commercial dairy industry has led to pasteurised milk being very popular, particularly in urban areas, with Kenyans ranked among Africa's highest consumers, according to industry data.
Raw and fermented milk is more widely drunk in rural areas.
The milk shortage has sparked widespread public concern with some people promoting unfounded conspiracy theories about supermarkets deliberately trying to profit.
According to the Kenya Dairy Board (KDB), the government body that oversees the dairy sector, formal milk deliveries to processors fell by 3.7% from 84.4 million litres in June to 81.3 million litres in July, while preliminary investigations suggest deliveries declined further in August.
The Consumer Federation of Kenya (Cofek) says there has been a downward trend of supply since the beginning of the year.
It attributes this to a delay in the seasonal rains, which has reduced the grazing ground available, coupled with a 45% rise in the cost of animal feed.
Cofek has expressed concern over the rationing as well as the increasing cost, saying fresh milk prices have risen from 70 to 80 Kenyan shillings ($0.54 to $0.62; £0.40 to £0.46) a litre.
"This shortage was foreseeable, and in material part, avoidable," it says.
The consumer body says dairy processor New KCC, a state-owned company, and the KDB did not adequately absorb the milk surplus last year, adding that powder processed from the excess milk would have helped resolve the current crisis.
Some of the milk processors in Kenya often reconvert the powder into the more-preferred liquid milk during dry seasons when the supply of fresh milk goes down.
"Had these buffers been in place, today's supply shock would have been substantially cushioned," Cofek says.
It has demanded a recovery plan to include fodder and subsidy support for farmers.
This would include waiving of taxes on animal feed inputs, as well as "active retail price monitoring to deter opportunity price gouging and rationing".
In response to media enquiries, the dairy board's managing director William Maritim assured that despite the "temporary supply constraint", milk continued to be available.
Fresh pasteurised milk, which has a shorter shelf life, had been more affected than the more long-life UHT milk, he said.
Customers at Nairobi supermarkets on the hunt for milk told the BBC they were worried about rising costs.
"Sometimes when I go to the supermarket I find there is none. When I do find some, the price has gone up. Today it is this price, tomorrow it has gone up again," said Bernard Abok, who does his shopping after finishing work.
Patricia Gathoni said if the prices kept going up she would have to rethink what she gave her children, saying she had resorted to adding water to the milk that she managed to buy.
On Thursday, agriculture ministry officials held a meeting with the association of dairy processors about the problem, with the ministry committing to support farmers, stabilise milk supply and protect consumers.
The ministry's top official in charge of livestock development, Jonathan Mueke, said the immediate focus was to get more feed for farmers, including through duty-free importation of yellow maize.
He said they were also looking at longer-term solutions that would manage stability across periods when there was surplus milk and when there were shortages.
Reports of milk going to waste are not uncommon during periods of a dairy glut. Farmers have often complained about how little they are paid for their perishable produce at such times - but they have few options because of limited processing or storage capacity.
According to Mueke, the government is considering setting up a fund to help support the preservation of milk during such periods.
In the meantime, the government is also considering temporarily importing milk from the neighbouring countries to ease the shortage.
For the devoted Kenyan chai lover, that may offer some respite.

Tuesday 8 September 2026 17:07, UK
Buffalo Bills head coach Joe Brady is under the most pressure in the NFL as he seeks to lead Josh Allen's side from 'bridesmaid to bride', says Sky Sports' Phoebe Schecter.
The Bills renew their Super Bowl quest this season having endured more playoff agony earlier this year when they were beaten by the Denver Broncos in overtime of January's Divisional Round clash.
It had been deemed a premature end to one of their best opportunities yet to end prolonged Super Bowl agony, with Patrick Mahomes' Kansas City Chiefs absent from the playoffs for the first time since 2014 and the likes of Lamar Jackson and Joe Burrow also nowhere to be seen.
Sean McDermott was subsequently fired after nine campaigns in charge, with Brady being promoted to head coach from his post as offensive coordinator.

Their 73 victories in that period are notably more than any other team in the league, Allen consistently spearheading one of football's most potent offenses.
Buffalo sought to strengthen their quarterback's aerial options by trading for Chicago Bears wide receiver DJ Moore, who hasn't recorded a 1,000-yard campaign since 2023.
"You look at what DJ Moore does for the team when you bring him in," Schecter continued. "That already elevates an offense that has never really had a star receiver.

Joe Burrow and the Cincinnati Bengals stake their only claim as NFL 'nearly men' alongside both Allen's Bills and Jackson's Baltimore Ravens.
The Bengals have missed out on the playoffs for three straight years and managed just one postseason appearance since their defeat to the Los Angeles Rams at Super Bowl LVI.
Burrow, who has missed 16 games through injury over the last three seasons, demanded urgency from his team this offseason as he seeks to maximise, when healthy, one of the most explosive passing attacks in football.

"But bringing in Boye Mafe, Jonathan Allen, you get Kyle Dugger from the Patriots, you've got a smart defense. You've got a safety who can now organise everybody.
"They've got to be able to go down and capitalise on having this fantastic trio on offense with Burrow, Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins and go attack it. This city needs it.
