The recipe for most fall outfits starts with a good pair of jeans.
High-quality denim lasts for years and can be styled again and again with whatever the next season calls for. And although trends come and go, no fit is more versatile or reliable than a standard straight-leg jean.
I was overdue for a new pair, so I turned to Gap, Banana Republic, and Old Navy (all owned by Gap Inc.) to find my new closet staple.
I ordered a similar style from all three retailers and wore them each for one day on a variety of outings. Then, I evaluated them based on design, fit, fabric, price, and the overall online ordering experience.
After putting them to the test, there was one clear winner, one that was just OK, and one I probably wouldn't order again.
Honestly, I was disappointed by the straight-leg jeans from Old Navy
I admire Old Navy for offering both classic and trending pieces at approachable price points.
I had originally ordered the mid-rise slouchy straight jeans in my usual size, but when they arrived, they were way too big on me. In fact, the pair fit so loosely that they were unwearable, so I had to return them.
Unfortunately, the smaller size wasn't in stock, so I ended up buying the mid-rise Wow boyfriend straight jeans and sizing down.
The new pair still fit a bit awkwardly around the waist and thighs, but overall, they were much better. I liked the versatile dark wash, which goes well with both casual and more elevated outfits.
I wore these on a weekday while working from a coffee shop, and they were comfortable both while walking there and when sitting for a few hours at a time.
The fabric — made from 80% cotton, 13% recycled polyester, 5% recycled cotton, and 1% spandex — felt a bit stretchier than what I would expect from denim. However, it made the pants feel soft and chafe-safe.
Although I probably wouldn't order these again due to the unpredictable fit, for $40, they're a solid low-cost option (and I later saw them on sale for only $22).
I'm also excited to see how the brand's offerings evolve in the coming months, given that Old Navy's new president and CEO, is set to take over in November.
The Banana Republic jeans were nice, but came with a hefty price tag
Banana Republic is Gap Inc.'s "attainable luxury" brand, and I'm always a bit surprised by how highly priced some of their styles are. However, I was excited to give the denim a try.
I ordered the mid-rise 90s classic jean, and I immediately loved the medium wash and shape of the pants.
These were a bit too large around the waist and in length, and although I didn't necessarily need to exchange them, I'd likely get them tailored for a better fit for my body type.
The structure of the straight-leg cut was incredibly flattering and would pair nicely with any blouse or sweater in my closet. I also thought the construction around the zipper and pockets seemed high-quality and durable.
When wearing these for a date night out to dinner and drinks, I felt both fashionable and comfortable throughout the evening.
I could feel the difference in fabric quality compared to the pair from Old Navy, too. Made from from 70% cotton, 28% Tencel lyocell, and 2% elastane spandex, the fabric felt more structured and crisp.
However, that also meant a significant difference in cost — this pair cost me $130. I think they'd be worth the investment, but I'd consider sizing down next time.
The Gap straight-leg jeans really won me over
Gap has always been a hub for closet staples. Lately, the brand's denim marketing and ad campaigns have been especially notable, from the KATSEYE "Better in Denim" commercial to the Hailey Bieber collaboration.
So, I was excited to put the brand's denim to the test and ordered the Gap mid-rise straight taper jeans.
I ordered these in my usual size, and they fit me perfectly. These had a slightly lighter medium wash, which is perfect for daytime and summer-to-fall transition looks. They hugged my curves well, and the waistline sat nicely at my hips.
I wore these jeans for coffee and shopping with a friend, paired with a simple blouse and kitten heels. I felt comfortable and confident wearing them, and the straight silhouette elongated my legs (which can be rare as a short person).
This pair is made from 100% cotton (95% cotton, 5% recycled cotton), so they were durable yet still soft enough on my skin. They cost $90, but are well worth the price for a pair of jeans I know I'll wear for years to come. Plus, I later saw them on sale for $53.
Business Insider reached out to Old Navy, Banana Republic, and Gap for comment.

Days before Hamas stormed into Israel on October 7, 2023, UAE president Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed reportedly delivered prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu a direct warning that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was preparing a major attack. Netanyahu, however, did not share the warning with Israel’s senior security leadership, according to a new investigation report.
According to Israeli publication Haaretz, which based its report on the new book, ‘Kidnapped: 843 Days of Abandonment’, MBZ spoke to Netanyahu for 45 minutes from Abu Dhabi, around 10 days before Hamas launched its October 7 attack.
Haaretz said the three senior foreign officials were updated on the contents of the 45-minute phone call at the end of September. The account, additionally, draws on interviews with senior Israeli officials, recordings, internal documents and correspondence.
A close adviser to bin Zayed, who was aware of the conversation, told Haaretz that the Emirati president had sought to convey the seriousness of the threat.
“The emir explained that, in his assessment, Sinwar was preparing for a major event,” the adviser said. “He told Netanyahu that Israel should be ready.”
Bin Zayed also urged Netanyahu to address the wider sources of instability, including the economic situation in Gaza and rising tensions in the West Bank.
According to the adviser, MBZ was surprised by Netanyahu’s response, as he did not appear alarmed. He told bin Zayed that he believed Hamas was preparing to act in the West Bank and assured him that Israel was ready to respond to any scenario.
The Emirati leader later discussed the warning with CIA director William J Burns, according to Haaretz. Bin Zayed reportedly described his concern that ‘something there is about to explode’ and said Netanyahu had focused instead on the West Bank.
The information reaching bin Zayed had reportedly originated with Yahya Sinwar. Haaretz said a Fatah figure involved in contacts over a prisoner deal had received repeated warnings from the Hamas leader after negotiations stalled.
“Tell the Israelis if they don’t advance, I’m preparing a huge surprise for them,” Sinwar reportedly said in one exchange. “Tell them to expect an earthquake.”
In another conversation, he described his plans as “a formidable operation”, according to the report. The Fatah interlocutor subsequently passed the information to a person connected to bin Zayed.
"The emir hoped that despite his reserved response, Netanyahu would take the message seriously and take action," the adviser says. Instead, Netanyahu chose not to brief the heads of his defense establishment. Israel’s top security chiefs, including the Shin Bet and Mossad heads and the IDF chief of staff, were not informed.
Haaretz also reported that Egypt’s intelligence chief, gen. Abbas Kamel, separately warned Netanyahu around the same period about “something unusual, a terrifying operation” that Hamas was preparing.
Netanyahu reportedly responded, “In Gaza, we are in the picture, we are in control. Our problem is with the West Bank, and that's where we are also diverting forces.”
On October 1, Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar again raised the possibility of taking proactive action against Hamas, including targeting senior figures. Haaretz said Netanyahu did not approve or reject the proposals and did not disclose his reported conversation with bin Zayed.
A senior Shin Bet official told Haaretz that knowledge of the warning could have changed how the agency interpreted other intelligence.
“If we had known about the warnings, there’s a chance it would have given much greater weight to the initial message that reached us from Sinwar,” the official said.
The official added, “Perhaps it would have also clarified what was behind his sudden withdrawal from the de-escalation talks in early September. It’s possible we would have put two and two together and reached a completely different conclusion from the one we arrived at, one that might have altered our entire intelligence picture.”
Netanyahu’s office has rejected the central allegation. In a response cited by Times of Israel, the Prime Minister’s Office called the report “a total lie!” and said, “Prime Minister Netanyahu did not speak with the president of the United Arab Emirates during the period in question and received no warning from him.”

On 26 August 2026, massive flash floods struck parts of Nepal and Tibet after an ice-and-rock avalanche triggered a surge of water and debris through the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river systems. The disaster destroyed homes, roads, bridges, hydropower projects and other infrastructure. As of 04 September, at least 1,252 people have died in Nepal, and more than 4,200 remain missing. Search and rescue operations are continuing, with two hydropower workers rescued alive from a tunnel on 4 September, nine days after the disaster (here, here, here, and here).
Amid this, a photo is being widely shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows a young girl being protected by her brother, who were victims of the Nepal floods. Let’s verify the truth behind the photo in this article.
Claim: The photo shows a young girl being protected by her brother, who are victims of the August 2026 Nepal floods.
Fact: The photo is not related to the August 2026 Nepal floods. Vietnamese photojournalist Na Son Nguyen took it in October 2007 in Can Ty, a remote village in Hà Giang province, Vietnam. The photo shows two Hmong siblings, with the boy comforting his younger sister while their parents were away working in the fields. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A Google Lens search of the viral photo led us to a BBC report (archived) dated 4 May 2015 featuring the same photo, confirming that it predates the 2026 Nepal floods. According to the report, Vietnamese photographer Na Son Nguyen took the photo in October 2007 in Can Ty, a remote village in Ha Giang province, Vietnam. Talking to the BBC, he said the photo shows two Hmong siblings, with the boy comforting his crying sister while their parents were away working in the fields. He also said this was his most-shared photo, but unfortunately, it was repeatedly circulated online in the wrong context.
We also found (archived) an Instagram post by Vietnam-based photojournalist Na Son Nguyen featuring the same photo, published on 2 April 2015. The post states that Nguyen captured the photo in October 2007 in a mountainous village in Hà Giang province, Vietnam. He said the photo shows a young boy comforting his younger sister while their parents were away working in the fields. This confirms that the viral photo is unrelated to the recent floods in Nepal.
To sum up, this viral photo does not show children affected by the August 2026 Nepal floods; it was taken in Vietnam in 2007.

Mumbai, Sep 08: Stock market benchmark indices Sensex and Nifty declined in early trade on Tuesday as rising crude oil prices and the US-Iran hostilities kept risk appetite subdued.
The 30-share BSE Sensex dropped 382.25 points to 75,750.56 in early trade. The 50-share NSE Nifty declined 97.80 points to 23,681.80.
Among the 30 Sensex firms, Mahindra & Mahindra, Trent, Sun Pharma, Axis Bank, ICICI Bank and Tata Consultancy Services were the major laggards.
Bharat Electronics, Eternal and Adani Ports were the gainers.
Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, traded 0.54 per cent higher at USD 97.52 per barrel.
"Rising crude prices and renewed US–Iran hostilities kept risk appetite subdued," Rajesh Palviya, Head of Research, Axis Direct, said.
In Asian markets, South Korea's Kospi, Japan's Nikkei 225 index and Shanghai's SSE Composite index quoted higher, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng index traded lower.
US markets were closed on Monday for the Labour Day holiday.
"Global cues are mixed. US markets were closed overnight for the Labour Day holiday, while Asian markets are trading mixed this morning, with the unresolved geopolitical crisis and elevated crude oil prices remaining the dominant variables for investor sentiment," Hariselvan Radhakrishnan, Founder & CEO of HST Wealth, a research analyst firm, said.
Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) bought equities worth Rs 280.13 crore on Monday, according to exchange data.
"The geopolitical backdrop remains fragile as the US-Iran conflict shows few signs of easing. Uncertainty surrounding the Strait of Hormuz and the timing of its full reopening continues to underpin concerns over global oil supplies and broader market sentiment," Ponmudi R, CEO of Enrich Money, an online trading and wealth-tech firm, said.

Back to school: Everything you need to know about Ontario's education policy changes
A cheat sheet on the major changes for the 2026-2027 school year
Tuesday marks the official return to school for hundreds of thousands of Ontario students, but the academic landscape inside those halls will look a little different this fall.
If you’ve just come off a busy summer full of beach days and cottage trips, here are some of the major updates you may have missed.
Mandatory final written exams for high school courses
In June, Education Minister Paul Calandra announced a string of changes, including making final written exams mandatory for most high school courses.
The move is “intended to provide a more consistent approach to assessment and evaluation for students in Grades 9 to 12,” according to the province’s website.
For Grades 9 and 10, mandatory final written exams are now worth 20 per cent in core subjects like english, math and science. The EQAO Grade 9 mathematics assessment counts as a written final exam.
In Grades 11 and 12, exams account for 25 per cent of the grades in core subjects, while non-core subjects split final evaluations between a written exam and a culminating project.
Workplace preparation, co-op and special education courses remain exempt from written exams, though final non-written evaluations are still required.
Attendance will now factor into final grades
Starting this school year, attendance and participation will account for 15 per cent of a final mark in Grades 9 and 10. In the upper years, it will count for 10 per cent.
A student who has more than two unexcused absences won't be able to get that full 10 or 15 per cent.
After the change was announced in June, Calandra told The Canadian Press attendance rates in Ontario high schools have been among the worst in the country.
"My advice to parents is, keep them in school," he said at the time. "Education should be their priority.”
Illnesses and religious holidays are categorized as excused absences and will not affect grades.
New financial literacy graduation requirement
Ontario high school students also now need to pass a financial literacy test in order to graduate.
Grade 10 students will take the new standardized financial literacy evaluation in Career Studies (GLC2O) and must score at least 70 per cent to pass.
According to the province's website, students will have two opportunities during the course to achieve that benchmark. If they don’t succeed, they will be provided more opportunities outside the course.
The education minister announced the requirement last spring, saying students need practical, real-world skills, including on how to manage money and budgets.
The evaluation will focus on essential financial life skills, including household budgeting, interest rates, credit cards, saving strategies and consumer awareness, the province says.
Student and family support offices at all school boards
Last week, the province announced student and family support offices will open at all 72 school boards.
The province first announced the program last fall, when it placed five school boards under provincial control for alleged mismanagement, ordering those boards to open support offices by January 2026.
When announcing the program expansion in Hamilton last week, Calandra said the offices are meant to give parents and caregivers a clear next step when concerns cannot be resolved at the school level.
“We know there are going to be times when parents have questions and concerns,” he said. “Most of these can and should be resolved with the teacher or principal.”
But parents should not have to spend weeks trying to determine who is responsible for handling more complex issues, Calandra said.
New 'back to basics' kindergarten curriculum
A new kindergarten curriculum will take effect this school year.
The new "back-to-basics" curriculum shifts away from play-based learning towards academic rigour, according to the province.
It includes new learning requirements in math, science and language skills, where the previous curriculum emphasized learning through exploration and play.
Some teachers have expressed concern over whether the new expectations are age-appropriate for four- and five-year-old children.
The province says the curriculum maintains learning through play while introducing more structured lessons in reading, writing and math.

Allow overseas stars to play for England - Lawes
- Published
England selection should no longer be restricted to players based at domestic clubs, according to cap centurion Courtney Lawes.
The 37-year-old is back in contention to add to his 105 England appearances, having signed a one-year deal with Sale after two seasons at Brive in the French second tier.
A clutch of English talent - notably Toulouse star Jack Willis - remain across the Channel and out of reach for England head coach Steve Borthwick.
"I can see why they do it because they don't want all their players playing abroad, but I don't think that's necessarily going to be the case anyway," said Lawes.
"It's important that you have the best players available for selection. If we want the game to develop and more people to watch it, I think it has to develop.
"I just reckon you make your best players available and by any means necessary.
"I don't see why you'd limit yourself."
In addition to Willis, who was voted the best player in France in 2024-25 and could well retain the award after a player-of-the-match performance in the Top 14 final in June, Willis' brother Tom, Kyle Sinckler, Manu Tuilagi, David Ribbans, Billy Vunipola, Lewis Ludlam and Junior Kpoku also ply their trade in France.
England have better access and control over players who are at Prem clubs. The clubs, in turn, benefit from central payments from the Rugby Football Union (RFU) and more chance of retaining their biggest stars, who face international exile with a move overseas.
Other nations, such as New Zealand, France and Ireland, have a policy of picking home-based players, but some of England's other rivals, such as South Africa, Australia and Scotland, lean heavily on players based abroad.
Borthwick has opted not to include either Lawes or Joe Marchant, his new Sale team-mate who has spent the past three seasons at Stade Francais in Paris, in his first training camp of the season, asking them to prove themselves in the Prem first.
The England coach adopted a similar approach when Owen Farrell returned from Racing 92 at the start of last season.
"I spoke to Steve a little bit," said Lawes, who played 80 minutes in a 50-28 win over Bath in the Prem Rugby Cup on Sunday, to Rugby Union Weekly.
"It was just what I would expect - he knows I'm coming back and he's going keep an eye on me, but he wants to see me play in the Prem first and I think that's a good idea.
"I've spent two years away, let's see how I go in the Prem first, I'm not really thinking about England before I can get up and running for Sale so that's there's no point."
Lawes, who initially retired from Test rugby after the 2023 Rugby World Cup semi-final defeat by South Africa, said his return to England was not something he expected when he departed boyhood club Northampton in the wake of lifting the domestic title the following year.
"Probably not, no [I didn't expect to be back]," he added.
"All options were on the table last season - potentially staying at Brive, potentially coming back or retiring. They were all on the table but you're a long time retired and I can still move really well so, why not when you've still got it in your legs?"
Watching from afar, he believes England have the talent to improve on an erratic 2025-26 campaign.
"It's obviously been pretty up and down more recently," he added. "They had an unbelievable autumn and then struggled in the Six Nations.
"It is hard to know exactly what's going on in camp, but obviously there's some issues otherwise they'd probably be playing a bit better than they are.
"With the squad they've got they should be doing quite well."

There is much to be said for the extraordinary women living ordinary lives, who nonetheless shaped India. Women have changed public life in the country far more than their presence in formal politics would suggest.
And so, as India marked its 79th birthday over the weekend, I found myself reflecting on the multitude of people’s movements, big and small – as well as the women who helped shape them. During India’s struggle for freedom from British rule, women organised boycotts of British goods, made contraband salt and marched to confront the police, taking on roles usually dominated by men. In the 1970s Chipko movement, protesting deforestation, women put their bodies on the line, wrapping them around trees to stop them being felled, turning a local struggle into a national reckoning over environment and development. More recently, grandmothers in Shaheen Bagh sat to protest the citizenship law, which critics have denounced as discriminatory, creating space for dissent when many thought none existed.
Today, routes into public life for women have multiplied, with social media enabling people without political links to be in the public eye. But not all barriers have disappeared. Electoral politics remains notoriously hard to break into, especially for women. Almost half of all female parliamentarians and state legislators come from political families, while for men it is 18%, a 2025 analysis by Association for Democratic Reforms showed.
What makes a woman leading an ordinary life suddenly want to put her head above the parapet to change things for everyone? I spoke to women thrust into the spotlight in the recent student movement, who have stepped in front of vans, starved themselves and had abuse hurled at them in the process – to find out why they do it.
‘Politics is not just slogans and protests’: Neha Bora, 29
The president of the leftwing All India Students’ Association, Bora fasted for 23 days, demanding accountability over exam paper leaks and the resignation of the Education Minister during the Cockroach Protests. Now, she is touring the country as part of a Gen Z Rising outreach campaign on education reforms.
“I am a PhD student at Jawaharlal Nehru University in theatre and performance studies. My family’s political understanding is very different from mine. I ended up joining politics because that was the only way I could make sense of the times that I was living in – to not be … completely helpless in the decisions that are made for me, that should be made by me. To have a say in what I do, how I do it and what gets done around me. What is tolerable, what is good, what is injustice – all these definitions made sense to me through politics. Theatre was the first thing that taught me that politics is not just slogans and protests. Politics is the very language in which you talk to yourselves, the thoughts you formulate in your head, the relationships you have with your friends, family and peers. Student politics reaffirmed this idea.
Freedom as a student means the ability to study in a university where the model of education has not been turned into an opportunity for profit. Where education is something that helps societies move forward from dogmatism, conservatism and orthodoxy.”
‘Freedom for me is to have a voice – and not be ashamed’: Rhiya Ahir, 27
A model, actor and theatre artist from Mumbai, Ahir made the split-second decision to physically block a police van holding detained protesters – an act that exposed her to an organised hate campaign.
“I started doing theatre when I was four and a half. It taught me empathy and understanding other people’s pain, even people I don’t know. I’ve always been raised with the belief that if you see something wrong you have to step in.
Freedom for me is to have a voice, to put it across confidently and to not be ashamed. I was trolled for a photo in a swimsuit. But what about the uncles who wear chaddis at the Ganga ghat? My clothes are not my character. My clothes cannot overshadow the point or the fact that I was there, and I helped 20 students get back home safely that day. So, my clothes are just my clothes.
The hate did make me second-guess myself. The first two days [after the Mumbai protest] were very difficult because I was still trying to wrap my head around what had happened. They couldn’t find fault with my argument, so they started questioning my character. They went through my Instagram and found that I was a model. They talked about what I wear. They said she’s doing it for the camera.
When the hate started pouring in I was like, ‘What did I do to offend someone? Did I do something wrong?’ Then I realised this doesn’t change my reality. This doesn’t change who I am as a person. I don’t have to prove myself to anyone.”
‘The police have visited my ancestral village asking for information on me’: Danish Ali, 24
Ali was among the student activists on hunger strike at Jantar Mantar. A member of the Jawaharlal Nehru University student union, she faces a year-long suspension for dismantling a facial recognition system at the campus library. For her, freedom is deeply personal and rooted in her identity as a Muslim woman.
“I come from a very small town in Madhya Pradesh. No one in my family had even visited the city, so going to Delhi for higher education was almost like going abroad for education. Since the protest, the police have visited my ancestral village asking for information on me. They called my father, asking him to tell me to focus on my studies.
As a student activist, freedom means to be able to critique the government openly and say that we don’t like their policies. Freedom is being assertive about your individuality and not caring what the society would says, what your parents might say or what the state might do to you.
Freedom also means being an equal citizen in this country. Muslims in this country are being made to feel as if they are secondary and that they don’t have any right to express their religious or cultural identities. I am an equal citizen and I don’t want anyone to tell me otherwise.”
‘What used to work … won’t work with the youth’: Ratna Singh, 31
She traded a career in the law and journalism to join the Cockroach Janata party, where she now serves as the legal head. She felt drawn to the protests, seeing her work reflected in the students’ demand for accountability. Initially hesitant to become its public face, she stepped forward as spokesperson when they needed female voices.
“When I was in law school, most of my classmates would go to law chambers for internships but I would spend the summers teaching children at NGOs. Education has been something I have been very sensitive towards, and I believe every child should have access to it.
A lot of people were criticising us [and calling us] an impatient generation. We are impatient because we want to see change. We can’t be protesting and be OK with not getting answers from the government. We are also just done with divide and rule politics on the basis of religion. Political parties need to understand that what used to work for a certain mindset of people – it won’t work with the youth.
There are so many protests which have begun in different parts of the country. The fear of speaking up is gone. We are seeing a lot of leaders coming up in their own districts. They are starting their own initiatives. I think that’s giving us all hope to keep going.”
What else we’re reading about
Political promises | In his Independence Day speech, Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced a series of youth-focused initiatives, including an AI skills programme, free online coaching for competitive exams and a countrywide sport talent hunt. His call to identify “dimagi naxals”, or people aligned with Naxal ideology, referring to the armed guerilla movement in central India, was criticised by the Opposition as a threat to suppress critics and rivals.
Environment targets missed | The Green India Mission, for protecting and restoring the country’s declining forest cover, fell short of its target by 97% over the past decade, according to an audit report tabled in Parliament. New forest cover added was just 0.03409 million hectares, the report said, citing poor planning and inadequate funding.
Sister act | Two women of Indian origin adopted by separate Dutch families 40 years ago, who became friends as children, recently discovered they are sisters after a DNA test, Reuters reported. “It’s like a missing puzzle piece has been found,” one said.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Actor Imran Khan (@imrankhan) recommends: “Rang De Basanti is an extremely timely and relevant film for this moment; it follows a young English film-maker who befriends a group of Indian students. They set out to make a film about the Indian freedom movement. A tragic accident blurs the lines between past and present, throwing them into their own conflict against an unjust power structure. The film is funny but also heartbreaking. It celebrates the spirit of the great revolutionaries, and imagines what their modern counterparts might stand for. And the soundtrack gives us AR Rahman at his most audaciously experimental. It rocks.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
Two
Question hour in Lok Sabha functioned for 1% percent of its scheduled time during the parliament’s monsoon session, the lowest since 2019, according to PRS Legislative Research, a nonprofit that tracks the functioning of the parliament and state assemblies. The key forum for members of parliament to question the government saw two questions answered in nine minutes, PRS said.
Vibe check
For creator Maroof Umar (@maroofculmen), storytelling can change the way we see the world. And the stories he tells, rooted in heritage and culture through cinematically shot videos, can both break and mend your heart. Each has a person at its center but the stories also belong to the city and its communities. His short videos capture his (and my) hometown of Lucknow most frequently, but his latest work takes us to a sweet shop in Varanasi. In it, Ram Bhandar makes tricolor treats in a nod to the colors of the Indian flag, carrying on a tradition begun by his ancestors decades before, as they tried to spread patriotic fervor during the freedom movement.

Parents are pushing back on classroom screen time in a 'techlash' over too much technology in schools
'We do not need a Google account to learn,' says parent and educator
As an occasional substitute teacher for middle- and high-schoolers in Nova Scotia, Kim Herrick often gets a front-row seat seeing how teens use tech at school.
Whether students are tasked with assignments, work for another class or granted free time, Herrick regularly sees them checking Snapchat, TikTok or Instagram accounts, shopping online, gaming or even trading Bitcoin — easily bypassing school board security methods aimed at blocking such use.
The ubiquity of students engaging in non-educational online activities — and the futile attempts to clamp down on it — have contributed to her view that we need to reconsider the tech used by default in classes today.
But the alarm bells really started going off for Herrick when she discovered her elder daughter — who's starting Grade 2 this fall — has had a school Google account for three years, without Herrick knowing. Herrick said she couldn't log into the account and school officials said she couldn't opt-out or have it deleted, saying it was necessary for access to educational apps and "a requirement" for learning.
We have hundreds of years of going to school as humans, Herrick said. "We do not need a Google account to learn."
Many parents, educators, advocacy groups and experts are pushing back against the amount of screen time in schools and the prevalence of tech tools woven into the current education system, with some making links to a range of woes, from behavioural issues to distracted students to data breaches that put youngsters' privacy at risk.
Yet a rollback to classroom practices of the past isn't the answer to the current "techlash," say some education experts, who favour intentional and thoughtful use of technology as the way forward.
Changing approach to tech in education
For years, a one-to-one student-to-device ratio, web access and learning through game-like applications have been seen as symbols of educational progress. But amid a worldwide push to reduce teen smartphone and social media use, a vocal wave of parent groups — including Skills Before Screens in Canada, the U.K.-based Close Screen Open Minds, as well as Schools Beyond Screens and ScreenSense in the U.S. — is broadening this scrutiny to encompass educational tech usage more generally.
After having prioritized digital schooling for the past decade, for instance, Sweden has recently shifted back toward physical textbooks, pen-and-paper homework, reinvesting in libraries and screen-free classrooms (particularly for younger students), citing falling scores on international assessments.
Poor reading scores have tech-friendly Norway making a similar return to physical books in its schools, as well as introducing a near-ban on Generative AI usage in elementary, with restrictions for high-schoolers.
In the U.S., parental demands have led to stricter tech policies at the country's two largest school boards. The Los Angeles Unified School District has already started the school year with limits on screen time in every grade, including a total device ban before Grade 2. On the opposite coast, New York is restricting one-to-one device time for Grade 2 and below and suggesting caps for older elementary students. It's also halting student-facing Generative AI use through Grade 8 and limiting use for high schoolers, for now.
Herrick says many parents, such as herself, are in the dark about the screens and apps their youngsters access in class, let alone what the responsible use or data privacy agreements are regarding those apps and school accounts.
Beyond privacy, the mother of two and former wilderness leadership educator in the U.S. is also concerned about what unfettered school tech use means for the long term.
She worries about susceptibility to distraction — she's had secondary students claim they're multitasking as they juggle a bevy of browser tabs, apps or screens — not to mention negative impacts on their mental and physical health down the road.
In the meantime, overreliance on tech also bogs down educators' precious time with policing student usage and dealing with tech support, rather than teaching, Herrick said.
Intention versus novelty
Classroom tech use varies across Canadian regions, schools and educators, but it's indeed integrated into teaching today, according to Johanathan Woodworth, an assistant professor at Mount Saint Vincent University in Halifax.
Whether teachers are getting students to research a project online, study the solar system via a virtual reality simulator or test out an AI chatbot, Woodworth emphasizes that tech use must be intentional, thoughtful and directly connected to the skills students are expected to learn.
"A lot of times teachers use technology in the classroom because of the novelty effect and engagement — but the novelty effect wears off," Woodworth said from Halifax, where he teaches educational technology to existing and prospective teachers.
"The first step is to think about 'Do I even need to use it? What is the purpose of me using it? Does it actually help me in my classroom?'"
It's important teachers are supported with guidelines and enough training on how to carefully and effectively use technology, he says, in order to understand it and, in turn, teach and model that knowledge to their students.
Striving for balance
Rolling back to no-tech classrooms isn't necessarily the answer either, Woodworth said, since a main reason schools employ tech today — text-to-speech and speech-to-text applications, for instance — is to accommodate students with disabilities.
Schools must balance "purposeful" tech use with the need to prep students for a tech-filled world, while also ensuring it's "not used as a distraction," according to education consultant Tom D'Amico, former director of education of the Ottawa Catholic School Board.
He says the concerns raised by parents — both the ones driving the current "techlash" and those pushing for their kids to build tech skills — are contributing to a "balanced and focused" approach by school boards.
In his current work advising school districts across Canada about artificial intelligence, D'Amico says he's noticing a shift: schools taking a more developmentally and age-informed approach to technology.
For instance, "that means regardless of the province, you're looking at the earliest grades not having a lot of device time, but still getting AI literacy. They still need to learn about digital citizenship, what it means to use a computer," he said, noting gradual introduction of more technology in middle and high school.
- As more teens turn to AI for emotional support, experts say it's no substitute for human connection
- What's the secret to perfect marks? Family, community, discipline and time management, top scholars say
"Critical thinking can be [taught] without the technology as well in the early ages," D'Amico added, emphasizing that this learning must be "embedded in the curriculum, so it happens every single year, in an age-appropriate manner."
Ultimately, he says, the top focus of schools should be student learning and strengthening students' connections with teachers and their classmates.
"What's the number one technology in a classroom? It's the student and their brain," he said.

Last month, I injected myself with a GLP-1 drug and became my own lab rat for three weeks.
As a fitness coach with my weight well under control, I didn’t need this. And yet, I took it. Why?
I work with people to treat their metabolic disease — obesity, diabetes, fatty liver, PMOS, metabolic syndrome. GLP-1 medicines, including semaglutide (the drug in Ozempic) and tirzepatide (the drug in Mounjaro), are among the tools we use. My job is to guide users to a healthy lifestyle (the right kind of activity, better food, improved sleep), while my medical team monitors their health markers. Our goal is to get them off the drug, with their health intact.
For the last 15 years, I’ve coached thousands of people on their strength and health. The single biggest pattern, which shows in their urgency and commitment to the cause, is the trigger moment. A doctor check-up, a wedding, or even a small event like finding themselves unable to bend down and tie their shoelaces helps them prioritise their health and wellness. As they get stronger and start building good lifestyle habits, good things happen.
But for a large percentage, the struggle with weight is real. And it never really ends. While people who lose weight see improvement in their quality of life across the board, maintaining that weight is an uphill struggle, especially when the reality and demands of life hit. As work mounts and stress amplifies, many of these habits crack, especially given the tremendous strain on our time and mental health and the way the environment is structured around us. You may have the best intentions, but you may still end up skimping on sleep or reaching for junk food.
Which is where GLP-1 drugs come in: this new tool in a weight loss toolbox, which I recently tried firsthand – something I always do, even when it comes to designing training plans. I always test-drive anything I recommend for my clients to coach well; I don’t know any other way.
How it went
I’ll start with a caveat: do not do this yourself. While I had no prescription and did not medically need the drug, I did this systematically. I tracked my vitals daily and weekly and reported my subjective and objective experience nearly every day to my doctor and my dietitian.
The drug I opted for was Mounjaro, the most advanced GLP-1 drug on the market today, opting for a starter dose of around 2.5 mg/ week, after consulting with my doctor. Honestly, I did not expect much, since my baseline lifestyle is good. I eat well 85% of the time; I’m active five or six days a week; my sleep hygiene is decent (even if my sleep, lately, hasn't been). But the experience surprised me more than I expected.
Food noise — the constant background hum of thinking about food — simply disappeared. I wanted simple, sattvic food, finding anything greasy immediately unappetising. Over-eating was not possible, whether it was my favourite dessert or the potato chips with my rice. The ease with which I could move through a world of hyper-palatable food, whether I was eating out, ordering in, or eating home-cooked meals, was mind-blowing.
That is the beauty of these drugs: they allow for mindful eating, making that admittedly woo-woo term accessible to all. I wasn't constantly thinking about food or tempted by the package of cupcakes being passed around at work, and I made sensible, adult decisions about food quite naturally, indulging in my favourite snacks without overeating.
In fact, I naturally wanted to eat more nutritious meals because they make me feel good. And I paid attention to my body and how it responded. Also, because I simply could not overeat, my energy levels started to improve, making it a truly liberating time.
Add a doctor, diet and activity
Dr Arun Raghavan, diabetologist and co-founder of Chennai’s Revivo Clinic, which focusses on metabolic care for obesity and diabetes, explains that GLP-1s in India are for adults with a BMI of 30 or higher who have at least one weight-related condition, such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol, or Type 2 diabetes. “They work alongside diet and activity. They are not a stand-alone fix,” he cautions.
And yes, some people should not touch them at all, he adds: anyone with a personal or family history of certain thyroid cancers or a rare inherited hormone disorder, and those with a history of pancreatitis or gallbladder disease. “Most bad reactions come down to the wrong patient, no baseline work-up, or no monitoring.”
The side effects are mostly gastrointestinal and are worse when starting or increasing the dose. His real warning is about stopping. “Come off the drug without having built the lifestyle, and the hunger returns. People lose muscle and regain the weight, often as fat.”
Battling the side effects
It was not all rosy. For the entire three weeks I was on the medication, I had a mild headache and low-grade nausea. It eased after the first week, but it never fully left. My resting heart rate climbed 15%. My heart rate variability — a marker of recovery, where higher is better — dropped 15%. I had frequent palpitations and a mild brain fog, all symptoms that I discussed with Dr Arun Raghavan.
While there is nothing particularly abnormal about these patterns, these were indeed high costs for someone who did not need the drug. For someone who does, going unmonitored is a gamble.
So, did it work?
The results of all this weren’t insignificant: my muscle mass increased by 1.2 kg (a lot!), and fat decreased by 3.2 kg. I was active six days a week, following a hybrid (strength plus conditioning) protocol I developed, which translated to about four 4-hour sessions a week. (Disclaimer: These measurements were taken with a high-end body composition machine, and while the data is reasonably accurate, what we can look at are trends only)
The downside, however, was that my sleep was affected a fair bit, especially at first. Practising some pranayama helped, and it did get better once my body got used to the drug, but the first few days were a struggle.
So, will I recommend this to my clients? It depends.
For people who struggle with weight loss, the first step is to understand the underlying reason for their struggle, whether it be environment, lifestyle, psychological, or an underlying health condition. Only then can an action plan be structured, and GLP-1 could be a valid tool for some people. While you are on the drug, you need to do physical activity, get enough sleep and manage nutrition.
Sure, the last may become easier than before, but it still requires discipline – adding adequate protein, avoiding junk food, increasing your vegetable intake and drinking enough water. And during this window (we see this as a six- to 24-month window, depending on the person), shift your lifestyle to one that is sustainable and significantly better.
Shedding that old lifestyle and identity is a relevant part of this metamorphosis. It is not possible to undergo a simplistic change, i.e. take the drug, lose weight, be happy forever and ever. That isn’t going to happen, because there is a very high chance you will put it back on.
Is using Mounjaro a short cut?
I see a lot of moral dilemmas around taking this drug. Do I want to use a crutch? Do I want others to know that I use a crutch? How will this affect my social life? And of course, the wariness in taking a drug in a world where trust in Big Pharma is rightfully eroding.
I understand and empathise with most of these dilemmas. After all, would I trust a drug to only do positive things for me? I don’t think so. But if it serves the purpose and there’s no long-term cause for concern, then I would use the tool for the job. Because every day with subpar health is affecting you: that’s my simplistic thinking.
I also see people taking the drug and not seeing results because they refuse to take responsibility for their actions and lifestyle. These are people that no drug or coaching can help, until they choose to help themselves.
Most of us eat too much. We think about food too much. We have too many options. Year on year, our weight-loss resolutions don’t change. And neither does our weight. We don’t struggle with knowing what to do. The people I’ve coached over 15 years struggle with food noise. With an environment that makes it hard to be healthy. And life getting in the way — work, stress, kids, the usual.
The drug silences that noise, and that’s why it feels like magic. It’s also why selling only the drug is dangerous: the day you stop, the struggle comes back. The injection is the simple part, but life isn’t always that way. Even Johann Hari, a journalist who took these drugs, lost 20 kilos, and wrote a book about them, refuses to call it a miracle. He calls himself one of the “guinea pigs” in a “mass experiment.”
It is a tool.
I profit from saying this, but I’m saying it anyway: the people selling you only the needle are selling a return ticket and calling it a journey. It buys you a window. What you build in that window is everything.
Disclaimer: This is a first-person account of a three-week self-experiment. It is not medical advice or a recommendation to use GLP-1 medicines without a prescription or medical supervision.
Arvind Ashok has coached strength and fitness for over 15 years. He is co-founder of The Quad and of Revivo Clinic, a metabolic-health practice that pairs medical care with lifestyle change.

A closely watched cardiovascular drug from Novartis failed in a pivotal study, the company said Friday, a major blow to the firm and to efforts to target a common heart disease risk factor.
The drug, called pelacarsen, had shown in earlier trials that it could drastically lower levels of what’s called Lp(a), a little blob of lipids and proteins that at elevated concentrations increases the likelihood of severe heart problems.
But Novartis said that in the Phase 3 HORIZON trial, pelacarsen failed to reduce the risk of cardiovascular death or emergencies like heart attacks or stroke compared to placebo.

Cooling from air conditioning saves lives — more than 5,000 a year in the United States alone — but it also heats up the planet and taxes our electrical grid, scientists say.
As the world warms, heat waves strike nearly every continent and United Nations officials estimate that about half a million people die a year from heat, air conditioning is needed and being used more than ever. A study in Nature Health reported Monday that air conditioning saved nearly 58,000 lives between 2010 and 2020 in the U.S. Air conditioning use is skyrocketing around the world, with electricity demand from cooling expected to triple, according to the International Energy Agency and the United Nations Environment Programme.
It’s also more of a problem than ever. Because most of the electricity for cooling comes from the burning of fossil fuels, the U.N. projects the amount of heat-trapping gas spewed into the atmosphere from air conditioning use to rise from 4.5 billion to 7.2 billion tons in the next 25 years or so. That 7.2 billion tons is almost as much as the carbon pollution from the United States and Europe now.
“Everyone knows air conditioning works, but air conditioning from a climate change perspective is not an ideal,” said Kai Chen, an epidemiology professor at the Yale School of Public Health who was the senior author on the new study. “It leads to more carbon emissions ... then it accelerates the climate warming problem.”
Because of a global energy crunch triggered by the war in Iran, eight countries — Bangladesh, Cambodia, Jordan, Malaysia, the Philippines, the Seychelles, Singapore and Sri Lanka — have limited how cool air conditioning can be in offices or even mandated one day a week for public offices to switch it off, according to the IEA. In 2025 the Indian government proposed limits on how cool air conditioners can go.
Experts from 75 countries and 250 cities are trying to walk the tightrope of creating more cooling to reduce deaths from the rising heat, but without worsening climate change. The Global Cooling Pledge will meet in September in Singapore.
One measurement experts use to tally accumulated heat as related to potential air conditioning use is something called “cooling degree days,” a calculation of how much energy is needed to cool buildings when it’s hot outside. The number of cooling degree days in the United States has increased by 28% since 1990, with 2024 setting a record, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Through May, 2026 has been on pace to beat 2024 for the most cooling degree days, EIA data shows.
In Europe, the number of cooling degree days has more than doubled since 1990, and air conditioning use there has jumped up by 44%. Meanwhile, usage has tripled in India and more than doubled in Southeast Asia, the IEA reported.
In the new study, Chen and his team went through 30 million U.S. death records over an 11-year time span, used county-by-county calculations for levels when heat becomes dangerous and calculated how many lives air conditioning saved during extreme heat. The most lives saved were in Arizona, Florida, Texas, Louisiana and southern parts of Nevada, Alabama and Mississippi. More than a dozen northern states, from Washington to Maine, had fewer than 10 lives a year saved, according to the study.
Chen said the study concluded that “the essential role” of air conditioning saved on average 5,267 lives a year. But it also found that has to be balanced with “overuse.” He pointed to offices — like his — which are cooled so much that many workers wear sweaters even in the summer. More than half the cases researchers looked at could be considered overuse, he said.
Many places use 75 degrees (24 degrees Celsius) as a reasonable limit for air conditioning, Chen said.
He also said the study found that using more air conditioning than needed doesn’t save more lives, but it does worsen climate change.
Air conditioning in cities adds extra warmth to the urban heat island effect, as anyone who walks by air conditioning units knows because that’s where waste heat is expelled outdoors, Chen said. And the added power use increases traditional soot and smog air pollution.
It’s also an issue of fairness since many of the world’s most vulnerable populations don’t have access to or can’t afford air conditioning, according to both Chen and U.N. officials.
Lily Riahi, head of the cooling buildings and energy unit at UNEP, said that in this year's heat waves, “many families had to choose between paying for medicines or running their air conditioner.”
“In a warming world, thermal comfort should not be a luxury,” UNEP chief heat officer Eleni Myrivili said. “It’s becoming a prerequisite for health, dignity and increasingly survival.”
Riahi said the goal is not less cooling but rather “smarter and more equitable cooling,” and she pointed to Singapore as an example for effective solutions.
“Singapore is a country I think has really tackled cooling from a very comprehensive perspective, looking at individual adaptation measures, early warning systems, passive measures in the city in terms of urban greenery, which saves them, I think, $35 million in energy costs per year,” Riahi said. Officials there also require new and old buildings to have more efficient cooling and ventilation systems.
Singapore has lowered temperatures in some places by 14 degrees (8 degrees Celsius), Riahi said.
But sometimes it can get so hot and humid in places that even green solutions aren't enough and air conditioning will be needed, Riahi said.
Until it's too hot and humid, fans and a low level of air conditioning work, Chen said.

Who will reach Super Bowl? - NFL predictions for 2026 season
- Published
The NFL is notoriously difficult to predict and last season was no different.
Seven of the eight division winners were different from 2024, with two of the Super Bowl favourites missing out on the play-offs entirely - the Baltimore Ravens and Kansas City Chiefs.
Two outsiders then made it all the way to the big game, with the Seattle Seahawks beating the New England Patriots for their first NFL championship in 12 years.
So, who will be this season's surprise package? Who will be playing at Super Bowl 61 next February? And who will be the main men?
Here, the BBC's NFL experts make their picks for the 2026 season, which begins this week. Plus you can predict your Super Bowl winner at the bottom of this page.
Who will reach the Super Bowl?
Rob Staton: I think the NFC will be another battle between the Los Angeles Rams and Seattle Seahawks. I'm going to go with the Rams, simply because only two teams have repeated since the turn of the century. I have them facing the Buffalo Bills. Josh Allen finally gets to the big game.
Hugh Ferris: You could argue that, aside from an underwhelming head coach hire, there's little reason the 2026 Bills will be any different to the recent incarnations. I'm picking them to finally get over the line, though, and reach the Super Bowl, but to lose nonetheless. It's incredibly difficult to choose anyone else rather than the Rams, isn't it?
Haydn Parry: Surely the Bills can convert Allen's talent and make it to the season showpiece? Joe Brady's promotion to head coach might prove to be the missing ingredient. From the NFC, I think the Rams look most likely to have a strong tilt this campaign, and I see them winning it.
Joe Bradshaw: The last time the Super Bowl was at SoFi Stadium in 2022, the Rams won on home territory and they look primed to repeat next February. From the AFC, surely Bills quarterback Allen is overdue a trip to the NFL's biggest game, even if it will ultimately end in defeat.
David Brindle: After losing Bo Nix to injury in last season's play-offs, I expect the Denver Broncos to use that as motivation and at least go one further this season. As for the Rams, it's very difficult to look past the consensus predictions for the Super Bowl.
Ben Collins: Full disclosure, I'd seen the above before writing this so here's some leftfield picks... imagine if it's the Los Angeles Chargers that actually get to play in the Super Bowl in their own stadium, and it's former Rams quarterback Jared Goff that leads Detroit to victory.
Who will be the NFL's MVP?
Rob Staton: I'm going with Josh Allen. He now has an offensive-minded head coach running the team. Everything will be geared towards him having a big season.
Hugh Ferris: In an attempt to think outside the box, I'm picking Justin Herbert of the Chargers. You might suggest a quarterback in a Jim Harbaugh team isn't likely to get the chance to have an MVP-level season, but the hiring of Mike McDaniel as offensive coordinator might change that.
Haydn Parry: I might be wearing my blue-star goggles here but Dak Prescott has the ability and the weapons to have an outstanding season. Offence was not the Dallas Cowboys' problem last year and it certainly wasn't Prescott's fault that the team failed to deliver. Dallas just need to find a 'D'.
Joe Bradshaw: Buffalo's new head coach Joe Brady has stepped up from offensive coordinator so knows how to get Josh Allen purring. If the Bills make the Super Bowl, their quarterback will be the obvious candidate for his second MVP award.
David Brindle: If it wasn't to be a quarterback, I fancy Jahmyr Gibbs. He's signed a new deal and now has no running back competition at Detroit so expect him to see lots of action on a Lions team who are NFC contenders.
Ben Collins: Cincinnati have remedied their defence and still have a top offence. After twice winning comeback player of the year, quarterback Joe Burrow stays fit long enough to bag the award he really wants as the Bengals make a deep play-off run.
Who will be coach of the year?
Rob Staton: It could be Joe Brady if he can help Josh Allen reach MVP status, but in order to mix things up I'm going for DeMeco Ryans. The Houston Texans are going to lead on their defence and I think they'll be really strong.
Hugh Ferris: If the Bills reach the Super Bowl, then it stands to reason Joe Brady gets the nod as a first-year head coach, putting to shame people (like me) who called him an underwhelming hire.
Haydn Parry: I have always been a big fan of John Harbaugh. He will start from a comparatively low base in New York with the Giants, but with their passionate fanbase and the enormous potential of Jaxson Dart lift-off could be achieved early.
Joe Bradshaw: There has been such turnover on the NFL's coaching carousel, it has been hard to keep up this off-season. In the face of such instability, I'll opt for Sean McVay as he steers the Rams to their third Super Bowl title.
David Brindle: I'm going for Sean Payton to pick up his second award, 20 years after winning it with New Orleans. With the work done so far and decisions Payton has already made at Denver, this is the year I think it'll be formally recognised.
Ben Collins: After Detroit were hindered by a defensive injury crisis last season, Dan Campbell is rewarded as he gets the Lions roaring again.
Who is the NFL rookie to watch?
Rob Staton: I'd expect Rueben Bain to have an immediate impact in Tampa Bay. Jadarian Price will get opportunities to shine in Seattle. I was a big fan of De'Zhaun Stribling, taken by the San Francisco 49ers. But in terms of pure impact, give me Caleb Downs, the safety in Dallas.
Hugh Ferris: The 49ers have one wide receiver AWOL, another out for the season, and injury question marks over Mike Evans and George Kittle - who's recovering from a torn Achilles - so along with a returning Deebo Samuel, there's a gap for De'Zhaun Stribling to fill.
Haydn Parry: It will be interesting to see how wide receiver Carnell Tate, fourth overall pick by Tennessee, adapts among the big boys. With his versatile skillset, the Titans expect him to contribute right from the off - the pre-draft scout reports highlighted his maturity, intelligence, sure hands and catch radius.
Joe Bradshaw: De'Zhaun Stribling was a surprise selection by the 49ers at the start of the second round but given their annual injury issues, he could be in line for plenty of work this season. Some fine displays in pre-season have only increased the hype.
David Brindle: After Kenneth Walker departed, the Seahawks picked Jadarian Price in the draft. He'll start the season as their lead back, with Zach Charbonnet still recovering from an ACL tear. I expect him to keep that job and become a top running back in the league for many years.
Ben Collins: Sonny Styles' athleticism caught the eye of NFL teams during the pre-draft process. He could have a big impact at linebacker for the Washington Commanders and soon become one of their leaders.
Who will be the NFL's surprise package?
Rob Staton: I'm not suggesting the Las Vegas Raiders are going to go on an improbable run or anything, but Klint Kubiak did an excellent job in Seattle [as offensive coordinator] and should make the transition to head coach with ease. I think this will be the year, finally, that the Raiders show signs of growth.

F1 title race: Why championship is not over despite spectacular Kimi Antonelli win at Italian Grand Prix
Kimi Antonelli showed why he is championship leader after his superb win at Monza; but Antonelli and Mercedes still have hurdles to overcome in remaining races; watch every session of the Spanish Grand Prix at a new track in Madrid from this Friday, live on Sky Sports F1
Tuesday 8 September 2026 06:23, UK
Kimi Antonelli's stunning Italian Grand Prix victory felt like a key moment in this year's championship as he landed a psychological blow on his title rivals by winning from 19th.
Antonelli now leads George Russell by 66 points, Lewis Hamilton by 76 points and Lando Norris by 96 points with 10 scheduled rounds remaining.
Without doubt, the Italian is favourite for the championship - and would be the youngest driver ever to become world champion should he do it - but the season is far from over yet...

Monza was a one-off track
The long straights at Monza put high emphasis on a strong power unit and Mercedes have been the benchmark in this department, even though the FIA ruled earlier this year that Red Bull have the best engine.
It is the deployment of the Mercedes though - which was not measured by the FIA - which stands out and they were effectively able to get more out of the electrical side of their power unit to excel on the straights.
There are no further tracks that will be reliant on the power unit to the extremity of Monza, although Baku later this month and Las Vegas in November feature long full throttle sections. However, both circuits have more corners than Monza.
"I'm quite happy, first of all, that we were able to perform in Monza like we did, because we weren't sure. Ferrari brought an engine upgrade and others on the chassis side, and this is a development race," said Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff.
"But we have to consider the fact that Monza is an outlier on the track. It's on one end, and then there is Monaco on the other."
This weekend's new race in Madrid is a complete unknown but the track layout looks very twisty and cars that are strong in the corners - which should suit McLaren and Ferrari - will be fast.
Azerbaijan follows, which can be a chaotic race, then the more traditional tracks of Sepang in Malaysia, Austin in the USA and the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez in Mexico should see the field be much closer - depending on upgrades...
Lots to play out in development race
The two races prior to Monza saw McLaren with a car that was capable of winning as Norris drove superbly to victory in Hungary and the Netherlands.
Most teams have gained big chunks of performance when fitting new parts to the car and Mercedes are not bringing any upgrades until Malaysia at the start of next month.
"We must not get ahead of ourselves now, thinking, 'well, we can wait for the upgrade until Malaysia'. We know that it's going to be a big fight in Madrid. Our car hasn't got the performance levels that it has in Monza for the next race in Madrid," said Wolff.
"We know that our upgrades would help a lot in Madrid but we haven't got them. So we just need to do our best and that could mean that some of the race weekends, not winning, but just scoring points."
McLaren boss Andrea Stella says the team's realistic target is to "consistently" be in the fight for wins until the end of the season.
"I think our tracks will be more the likes of Malaysia, Austin, Brazil. I think where we have some long corners, the car seems to express its potential well," said Stella.
"We have some new upgrades that we will take to Baku, but we still think that tracks like Baku and Madrid where you have to be very precise with the trajectory, short corners, maybe they don't play to the best of our car. Yet we have to say that in Zandvoort and Hungary we were in a position to win races and in Monza while we were not, we know that it's a special race.
"The drag will be less important in Madrid, there's a much higher density of corners, so we will definitely give it a go, but from a championship point of view I think we have to remain very realistic, don't get conditioned by looking at the classification, just focus on one race at a time."
Will Antonelli crack under increasing pressure?
Right now the answer is a firm no. Antonelli is a generational talent with bundles of speed and it's his sheer pace which has made the difference this year.
He's only 20 years old though and in his second season, so most drivers would still be making costly mistakes at this stage of their career.
There has been no sign of that from Antonelli though but you would expect that he will be tested several times in the remaining races - whether that's due to the closeness of the field and being on the right side of the stopwatch, or a rainy Sunday where a small error can suddenly fire you into the barriers.
"Definitely it's been a very strong year so far, but still many races left and so, still anything can happen," said Antonelli.
"And we've seen how things can swing very quickly. So, on my side, as I said many times, just take it race by race, focus on things that I can control and just maximise every opportunity I get.
"In Monza we were fastest, but we never know. We might go to another track and all of a sudden, McLaren is the fastest, or Ferrari is up there, or even Red Bull, with Max."
Indeed, should McLaren or Ferrari suddenly have the fastest car for consecutive races, and Antonelli is not on the podium - Hamilton or Norris could gain double figures in points from one Grand Prix, then the pressure will inevitably ramp up too on Antonelli.
The outlook is actually bleaker for Russell as he has the same equipment as Antonelli but does not have the pace to match his team-mate.
It is harder to see how that changes, whereas - as Antonelli points out - McLaren or Ferrari may have the best car over the final 10 rounds.
Perhaps Wolff sums up best how the F1 title race stands when he stated: "It's motor racing. It's a technical sport. Things can break, accidents can happen and that's why we have to do our best job for both drivers. Continue to bring our best game."

India is all set to host the 18th BRICS Summit in the national capital this weekend. The high-profile Summit, scheduled for 12–13 September 2026 at Bharat Mandapam, brings together leaders of BRICS Member and Partner Countries, as well as Outreach Invitees. India is the BRICS Chair for the 2026 edition. The BRICS Chairship is guided by the theme: “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability.” At the two-day Summit, the leaders will also exchange views on strengthening intra-BRICS cooperation on common priorities and share perspectives on global and regional matters of mutual importance. As many as 350 meetings and high-level engagements have already been held in over 25 cities across India to further strengthen the BRICS strategic partnership under India’s Chairmanship this year. A final meeting of theBRICS Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors will be held in Mumbai on September 9-10. The Mumbai meeting will bring together finance ministers and central bank governors of BRICS member countries and comes just days ahead of the BRICS Leaders’ Summit. BRICS was formed in 2006 as an informal group, with its first formal summit held on June 16, 2009. BRICS brings together eleven major emerging markets and developing countries worldwide: Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa, and the United Arab Emirates. It serves as a useful platform for consultation and cooperation on contemporary issues of global and regional significance. India is a founding member of BRICS and has previously held its Chairmanship three times: in 2012, 2016, and 2021. India assumed its fourth BRICS Chairship on 1 January 2026. The year 2026 also marks a significant milestone as BRICS completes twenty years since its establishment. A BRICS overview published by Brazil's central bank puts the expanded grouping at about 49% of the world's population, 39% of global GDP and 23% of international trade. BRICS is not a formal organisation, but a loose bloc of non-Western economies that coordinate economic and diplomatic efforts around a shared goal, according to the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), an independent think tank. BRICS countries seek to build an alternative to what they see as the dominance of the Western viewpoint in major multilateral groupings, such as the World Bank, the Group of Seven (G7), and the UN Security Council, CFR says. The formal BRICS expansion became effective on 1 January 2024, welcoming Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, and the United Arab Emirates as new member states The 2024 expansion came with a range of geopolitical implications representing growing economic and demographic heft: the eleven BRICS countries now comprise more than a quarter of the global economy and almost half of the world’s population, according to CFR. “The group is poised to exert influence over the wars in the Gaza Strip and Ukraine, the shape of the global economic system, the competition between China and the West, and efforts to transition to clean energy,” writes Zongyuan Zoe Liu, CFR Expert and Maurice R Greenberg Senior Fellow for China Studies Growing membership also brings new challenges, however, including increasing pushback from Western countries and divisions within the bloc. Experts say that how BRICS members navigate those tensions will determine whether the group can become a more unified voice on the global stage. From being largely an economic grouping of emerging economies, BRICS has over the years evolved into something much bigger: a platform through which countries of the Global South seek greater influence over the global economic and political order. For India, BRICS brings it to the same table as China and Russia while also connecting it with major economies and energy producers across the developing world. The bloc provides an important platform for INDIA to position itself as a voice for developing and emerging economies, a major central foreign-policy objective. The grouping has consistently pushed for reforms to institutions such as the United Nations, the International Monetary Fund, and the World Bank, arguing that their governance structures do not adequately reflect the economic weight of emerging economies, something India also supports. BRICS allows India to engage with China and Russia without abandoning its partnerships with the US, Europe, Japan, Australia and other countries. The likely participation of Chinese President Xi Jinping at the September 2026 BRICS summit in India is particularly significant, as it could provide another high-level channel for managing the complex India-China relationship. During India's 2026 BRICS chairship, New Delhi has pushed for greater and more balanced trade among members, stronger trade in services, resilient global value chains and easier access to finance for small businesses. For India, the challenge would be to strike a balancing act because the expanded BRICS includes both Iran and the UAE, which have opposing interests in the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. At the same time. New Delhi also has important strategic and economic relationships with Washington and Gulf countries. That makes India's BRICS chairmanship even more important. At the recent BRICS Trade Ministers' meeting in Jaipur, members endorsed principles to strengthen MSME access to global markets and narrow the trade-finance gap.India also pushed for more resilient and diversified global value chains at the Jaipur meeting. This matters because India's economic interests are increasingly tied to markets outside the traditional Western economies. And the stakes are not merely diplomatic. The US-Iran war has affected energy security, shipping and global oil markets, with the Strait of Hormuz becoming a major vulnerability. Reuters reported on 31 August that analysts expected oil prices to remain above $80 per barrel in 2026 due to ongoing supply disruptions linked to the US-Iran conflict. For India, this is particularly significant because West Asia is central to its energy security, trade and diaspora interests. Any prolonged disruption in the region can raise India's import bill, put pressure on inflation and complicate economic growth. The US-Iran war has exposed the central contradiction within BRICS, according to analysts. While the grouping seeks to challenge a Western-dominated global order, its members have different interests when an actual geopolitical crisis erupts. For India, the opportunity is to demonstrate whether its much-discussed strategic autonomy can translate into leadership, analysts believe. This is also a diplomatic challenge, they said. Iran has sought to use BRICS to rally opposition to US military action, urging India, as chair, to help build a common position. On 31 August, Prime Minister Narendra Modi met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan. This was the first meeting between the two leaders since the US-Iran war broke out, impacting the Middle East and beyond, following US and Israeli attacks on Tehran earlier this year. Pezeshkian urged Modi to use India's extensive contacts with various parties to help them move away from the path of war and bloodshed and return to the path of dialogue and agreement. "We believe that the solution to the issues we face lies in dialogue and cooperation, and that all available capacities must be mobilised to prevent the spread of insecurity and conflict," he said, according to an Iranian readout. Prime Minister Narendra Modi will host the summit. Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to attend, though China has not formally confirmed his participation. If Xi visits, it would be his first trip to India since the 2019 informal summit in Mamallapuram with Modi. A Modi-Xi bilateral meeting on the sidelines is widely anticipated. The Chinese leader's delegation could run to around 400 officials, roughly double the 2019 contingent, according to some media reports. There has been intense diplomacy between China and India, the latest being the 25th round of Special Representative talks, held in Beijing on 28 August, between National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi. Russian President Vladimir Putin will attend the Summit. This would be his second visit to India in under a year, following the annual bilateral summit in New Delhi in December 2025. Modi renewed the invitation to Putin in person when the two leaders met at the SCO summit in Bishkek on 31 August.
