This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Lisa Eder. It has been edited for length and clarity.
For 10 years, I worked my way up in luxury hospitality, eventually becoming a director at a high-end hotel group. It had always been my dream position, and I loved my job.
Everything about it was exciting, and no two days were ever the same. There were important VIP arrivals, high-profile events, and constant challenges. I became consumed by it all. The job was a lifestyle, and for a decade, it was the lifestyle I wanted for myself.
I loved working 12-hour days, most days of the week. I loved leading a team of 100 people and six department heads. I loved the responsibility, the pace, and having to be "on" all the time. But I didn't have much of a life outside work. The job was my life.
When my husband and I moved from Austria to Australia in January 2024 for his job, however, my mindset about work began to change.
I didn't burn out
Australians are generally more relaxed about work. I saw how much they enjoyed the different aspects of life outside their jobs, and I found myself wanting the same for my own life.
Slowly, I began to wonder whether I had outgrown my career.
I hadn't burned out. I didn't hate my job. In fact, I still loved many aspects of it. It just no longer felt like it was for me. I no longer wanted to fit into the corporate box. I wanted something else.
I wanted to have dinner with my husband at night and completely switch off from the day. I wanted the autonomy to decide how I spent my time. I wanted to discover new hobbies and interests that made me feel alive again.
For months, I sat with these newly emerging desires, trying to work out what to do with them.
I asked myself what I wanted from life
I had spent years working to get where I was professionally. What would other people think? Was I giving up? Was I throwing away everything I had worked so hard for?
At the same time, I was asking myself bigger questions: What did I actually want from my life? Who was I now? What were my values?
Throughout the entire process, my husband made it very clear that I could choose whatever I wanted. The decision and drive mainly came from me, but he supported it because he understood that I was serious about it
In early January 2026, I quietly decided to resign. In February, I resigned, and I left the company in March. I'd like to say it was easy, but it wasn't.
I took a waitressing job
I grappled with who I was now that I was no longer a leader in the corporate world. I had spent so long building a professional identity that I wasn't sure who I was without it. I also had to learn how to live with the uncertainty of not knowing what would come next.
Financially, I had been preparing for the transition by saving money to support myself. My husband was also incredibly supportive. But I wanted to make my own money, so I took a part-time waitressing job at a café in Sydney.
Unexpectedly, that job became about much more than income. It gave me joy.
I loved being around people, food, and coffee. I loved finishing work and coming home without the weight of a corporate job on my shoulders. I had the freedom to decide what I wanted to do with my evenings, whether that was something on my own or spending time with my husband.
I also started playing volleyball, running, and tennis — sports I had loved before my corporate life took over.
Then I started dreaming about becoming a Pilates instructor. I enrolled in a training course, which I'm still completing, with the goal of becoming an instructor.
I found myself again.
I won't say I have everything planned out. That wouldn't be honest. But having space in my head has given me the ability to keep asking myself whether my life aligns with my values — and to make changes when it doesn't.
My journey is my journey, but it won't be right for everyone.
If you aren't willing to do the mindset work — to question your identity, understand your values, and rethink what success means to you — to live with uncertainty and wrestle with doubt, then giving up a corporate career may not be the right choice for you.
But for me, it feels almost unthinkable how different my life looks now. And I don't regret it.

Welcome to the first edition of Power Play! From now until the midterms, senior writer Molly Taft will be sharing their thoughts every Sunday on this political season’s hottest issue: data centers. We welcome reader comments, and will be answering questions from the comments section in future editions.
Be sure to catch WIRED’s first livestream on data centers this Thursday, September 10, featuring Molly, senior politics correspondent Hugo Lowell, and senior business writer Max Zeff! You can submit questions here.
It’s been a rough summer for data center boosters. Polling is getting even more dismal—as many as 75 percent of Americans now say they would oppose a data center being built in their area, up from 42 percent last year. Politicians from both parties who were previously advocates, like Texas governor Greg Abbott and Pennsylvania governor Josh Shapiro, are now switching up as the midterms approach, looking to convey to voters that they’re talking a hard line on the hated infrastructure.
But while some Republicans are turning tail on the issue even in the face of President Donald Trump’s vigorous support for data center construction, others are joining prominent tech leaders in doubling down on an old narrative: That China is responsible for all this malaise.
In late August, X announced that it had identified 200 accounts linked to China that were helping to spread anti-data center talking points on the platform, causing a flurry of alarmist headlines and tweets. (“China is secretly fueling America's data center rage,” Axios trumpeted in an article on X’s report, which data center-friendly politicians and right-wing figures amplified using X itself.) Even the president joined in: “China could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement,” he wrote in a Truth Social post defending data centers (“let Data Reign!”) made just a few days after the X report.
The idea that Americans hate data centers because of a nebulous foreign influence operation—not because of a slew of environmental worries, an oligarch-friendly political system, or a general resistance to AI—is a handy excuse for the technology’s backers and their allies. And it’s one that’s been hanging around for a few months. In the spring, a handful of reports from right-wing policy shops were used by lawmakers and pundits alike to point fingers at the Chinese Communist Party for purportedly seeding anti-data center narratives among the American public. In June, OpenAI banned a cluster of users it had found that, the company said, were linked to the Chinese government and “testing narratives against AI infrastructure.”
But claims that Americans hate data centers because of Chinese influence are based on pretty thin evidence. The biggest report circulating around DC claiming foreign influence, China experts told me earlier this year, leans heavily on insinuations and assumptions with precious little hard evidence. In its own report from June, OpenAI acknowledged that the cluster of accounts it identified was simply exploiting existing discontent around data centers. It’s possible X’s recent purge may be linked to the accounts flagged by OpenAI: They use similar hashtags and images, and several link to the same obscure local news article. X ultimately identified 200,000 accounts in the same bot farm; the 200 anti-data center accounts were just a drop in the larger bucket.
Do blue-check tech types and Republicans keep hammering on the China angle because they know something that the public doesn’t? Graphika, a social media analytics firm that has been tracking data center sentiment online, told me in June that most of the opposition they had seen thus far was homegrown. That hasn’t changed: There’s still very little evidence of significant foreign intervention, Tyler Williams, vice president of intelligence at Graphika, told me this week.
Blogger Andy Masley has a healthy skepticism of the China narrative. Masley, whose blog is largely funded by a grant from effective altruist philanthropy Coefficient Giving, is popular with tech boosters on X for his pro-data center takes. But “as soon as I start talking China, they get quiet,” he tells me. “It seems like a very convenient belief. I have my own biases as a Democrat, but I sometimes look at these [tech] guys and think, ‘Oh, they had to meme themselves into being more right-wing a few years ago. They think right-wing people like it when you talk about China.’”
Masley has put out a public call for any insider information from the tech world about Chinese intervention; he says he hasn’t gotten anything solid yet. It’s also worth noting that right-wing attempts to blame China for sowing data center discord come as members of the Trump administration complain that Chinese firms are stealing American advances in AI. If you’re having trouble wrapping your head around why China would try to muddy the waters around the infrastructure that its AI models are allegedly coasting on, you’re not the only one.
I took my obsession over this topic to Louise Matsakis, WIRED’s senior business editor and resident China expert. She says that this whole episode belies a basic misunderstanding of what Chinese influence campaigns actually look like—and she also didn’t seem surprised that this narrative was taking off like wildfire among factions on the right, which has a long history of pointing the finger at China for American problems. Louise tells me that, at the end of the day, panics like these are not really about China at all.
“It is endlessly fascinating to me how China becomes a scapegoat,” she says. “Americans often find it easier to put the blame on a nebulous other, rather than to actually look at themselves.”
What WIRED’s Writing
My colleague Paresh Dave wrote an eye-opening piece recently about Meta’s push to build out a robot workforce in data centers. “I was surprised to learn that some data centers have cafeterias, with full-on kitchen staff,” he tells me. “It's important to realize that as data centers automate some of the more technical work and reduce on-site jobs, operators could also save money on items such as food and janitorial services—and all those people would also be losing work.”
What We’re Reading
- An outrageous story is unfolding in Arkansas, where Entergy tried to get a restraining order against the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette, which published details of the utility’s data center-related deal with Google that were obtained via a records request. The utility claims that trade secrets were accidentally released, and also dragged the young mom who made the original records request into court. More coverage from the Arkansas Times.
- The Financial Times covers how AI has caused high unemployment for college graduates in Texas—a state that has one of the largest number of data centers in development.
- And The Washington Post reports on a massive new influx of state legislation around data centers heading into the 2026-2027 legislative year.

Four Renoir paintings worth millions stolen in French museum heist
- Published
Four paintings by the impressionist artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir have been stolen from a museum in the south of France.
Two thieves broke into the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer on Tuesday morning but dropped two of the paintings in the institution's garden as they made their escape, local Mayor Bryan Masson said.
The paintings, each worth €9m (£7.7m; $10.4m), are the latest high-profile pieces to have been stolen in a string of recent heists in Europe which have thrust the security of art in galleries and museums into the spotlight.
One of the most high-profile was in October last year, when a brazen heist at the Louvre Museum in Paris saw France's priceless crown jewels being stolen.
CCTV footage captured the thieves entering the Renoir museum gardens by cutting through a fence before they cut through structures holding the paintings' frames in place, the local mayor said.
The alarm went off at 05:48 (05:48 GMT), and police were at the scene within five minutes, Masson explained, saying the thieves fled the scene upon hearing the security alarms.
He later told reporters that the thieves seemed to be "well-equipped" and "well-informed".
They were "wearing helmets, gloves, and combat gear" and carrying "an electric knife and hacksaw," he added.
Investigators have found two zip-up bags at the scene, which may have belonged to the suspects.
The mayor said that two paintings were "abandoned" in the gardens and have now been recovered.
The two paintings that are still missing are:
- Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910)
- Jeune fille au puits (1886)
And the two pieces that were recovered are:
- Portrait of Madame Pichon (1895)
- Coco Lisant (1905)
"Attacking the Renoir Museum is attacking a part of the history and heritage of Cagnes-sur-Mer," the mayor told reporters at the museum.
"It's Renoir's, it is priceless, you cannot sell it like that," he said.
The Renoir Museum is home to 12 of the famous painter's artworks.
Opened in 1960, it was Renoir's last home before his death in 1919, and also features many things that once belonged to him, including his easel and wheelchair, as well as photographs and personal letters.
Last month, four Renaissance paintings being stolen from a museum in Sicily, Italy.
"Beyond Cagnes-sur-Mer, this incident should serve as a warning about the protection of our museums, which now face a new form of organised crime targeting works of art," the local French mayor warned.
Masson called on the French government to provide more financial support to local areas and museums to protect artwork from "increasingly organised and determined criminals".

Nepal authorities have said they are “confident” that dozens of workers in Nepal’s Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant are still alive, more than a week after deadly flash floods left them trapped in an underground chamber.
Authorities said that at least 639 workers were still missing from hydropower plants built along Nepal’s Bhote Koshi and Triushuli rivers.
Most of the projects were destroyed when a surge of water, debris and mud came coursing down the river valley last week, triggered by the collapse of a melting glacier on the border between Nepal and China-controlled Tibet.
The deadly flash floods reached up to 100mph (160km/h), according to scientists, and travelled more than 60 miles down the river valley, wiping away whole villages, bridges, and hydropower dams.
At least 1,252 people have been confirmed dead from the floods. More than 4,200 remain missing.
According to a preliminary estimate by the UN Development Programme, the disaster created at least 2.2m tonnes of debris, including parts of buildings, rocks and sediment. Large boulders and flood waters deluged the hydropower tunnels, blocking off the entrances, and some were buried deep in mud.
Rescue efforts have increasingly centred on these tunnels, where authorities believe workers may have survived for more than a week due to air pockets. So far, more than 270 people have been rescued from the hydropower projects.
Speaking on Wednesday, officials said they believed 46 people were still alive in an underground room in Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant, and efforts were ongoing to locate them using excavators and other heavy equipment.
“We are very confident that they must be alive after one week because … they have food and water over there in the building,” Amhsu Kiran Shahi, a board member of the Nepal electricity authority, told Reuters.
Durga Gurung, 60, said his brother Jhappad Bhujel was among those trapped in a hydropower tunnel. “Right now, we are just relying on God,” he told the Guardian. “We have not been given any information about whether the people inside are alive or not.
“Neither the army nor the people from the electricity authority are telling us anything. So many days have passed that we have reached a point where it feels like all we can do is hope for a miracle.”
“Our relatives are sitting inside a dark tunnel,” he added. “How long can they possibly survive?”
Major rescue operations were under way or planned at four hydropower projects. Two sites – the Rasuwagadhi hydroelectric project and the Upper Trishuli 3A facility – where about 90 people are missing, offered the strongest prospect of finding survivors because of the presence of air inside the tunnels, Shahi said.
The Rasuwagadhi hydroelectric project is located in Rasuwa district, about three miles away from the border with Tibet, which was one of the areas of Nepal hardest hit by the floods, and remains almost inaccessible except by helicopter. “This is the only project where it’s possible to walk through the tunnel,” Shahi said. “The army tried doing that three days ago, but they didn’t find the room. We are going in again.”
At the Upper Trishuli 3A facility, another project hit by the floods, it took rescue workers almost six days to find the tunnels because of the thick mud. The authorities believe about 30 to 40 people may still be alive in the tunnel. “We are expecting [survivors] in there because we are told there is a dry space inside. We are trying to break into the tunnel now,” said the Nepali army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet on Wednesday.
The army said the search and rescue operation would go on for as long as there was hope for survivors, but that efforts would also continue to recover the dead bodies. “We are using every technology available in Nepal right now, and we are taking help from the Indians, Chinese, Koreans. We have experts from Australia too,” added Basnet.
Families of those still trapped in the projects have returned to the Nepal electricity office for the past eight days, in the hope for information. Laxmi Adhikari’s brother Jeevanlal Adhikari had gone to the Trishuli 3A Hydropower Project to test the machines, when the floods hit.
She accused the authorities of withholding information from the families, and of not acting fast enough to save their relatives. “We have been running from one ministry to another and from disaster management authority to another government office, trying to find my brother,” she said. “We keep going from place to place, but the rescue operation has not been accelerated.”
She said the lack of answers made the wait even more painful: “When the water came rushing in, where did he go? Did he manage to get to safety? They haven’t even given us definite information about whether our people are alive or not.”
Nepal has invested more than $9bn (£6.7bn) in building hydropower dams across the mountains, huge sums given the country’s small economy. According to preliminary surveys, the floods debilitated or destroyed 11 hydropower plants and knocked out about 10% of Nepal’s total electricity-generation capacity.
According to the authorities, more than 20,000 houses will have to be rebuilt in the aftermath of the flood. Nepal has put the cost of recovery at more than $5bn (£3.7bn).

Pusheen is getting her first game, and it will appear exclusively on Apple Arcade. Launching October 1st, Pusheen’s Place lets you collect and care for more than 100 Pusheens as you play minigames and decorate rooms for Pusheenicorn, Pancake Pusheen, and other variations of the cartoon cat.
Pusheen’s first game is coming to Apple Arcade
Pusheen’s Place lets you collect and care for more than 100 variations of the cartoon cat.
In the mix of minigames, you’ll “sort color cakes in Snack Stack,” “pop cute Pusheen fruit bubbles in Parfait Pop,” “make delicious matches and blast blockers in Batch Match,” and solve puzzles, according to the game’s description on the App Store. The game’s developers will also continue to add “more Pusheens, decor themes, games and features” over time.
Along with Pusheen’s Place, Apple is adding several other games to its $6.99 / month Arcade subscription next month, including the sandbox adventure game Terraria, a zombie horde-fighting game River City Survivors, the physics-based BMX stunt game Touchgrind BMX 2, and the puzzle game 4 Pics 1 Word.

- Marvel Rivals has removed Loki from the hero roster and hero gallery ahead of season 10's release.
- The disappearance of Loki is connected to NetEase Games' marketing campaign for Marvel Rivals Season 10.
- Loki has been disabled in Quick Play, Arcade, Practice vs. AI, and 18 vs. 18 game modes, but is available in competitive matches.
In a sudden turn of events, Loki has been removed from the Marvel Rivals hero roster ahead of Season 10’s launch later this week. The God of Mischief has vanished from both the hero selection screen and the hero gallery in the main menu. The hero’s icon has been replaced by a poster reading “missing” in an Asgardian font.
Loki Gets Disabled in All Marvel Rivals Game Modes Except Competitive
Marvel Rivals Season 10 is right around the corner, and fans are gearing up for the arrival of new heroes. Earlier today, many players, as well as popular content creators like Necros, claimed that Loki had been suddenly removed from the game.
True to these reports, the God of Mischief has been removed from the hero roster in Quick Play, Arcade, Practice vs. AI, and 18 vs. 18 game modes in Marvel Rivals. However, Loki is still available in competitive mode and in in-game social hubs like Times Square and Hellfire Bay Beach.
If you are wondering why Loki has vanished all of a sudden, this isn’t one of his illusion tricks. In case you didn’t know, Gorr the God Butcher is seemingly the new hero of Marvel Rivals Season 10, according to the list of Marvel Rivals leaked characters.
The PlayStation Store also accidentally leaked the cover art of the upcoming season yesterday and confirmed that Gorr is indeed the next character in line to join the hero roster. Thus, NetEase Games has begun teasing the arrival of Gorr the God Butcher, by taking the God of Mischief out of the game today.
So, did Gorr kill the Asgardian god Loki, or has the God of Mischief gone into hiding now that Gorr is making his debut? We have to wait and find out later today during the new Marvel Rivals dev vision for season 10. NetEase Games hasn’t released a statement regarding Loki’s disappearance yet at the time of writing.
NetEase Games always prefers a special marketing campaign for new Marvel Rivals seasons and character reveals. Thus, Loki’s vanishing perfectly ties in with the season 10 promotions.
Now that Loki is gone, will his Asgardian siblings, such as Thor, Hela, and Angela, disappear from the game next? Let’s patiently wait and see.

When I first visited Japan more than 30 years ago, the Cold War had ended, China had not yet risen, and the country—although it was no longer the Japan as Number One of Ezra Vogel’s best-selling 1979 book—was formidable. Japan’s GDP was not very far behind that of the United States, was larger than that of most of the rest of Asia combined, and was seven times that of China.
On a recent visit, I found a very different country. Even in 1995, there were ominous signs: the collapse of property prices and several years—which would stretch into decades—of economic stagnation. Birth rates were below replacement, at roughly 1.4 per woman, although they have since fallen further, to a bit more than 1.1. But some of the biggest changes lie in Japan’s geopolitical environment.
Today, Japan’s GDP is roughly a fifth of China’s, and although the size of its armed forces remains roughly the same as in the past, it is now far outstripped by that of its continental neighbor. Back in 1995, North Korea was still a decade away from testing a nuclear weapon; today, it has dozens or even scores of weapons that it can deliver. And back then, Russia was still recovering from its rocky transition out of Communist rule; today, it is aligned with China and routinely provides military technology to China and North Korea.
Small wonder that the Japanese political, military, and intelligence leaders as well as academic experts I recently spoke with were grim. They cling to their security treaty with the United States, but their government is also doing once-unthinkable things to ensure their own defense.
For most of the postwar period, Japan relied on its defense treaty with the Americans and on robust economic growth. Defense spending was held at 1 percent of GDP, but its economy was so much larger than those of its neighbors that this meant a relatively substantial investment in the Japan Self-Defense Forces. Despite its love of samurai movies and martial arts, Japan remained a pacifist country that did not export weapons, focused on defensive missions, and pledged not to produce, possess, or host nuclear weapons.
All of that has changed. Under plans adopted in 2022, Japan has increased its defense spending to something like 1.4 percent of GDP, and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has indicated that it will rise to 2 percent. It is likely to go beyond that, possibly even as far as the 3.5 percent target now generally accepted in Europe. The result is not just an improvement of Japanese weapons systems across the board (numbers of service personnel remaining stable), but the acquisition of new capabilities. Japan is now openly acquiring what it calls “counterstrike” weapons—that is, missiles of various kinds that can hit targets on the Chinese mainland. It is investing in cyber and space operations, as well as in much greater air and missile defenses. It is building concrete shelters and digging tunnels for passive defense against Chinese attacks on its bases, something that the United States has inexplicably failed to do in either Asia or the Middle East. Japan is newly willing to sustain its defense industries by exporting weapons. This year it created its first centralized intelligence agency—the National Intelligence Bureau—since World War II.
Most interesting of all is the shift in Japanese attitudes to nuclear weapons. The Japanese policy toward those weapons after World War II was grounded in the trauma of being the only country to have suffered a nuclear attack. On this trip, I heard nary a word about Hiroshima or Nagasaki, but a great deal about deterrence.
More to the point, Japanese officials and experts were virtually unanimous on the need to drop at least one of the three legs of its nuclear policy: the prohibition of introducing nuclear weapons on Japanese soil. They were eager to explore the possibility of arrangements with the United States comparable to those with Germany or other European countries, under which both countries have their finger on the nuclear button, a so-called dual key. A submarine-launched cruise missile with a nuclear warhead, now under development in the U.S., seems to be the preferred system.
Japan could easily develop nuclear weapons. It has ample supplies of plutonium and outstanding engineers. It would much prefer not to, for a host of reasons, including lingering domestic opposition and fear of preemptive attack. But the arguments I heard against a purely Japanese nuclear deterrent are now cast in prudential terms, not emotional or historical ones.
These changes emerge from a heightened Japanese sense of threat. Almost every day, Chinese coast-guard vessels enter the contiguous zone (12 to 24 miles out) around the Senkaku Islands, which stretch almost to Taiwan, and they commonly intrude into Japanese territorial waters there. The Chinese coast guard, it should be noted, has vessels the size of frigates or destroyers in other navies, and that have mounted automatic cannons of the type used for combat rather than law enforcement. Their belligerent rhetoric upon encountering their Japanese counterparts matches that of their government.
Joint Chinese and Russian air patrols unnerve Japan’s air defenders, as do increasing flights of Chinese drones near Japanese islands. China’s insistence that the Senkaku Islands are Chinese is of long standing but has become more strident in recent years. Meanwhile, Japan looks with dismay at a China whose nuclear arsenal is growing quickly, as is that of North Korea. And both are aligned with a Russia whose navy and air force remain active in the Pacific despite the demands of the fighting in Ukraine.
Japan is in a tough spot, and for that and other reasons, its attitude to the United States is different from that of many European countries. In Japan, one seldom hears complaints about democratic backsliding or accusations of betrayal. Rather, the Japanese are desperate to put their faith in the U.S. at a time when alternatives are few.
There is no Pacific NATO, and even the combined command of U.S. and Japanese forces is not nearly as organizationally robust as that of the United States and South Korea. There is only the presence of American forces (oriented for the most part toward Korea and Taiwan) and America’s good word, as well as Japan’s determination to resist encroachment—or, as its defense documents call it, “invasion”—by a hostile China.
Japan’s anxieties around Taiwan are high. Even a peaceful takeover of the island by China would represent a major setback. It would unhinge Japan’s and the United States’ strategic posture in East Asia, and encourage (in Japan’s view) accommodation or worse from some of China’s neighbors. In a seemingly spontaneous remark in late 2025, Prime Minister Takaichi indicated that a Chinese naval blockade of Taiwan would count as a “survival-threatening situation” that would, by implication, permit Japan’s use of force for collective self-defense. Despite the furor that erupted, she has not withdrawn those remarks.
The next few years may be perilous in East Asia if China sees an opportunity created by a distracted and underequipped America to accomplish its goal of unifying an unwilling Taiwan with the mainland. Thankfully, the U.S.-Japan relationship is an alliance that the Trump administration has not yet heedlessly and willfully damaged. For the sake not only of Tokyo, but of peace in the region, one hopes that will remain the case.

The normally genteel world of international space policy turned ugly this week as several prominent US space companies—including SpaceX, Blue Origin, Stoke Space, K2, and Starcloud—pulled out of a high-profile French space summit organized by the country’s president, Emmanuel Macron.
Politico first reported the diplomatic turmoil, saying that the White House “pressured” US space companies to skip Macron’s space summit in Paris next week. Since then, the companies have largely pulled out of the meeting without commenting publicly, though some US representation remains on the two-day program.
Multiple sources confirmed to Ars that an official with the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, or OSTP, led the call with US space companies late last week. The call was convened in response to queries from US industry about the French meeting, which is not part of the traditional circuit of international space conferences.
What is the Space Summit?
Macron announced his plans for the meeting during a June 2025 speech on the importance of space to defense and Europe’s need to remain competitive in the domain. He said France would hold a “Space Summit” at the beginning of 2026 to consolidate French and European strategy in space and “mobilize our public and private partners from around the world.” Later, Macron announced that some of France’s most visible space officials, including astronaut Thomas Pesquet and entrepreneur Hélène Huby, would serve as special envoys.
The meeting subsequently slipped from the spring to the fall, and in the meantime, US companies received invites to attend. As is customary in such situations involving geopolitics, the government relations officials with these companies reached out to the White House OSTP with questions about the nature of the summit.
The White House officials were growing concerned that this was not a normal space industry trade show or conference but would instead include some policy prescriptions around contentious issues such as sharing of spectrum. US officials believed that at the end of the summit, European space officials may move to adopt some policies that were not necessarily beneficial to US companies.
This led to the teleconference with the OSTP and some US space companies late last week, during which the government relations officials were advised that the US firms should not necessarily expect to be treated fairly and might be pressured to endorse policy positions that misrepresent their preferences. The companies were not told they must pull out by the Trump White House but were instead advised that attending might not be in their best interests.

U.A.E. warned Netanyahu of major Hamas operation days before Oct. 7 attack: Israeli newspaper
Haaretz says Netanyahu's office called report 'absolute lie'
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was directly warned by the president of the United Arab Emirates that Hamas was planning a major offensive just days before the militant group led an attack on Oct. 7, 2023 , according to an Israeli newspaper.
U.A.E. President Mohammed bin Zayed spoke with Netanyahu 10 days before the attack and said Yahya Sinwar, the leader of Hamas in Gaza at the time, was planning an operation, the Haaretz daily said.
Bin Zayed said it would lead to bloodshed and could destabilize the region and undermine the Abraham Accords, the normalization agreements between Israel and several Arab and Muslim-majority nations, the newspaper reported.
But Netanyahu "reacted with relative calm," according to Haaretz, which said he assured bin Zayed that Israel was prepared for any scenario and a possible attack was more likely to come from the occupied West Bank.
The attack led by Hamas militants on Oct. 7 killed some 1,200 people and took another 251 hostage, according to Israeli officials.
Haaretz reported Netanyahu's office called the report an "absolute lie" and said Netanyahu did not speak with the U.A.E. president "during the period in question and received no warning from him."

Netanyahu has rejected calls for an official government inquiry into the events surrounding the Oct. 7 attack. His office did not respond to a request for comment.
The U.A.E.'s Foreign Ministry also did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Israel is holding national elections next month and Netanyahu's actions around the time of the Oct. 7 attack are a key issue in the campaign.
Gadi Eisenkot, a former top general seen as Netanyahu's main opponent in the election, accused the prime minister of ignoring dozens of warnings ahead of the attack.
"He is unfit," Eisenkot wrote on social media.
Another Netanyahu rival, Naftali Bennett, said, "Netanyahu bears personal and direct responsibility for the failure that led to the deaths of thousands of Israelis on his watch."
Israel's offensive in Gaza has killed more than 73,650 Palestinians, according to Gaza's Health Ministry.

Iran-backed Houthis attack Saudi oil facilities, injuring dozens
Attacks on Saudi facilities threaten to worsen the global economic impact resulting from Iran war
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis attacked four cities in the south of U.S. ally Saudi Arabia on Tuesday, wounding more than 70 people and setting oil installations ablaze in what appeared to be a major expansion of the six-month-old Middle East war.
The Houthis, who control most of Yemen's populated areas, including the capital, said they had launched a broad operation deep into Saudi territory. They used drones and missiles to strike a Saudi airbase in the southern city of Khamis Mushait, and targets belonging to Saudi Arabia's state oil company in nearby Abha, Najran and Jazan, a major Red Sea port.
Saudi authorities described blazes at the sites and said women and children were among the 73 people hurt. The reports of such large numbers of wounded suggested the attacks were among the biggest carried out against Saudi Arabia since the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran in February.
Confirmed images of the aftermath of the attacks were not immediately available. The Houthis released pictures of an explosion of what they said were trucks from Saudi Arabia they had struck at the border in another area.
Houthi attacks on southwestern Saudi Arabia have the potential to worsen the war's global economic impact by disrupting Middle East energy supplies beyond the blockaded Strait of Hormuz.
After a month of calm in August, fighting in the Gulf has resumed, with Iran and the U.S. exchanging fire, sending global oil prices back up to levels unseen since July. Brent crude prices were up more than two per cent on Tuesday, above $99 US a barrel.
The fighting has caused global shortages of crude oil and, more acutely, the fuels that are produced by refining it. Diesel fuel in the United States is now at a record average retail price of more than $5.90 a gallon less than two months before midterm elections that could threaten the hold of Donald Trump's Republicans on one or both chambers of U.S. Congress.
Test of wills
Saudi Arabia has led an Arab coalition battling against the Houthis in Yemen for more than a decade. That war had calmed in recent years, but a ceasefire there has broken down, with the Houthis threatening shipping at the mouth of the Red Sea.
"The coalition will take all necessary operational measures to deter this terrorist militia and resolutely confronts its hostile approach," Col. Turki al-Malki, spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition, said in a statement on X.
Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree accused Riyadh of having escalated the war by launching airstrikes on Yemen, and said the Houthis would respond.
The war in the Gulf has turned into a test of wills between the U.S. and Iran, with each side hoping that economic pressure from competing blockades will force the other to yield.
Washington is trying to increase the flow of oil to world markets by guiding ships through the Strait of Hormuz at the mouth of the Gulf, while cutting off Iran's exports with a blockade just beyond it.
Tehran has announced new measures to seal off the strait, saying it will soon unveil details of a "maritime exclusion zone" that will extend from the perimeter of the U.S. blockade, through the strait and into the Gulf itself.
The U.S. fired at Iranian tankers over the weekend in retaliation for Iranian fire at American warships. Iran said it had used new, more capable ballistic missiles to attack.
"In recent days, Washington has received a clear warning from Iran’s new missiles," Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council said on X. "Economic warfare will be met by a maritime exclusion zone across the Persian Gulf to the blockade perimeter. The operational posture toward U.S. warships and bases has been fundamentally recalibrated."
Thousands on the move in Yemen
Despite U.S. barrages that have degraded Iran's conventional forces and punished its already ailing economy, Iran still possesses missiles and drones that can threaten oil tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz and have been used to attack U.S. military bases scattered throughout the region.
About one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments passed through the strait before the war.

The flare-up between the Saudis and Houthis has displaced about 18,500 people in Taiz and Hodeida in southwestern Yemen, further pressuring communities in southern Taiz and the West Coast, according to the International Organization for Migration.
"Families are arriving with nothing: no shelter, no food, no way to know if it's safe to go back," said Abdusattor Esoev, IOM chief of mission for Yemen. "Many of these are people who have already been displaced once, twice, even four times before."
Yemen's civil war began in 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, and much of northern Yemen and forced the government into exile. A Saudi-led coalition intervened the following year to try to restore the government to power.
The civil war has killed at least 150,000 people, according to UN estimates, and at times pushed the country to the brink of famine.

‘Conduct worthy of derision’: HC rebukes Noida DM over illegal NSA detention
The Allahabad high court said IAS and IPS officers must remember that their loyalty is to the Constitution and not the political executive.
The Allahabad High Court has directed that ₹5 lakh compensation be paid to 25-year-old Delhi University graduate Akriti Chaudhary, who had been in judicial custody for around five months in connection with the April 2026 Noida workers’ protest, with the amount to be recovered from the salary of the Gautam Buddha Nagar district magistrate who ordered her preventive detention under the National Security Act (NSA), which the court quashed on September 2.
In its detailed order made public on Monday, a bench of justices Atul Sreedharan and Achal Sachdev delivered a scathing indictment of the administration’s conduct, describing district magistrate Medha Roopam’s conduct as “worthy of derision” and saying she had sought to “set an example” out of a peaceful student activist to deter others from protesting. The court also directed that its displeasure with the DM and the police be recorded in their service records.
The court also criticised what it described as bureaucratic overreach, saying IAS and IPS officers must remember that their loyalty is to the Constitution and not the political executive.
“They (civil servants) should realise that their loyalty is towards the Constitution and not the political executive, and the honesty and impartiality are towards the people whom they serve while bearing in mind at all times that they are the servants who serve the people, the masters in a democracy,” the court said.
The court warned that officers who forget this risk reducing Uttar Pradesh to “an Orwellian Dystopia.”
The bench scrutinised the evidence relied upon by the administration to detain Chaudhary, including WhatsApp chats, videos, case diary entries and message timestamps retrieved from her phone, and found that the record did not support the prosecution’s version of events.
A key issue was a notice issued to Chaudhary under Section 130 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), under which police can require a person to execute a bond for “good behaviour” in certain circumstances. The police claimed Chaudhary was served the notice on April 12, requiring her to furnish a ₹50,000 bond, and was arrested only after she refused. Chaudhary, represented by senior advocate Colin Gonsalves, had argued that she had actually been taken into custody on the evening of April 11 and was never given a genuine opportunity to furnish the bond.
The high court found that the General Diary entry number mentioned in the notice could only have been generated after her arrest, suggesting that the notice itself was prepared retrospectively.
“Mentioning the G.D. number in the notice under Section 130 of the BNSS reveals that the Petitioner was already arrested and the procedure of giving a notice under Section 130 of the BNSS was ex post facto the arrest and nothing more than a sham,” the court said.
When the state government was asked to explain the “visible fabrication in the record”, the court said, “no answer” was forthcoming.
The bench also found that the WhatsApp messages and videos produced by the State did not contain “a single message” or video showing that Chaudhary had incited people to riot, commit arson or damage public or private property.
The violence that erupted on April 13 therefore could not, on the material placed before the court, be attributed to a conspiracy allegedly hatched by Chaudhary, it said.
The court said preventive detention under the NSA is an “exception” and cannot be used merely to keep someone incarcerated because they might otherwise secure bail in an ordinary criminal case. It stressed that the exercise of such extraordinary power directly affects the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 of the Constitution and “cannot be exercised lightly on the basis of surmises, biases, conjectures and opinions”.
The court also cautioned against restricting peaceful protests merely on the assumption that they could lead to a breach of peace. “Preventing people from gathering in public spaces or agitating their rights on the grounds of assumed breach of peace,” it said, would amount to “throwing the baby out of the bath water”.
Instead, the State should train its police force to manage large gatherings and use videography to ensure accountability when violence occurs, the court said.

As the secretary of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. holds a unique role in shaping national priorities and discourse surrounding public health. Even before he took office, Kennedy gained attention particularly for his views on vaccines — for example, claiming in 2017 that if a vaccine vial broke in a building, the building would have to be evacuated.
After stepping into the HHS role in 2025, he continued to spread false and misleading rumors, such as suggesting on multiple occasions that vaccines caused the 1918 Spanish flu pandemic and that the vaccine for measles, mumps and rubella contained tissue from aborted fetuses.
His views on vaccines and the use of medications such as Tylenol often bleed into conversations about autism. In April 2025, he claimed autistic children will never pay taxes, hold a job, play baseball or write a poem, and in May 2026, he cited highly critized studies that said children circumcised early had "double" the rate of autism because they were given Tylenol.

Canada braces for prolonged trade war as counter-tariffs on US take effect
- Published
Canada's retaliatory tariffs on a range of US goods came into effect on Tuesday, with no sign of a trade deal on the horizon.
The counter-tariffs will apply to nearly C$28bn ($20bn; £15bn) worth of American products, from steel to furniture to cotton T-shirts, and will be as high as 50%.
Fresh fish and lobster were also on the list, but Canada later omitted them after pushback from its seafood industry - a sign of the tricky balance it has to strike as it retaliates against its largest trading partner.
Both US and Canadian officials have said they would like to strike a deal, but no movement has been made to resume talks after they collapsed in late August.
Speaking to reporters last week, Prime Minister Mark Carney said that Canada is still in search of a deal with the US that is "durable" and in the best interests of both countries.
"We're ready to sit down and and strike that deal when the Americans are ready," Carney said.
US trade representative Jamieson Greer, meanwhile, said on Thursday that the ball is in Canada's court.
"We offered them the best deal, they looked at it square in the face and turned around," Greer said in an interview with Fox News, adding that there has been sparse communication with the Canadians since talks collapsed.
In a separate interview with Canadian broadcaster CBC, Greer cautioned against retaliation and suggested the US might hit back by banning the import of some Canadian products.
President Donald Trump threatened on Monday to halt all US business with Canada-based airplane maker Bombardier unless it moved its manufacturing south.
The company is one of the largest in the country, contributing over C$7bn to Canada's annual GDP in 2024, according to a report commissioned by Bombarier by public accounting firm PwC.
- What tariffs will really cost Canadians and Americans 
  - Published29 August
- The US-Canada trade war in 5 charts 
  - Published31 August
Trump took aim at Canada in a series of other Truth Social posts over the weekend, including one that called Canada's exchange rate with the US "unacceptable".
Another post showed a map of North America - including Canada and Mexico - and Greenland all overlaid with the US flag.
Canada and the US have the world's largest bilateral trading relationship valued at nearly $900bn in 2025.
With new US tariffs and Canadian counter-tariffs are now in effect, businesses on both side are scrambling to deal with what comes next.
The US currently has in place a 25% tax on Canadian cars and trucks, as well as taxes on Canadian steel, aluminium and lumber. In late August, President Donald Trump imposed new 50% tariffs on other goods like dairy, alcohol, hockey sticks and perfume.
Canada's counter-tariffs, which were described by Carney as "dollar-for-dollar", will be applied to hundreds of items coming in from the US as of midnight on Tuesday.
They are in addition to existing retaliatory taxes Canada had placed on finished American cars and trucks that are non-compliant with a free trade agreement between Canada, the US and Mexico, known as the USMCA in the US and CUSMA in Canada.
Polls suggest the majority of Canadians support, external their country imposing retaliatory tariffs on the US.
But economists warn that the latest counter-tariffs will raise prices for consumers, external on everyday goods like clothing, food and furniture.
The Canadian Chamber of Commerce has also urged the Carney government to take a surgical approach to retaliation.
"Businesses understand retaliation but don't want to see endless escalation," said the Chamber's CEO and President Candace Laing in a statement to the BBC on Friday, though she added that businesses "are preparing for this trade dispute to last".
Pushback from the fisheries industry was enough for Canada to alter its counter-tariffs by removing dozens of seafood items to avoid unintended consequences to its own economy.
The lobster industry in both Canada and the US are heavily dependent on the other, with American-caught lobster often sent to north to be processed before it is shipped back to the US and sold.
Ahead of the latest tariffs, Canada's economy had shown signs of resliency. Its GDP grew 3.3% in the second quarter and it had gained 181,000 jobs from April to July.
But around 41,000 jobs were lost in August, a period that coincided with the new US tariffs on Canada and the collapse in trade talks.
One sector that saw a modest bump was manufacturing - a gain the Canadian government attributes to consumers and businesses buying more made-in-Canada products.
Prime Minister Carney has vowed to diversify Canada's trade away from the US. July figures show the share of US-bound Canadian exports dropped to 66% from an average of 75% before the trade war.

When I first tested the developer beta of Apple's Siri AI by taking it as my tour guide around San Francisco, I was convinced the overhauled smartphone assistant would be an “everything tool” on the iPhone. The answers felt reliable enough and more helpful than previous versions of Siri. Also, the chatbot-style app for Siri felt very sleek, very Apple-y.
Over the next month, I kept experimenting with the Siri AI in the iOS 27 beta. The tool was quite powerful, especially with the personal context brought in by indexing the contents of my phone. Finding an ancient text message or photo has never been easier. Even so, my usage of the smartphone assistant slowly started tapering off.
It’s not that Siri AI isn’t better now. It is! This new version is quite the step change, which makes my reaction even more devastating. Siri AI isn’t revolutionizing how I interact with my phone the way I'd initially hoped, especially as an AI assistant built directly into the device and factoring in that Apple gives more thought to preserving my privacy than many other AI companies.
Even though I wasn't going out of my way to interact with Siri AI, I didn’t mind how it was now, essentially, the search bar for the smartphone. As the summer months faded, I wasn’t souring on Siri AI. Instead, I just grew more neutral.
Old habits die hard. Soon I was back to my regularly scheduled doomscrolling on Instagram and aimless Yelp expeditions. I was manually typing and swiping for myself rather than relying on a smartphone assistant for help. And I was already low-key locked in with another chatbot, Anthropic’s Claude, and already used that app fairly often on my phone.
Even though some AI power users may not go all in on this new Siri, analysts say this won’t matter, since everyday users are often fine with Apple’s default software. “Will Siri bear the weight of criticism for not being as good as some of its peers? Sure,” says Dipanjan Chatterjee, vice president and principal analyst at Forrester, a research and consultancy company. “Will it make a difference to the vast installed base of iPhone users and cause them to look elsewhere? Not a chance.” Some iPhone users trust Apple with their data in ways they don't with any other company. Siri AI may reap those same benefits.
Tech analysts see Apple’s long-cultivated consumer trust in data privacy as potentially a compelling distinction. Ramon Llamas, a research director analyzing the mobile device market at the International Data Corporation, believes users deep in the Apple ecosystem, who previously had qualms about the safety of other AI tools, may be open to trying the new Siri.
My experience with Siri AI—loving it and then leaving it for dust—may be an outlier. Many other beta testers are still rocking with the smartphone assistant.
“In the past, I was unwilling to trust that Siri could do anything useful,” says Avi Greengart, founder and lead analyst at Techsponential. “But with the latest beta software, I'm finding myself not only using it more, but for more things: Siri is now able to find information buried on my phone faster and more efficiently than any other method, its world knowledge is vastly better than before, and even dictation works better.”
That said, the cultural backlash to generative AI has been brewing. Another solid segment of iPhone owners may choose to avoid the new Siri altogether because of the AI attached to its name. Whether it’s a moral objection or broader distrust of AI tools, these holdouts are unlikely to be won over by Siri’s feature improvements.
Ultimately, my own summer fling with Siri AI was short-lived. But I promise, it’s not you. It’s me.

Exclusive: WWE legend Ric Flair claims ‘influencer talent agency’ duped him into handing over his digital life: lawsuit
‘The Nature Boy is not finished,’ according to court filings obtained by The Independent. ‘The case has just begun.’
Legendary pro wrestler Ric “Nature Boy” Flair is suing a digital talent agency he claims duped him into signing away the rights to his own image and likeness while promising him a six-figure monthly revenue stream that allegedly never materialized.
The 77-year-old Flair, whose real name is Richard Morgan Fliehr, spent four decades “building something… through his body, his blood, his pain, his persona, his craft, and his commitment to excellence at a level that only sixteen world championships can describe,” according to a $10 million lawsuit obtained by The Independent.
But, Flair’s complaint says, FAM Networks, a “cutting-edge talent-first management agency and media company representing some of the most unique and impactful influencers around the world,” pounced on an opportunity to rook the elderly performer out of what was rightfully his.
“What FAM did was simple: it waited until he needed help managing the digital legacy of everything he had built, presented him with a document he was not equipped to understand, told him he had lawyers when he did not, gave him fourteen minutes to read it, and walked away with a perpetual license to his identity,” the complaint contends, adding that the pending legal action is only “the beginning.”
“The Nature Boy is not finished,” the complaint states. “The case has just begun.”
Reached by phone at his home in Hillsborough County, Florida, Fliehr, who last wrestled in 2022, told The Independent that he “wants to bury” the people at FAM Networks, and said he lost out on at least $250,000 in revenues so far.
Messages sent to five different departments at FAM Networks were all returned as undeliverable. A contact form on the company’s website was inoperable on Tuesday; it does not have a publicly listed phone number.
As Ric Flair, Richard Fliehr “electrified arenas across the world,” his complaint explains, calling him “one of the most celebrated, decorated, and recognizable professional athletes in the history of his sport.”
His career transcended the ring and became an indelible part of American pop culture, it goes on.
“A name, a likeness, and an identity that carries commercial value precisely because generations of fans have given it meaning through their devotion,” the complaint states. “That identity – the product of a lifetime of work, sacrifice, and sacrifice again – is what FAM Networks, LLC came for.”
FAM, which maintains offices in New York City and Los Angeles, purportedly defrauded Fliehr by quietly taking control of his social media accounts, recategorizing them to make recovery near-impossible, and milked his persona for profits he never saw.
At 5:57 PM on December 5, 2025, Fliehr opened an email from FAM, which came with a contract attached, according to the complaint, which was filed September 5 in Manhattan Supreme Court.
“At 6:11 PM – fourteen minutes later – he signed it,” the complaint continues. “In those fourteen minutes, without the benefit of legal counsel, without a single attorney reviewing a single word on his behalf, and in direct contradiction of a contractual recital FAM itself drafted declaring that the agreement had been negotiated with counsel, Mr. Fliehr surrendered an irrevocable, perpetual, sublicensable license over his name, image, likeness, voice, accounts, and commercial identity – throughout the universe, without restriction, in all languages, formats, and media now known or later developed.”
FAM “knew he had no lawyer,” the complaint alleges. “FAM wrote the clause saying he did anyway.” (Fliehr has trouble discerning AI-generated content from reality, and often gets confused about things he sees online, according to his daughter Charlotte.)
The company, which promotes online influencers and pairs them up with corporate deals, offered Fliehr a full slate of speaking engagements and appearances with 90 percent of the proceeds going to him, the complaint states. It says FAM pledged 50 percent to Fliehr for “collaborative projects,” and 10 percent for “passive content.” FAM would also restore Fliehr’s “hacked, demonetized” Facebook page, which it claimed would throw off six figures on a monthly basis.
“These were not aspirations,” the complaint argues. “They were contractual obligations.”
However, it alleges, “FAM delivered none of them. It sourced not one speaking engagement. Not one in-person appearance. Not one personal project at the ninety percent royalty tier. It reposted existing content.”
At the same time, FAM enriched itself by as much as $20,000 a month by monetizing Fliehr’s Facebook page, while paying him “next to nothing,” according to the complaint.
It then transferred Fliehr's Facebook page to itself, effectively locking Fliehr’s existing team out and blowing a potential advertising deal they already had in the works, the complaint states. By taking “operational control” of Fliehr’s digital life, FAM was allegedly able to “entrench itself in a position from which it could demand a ransom for his own property's return.”
When Fliehr signed the contract with FAM, the company was already embroiled in an almost identical case involving ufologist Steven Greer, according to the complaint. Yet, FAM “disclosed none of this to Mr. Fliehr before he signed,” because, the complaint argues, “[d]isclosure would have ended the transaction.”
The complaint contends that the contract that FAM convinced Fliehr to sign and later “weaponize[d],” should be declared null and void. It describes the agreement as “not a contract,” but, rather, “a trap,” giving FAM the right to act in Fliehr’s name without his involvement and erecting practically insurmountable barriers preventing him from extracting himself from the deal.
“New York courts of equity do not enforce traps, and they do not enforce perpetual licenses extracted from elderly men in fourteen minutes without counsel on the basis of false recitals and undisclosed litigation,” states the complaint.
Last year, Fliehr sued a cannabis company he was involved in promoting, along with iconic prizefighter Mike Tyson, for $50 million, alleging fraud, self-dealing, and civil RICO conspiracy.
Fliehr is now asking a judge to rescind the agreement with FAM, to order control of his Facebook page returned to him, a declaratory judgment stating that FAM has no right to his name, image, or likeness, and for a “complete accounting of revenues generated in his name.”
He is also demanding compensatory damages, among other things, of at least $5 million for breach of contract; compensatory and punitive damages of at least $5 million for fraudulent inducement; compensatory damages to be determined at trial for violations of New York Civil Rights Law; compensatory and punitive damages for tortious interference with prospective economic advantage, also to be determined at trial; and disgorgement of all amounts by which FAM “has been unjustly enriched at [Fliehr’s] expense,” plus attorneys' fees and court costs.
A trial date has not yet been set.

Why thousands are paying to watch people play Dungeons & Dragons live
Live 'actual play' combines the unpredictable nature of sports with the intimacy of friends telling stories
There is no script, no fixed ending and no guarantee the heroes will make it out alive.
Onstage, performers build a fantasy world together while dice rolls and split-second choices can send the story to places nobody planned.
On Sept. 10, nearly 2,800 people will fill Vancouver's Queen Elizabeth Theatre for a sold-out performance of Endless Dungeon, led by comedian and game master Brennan Lee Mulligan. The Vancouver date follows a sold-out May performance at Toronto's Coca-Cola Coliseum.
Endless Dungeon is part of the growing world of "actual play" — tabletop role-playing games performed for an audience — a genre combining improvisational theatre, collaborative storytelling and game mechanics, with dice helping determine whether characters succeed or fail.
For performers and scholars, the appeal lies in uncertainty, intimacy and collaboration — and in knowing that no two performances will be exactly alike.
Mulligan told CBC News that part of the attraction is simply "the joy of live theatre."
"It's happening in front of your face," he said, adding that the audience reactions become part of the draw. "You are there, your gasps, your laughs, your groans at a bad D&D pun."
A roller coaster with no track
The term "actual play" is recent, but the practice is a longstanding one according to Emily Friedman, a professor of English at Alabama's Auburn University who studies the format.
Online shows such as Critical Role, Mulligan's Dimension 20 and The Adventure Zone helped bring actual play into the mainstream. Live performances are often self-contained, with clearer character goals and story beats designed to reach an ending in a few hours. That makes the action "heightened and brightened and made sharper and quicker and faster," Friedman said.
She compared its appeal to being on a roller coaster where "the track is being laid in front of you at high speed."
Vancouver comedian Jess Lupini, who is joining Endless Dungeon for this stop, compared it to another form of unscripted entertainment.
"Watching actual plays is exciting in many of the same ways that watching hockey is exciting," she said. "You don't know what's going to happen."
'The feeling of being in the room'
But that unpredictable nature only partly explains why people pay to see a format they can watch online.
Abdul Aziz, a Vancouver comedian joining Mulligan for this Endless Dungeon performance, says the attraction is "probably the feeling of being in the room."
Aziz also performs on the actual-play podcast Spout Lore, which has tried to preserve the atmosphere of friends playing together even as those conversations became entertainment for strangers.
"We sort of are more focused on each other while playing than we are focused on the audience," Aziz said.
- Level up your next Dungeons and Dragons adventure with these creative makers
- Tabletop role-playing games can be intimidating. Here's one anyone can jump into
Friedman says audiences are watching two things at once: fictional characters and the real people creating them reacting genuinely when another player's choice surprises them.
Mulligan says performers have to make the audience feel included without sacrificing their connection to one another.
"The best part of live theatre is the preservation of authentic connection between performers and feeling totally invisible as an audience member, even as everything has been arranged to include you," he said.
"Whatever you do to delight your players will delight the audience."
A place to imagine differently
For Aziz, fantasy also offers room to question rules that can seem fixed in the real world.
Aziz, whose parents are from Egypt and who immigrated to Canada as a child, says growing up in a mainly white community gave him an outsider's perspective on cultural conventions.
- How a Dungeons and Dragons club became a 'lifesaver' for a group of neurodivergent Ontario youth
- VideoFrom 'satanic panic' to church-approved, Dungeons & Dragons thriving after 50-plus years
That carried into Spout Lore. While building his barbarian character's homeland, Aziz drew heavily on Middle Eastern cultures.
"In a very literal sense, the outsider's perspective was immediately useful in our show," he said.
For Lupini, who is also a recurring cast member on BlackwaterDnD, an actual-play show streamed on YouTube and Twitch, taking on different characters became a way to explore herself.
Lupini, who is transgender, says tabletop role-playing games give people a chance to try on different identities, pronouns and personalities.
Before transitioning, she played characters who used she/her pronouns.
"That was really liberating and felt like a safe way of exploring a piece of myself that I had been conditioned to be really afraid of exploring," she said.
- VideoThese girls are learning to master Dungeons and Dragons
- The rise of Critical Role: How a crew of 'nerdy-ass voice actors' became Dungeons & Dragons rock stars
Friedman says women, gender-nonconforming people, 2SLGBTQ+ people and disabled people have always been part of tabletop gaming as players and creators, but were not always visible in traditional gaming spaces.
"It's just the shift of the spotlight in a lot of ways," she said.
Mulligan agrees, saying actual play didn't create those experiences, but made them easier to see.
"Actual play provided visibility for a reality that was always there," he said.
A safe place to play
That kind of exploration depends on trust, says Em Carlson, CEO and creative director of BlackwaterDnD and another performer joining Vancouver's Endless Dungeon.
Carlson, whose professional background is in mental-health therapy, says the group does extensive preparation around safety and collaboration and notes that "play can't happen if you're not safe."
Tabletop role-playing culture still hasn't fully achieved its ideals of inclusion, Carlson says, but the stories reaching audiences have broadened as people want stories that help them feel included in the narrative.
"They can be a part of that joy that the players experience at the table."
For Carlson, Endless Dungeon offers something increasingly uncommon in an era of endlessly replayable media: a story created once, for the people present.
"It's a one-night experience where a fantastic, amazing audience gets to come in and laugh with us and cry with us and feel big feelings and cheer."

If you opt for an Android phone over an iPhone, there are certain features you get as standard as part of Android. Then there are other features specific to certain manufacturers, as each Android phone maker puts its own spin on the software.
Pixel phones, for example, get the Now Playing widget on the home screen and lock screen that works like an instant Shazam. It'll tell you the name of the song playing in your environment before you've even searched for it.
With Samsung phones, one of the best perks isn't as widely known about or used as it should be. It's called the Edge Panel, and it works like a customizable shortcut bar that gives you speedy access to the other parts of your phone.
If you own a Galaxy device and have never come across the Edge Panel, or you used it once but have since forgotten about it, here's what it's capable of now—and how you can make the most of it to optimize your mobile experience.
How the Edge Panel Works
You can think of the Edge Panel as being a little bit like the Start menu on Windows, or the dock on macOS. It provides something that Android doesn't have by default, which is a user-configurable launcher for collecting your favorite apps and feature shortcuts.
When it's enabled, the Edge Panel appears as a faint line along the side of the screen, and you can swipe across it to open the pane. If you don't see it, head to Settings and choose Display > Edge Panels to turn it on (via the toggle switch) or customize what the panels show (by tapping the menu entry).
There are actually seven different types of panel to choose from, as you'll see when you start to customize the feature: Apps, People, Tasks, Weather, Tools, Clipboard, and Reminder. You can have just one of them active, or all seven, or something in between (once you've got the Edge Panel up, swipe across it to switch between the different types).
The names of these panels give you some idea of what they can do. You can use the Apps panel to access the apps you use the most, without having to hunt for them in the main app drawer or having them clutter up your home screen. You can also jump to your most important people on the Contacts panel in the same way.
The Clipboard panel gives you quick access to the phone clipboard, while Tasks features shortcuts such as taking screenshots, adding new calendar events, adding alarms, and taking a screenshot. Having these shortcuts on the Edge Panel means you don't have to dig through menus or remember key combinations for the same functions.
Tools is actually just a single tool: a compass that tells you your current location and points you north, south, east, or west. Weather is pretty self-explanatory, while Reminder syncs information from the Reminder app that comes preinstalled on Galaxy devices.
Customize the Edge Panel
The Edge Panel works fine in its default state, but to make the most of it you really need to set it up to suit you and the way you use your phone. From the main Settings menu, choose Display, then tap Edge Panels.
First, select Panels to pick which panes are shown. Put a check next to the panes you want to have available. If you tap the three dots (top right) then Reorder, you're able to choose the order they appear in as well—place the panes you use most often furthest to the left, as they'll be available in fewer swipes.
You can also tap the three dots then Hide on Lock screen if you don't want the Edge Panel to appear before you've unlocked your phone. Bear in mind that you might not want some information—such as the contents of the clipboard or your reminders—being available to anyone who picks up your handset.
With Apps, People, and Tasks, you can customize what's included. Just tap the Edit button underneath the pane. In each case, there are more available options than there are slots on the Edge Panel, so you need to prioritize accordingly.
Back on the Edge Panels screen, there are a couple of other options worth knowing about. If you pick Handle, you can set the properties of the little onscreen strip that Edge Panel is activated through. Pick the size and transparency level of the handle, its color, and which side of the screen it appears on.
Finally, there's the Show in landscape mode toggle switch; disable this if you don't want to see the Edge panel when you're using your phone in its landscape orientation. This mode is mainly used for watching videos and playing games, in which case the Edge Panel and its handle might distract you.
