First Opinion is STAT’s platform for interesting, illuminating, and provocative articles about the life sciences writ large, written by biotech insiders, health care workers, researchers, and others.
To encourage robust, good-faith discussion about issues raised in First Opinion essays, STAT publishes selected Letters to the Editor received in response to them. You can submit a Letter to the Editor here, or find the submission form at the end of any First Opinion essay.
The story
“Tear down the wall between M.D. and D.O. education,” by Abigail MacKenzie and Vijay Rajput
The response
While I appreciate Drs. MacKenzie and Rajput for helping to shine a light on the bias and unfair challenges graduates of osteopathic medical schools face in residency placements, the answer is not for D.O. grads to surrender and give up the principles and practices that they bring to the health care system. While it may be hard for some M.D. physicians to understand, the separate pathways are more than just logistics. Organizations, examinations, accreditation systems, and professional structures matter, but they are not what makes osteopathic medical education worth preserving.
We need to preserve something much more fundamental: the cognitive architecture of osteopathic medical education. By cognitive architecture, I mean the intentional organization of knowledge, experiences, scientific disciplines, and professional values to shape how physicians perceive, reason through, and solve clinical and health system problems. Every allopathic medical school (M.D.) teaches biomedical and clinical science. Increasingly, they teach health systems science as well. The distinction between allopathic and osteopathic education is not whether these subjects exist elsewhere. The distinction is how they are intentionally integrated.
Osteopathic principles and practices are more than just an add-on elective. Osteopathic medical education intentionally integrates biomedical, clinical, health systems and biomechanical sciences, and concepts aligned with complexity science into a coherent framework for physician formation. Osteopathic philosophy serves as the integrative lens through which these domains influence clinical reasoning. For the D.O. community, the result is physicians who strive to excel at both promoting and maintaining health and treating disease; who value relationships as well as diagnoses; who recognize that structure and function are linked; who appreciate context, adaptation, prevention, and community; and who use medical, surgical, manual, behavioral, and social interventions as complementary tools in patient care.
Given the incredible growth of osteopathic medical education, this philosophy and these principles are resonating with prospective medical students and patients in record numbers. Today, about 30% of all medical students in the U.S. are educated at a college of osteopathic medicine, and that percentage is growing every year. Those students deserve equal opportunities, and that is why the American Association of Colleges of Osteopathic Medicine is working with our peers in the medical community and why we’re supporting the Fair Access in Residency (FAIR) Act. The answer to our nation’s physician shortage crisis is to fully open the doors to residency for all qualified candidates, not to close the door on those who choose the osteopathic pathway.
— Robert Cain, American Association of Colleges of Osteopathic Medicine
The response
Excellent article and well researched. Most of my colleagues never knew or cared that I was a D.O. They cared more about the care I offered and whether I could accept constructive criticism when it was due. I completely agree with the article, but I think the credentialing boards generate so much revenue that they are reluctant to combine (and possibly line their pockets a little less) and work together. Perhaps we even do away with the maintenance of certification altogether. Isn’t passing boards and maintaining continuing medical education credits, along with the threat of lawsuits always looming, enough to ensure we keep up with the science?
— Sharon McKelvey
The response
There are more differences in the training of M.D. students and D.O. students than just the modality of osteopathic manipulative treatment. The entire approach to the patient is different. Holism (a term that has been grossly overused and misunderstood) is a tenet that stresses a more global understanding of a patient and all that influences their health and well-being. This approach begins in year one and continues throughout all (usually) four years. D.O. training focuses heavily on history and physical diagnosis and tends to create a higher percentage of primary care providers because of this broad approach. All facets of scientific evidence-based medicine and surgery are taught and complementary, and alternative medicine is not avoided. In fact, osteopathic manipulative medicine focusing on circulation and innervation is a central modality during training.
Most of us who have spent careers as osteopathic physicians in a largely allopathic American health care system have learned to value and embrace these unique aspects. Vive la différence!
— Alfred Sassler, University of Cincinnati Medical Center/UC Health
The story
“AI won’t enhance physician autonomy. It will further diminish it,” by Frances Mei Hardin
The response
Thank you for this article. I couldn’t agree more that “lack-of-autonomy creep” has been happening for a long time. It would be OK if the new structures and “tools” were mostly in the service of better patient care, but let’s be honest, most new “advancements” are not. As the author points out, our autonomy has been removed from us piece by piece. The power is in the hands of the owners of the means of production, and that is not the doctors. We are the workers, not the factory owner, albeit well-paid ones, which is one reason we don’t complain. How can money-driven incentives improve patient outcomes?
Let’s be honest about that. Venture capital couldn’t care about patient outcomes as much as we do. AI will be deployed for cost savings primarily. The AI we happily use for our notes will be the loser to the AI the insurance companies use to tell us we have “overcoded.” Physicians are suffering from a history of autonomy that is currently an illusion. This long-defunct echo prevents us from organizing and exerting the power we do have to influence our destiny. I am by no means a Marxist, but in this case the metaphor is apt. We have gone from being respected autonomous experts to unempowered, well-paid “factory workers.” The attribution of liability that the author references is but one example.
The answer is to not passively accept what is given but to organize to make our voices heard. And sorry, our professional organizations as they currently exist are not the answer, as they are in bed with corporate (insurance, pharma) interests, something almost too obvious to have to state.
— Jody Whitehouse, M.D.
The story
“Whale songs: the sounds of love and loss as heard by an OB-GYN,” by Caroline Cherston
The response
These observations rang true to me because of my experience working in the pit right after Sept. 11. My therapy dog and I accompanied grieving families to ground zero in the days following the attacks. Mothers accompanied by their adult children would arrive at the still burning disaster, still in denial that their child had been killed. Once there, staring at the devastation, there was no denying the reality of death. These women would scream a very distinctive wail, something I had never heard before and will never forget. As a park ranger living with brown bears in Alaska, I have witnessed what I interpret as grief when a sow loses a cub. Now I work at a national park where we teach our visitors about whales. Grief is human, grief is universal. Would that we studied it more and embraced its process.
— Naomi Boak, National Park Service
The story
“The Lindsay Clancy case shows the limits of postpartum psychiatry,” by Jamie Maguire, Lauren M. Osborne, and Jennifer Payne
The response
The authors are right on the mark arguing that scientific knowledge on postpartum psychopathology is lacking, and that this gap is likely to have played a role in the tragic Clancy case. I agree with their argument whereby the major flaw of extant knowledge is lack of precision, particularly concerning risk factors for developing severe, even lethal, conditions. Most importantly, by focusing on science, the authors steer the discussion away from (unsubstantiated) claims about psychiatry’s negligence and toward where we, collectively (science, mental health services, policymakers, and the public) should head to prevent such tragedies. I particularly identify with the article’s ending, which suggests that ultimately, precision enables compassion.
One aspect, however, is conspicuously absent from the authors’ vision: the role of clinical psychological science in achieving such precision. The past four decades have seen a proliferation of methodologies enabling increasingly precise assessment of risk and protective factors in psychopathology, including psychometrically sophisticated self-report measures, investigator-based semi-structured interviews, computerized tasks targeting cognitive-affective processes, and the validation of these methodologies against neural processes and overt behavior.
Perhaps the most intriguing risk factor for psychopathology gleaned from clinical psychological science, and one that is particularly relevant to the assessment and treatment of postpartum psychopathology, is malignant self-criticism. Defined as the tendency to set impossibly high self-standards and to adopt a punitive self-stance once these standards are (inevitably) unmet, self-criticism emerged as a robust predictor of virtually all forms of psychopathology, including suicide and violent behavior. Self-criticism has also been shown to derail evidence-based psychotherapeutic and psychopharmacological treatment of depression, even though more recent studies have shown that self-criticism responds well to distinct forms of treatment.
Importantly, such research demonstrated the formidable risk associated with self-criticism for postpartum depression and anxiety, as well as for disruptions in mother-child communication, which might exacerbate postpartum psychopathology.
Of course, we cannot know the extent to which malignant self-criticism played a role — if any — in the Clancy case. Other psychological risk factors may be in play. The bottom line, however, is that psychiatry and psychology should not compete over markers. Rather, they must join forces, in science and practice, in identifying a wide spectrum of factors that increase vulnerability to the chilling outcome manifested by the Clancy case and other tragic ones. The aim, therefore, is biopsychosocial precision in mental health science and practice.
— Golan Shahar, Ben-Gurion University of the Negev
The story
“8 steps to making surrogacy more ethical for everyone involved,” by Arthur Caplan
The response
The problem is with the very concept of “surrogacy,” which means acting on behalf of someone else. Our ideas of surrogacy are based on a patriarchal notion that the essence of the baby is in the seed. While the original idea was that men had the seeds, medicine eventually had to acknowledge that women have seeds too, and babies are thus “half his and half hers.” Our society, and this discussion, claim that the real, the meaningful relationship is with the seed, and the pregnant woman is just a place, a spot you plant the precious seed. (In ordinary English we refer to the earth itself as dirt, soil in which we plant seeds.)
But pregnancy is not a location — it is a relationship. Babies are born recognizing the language the pregnant woman spoke. The comfort “rocking” offers a baby is its duplication of the walking motion. Hiring someone to be the location disregards the relationship. Can I hire someone else to be the wife for a husband, live with him, interact physically and socially — and then fire her, take him back, claim she was only a surrogate? We need to acknowledge and respect the relationship that is pregnancy.
— Barbara Katz Rothman, City University of New York
The story
“Medical aid in dying and the burden of choosing to live,” by Monika Piotrowska
The response
I am 82 years old and still healthy, but — let’s face it — for how much longer? The analogy the author makes between a student learning that they are not doing well academically and facing the inevitability of dying does not work for me at all. The author speaks of autonomy, and I don’t understand that, either. Because my husband has died of dementia with no autonomy at all and it wasn’t pretty. Because I want to be able to decide I am ready to die and I know that I soon will be ready to die (but still hoping to outlive Trump). I have had a long and really wonderful life and I am content. What I fear is burdening others with my care. I don’t want to impose that on my children. I want to be able to make the choice about the timing of my death so as to retain my autonomy and my ability to make choices, to have quality, not quantity of life. MAiD promises this to me, and is such a tremendous relief.
— Nora Staffanell
The story
“AI has created a shadow medical system,” by Arya Rao and Marc Succi
The response
In their recent essay on AI and the “shadow medical system,” Arya Rao and Marc Succi close with the 1979 IBM assertion that “A computer can never be held accountable, therefore a computer must never make a management decision.” Applied to health care, that claim has been outdated at least since 2018. That was the year LumineticsCore received the first FDA de novo clearance for an autonomous medical diagnosis — diabetic retinopathy — and began carrying malpractice insurance for its no-clinician-in-the-loop system. And just this year, Doctronic launched a prescription-renewal pilot that has some physician oversight, but not over every clinical decision made by the AI. Accordingly, Doctronic also carries a malpractice policy holding the system to physician-level accountability.
The problem of AI accountability for health decisions is real and important. It is no longer accurate to say it is unsolved.
— Joel Selanikio, M.D., futurehealth.live
The response
While the article makes several insightful points about AI assuming clinician responsibilities, the bigger picture should be on who is accountable for those decisions. Rao and Succi correctly identify accountability as the dividing line between a useful medical tool and a functioning medical system. Accountability is more complicated than ensuring a physician remains nominally involved. “Human oversight” becomes meaningless when responsibility and authority are separated.
We’ve seen this problem with clinical decision support for years. Technology identifies an abnormality or recommends action, while the difficult question — who owns the next step? — remains unanswered. AI makes that long-standing design failure much more consequential. If the default is to lay accountability at the clinician’s feet, we are in danger of creating an unsustainable system. A clinician cannot meaningfully be accountable for AI decisions if they did not select the model, cannot interrogate its reasoning, cannot see its underlying data, or do not have a realistic opportunity to intervene.
The American Medical Association has called for transparency, accountability, physician oversight, regular auditing, and clearer standards around AI-enabled clinical decision support. It has also argued that liability should be appropriately apportioned rather than automatically falling on physicians. “Human in the loop” is not an accountability model. Requiring a clinician to approve an AI-generated recommendation may create the appearance of oversight without giving that clinician genuine control. “Clinicians must review an AI output” is closer to a disclaimer than a governance policy unless an organization clearly defines where human judgment is required and leaves space for clinicians to exercise that judgment.
That thinking applies to the shadow system. A click, signature, or brief review should not magically transfer responsibility from an AI developer or platform to a physician. Accountability has to extend beyond the diagnosis to the care loop. Technology often succeeds at identifying a problem while failing to establish who owns what happens next. We must design clinical systems around explicit responsibility and completion of the care process, rather than merely generating alerts or recommendations. This idea maps to Rao and Succi’s concern about AI correctly identifying abnormal lab values and the trail of questions that follow: Who confirms it? Who determines its significance in context? Who ensures follow-up occurs? Who recognizes when the algorithm missed the dangerous alternative diagnosis? That’s where “answering a medical question” becomes practicing medicine.
— Craig Joseph

Shares of enterprise cloud and AI company ESDS Software Solution hit the 20% upper circuit for the third consecutive session today, taking the stock to more than three times its IPO issue price. The stock was locked at ₹1,289.55 apiece on the BSE, taking ESDS’ market capitalisation to ₹15,114.9 Cr ($1.6 Bn). On the NSE, the stock was locked at ₹1,308.05 as of 12:36 PM IST. At these levels, ESDS shares were trading 200.6% above their IPO issue price of ₹429 apiece on the BSE. On the NSE, the stock was up 204.9% from the issue price. ESDS made its stock market debut on Friday (September 4), listing at ₹757 on the NSE, a premium of 76.5% over its issue price. On the BSE, the stock debuted at ₹746.30, a premium of nearly 74%. The shares subsequently hit their 20% upper circuits at ₹908.40 on the NSE and ₹895.55 on the BSE on the listing day and remained locked at their respective upper limits during the following session. Meanwhile, Choice Institutional Equities has initiated coverage on ESDS with a ‘buy’ rating and a target price of ₹1,550. While the brokerage’s target represented an upside of about 71% from its reference price of ₹908, the stock’s subsequent rally has narrowed the potential upside to 18.5% from its NSE price of ₹1,308.05. The brokerage expects ESDS’ $1.25 Bn AI infrastructure contract with Australia-based Sharon AI to be a key growth catalyst. It has projected the company’s operating revenue to increase nearly 9.7X from ₹472 Cr in FY26 to ₹4,581 Cr by FY28, driven primarily by the ramp-up of its AI infrastructure business. However, Choice flagged the execution of the Sharon AI contract as a key risk, along with customer concentration, the capital-intensive nature of ESDS’ expansion plans, and growing competition in the cloud and AI infrastructure market. The company’s ₹720 Cr IPO, comprising entirely a fresh issue of shares, was subscribed 135.88X during its three-day bidding period. The QIB portion was subscribed 261.51X. Before the IPO, ESDS raised ₹216 Cr from anchor investors by allotting 50.34 Lakh shares at ₹429 apiece. Its anchor book included Motilal Oswal Mutual Fund, Bandhan Mutual Fund, Quant Mutual Fund, ITI Mutual Fund, and JM Flexicap Fund, among others. Founded in 2005, Nashik-based ESDS provides cloud computing, data centre, managed services and AI-led digital infrastructure solutions to government and enterprise customers in India and overseas. ESDS operates across infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS), managed services and software-as-a-service (SaaS), serving customers across banking and financial services, government and enterprise segments. ESDS plans to use ₹576 Cr, or 80% of the IPO proceeds, to purchase and install cloud-computing equipment and other data-centre infrastructure. The remaining proceeds have been earmarked for general corporate purposes. Its operating revenue increased 30.7% YoY to ₹472.2 Cr in FY26 from ₹361.3 Cr in the previous fiscal. Consolidated net profit more than doubled to ₹120.8 Cr from ₹55.6 Cr during the period.

Congress has handed Sachin Pilot a familiar problem and a bigger opportunity.
NEW DELHI: The Congress leadership last week finally responded to 'Mayday' calls from Punjab rebels and brought in Sachin Pilot, replacing Bhupesh Baghel, to prevent a crash landing of the deeply fractured state unit ahead of the assembly elections early next year.Months of open infighting between Charanjit Singh Channi, the former chief minister leading the rebel camp, and Raja Warring, the state unit chief, not just embarrassed the Congress but also threatened to derail its 2027 campaign.Before being put in the driver's seat in Punjab, Pilot was in charge of Chhattisgarh, where Baghel remains a key Congress leader and former chief minister.
Why Congress was forced to budge
The Congress had sent former Chhattisgarh chief minister Bhagel to Punjab in February this year to defuse the brewing Channi vs Warring crisis in the state unit. Ironically, as things turned out, Baghel faced resistance and became part of the crisis, with the Channi camp openly accusing him of siding with Warring. More so, since July, after the party’s central leadership decided to ignore Channi’s claim for the top post in the state and announced that it would continue with Warring as state Congress president.
Bhupesh Baghel had asserted that it is not a 'child's play' and the decision of the high command will not change.
With several senior state leaders backing Channi, the fight turned ugly and Baghel became ineffective.
Congress meetings in the districts saw open “Go back Baghel” chants from Channi supporters, taking the infighting to the streets and embarrassing the top leadership.So, while the ruling Aam Aadmi Party was already in full election mode with chief minister Bhagwant Mann at the centre of its campaign, the Congress was still struggling to get its senior leadership to sit across the table.Not just the AAP, even the BJP and the Akalis had their house in order and were planning their electoral moves on the ground. With the party's 2027 campaign failing to take off under Baghel, the Congress was forced to budge and turn to Pilot.
Why Sachin Pilot
The Congress decision to send Pilot to Punjab, while ironic, may still be the best bet for the leadership. Sachin Pilot, during his years in the Congress, has seen enough internal wars to know how quickly a fight over one post can turn into a larger battle over leadership, political space and, of course, eventually the chief minister's chair.Throwback to Rajasthan, where he spent years at the centre of a similar leadership tussle with senior leader Ashok Gehlot. Pilot brings something the Congress needs badly right now: the experience of being at the centre of a difficult internal power struggle.
Punjab Congress working president welcomed Sachin Pilot’s appointment, saying it will help iron out differences within the state unit.
Pilot has led the Rajasthan unit, worked closely with the high command, weathered the bitter internal battle, survived the fallout and then rebuilt his position within the Congress.He was appointed Rajasthan Congress chief in 2014, after the party's abysmal performance in the 2013 assembly election. Over the next four years, he emerged as one of the key faces of the party's rebuilding effort before Congress returned to power in 2018. That victory, however, did not give him the chief minister's chair.Ashok Gehlot became chief minister, while Pilot was made deputy chief minister and continued as PCC president. While both sides got something, the arrangement never really settled the rivalry between Gehlot and Pilot.By 2020, those differences exploded into an open rebellion.Pilot left Jaipur with a group of MLAs and challenged the Gehlot government. Congress responded by removing him as deputy chief minister and state president. The Gehlot camp even accused him of working with the BJP. A truce was eventually worked out, and Pilot stayed with Congress.But he never quite returned to the position he had occupied before and has been on the sidelines ever since. He remained a prominent face in the party and was later given charge of Chhattisgarh, but his role in Rajasthan remained limited.It is interesting how, in Rajasthan, Pilot was the leader asking the Congress high command to listen to a dissatisfied camp. In Punjab, he now has to convince dissatisfied leaders to accept the high command's decisions and work together.That may be why Congress believes he is best suited for the job.
Baghel gone. Will Warring be next?
But will Pilot’s appointment end the crisis in the Punjab unit?Channi's supporters had demanded Warring be removed as Punjab Congress chief, and the Jalandhar MP be declared Congress’s chief ministerial face for the 2027 assembly polls. The Congress has not accepted either of the two demands. So, while Channi has not made any significant gains, Warring has been left wondering if he will be the next to be axed.Warring was picked up to lead and rebuild the Punjab unit after the Congress was decimated in the 2022 assembly polls. Channi, who was the chief minister then, led the Congress to its worst-ever performance in the state. The Congress not just lost its government to AAP but was also reduced to 18 seats in the 117-member assembly.The leadership tussle between the two had been brewing for quite some time. But as is the Congress’s wont, the party kept dilly-dallying on the issue for nearly 4 years. Finally, when the Congress did take a decision, it ended up opening deep faultlines.For now, both camps have welcomed his appointment. Warring said Pilot's energy and dynamism would "for sure" add to the vigour of the party ahead of the crucial polls, while Gurdaspur MP Sukhjinder Singh Randhawa, a close associate of Channi, said Pilot's experience, leadership and connect with the people would give new strength and momentum to the Congress in Punjab.Punjab Congress working president Raj Kumar Verka hopes that under Pilot’s leadership all state leaders would come together. "Pilot knows all leaders of Punjab, and they also have confidence in him," said Verka.For Pilot, this may be his first real test. If party leadership decides to keep Warring, he has to get Channi, Randhawa and other leaders to fall in line. If Warring goes, he has to make sure one problem is not replaced by the other.
Congress has a lot at stake
The Congress, which remains the main challenger for now, cannot afford this infighting because Punjab is one of the states where it still has a real chance. There is anti-incumbency against the Bhagwant Mann-led AAP government.In 2022, AAP swept 92 of the 117 assembly seats, while Congress was reduced to 18. But the 2024 Lok Sabha election brought some relief for the grand old party. The Congress won seven of Punjab's 13 seats, compared with AAP's three, showing that the party still has enough ground to be a serious challenger.AAP is perhaps no longer riding the wave that brought it to power in 2022 and is now defending its record under Bhagwant Mann. Raghav Chadha's exit has also added to the churn in the party.The BJP and the Akalis are still on the margins of the state’s politics. But the scenario could change very fast. The BJP is going all out to broaden its organisational base and rope in leaders from other parties. There are also reports of talks between the BJP and the Akalis to revive their old alliance. The Congress needs to remember that the BJP is coming off a massive victory in West Bengal and is looking to expand its footprint in Punjab as well.
Punjab could shape Pilot's Rajasthan future
Pilot has already made it clear that he sees Punjab as a comeback opportunity for the Congress. On Monday, he said he was confident that with a strong organisation, collective effort and the energy of party workers, Congress could return to power in the state.
Pilot has the experience of being a part of successful strategising in Himachal Pradesh in the previous assembly polls and has also been a senior observer for the Kerala polls, where Congress returned to power after a decade.If Pilot can manage to bring the rival Punjab camps together and help the Congress put up a strong show in 2027, it will add to his standing within the party at a time when Rajasthan is already looking ahead to the 2028 assembly election.There has long been speculation over a bigger role for Pilot in Rajasthan. He may not have got it yet, but a successful Punjab stint could considerably strengthen his case.For a leader who has had to rebuild his own position in the party before, Punjab could well become the next big step in that comeback.

In a pair of late-stage trials, a drug from AstraZeneca reduced the dangerous flare-ups that drive the worsening of COPD, positioning it as a potential new option for the vast numbers of patients with the debilitating lung condition, according to data released Tuesday.
Results from the Phase 3 trials of the drug, called tozorakimab, also amount to a re-assuring victory for AstraZeneca, which is known for its metronomic success in trials but has seen some notable misses in recent months, most dramatically with a heart disease drug. Analysts and the company have projected that “tozo,” as the injectable drug is dubbed, could reap billions in annual sales if approved, both in COPD — which, as the third-leading cause of death globally, remains greatly underserved — and in other conditions including asthma.
In the trials, tozo reduced COPD exacerbations — any sudden worsening of the disease requiring medical care, whether a severe cough or breathlessness — by about 30% across all patients over a year, according to data presented at the European Respiratory Society’s annual conference in Barcelona and published in the New England Journal of Medicine. That finding makes tozo competitive with other COPD treatments that have reached patients in recent years, but notably, the tozo trials included participants not eligible for the other new drugs. The benefits seen in those patients could give AstraZeneca a large segment of the market to itself.

A day after the president of the West Bengal unit of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) Samik Bhattacharya said Bengalis would eat fish and meat during Durga Puja, rejecting the advice of the chief priest of Bageshwar Dham Dhirendra Krishna Shastri to follow a vegetarian diet during the pujas, several other BJP leaders came out in Mr. Bhattacharya’s support.
From Ministers of the West Bengal government to veteran party leaders, everyone followed the line taken by Mr. Bhattacharya. However, none of them criticised the self-styled godman, and some said that there was nothing wrong in promoting vegetarianism.
“Our State party president has clearly said that any person coming from outside will not understand our culture. In other States, during Durga Puja, everyone eats vegetarian food. But if he thinks that the same culture is here, it is not the case here. Here (in West Bengal) we save money so that we can have mutton and fish,” Minister for Municipal Affairs and Urban Development Agnimitra Paul said.
There was a tradition of offering animal sacrifices during Durga Puja and Kali Puja, and meat is offered as ‘prasad’’, Panchayat Minister and former State BJP president Dilip Ghosh said. “Some saints say that eating vegetarian food is good, but that is not a compulsion in West Bengal,” Mr. Ghosh said.
Senior BJP leader and West Bengal Industries Minister Tapas Roy, said that “each religion has its own rules but people will eat whatever they want”. “Our president Shamik Bhattacharya has also clarified that people will follow their own rules relating to religion and eat what they want,” Mr. Roy said.
West Bengal BJP veteran and former Tripura Governor Tathagata Roy said Dhirendra Shastri’s remarks were a non-issue. “Those who want to follow him, do so by all means — not eating non-veg food will hurt no one. And those who, like me, will eat non-veg food anyway, will ignore him. So, what’s all this hullabaloo about?” Mr. Roy said.
Dhirendra Shastri, also known as ‘Bageshwar Baba’, made the remark while addressing his devotees at an event in Liluah on September 6, 2026. “I want to appeal to the Hindus of Bengal that during Navratri, even if you don’t keep the idols of the Goddess, do not sell non-veg near the idols,” the self-styled godman said.
The remark had triggered strong reactions from the people of the State, including leaders of Opposition parties. The Madhya Pradesh-based religious preacher was welcomed to the State by Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari who, along with members of the Cabinet, had dinner with him.
On September 7, Mr. Bhattacharya appeared to attempt damage control by saying nobody could ask Bengalis to give up non-vegetarian food.
“How can Bengalis not have fish and meat? Even Swami Vivekananda said Ma Kali will have mutton [as an offering]. It is dangerous if someone tries to rise above Vivekananda. This is his (Shastri’s) personal opinion,” Mr. Bhattacharya had said. The BJP leader, however, added that there was no sin in advocating vegetarianism.
Political parties in the Opposition have targeted the BJP over the issue. While the Congress party lodged a police complaint against Dhirendra Shastri at the Bhawanipur police station, Communist Party of India-Marxist (CPI-M) leader Bikash Ranjan Bhattacharya said it was not Bageshwar Baba but those who had invited him to the State who were to be blamed.
Trinamool Congress MLA Kunal Ghosh said the State government, and Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari, who was patronising Bageshwar Baba, should offer clarification. “This is not just a matter of filing a complaint…There is a government that is patronising all this. The friends of this government come and insult Bengal and Bengalis whenever they wish,” Mr. Ghosh said.

Arunachal Pradesh – A Living Treasure of Biodiversity
Arunachal Pradesh is one of India’s most biologically diverse states, where forests, rivers, wetlands, mountains and communities are part of one interconnected ecological landscape. Its extraordinary range of habitats supports thousands of plant and animal species, including several rare, endemic and threatened species.
The State’s biodiversity is shaped by its remarkable variation in altitude and climate. From tropical forests in the foothills to temperate forests, alpine meadows and high-altitude ecosystems, Arunachal Pradesh offers a continuous range of habitats within a relatively compact geographical area.
With more than 80 per cent of its geographical area under forest cover, the State plays an important role in maintaining the ecological balance of the Eastern Himalayas. It is also part of the Eastern Himalaya Biodiversity Hotspot, one of the world’s globally recognised regions of exceptional biological richness and conservation importance.
A Landscape of Remarkable Ecological Diversity
The geographical diversity of Arunachal Pradesh is reflected in its forests. Depending on altitude and climatic conditions, the State has tropical evergreen and semi-evergreen forests, moist deciduous forests, subtropical broad-leaved forests, pine forests, temperate forests, coniferous forests, sub-alpine vegetation and alpine meadows.
This remarkable transition from the warm foothills to the high Himalayas creates habitats for species with very different ecological requirements.
The State is home to more than 5,000 species of flowering plants, around 600 species of orchids, about 75 species of rhododendrons, 45 species of bamboo, 17 species of cane and hundreds of medicinal plants. Arunachal Pradesh is particularly renowned for its orchid and rhododendron diversity.
The forests also support a remarkable variety of mammals, including the tiger, leopard, clouded leopard, snow leopard, golden cat, marbled cat, Asiatic elephant, red panda, takin, hoolock gibbon and several other rare and threatened species.
A Paradise for Birds
Arunachal Pradesh is equally celebrated for its avian diversity. Its forests and mountain ecosystems provide habitats for hundreds of bird species, making the State one of the most important birding regions in India.
The Eaglenest Wildlife Sanctuary in West Kameng is one of the best examples of this extraordinary richness. Located within the Eastern Himalaya Biodiversity Hotspot, Eaglenest is home to a wide variety of hornbills, pheasants, kingfishers and other birds. The sanctuary is also known for the discovery of the Bugun liocichla, a bird named after the Bugun community that lives in the region.
Protecting Arunachal’s Wildlife
Arunachal Pradesh’s biodiversity is protected through an extensive network of national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, tiger reserves and other conservation landscapes.
The state is home to important protected areas such as Namdapha National Park and Tiger Reserve, Kamlang Tiger Reserve, Pakke Tiger Reserve, Mouling National Park, Eaglenest Wildlife Sanctuary, Sessa Orchid Sanctuary, Dibang Wildlife Sanctuary and Mehao Wildlife Sanctuary, among others.
These landscapes support an exceptional range of wildlife, from high-altitude species such as the snow leopard and red panda to tropical forest species including the clouded leopard, hoolock gibbon and numerous birds, reptiles and amphibians.
Recent wildlife surveys have continued to expand scientific knowledge of these ecosystems. A 2024 WWF-India survey in Arunachal’s high-altitude rangelands recorded six wild cat species, including photographic evidence of the elusive Pallas’s cat, marking the first such photographic record from the state. The survey used 136 camera traps across 83 locations, covering approximately 2,000 sq km.
The Orchids of Arunachal Pradesh
Among the many botanical treasures of the State, orchids hold a special place.
Arunachal Pradesh has one of the richest orchid assemblages in India, with hundreds of species occurring across its varied habitats. The Sessa Orchid Sanctuary in West Kameng was established in 1979 to conserve and study orchids in their natural habitats. The sanctuary has recorded a remarkable diversity of orchid species, including epiphytic and terrestrial orchids.
The Orchid Research and Development Centre at Tipi further strengthens conservation and research efforts. Its facilities include orchid species houses, natural orchidaria, a herbarium, tissue culture laboratory, museum and hardening units. These initiatives support both ex-situ conservation and the rehabilitation of orchids in their natural habitats.
Glaw Lake: Arunachal Pradesh’s First Ramsar Site
A landmark development came in August 2026, when Glaw Lake, located within the Kamlang Tiger Reserve in Lohit district, was designated as India’s 101st Ramsar Site and became Arunachal Pradesh’s first Ramsar Site.
Situated at an elevation of around 1,168 metres, Glaw Lake covers approximately 82 hectares and forms part of the catchment of the Kamlang, Lang and Lati rivers, which flow into the Lohit River. The lake is recognised by the State Forest Department as an important repository of aquatic biodiversity.
Its Ramsar designation gives international recognition to the ecological importance of the wetland and strengthens the focus on its conservation and sustainable management. The recognition is also significant for Arunachal Pradesh’s wider efforts to protect wetlands and the ecosystems and communities that depend on them.
A State Where New Discoveries Continue
Arunachal Pradesh’s biodiversity story is still being written.
Recent scientific discoveries demonstrate how much remains to be documented within the State’s forests and mountains. The rare plant Vaccinium piliferum, a relative of the wild blueberry that had not been documented for nearly 188 years, was rediscovered in Vijoynagar in Changlang district recently.
New orchid species have also been identified in different parts of the State, while researchers have recorded new cascade frog species from Arunachal Pradesh. In 2026, scientists also identified a new butterfly species, Euthalia zubeengargi, from Basar in Leparada district.
Such discoveries are a reminder that Arunachal Pradesh is not merely a repository of known species. Its forests and mountains continue to offer opportunities for scientific research and the discovery of life forms that may not yet be fully documented.
Biodiversity and Indigenous Knowledge
For generations, the indigenous communities of Arunachal Pradesh have lived closely with their natural surroundings. Forests provide food, medicinal plants, fibres, fuel and other resources, while traditional knowledge has helped communities understand seasonal changes, plants, wildlife and sustainable use of natural resources.
Today, this relationship is increasingly important to conservation.
A recent example comes from West Kameng, where indigenous communities are sustainably harvesting Zanthoxylum, locally known as Khagi, a wild Himalayan spice. The initiative has reportedly involved around 200 families while contributing to the protection of approximately 100 square kilometres of forest and generating livelihood opportunities.
Such efforts demonstrate that conservation and livelihoods can move together when local knowledge and sustainable practices are placed at the centre of biodiversity management.
Conservation: Protecting a Living Legacy
Arunachal Pradesh’s biodiversity is a natural asset of national and global importance. At the same time, ecosystems across the world are facing growing pressures from habitat loss, climate change, pollution, invasive species and unsustainable exploitation of natural resources.
Protecting Arunachal’s biodiversity therefore requires more than creating protected areas. It calls for habitat restoration, scientific research, responsible tourism, community participation, sustainable livelihoods and greater awareness among citizens.
The State’s protected areas, community conservation initiatives, biodiversity documentation programmes and institutions dedicated to research and conservation all contribute to this larger effort.
Looking Ahead
The story of Arunachal Pradesh is inseparable from its forests, rivers, mountains and wildlife. Its biodiversity sustains ecosystems, supports livelihoods, enriches traditional knowledge and strengthens the ecological security of the Eastern Himalayas.
From the orchids of Sessa to the forests of Namdapha, from the bird-rich landscapes of Eaglenest to the wetlands of Glaw Lake, every ecosystem adds another chapter to the State’s natural heritage.
The recent recognition of Glaw Lake as a Ramsar Site is an important milestone, but it is also a reminder of the responsibility that comes with being home to such extraordinary natural wealth.
Arunachal Pradesh is a living treasury of biodiversity and conserving it is not only about protecting nature today, but ensuring that its forests continue to breathe, its rivers continue to flow, and its remarkable species continue to thrive for generations.

Ross Wilson: Newcastle chief reveals club prepared for Eddie Howe exit in summer that 'never felt chaotic'
Newcastle chief Ross Wilson reveals club were prepared for Eddie Howe's exit; Magpies also lost key players this summer, including captain Bruno Guimaraes; Wilson admits midfielder's Arsenal exit was not "part of plan" - but Wilson insists: "[This summer] never felt chaotic inside"
Tuesday 8 September 2026 08:42, UK
Newcastle sporting director Ross Wilson says they were "prepared for a number of months" for Eddie Howe's exit in a summer that "never felt chaotic".
Howe's shock resignation in July led to the swift appointment of Matthias Jaissle, who has enjoyed an unbeaten start to his reign.
Howe's exit was part of a turbulent summer for the Magpies which also included the departures of key players Bruno Guimaraes, Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon.

Toon chief Wilson revealed Howe's resignation was not "painful" because of their Jaissle contingency, but Guimaraes' £75m move to Arsenal was not "part of the plan".
Wilson said: "Eddie is an exceptionally talented coach and at some point that meant he was probably going to do something else and we had to be prepared for that.
"It didn't feel painful. Clearly the timing was not one we had planned for. But we had a plan in place which is why we executed it as quickly as we did.
"It might have caught some people off guard, but the reason we could move so quickly on it was because we had prepared for a number of months."
Wilson added: "I think we want Newcastle United to be a club with anticipation and excitement. If we're not it probably means we're doing it wrong.
"[This summer] never felt chaotic inside. There is no point us pretending otherwise - we did not want to lose Bruno Guimaraes. That was really disappointing that we got to that place in the end.
"We were happy where we got to in terms of numbers but that was not part of our plan. But everything else that happened during the window was part of the plan."
'Trading an important part of Newcastle plan'
Wilson believes success for Newcastle rests on them being a trading club going forwards after a summer of fluctuating fortunes in the transfer window.
Newcastle raised nearly £250m in player sales but signed eight players aged 24 or under, with much enthusiasm over the big-money arrivals of Nico Gonzalez and Matias Fernandez-Pardo.
"If you want to be a successful club in the Premier League, you have to trade players and if you don't the chances are you won't be a successful club in the Premier League," said Wilson.
"This is what we've got to do. And if you don't do it, then just keep the squad you've got and forevermore they'll grow old, achieve less and leave for nothing."
The outlook is shaped by Newcastle being fined £5.2m for breaching UEFA's financial sustainability regulations, with £6m suspended pending future compliance.
They have not qualified for Europe this season, and chief financial officer Simon Capper has forecast the club will be "compliant" with the more relaxed Premier League financial rules.
Woltemade exit allowed Fernandez-Pardo signing
Wilson and Capper also revealed that club-record signing Nick Woltemade had to leave on loan to allow the arrival of Fernandez-Pardo.
On Deadline Day, Woltemade, who joined last summer in a £69m deal, moved to Juventus on loan, with Newcastle confirming the £51m signing of Fernandez-Pardo from Lille.
Wilson said: "Because we try to link things together, the ultimate deal for Fernandez-Pardo was only possible because we did the Woltemade deal. The ultimate [Fernandez-Pardo] deal.
"If we didn't do the Woltemade deal, we might have done another deal, but that's what we mean by linking things together."
Capper added: "So the conversation we were having internally was, 'If you want to do that [sign Fernandez-Pardo] you're going to have to give me something back…otherwise we'll be in a position we're not comfortable with'.
"We managed to get that. That's how we work together as a group, as a senior management team, to deliver the best result we can out of a transfer window."

Queiroz returns as Ghana head coach
- Published
Carlos Queiroz has been reappointed as head coach of Ghana's men's national team.
The 73-year-old, who had two spells as assistant manager at Manchester United under Sir Alex Ferguson, took charge of the Black Stars in April and led the side to the last 32 at this year's Fifa World Cup, where they were beaten 1-0 by Colombia.
Queiroz appeared to announce his own departure on social media shortly after that defeat, but the Ghana Football Association (GFA) has decided to re-engage him for another spell in charge following internal discussions.
The GFA has not announced the length of his new deal but said he will prepare the team for "a successful new phase on the international stage".
"The GFA believes Queiroz's extensive international experience, technical expertise and knowledge of the Black Stars position him strongly to lead the team into this next chapter," a statement added.
Queiroz has previously led Iran, Portugal and Egypt at major tournaments and has had stints in charge of South Africa, Colombia and Qatar.
Further details on his mandate will be announced by the GFA in due course.
Queiroz said the chance to continue in the role gave him "immense pride and honour".
"Serving Ghana is far more than coaching a football team," he added in a post on Instagram.
"It is a privilege, a responsibility and a mission to honour one of Africa's greatest football nations and its incredible and passionate football people.
"Our ambition is clear: improve every day, unite the nation, make Ghana stronger and fight for every victory with passion, humility and pride. The mission continues."
Queiroz will begin his second spell in charge of the West Africans with qualifiers for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations, which begin later this month.
The Black Stars are yet to announce the dates and venues for their first two fixtures in Group C, where they have been drawn alongside Ivory Coast, The Gambia and Somalia.

20 December 2024 was a crucial moment for Luxembourg in supporting WHO and strengthening global public health, to make progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals in 2025–2028. A Strategic Partnership Framework (SPF) with the Ministry of Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Affairs was signed amounting to €46.5 million – the largest-ever agreement WHO has had with Luxembourg. Furthermore, the first-ever multiyear agreement with the Ministry of Health and Social Safety €1 million was launched, as the country’s first voluntary contribution to WHO.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General greets with Luxembourg's Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety and Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. © MAE Luxembourg
“From now till 2028, this contribution will help finance priority areas in Luxembourg’s collaboration with WHO” said Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety during the bilateral meeting, “notably for sanitary crisis preparedness and response and the fight against health inequalities, with a special focus on gender.”
The amount of €46.5 million contains fully flexible and thematic funding, and allocations for the Universal Health Coverage Partnership, tropical disease research and polio eradication. The fully flexible funding enables WHO to allocate the money to the areas of highest need.
“By signing two new partnership agreements, we have reaffirmed Luxembourg's continued support for the WHO and its mission,” said Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. “This reflects our strong commitment to promoting global health and multilateralism. We launch these agreements with WHO because we believe the best way to avoid is to prevent.”
To support the achievement of WHO’s priorities, the strategic partnership framework with Luxembourg includes support for WHO’s core work to develop, deliver and implement high-quality technical products – the guidelines, norms and standards on which many countries rely.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, remarked how symbolic it was that the agreements were signed on the International Day of Solidarity. They are “a strong statement of solidarity by Luxembourg, not just with WHO, but with the people of the world”, said Dr Tedros.
Xavier Bettel, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and Martine Deprez at the signing ceremony. © MAE Luxembourg
WHO and Luxembourg continue their historical strategic partnership, collaborating to fulfill a shared mission to promote, provide and protect health.

A claim that federal officials approved a plan to change the name of the state of New Mexico to "New America" spread online, with one popular post going so far as to claim U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order changing the state's name in early September 2026.
The claim emerged following a real order Trump signed Aug. 27, 2026, to change Lake Ontario to "Lake America" in the United States.
X user @DailyNoud shared the claim on Sept. 1 that New Mexico's name also would be changed (archived), writing: "Donald Trump has signed an executive order to change the name of New Mexico to New America." The post received more than 2.7 million views, as of this writing:
Variations of the claim also spread on Instagram, Threads and Facebook. Some people seemed to interpret it as true, and Snopes readers contacted us in search of more information.
To investigate the claims legitimacy, we first used search engines such as DuckDuckGo and Bing. If officials in Trump's administration had really approved plans to change the state's name — or if Trump had signed any such executive order — these searches would have uncovered such evidence.
That was not the case. We did not find any credible reporting about an official move to change the name of New Mexico.
We identified the claim's original source: satirical social media account Casper Planet, which describes its output as "Snews that doesn't matter." This post didn't explicitly say Trump signed an executive order, rather — it claimed that "federal officials have reportedly approved plans to rename the state of New Mexico to New America." (X user @DailyNoud also was a satire account.)
The Facebook page Casper Planet shared the related claim (archived) on Aug. 29, 2026:
New Mexico To Be Renamed New America Following Federal Geographic Naming ChangesWASHINGTON - Federal officials have reportedly approved plans to rename the state of New Mexico to New America, continuing a recent effort to update geographic names across the country.According to officials familiar with the change, the word "Mexico" was identified during a routine review of American maps and was determined to be geographically confusing.The change is expected to affect highway signs, government documents and approximately 14 million souvenir coffee mugs.Residents will officially become New Americans, while people born there before the change will reportedly be allowed to continue identifying as New Mexicans during a two-year transition period.Mexico has not been consulted.
In addition to a location tag on "Satire Street," its Facebook bio reads (archived):
Delivering the Snews that doesn't matter directly to your Snews feed. Did we say this is satire? Well it is, names/locations are made up
We reached out to the page owner for comment in January 2026 regarding a claim about AI-generated images of massive snow bank on Wyoming's Devils Tower. The account's administrator, Justin Hathaway, told Snopes over the phone: "I just love doing this satire stuff, it's such an outlet for me." He continued: "Another reason is people don't really read things fully anymore, and it's a good way to educate people on reading stories fully if they sound somewhat unbelievable."
Other Casper Planet posts Snopes has debunked include a claim that Yellowstone National Park rangers warned the public that ravens had learned to open car doors and another that a man received a DUI while riding a bear.
Because the effectiveness of satire is subjective, we use "originated as satire" or "labeled satire" ratings based on creators' description of their work.

If you’ve got limited closet space, it also helps if the backpack can pull double duty and be used for travel and/or hiking. When Sidhartha Bandha’s 63-year-old father suffered a stroke, the hospital did what it was supposed to do: it saved his life. But when he came back home, another struggle began.
His father could no longer do things on his own. The doctors told the family that rehabilitation and physiotherapy were important for his recovery. But the physiotherapy service available to them was far away. For a family dependent on daily earnings, travelling repeatedly for treatment meant spending money on transport, losing working days and managing the difficulty of moving a person who could barely move independently.
The family eventually had to give up on regular rehabilitation. Over time, Sidhartha’s father developed contractures, a condition in which muscles and joints become stiff and shortened when a person remains immobile for a long period. Sitting, standing, changing position and doing everyday activities can become a struggle.
Sidhartha remembers a different life for his father, a life where he worked in the fields and helped with household chores. His father was alive now, his life saved. But what kind of a life was it?
Where should healthcare end?
If a person survives a stroke but cannot regain the ability to move, work, participate in family life or live with some independence because rehabilitation was out of reach, is it fair to say that the job of healthcare was completed?
There is no doubt that acute medical care saves lives. But saving a life is only the first part of recovery. Rehabilitation helps a person live the life that has been saved in the way they want to.
In India, while a lot of attention has been rightfully given to improving emergency and critical care, far less has been given to what happens to patients after they leave a hospital. Physiotherapy and rehabilitation are crucial components of recovering after a number of conditions, including damage to the nervous system, heart disease and orthopaedic injuries. The question before the country today, however, is: how many people can physiotherapists actually reach?
What India needs
Global organisation World Physiotherapy’s profile of the Indian Association of Physiotherapists estimates 52,000 practising physiotherapists in India, equivalent to only 0.36 physiotherapists per 10,000 people, whereas, for instance, several countries in Europe have over 10 per 10,000 people.
The number tells only part of the story. The more important question is where these physiotherapists are and how many people each one can realistically reach. Are they available close to the homes of people living in rural areas? Can a person from a low-income family receive regular treatment that can last from days to months without spending a large part of the family’s income on travel and treatment?
The problem, therefore, is two-fold: there are not enough physiotherapists, and those that are available are not able able to reach the people who need them.
And the need is enormous.
Physiotherapy is not limited to treating back pain or helping an injured athlete. It can make a meaningful difference to people recovering from stroke, heart disease, injury, surgery and many other conditions. It can help a person stand again, walk again, use an affected limb, improve balance, become physically active and return to everyday life.
With India’s growing burden of non-communicable diseases, including heart disease and stroke, the need for physiotherapy is increasing. Someone with heart disease may need help becoming physically active safely. An older person may need help maintaining strength and balance. A person recovering from an injury or surgery may need rehabilitation to return to work. For all of them, physiotherapy can be the bridge between being medically stable and becoming an active, functioning member of the family and community. But that bridge is often missing.
Strategies that can help
There are a number of measures that can help, ranging from policy change to simple steps hospitals can take.
A model that has worked is community-based learning. This model gives physiotherapy students opportunities to work in rural and underserved communities and understand the barriers people face in accessing rehabilitation. Students are encouraged to see these communities not just as places for academic postings, but as places where physiotherapists can build meaningful careers and take rehabilitation closer to people’s homes. It deserves wider attention across physiotherapy education and healthcare policy.
Another measure is to teach families how to safely continue simple rehabilitation at home. A physiotherapist does not have to be physically present for every exercise. Families can be shown how to help with safe movement, positioning, walking and everyday activities, while the physiotherapist checks progress and changes the programme when needed.
Technology can help too. Tele-rehabilitation cannot replace hands-on treatment when a person needs physical examination or direct treatment. But it can allow a physiotherapist to follow up, demonstrate exercises, answer questions and keep in touch with patients who find regular travel difficult.
India also needs to think about where physiotherapists work. If most opportunities are concentrated in large cities and private clinics, many people who need rehabilitation will continue to be left behind. Students should have meaningful opportunities to work in villages, smaller towns, primary healthcare centres and underserved communities -- not as an afterthought, but as an important part of the profession.
It is high time we treated physiotherapy as an important component of lifesaving care, not as an optional service tacked on after the treatment. No one should be left unable to move simply because rehabilitation was too far away or too expensive.
(Dr. Shakeeb Ahmed Khan is a physiotherapist & disability and development professional khan.shakeebahmed@gmail.com; Dr. Christianez Ratna Kiruba is an internal medicine physician and a freelance health journalist based in Guwahati, Assam. christianezdennis@gmail.com)

Mac Allister 'sad' at no Liverpool contract offer
- Published
Liverpool midfielder Alexis Mac Allister says he is "very sad" not to have been offered a new deal by the club and had "options" to leave in the summer.
The Argentine, who joined on a five-year contract from Brighton in June 2023, saw team-mates Dominik Szoboszlai and Ryan Gravenberch extend their Reds deals this year.
"I received the news that the club was not in a position to offer me a new contract which, of course, makes me very, very sad," said the 27-year-old before Wednesday's Champions League game against Atletico Madrid.
"Everyone can see that I give my 100% for this football club every single day in training and games. Of course, I can have very good games [and] bad games, like everyone, but I always give my best.
"I see Dominik and Ryan renewing their contracts and that makes me very happy because they deserve it.
"At the same time it makes me a little bit sad that I didn't get mine. Of course, there is still time.
"The fans don't need to worry because I will give my 100% until the last day I am here."
Mac Allister, who has been linked with a move to Manchester City, said he has not had direct contact with Liverpool over the decision not to extend his deal.
"We won a Premier League together, we went through difficult times together and I always give my best so we will see what happens," added Mac Allister, who helped Argentina win the 2022 World Cup.
"I don't think I have to prove something - but I have to show the level I can perform and, hopefully, that's the case.
"I love this club. I love the fans. I know very well this is an amazing club and this city has something very special. I love being here."
He added: "There were options to leave this summer. I think right now I'm in the right club and I have the right mindset to give 100% for this club."
Andoni Iraola was appointed as Liverpool boss this summer after the sacking of Arne Slot.
Speaking about Mac Allister's contract, the Spaniard said: "We all have personal situations with different contracts.
"The important thing is he wants to be here. We haven't been together a long time but he has been an important player and I rate him very highly.
"There is still a lot of time to talk about those contract situations."

ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition (ICMR-NIN), Hyderabad, researchers have found that vitamin D3 is more effective than vitamin D2 in maintaining and restoring muscle and heart function, at least in animal studies in their latest study.
What does Vitamin D do to body?
Vitamin D is widely known for its role in maintaining bone health and regulating calcium levels. However, it also plays an important role in the functioning of skeletal muscles and the heart. The nutrient is available mainly in two forms: vitamin D2 and vitamin D3, both of which are commonly used in supplements and food fortification programmes.
Researchers conducted experiments on weaning male Sprague-Dawley rats to compare them. The animals were fed diets containing vitamin D2, vitamin D3, a combination of both, or a vitamin D-deficient diet. The team then evaluated body composition, muscle strength, muscle structure, energy metabolism and markers linked to heart function.
They found that rats receiving vitamin D3 showed greater improvements in muscle mass, muscle fibre size and grip strength than those given vitamin D2. Vitamin D3 was also more effective in enhancing biological markers associated with muscle growth and energy metabolism.
Similar benefits were also found in heart health as Vitamin D3 produced stronger effects on indicators of cardiac contractility and metabolism, especially among rats recovering from vitamin D deficiency. Scientist Ayesha Ismail, also the corresponding author of the study, said that while both forms of vitamin D improved calcium-related parameters, vitamin D2 was less effective in several measures related to muscle and heart structure and energy metabolism.
ICMR-NIN Director Bharati Kulkarni said the findings suggest that vitamin D3 may be a better option for maintaining and restoring muscle and cardiac functions. However, she cautioned that further studies are required to better understand the effects of the two forms of vitamin D and their implications for supplementation and food fortification programmes, as per a press release.

Mark Cuban is urging local governments to negotiate harder before approving data centers, saying towns should secure enforceable protections while they still have leverage.
In a series of X posts on Monday, the billionaire tech entrepreneur shared a 10-part playbook for communities considering their first project.
His basic rule: Every major promise from a developer should have a measurable limit, independent oversight, financial backing, and a practical remedy if it is broken.
# A town's first data center: what to require before saying yes
A data center can bring construction employment, tax base, and infrastructure investment. It can also impose demands on electricity, water, public services, and nearby neighborhoods that last for decades and outlive…
Cuban said towns should hire their own lawyers and technical advisors, assess the project's entire planned build-out, and impose clear limits on water consumption, noise, backup generation, and infrastructure costs.
He also called for upfront decommissioning funds and guarantees from financially credible parent companies.
Cuban paid particular attention to water use and noise, warning that "closed-loop" cooling systems can still consume water during hot weather and arguing that conventional noise limits may fail to capture the low-frequency hum produced by cooling equipment, which has become emblematic of many complaints about data centers.
## 5. Protect neighbors from noise before the equipment is ordered
Noise is now the most common post-approval complaint and the most active area of litigation, including proposed class actions in Wisconsin and Mississippi alleging sound carrying more than a mile past the…
Cuban also called for protection against stranded infrastructure costs if a project is delayed or abandoned. His proposals included upfront decommissioning funds, parent-company guarantees, and cash escrow or letters of credit before construction begins.
It's not Cuban's first warning about the data-center boom. In July, Cuban said communities should aggressively pursue operators who break the law or cause documented damage.
If the data center breaks the law or damages the community, the community should go after them with everything they have. 
The AI companies  need the data centers more than they need air.  Take advantage of that fact.  Tax the shit out of them if they do any documentable damage. https://t.co/OvaS6tr1zP
Later that month, he told the "All-In" podcast that technological advances could make some of today's computing capacity redundant, joking that unused data centers might become "pickleball courts."
Public opinion toward data centers is already dismal. A Gallup poll conducted in March found that 71% of Americans opposed having one built where they live, compared with 53% who opposed a nearby nuclear power plant.
The Environmental Health Project says data-center cooling systems and diesel generators can create a constant hum audible to nearby residents. The group also warns that their cooling needs can consume large amounts of water, worsening water insecurity in regions where supplies are already scarce.
The industry's image problem has become potent enough to sell beer. Former NFL star Jason Kelce recently starred in a satirical Garage Beer and Liquid Death ad asking people to send their urine to cool AI data centers — a campaign built around public concern over their water use.
Cuban described his latest framework as a work in progress and invited others to contribute. Its message was straightforward: Once a town grants approval, much of its negotiating power is gone.

GUWAHATI: Accused husband Ramanuj Goswami, arrested for allegedly killing and beheading his wife Riya Talukdar Goswami, has claimed he has “no regrets” and will offer “no apology” for the crime.
Goswami allegedly said that if he were released from jail, he would also kill the man he referred to as his wife’s “sugar daddy”.
The remarks come day after the gruesome killing of 25-year-old Riya, whose partially decomposed and decapitated body was recovered from the couple's flat in Guwahati's Beltola area.
Police said Riya's severed head was found wrapped in a polythene bag and kept inside the refrigerator. Her fingers had also allegedly been cut off.
The couple had married on September 22 last year. Police said the killing allegedly took place following a quarrel between the two on September 3, with the argument continuing into the early hours of the following day.
Ramanuj, a cab driver, later surrendered before police and allegedly confessed to killing his wife. Investigators said he claimed that frequent disputes over his allegations of an extramarital affair had led to repeated quarrels between the couple.
DCP Tabu Ram Pegu said the accused had disclosed certain details during questioning and that police were examining the circumstances surrounding the crime.
“We are verifying the facts as claimed by the husband. Detailed interrogation is yet to be done. We are examining the circumstances leading to the crime,” police said.
A ‘dao’, or machete, allegedly used in the killing has been recovered from the house.
The case came to light after family members reportedly failed to contact the couple for two days. Police reached the flat and found the door open, with Riya's body lying on the floor and her head severed.
A local court has sent Goswami to seven days of police custody as investigators continue their probe.

Thieves have stolen three paintings from the Renoir Museum in France, worth 9 million euros ($14.5 million).
Two thieves broke into the museum in the early hours of the morning, stealing four artworks, dropping one as they fled.
What's next?
The thieves have not been caught and are being "actively sought", according to local mayor.
Thieves have stolen three paintings from the Renoir Museum in France, the local mayor said.
Two thieves broke into the museum dedicated to French impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir in southern France early Tuesday, local time, stealing four works of art, dropping one as they fled.
Local French newspaper Nice-Matin reported the stolen paintings as Portrait of Madame Pichon (1895), Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910), Coco Lisant (1905) and Jeune fille au puits (1886).
The mayor's office estimated the value of the stolen works at 9 million euros ($14.5 million).
"Spotted thanks to the town's video surveillance cameras, the two individuals fled, abandoning one of the stolen paintings as they ran," said Bryan Masson, mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer.
"The museum alarm went off at 5:48am. At 5:53am, just five minutes later, our municipal police were on the scene," Mr Masson said.
"Since this morning, both the municipal and national police have been deployed to the site.
"The perpetrators are being actively sought, and the investigation is ongoing."
The Renoir Museum was opened in 1960 in the painter's last home before his death in 1919.
Its collection includes objects and furniture that belonged to Renoir, including his easel and wheelchair, as well as portraits, landscapes, and nudes painted by the artist.
The four suspected Louvre robbers have been arrested, but the stolen items still have not been found despite extensive searches by French investigators in the Paris region and exchanges with police in Belgium, Italy and beyond.
The artworks included Fish by Auguste Renoir, Paul Cézanne's Still Life with Cherries, and Odalisque on the Terrace by Henri Matisse.
Days after their recovery, another four paintings were stolen from another Italian museum.
Artworks by 15th century painter Antonello da Messina were taken from the Museo Regionale di Messina — the pieces some of the only surviving work by the Renaissance painter to have remained in his native city.

Dalgona coffee was one of the food trends that took off during the COVID-19 lockdown, popularising a whipped version of the traditional Parsi pheteli (beaten) coffee. Around the same time, proffee — a combination of protein powder and coffee—emerged as a home-made drink and has since become popular among gym-goers.
How is it done?
For proffee, the coffee needs to be brewed ahead and cooled before being mixed with protein powder. Hot coffee can make the powder clumpy, resulting in a less-smooth drink. The two can be mixed with a stirrer or frother. Proffee drinkers say there is no fixed recipe; variations include milk and flavoured syrups.
For those who want it readymade and save themselves from the task of brewing and mix, there are brands in India that sell proffee. A quick online search on e-commerce sites list brands like TrueBasics, Horlicks, Sleepyowl, Earthful for proffee. Most of them claim to be sugar free and offers choice of flavours like hazelnut, vanilla, chocolate etc.
The purpose
You get caffeine and protein in one glass instead of having coffee first and breakfast later. Nutritionist Dr Lovneet Batra categorises proffee as a drink of convenience. “If you drink coffee and add your protein to it, many consider it an easy ‘high-protein breakfast.’ From a nutrition standpoint, I don’t recommend it because it is an acidic combination. Even if one works out, caffeine comes as a pre-workout and protein as post-workout, so mixing them is just a matter of convenience.”
Hyderabad-based independent fitness coach Bilon Aristotle agrees that proffee is convenient, but says the combination can serve a purpose. “Caffeine and protein serve different, complementary jobs — one for alertness, one for satiety and muscle maintenance. Combining them into a single occasion is efficient rather than gimmicky. It’s a legitimate way to front-load protein earlier in the day, particularly for people who otherwise skip breakfast.”
But does it work during or after a workout? Businessman Ranjit Raja, who has trained consistently for over a decade and competes in bodybuilding shows, prefers to keep the two separate. He opts for either a banana or a plain protein shake after training. “That’s how I started and I have been following the same routine. Since I compete in the under-65 category, I need to maintain lean muscle. Post-training, I prefer real food such as steamed sweet potato or eggs.” Each to his own.
Chennai-based fitness and nutrition coach Raj Ganpath breaks down the role of each ingredient. Protein, he says, is not something the body needs only after a workout but throughout the day. It is one of the three macronutrients, alongside carbohydrates and fats, and the amount required varies according to individual needs and goals.
Caffeine, meanwhile, works well as a pre-workout, he says, helping with alertness, mental sharpness and exercise performance. It can also help mobilise fat for energy.
As for consuming protein before a workout, Raj says it can help limit muscle breakdown, particularly when training in a fasted state. “You want protein around your workout — some before training and some after is a good idea.”
Having explained the role of coffee and protein separately, Ganpath gives proffee a thumbs up, with one caveat: “Not if you are working out late in the evening, as caffeine is also known to interfere with your sleep cycle.”
