In Summary
- Apple’s new CEO John Ternus is expected to take centrestage on 9 September in Apple’s “Surprise and shine” event. This will be
- Ternus’ first appearance in an Apple event since he took over from Tim Cook.
- Apple is expected to launch new iPhones at the event, including the much-talked-about iPhone Ultra, its first foldable phone.
- As the event draws near, we write an open letter to Apple’s new CEO, requesting something that was once very much Apple – being different.
Dear John,
You will shortly be making your first public appearance as CEO at a major Apple event. Over the years, the iPhone launch pretty much sets out the tech agenda for the rest of the year. For the iPhone is not just a tech launch but a trend setter of sorts – it influences which colors, shapes, features, and functions matter in the industry in the coming days. About a decade ago, we would have laughed at the notion of a notch in any device. Until last year, orange was associated more with juice than tech. You get the idea.
Indeed, very few names have influenced our lives in the way in which Apple has over the past few decades. The brand made computers and touchscreen smartphones that were effortlessly easy to use, put thousands of songs in our pockets, created notebooks that could be carried in stationery envelopes, showed us that Bluetooth earbuds could exist without wires, added a third screen to many of our lives in the form of a tablet, got us looking at our watches for more than just the time, made us realize that there was “an app for that…”, and much more. It was seldom the first to come out with a particular product, but it often put a different spin on products, making them easier to use. It was the brand that thrived on its legendary motto, ‘Think Different’. Other brands could match Apple’s features and spec sheet, perhaps, but never the ‘feel’ or ‘vibe’ of an Apple product.
In recent times, however, this Apple feel or vibe has been getting increasingly diminished. Some would say that perhaps an “inspired” (read “copycat”) competition is closing the gap on the market leader. Perhaps. But then, it is not as if competition and “copy and paste” mode did not exist in the past. Remember how Steve Jobs went ballistic at Google for Android, claiming that it had been copied from Apple? “I’m going to destroy Android, because it’s a stolen product. I’m willing to go thermonuclear war on this,” Jobs raged when speaking of the topic, in Walter Isaacson’s biography. But even then, Apple’s products continued to be strikingly different. The competition could offer a similar appearance (camera units, straight sides, similar colors), but beneath that familiar surface, it was clear that they were just knockoffs.
That is no longer the case. Somewhere in its pursuit of market share over the past decade, Apple started losing its mystique, going from Hogwarts to Harvard. The brand’s sales volumes and capital value have shot up exponentially, but all this has come at a creative cost. Apple now seems more a part of the crowd rather than apart from it. Don’t get me wrong. Apple’s products are still very good, but while their pricing is more premium than ever, the products themselves are not as different as they used to be. In fact, in many cases, they do not even seem to be too different from their own predecessors.
The brand that championed “Think DIfferent” has been increasingly thinking similarly of late. From being among the first to popularise graphical UIs, capacitive touchscreens, app screens and face unlock systems, it has graduated to being last in line in the foldables and AI race. It might end up winning both of those contests even now, such is its market domination, but that would be a victory of volumes rather than delivered value, similar to how IBM ended up bossing the PC market in the early eighties even though it was a latecomer. IBM’s motto was incidentally “Think,” and is believed to have inspired Apple’s “Think Different.” Oh, the irony.
There has always been a large section of people who believed that most people who bought Apple products did so just to “show off the logo,” as products from other brands were just as good. For a while, this was a very unfair accusation, as in spite of their premium price tags (even more so in India, because of customs duties, we are told), Apple’s products seemed to be in a totally different league. Today, Apple still has the high ground in privacy and security and its face unlock remains unmatched, but in many other regards (yes, even in apps and interface), the brand seems content to swim in the mainstream, rather than walloping the competition from within its famous “walled garden.”
We are coming to the stage when a lot of people are actually buying Apple products for the logo on them rather than what they do. At one level, it tells us that the Apple brand has such equity that people are willing to invest large amounts in a product because it has an apple engraved on it. At another, it tells us that the products are now being defined by the brand rather than the other way around – a foldable phone is special because it comes from Apple, rather than Apple being special because it made a foldable phone.
Today, Apple is arguably the world’s greatest tech brand, but it has more money than mojo. For other brands, that would be just perfect. But since when was Apple just another brand? Mind you, money is a wonderful thing. After all, it enables one to do things and invest in ideas that don’t have a short-term payback. We did not say that; Steve Jobs did. Well, Apple has the money. Perhaps it is time for it to do things. Differently.
All this is easier said than done, of course. My colleague Akriti Rana recently wrote eloquently of how you now hold not just the reins of arguably the most high-profile tech company in the world, but also bear the burden of two massive, yet contrasting legacies. How you decide to honor them is your choice. You could choose to sail in a sea of successful sameness. Or maybe just spend more time in that walled garden.
Still, as someone whose first ever story in tech was about an Apple product (the iBook in 1999) and who confidently predicted that the first iPhone would fail (and was delighted to be proved wrong) in 2007, I have a request.
I am not asking for slimmer portfolios. Or lower price tags. I am asking for something much more basic – the experience of going to an event without having any idea of what will happen.
Of seeing a product without having seen it being leaked more often than a local municipal pipeline.
Of feeling a sense of wonder while using a product, because there is nothing else quite like it.
Of looking at the Apple logo and thinking of wizardry rather than wealth.
The universe is waiting, John Ternus. Go put a ding in it.
Regards,
Nimish Dubey

Kannada actor Kiran Raj recently shared a video on social media that showed him seemingly being attacked by a lion. The video quickly went viral, leaving fans concerned about the actor’s safety. Soon after, Kiran addressed the panic and reassured his followers that he was safe.
Responding to the concerns, Kiran commented, “Don’t worry, guys, if I am able to post this, I am fine.” He later shared another video clarifying the circumstances behind the viral clip.
Kiran revealed that the video was part of a project for which he has been training with a lion named Rocky. He explained that the training was aimed at helping him become familiar and comfortable with the animal.
“I would like to clarify: the captions and background music are creating panic and misinformation. The fact is, for the project, I’m training with Rocky, and it’s a very safe atmosphere,” the actor said.
Kiran further claimed that he has developed a “little bond” with Rocky and that adequate safety precautions are being taken during the training. He also thanked fans for their concern while urging them not to believe the misleading context surrounding the viral video.
“I have a little bond with him, so it is completely safe... Thank you so much once again. My concern is that the misinformation is being spread, (as translated)” Kiran added.
In the now-viral video, Kiran had explained that it was the “Day 1” of his training to learn how to work with lions named Roger and Rocky. Sharing a few lessons from his first day, the actor wrote, “Lion always try to make you fall, so always lean towards something strong” and advised keeping one’s face towards the lion even while moving away. He also claimed that “lions can read your eyes” and added, “They love to hug you and cuddle.” While the video showed Kiran in a seemingly dangerous interaction with the animal, his caption indicated that the footage was part of his training for a project.

WHO welcomed Mr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Spain’s Secretary of State for Health and his delegation on 23 and 24 April 2024 to discuss joint global health priorities. Amongst others, Spain's focus is on universal health coverage and health systems strengthening; pandemic response and emergency medical teams; organ and tissue transplantation; malaria and other tropical diseases; and polio.
During the visit, participants focused on plans and on-going work across a number of areas, including WHO’s Transplantation Program to increase availability; ethical access and oversight of transplantation of human cells; tissues and organs. They also discussed social determinants of health; tobacco and alcohol control; primary health care; access to medicines; universal health coverage; ensuring healthy lives at all ages; nutrition and food safety; health workforce; and emergencies.
Mr Javier Padilla was accompanied by Ms Paola Cannata Molero, Director of the Cabinet of the Secretary of State for Health, Mr Jacobo Fernández Álvarez, Technical Secretary General, Mr Héctor Tejero Franco, Advisor in the Cabinet of the Minister of Health and Responsible for Health and Climate Change, and Mr Roberto Carro Vázquez, Senior Technician of the Office of the Secretary of State for Health. The delegation also had representatives of Spain’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations Office and Other International Organizations in Geneva, including H.E. Ambassador Ms A. Díaz-Rato Revuelta, H.E. Ambassador Ms Clara Cabrera Brasero, and Counsellor Ms María del Carmen Martínez de la Peña.
The Spanish delegation met with Dr Ailan Li, Assistant Director General (ADG) for Universal Health Coverage, Healthier Populations, Dr Catharina Boehme, ADG for External Relations and Governance, Dr Yukiko Nakatani, ADG for Access to Medicines and Health products and ADG for Antimicrobial Resistance ad interim, Dr Michael Ryan, Deputy Director-General and Executive Director for WHO Health Health Emergencies Programme.
Left to right: Dr Maria Neira, Director, Environment, Climate Change and Health, H.E. Ambassador Aurora Díaz-Rato Revuelta, Dr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Secretary of State for Health, Michael Ryan, Deputy Director-General and Executive Director, WHO Health Emergencies Programme. Credit: WHO/Chris Black
WHO’s Management and their teams thanked Spain for their financial and technical support over the years. Spain’s support was instrumental in the last biennium in improving access to quality essential health services and medicines; addressing climate change and healthier environments; and strengthening country capacity in both data and innovation. Spain continues to be a champion of the Global Polio Eradication Initiative.
Spain also contributes to WHO’s work in tackling malaria and neglected and other tropical diseases, and has helped the Organization strengthen countries’ preparedness, readiness, prevention and response for health emergencies, epidemics and pandemics. Spain’s contribution to WHO’s Health Emergency Appeal has helped to protect health in humanitarian emergencies to break the cycles of poverty.
As a world leader in the field of organ and tissue transplantation, Spain plays a key role in WHO’s efforts through its Ministry of Health to improve the safety, quality, efficacy and access to transplants. WHO appreciates and acknowledges Spain as a partner who is not only leading and sharing expertise in support of countries’ development of sustainable, self-sufficient organ transplant systems, but also more generally, a key partner to WHO in health for all.

Lhasa (Tibet), Sep 8: The massive flash flood that struck the Tibet-Nepal border on August 26 has put China's numerous hydropower projects in the region, including the mega dam on the Brahmaputra River, under renewed scrutiny, as Chinese experts said global warming and accelerating glacier retreat may have contributed to the recent gigantic mudslide.
The disaster was likely the result of a combination of factors, including rising temperatures and accelerated glacier melt, glacier retreat, local geological and geomorphological conditions and broader climatic influences, according to Chinese climate experts.
“According to our monitoring, we can see the short-time rain days, or the imbalance of the rain pattern and the rising of the temperature in Tibet,” said Sun Xiaoguang, head of the Meteorological Observatory of the Tibet Autonomous Region.
The Tibet region may be affected by the climate change crisis, he said.
“As far as I know, and according to the reports published by the Meteorological Observatory of China, I think there are... there will be more and more extreme weather, or extreme weather incidents in China that was impact [of] or affected by the climate change,” he said, talking to PTI while on his way to the flash flood-hit area close to the Tibet-Nepal border on Sunday.
The August 26 disaster was triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border, sending a massive surge of water and debris downstream through the Bhotekoshi River and devastating settlements in northern and central Nepal, which killed more than 1,350 people, while around 5,000 remain missing.
On the Chinese side, the flash flood has killed 43 people, while 519 remain missing, according to authorities. The missing include 261 foreigners, of which 49 are from India.
The force of the mudslide, comprising huge boulders, ice and massive amounts of mud, wiped out the sprawling Chinese immigration centre building at Gyirong. Most of the dead and missing foreigners were on both sides of the building.
A group of foreign correspondents from Beijing, who were taken on a tour of the area by the Chinese Foreign Ministry on Sunday, saw that the entire area was devoid of any traces of the building, except for a few rods piercing out in some places.
The disaster has put the spotlight on the threats posed by the increasing volatility of the fragile environment in Tibet, the roof of the world, where around 10 transboundary rivers, including the Brahmaputra, originate.
Over the years, China has faced criticism over its hydropower projects, including the construction of a USD 167.8 billion dam on the Brahmaputra River in Tibet, which has been described as the world's largest construction project, upstream of India's Arunachal Pradesh.
Construction of the dam started in July last year. It is expected to generate more than 300 billion kWh of electricity each year, enough to meet the annual needs of over 300 million people.
The dam is being built at a gorge in the Himalayan reaches where the Brahmaputra River makes a huge U-turn before flowing into Arunachal Pradesh and then to Bangladesh.
While concerns earlier centred largely on earthquake risks, given Tibet's location along the collision zone of the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates, the August 26 disaster and its links to climate change and glacier retreat have added a new dimension to the risks facing the region.
Chinese researchers say climate change is emerging as a central driver behind the growing frequency and severity of such disasters across high-altitude border regions.
The August 26 event serves as a stark warning that rising temperatures are fundamentally reshaping the stability of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau and the Himalayan range.
Chinese officials who addressed the media close to the site of the disaster said on Sunday that Tibet has 33,000 glaciers, with 187 of them categorised as high-risk which require round-the-clock satellite monitoring to predict collapse.
Nie Yong, a researcher at the Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment of China, said there are now more than 14,000 glacial lakes on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, covering a combined area of more than 1,100 square kilometres, with many continuing to expand.
The area covered by glacial lakes in the region is increasing by an average of about one per cent a year, he told Chinese daily The Paper, warning that the continued expansion of the lakes is contributing to the accumulation of geological disaster risks in high-altitude areas.
Kang Shichang, director and researcher at the Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment, under the Chinese Academy of Sciences in Chengdu, said glaciers across the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau had shrunk by about 24 per cent in area over the past six decades.
The decline has been even more pronounced in the southern part of the plateau, particularly in the Gangdise Mountains, Nyenchen Tanglha Mountains and the Himalayas, where glacier area has fallen by about 40 per cent over the same period, Kang told The Paper on Monday, attributing the dramatic retreat primarily to global warming.
The continued loss of glacier ice has also contributed to a substantial increase in the number and size of glacial lakes across the plateau, raising concerns over the risk of glacial lake outburst floods and related landslides.
The Paper said specialists examining the Gyirong Port mudslide have confirmed the disaster is closely tied to global warming.
The chain of events began with accelerated glacial melting driven by higher temperatures.
As glaciers retreat, they destabilise mountainsides, loosen rock and sediment, and create conditions where heavy precipitation or sudden structural failure can trigger cascading hazards, including ice-rock collapses that swiftly turn into massive mudflows.
As glaciers vanish, they leave behind unstable terrain and rapidly expanding glacial lakes, turning remote valleys into potential hazard zones and raising the possibility of more disasters.

Some Target baskets carry a Bluetooth Low Energy Beacon that transmits its location to "smart" lights in the store. The lights can interact with the beacons and Target's app to find a shopper's location, help them navigate around a store or send location-specific offers. Because the basket-mounted beacons transmit only locations and do not collect information about the shopper, it is technically Target's app that tracks shoppers, not the beacons.
In August and September 2026, a claim (archived) circulated online that the retailer Target used a Bluetooth device on its baskets that tracked shoppers in store.
The claim came from an Aug. 29 TikTok video in which a person who appeared to be a Target employee claimed the retailer fitted its baskets with trackers that followed shoppers throughout the store.
The alleged employee said:
Hello, I just want to make a PSA: You are now being tracked at Target. These baskets, this thing, that's a tracker, so they're now tracking shoppers at Target, at your local Target, for, supposedly, "consumer habits."
Other users shared similar claims about Target's alleged tracking on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), Threads (archived), X (archived) and Reddit (archived). Snopes readers also contacted us about the claim.
In short, Target does track shopper locations using the basket-mounted Bluetooth beacon that the TikTok user showed in their video. The beacon transmits its location to Target's "smart" overhead LED lights, which in turn can communicate location information to its app.
Acuity Brands, which Target said supplied its LED lights, explained in a news release in 2017 that by using its lights and beacons attached to items such as shopping carts it could deliver "highly accurate, real-time positioning services for customers" through a retailer's app. Acuity Brands said Target renewed a multiyear deal for products including its indoor location services in 2020.
According to its privacy policy, Target still used LED light and Bluetooth technology to track shoppers in-store in August 2026. The policy advised that customers who did not want to share their store location data could disable location sharing on their device or in the Target app.
We contacted Target to confirm how it collected and used data about customers in store using Bluetooth beacons, as well as how customers could opt out of tracking. We await a reply to our query.
What we know about Target tracking
The TikTok user who shared the video about Target's basket-mounted beacons on Aug. 29 shared another video (archived) the day after, identifying the exact product Target used to track shoppers as a Bluetooth beacon from Acuity Brands. A Reddit user who posted (archived) about the device six months earlier showed a device with the same FCC ID as the one the TikTok user identified.
The Federal Communications Commission grants FCC IDs to products that meet the necessary regulatory standards for wireless communication.
The product's user manual said it is a Bluetooth Low Energy Beacon that "communicates its position to Atrius Assets," the software that Target has used since at least 2020 for indoor location services.
Bluetooth Low Energy Beacons are small devices that send out radio signals that can be picked up by nearby devices. Beacons can only transmit — not receive — data, so they generally rely on apps to interpret and use the data they are sending.
In terms of tracking, if many beacons are sending their location, a device can interpret those signals and triangulate the location of an individual beacon, or individual shopper holding a basket fitted with a beacon. Target wrote in its news release in 2019 that its lights interacted with its app to find customer locations, suggesting that the basket-mounted beacons sent their signals to the lights.
It was unclear from the available information whether Target used the data it gathered about individual shoppers' routes through their stores beyond providing location-based offers through the app or guiding customers to specific products.
Target used Bluetooth beacons since at least 2015
The technology publication TechCrunch reported that Target and other retailers have used beacon technology to track shoppers in store and send them location-based offers since at least 2015 and that the retailer added Bluetooth beacon-driven indoor mapping to its app in 2017.
Target appeared to still use this technology in 2026. Its privacy policy in August 2026 said Target might use location information shared by customers' phones to "help you find nearby Target stores; or, in-store location through the use of your phone's blue tooth signal, LED light chip technologies or other technologies will permit Target to find nearby products for you, get you real-time deals, auto-sort your shopping list and more."
Target said in its privacy policy that shoppers who wished to opt out of sharing their in-store location could prevent their devices from sharing their location with Target "by adjusting the permissions on your mobile device or within the relevant app."
It did not appear from the beacon's manual that shoppers could turn the device off themselves, meaning Target would still collect information about where the basket traveled if a shopper used it, but could not connect that data to a specific phone or customer if the device's owner turned off location sharing or did not use the Target app.

Tobacco use is linked to infertility in women as well as poorer sperm quality and sexual function in men, according to the latest World Health Organisation (WHO) report, which further warned that second-hand smoke may also affect fertility. Women who quit smoking may have a 25% lower infertility risk than continuing smokers, it said.
The report highlighted evidence that tobacco use is associated with potentially lower chances of success for some fertility treatments. It said that evidence on newer products, including e-cigarettes, waterpipes, and smokeless tobacco, is still emerging, stating that while evidence is strongest for cigarette smoking, other tobacco and nicotine products may also pose risks to fertility and require further research.
Globally, one in six people of reproductive age will experience infertility at some point in their lifetime. Infertility is defined as the failure to achieve pregnancy after 12 months or more of regular unprotected sex.
40% rise in risk
The publication cites decades of evidence showing that smoking can harm women’s reproductive health. A systematic review of studies conducted between 2000 and 2026 found that women who currently smoke tobacco have a 40% higher risk of infertility compared to those who do not smoke.
The publication also notes that women who smoked tobacco in the past but are not currently smoking may have a 25% lower risk of infertility compared with women who continue to smoke, suggesting that quitting tobacco can make a meaningful difference.
The WHO stressed that infertility is not only a women’s health issue. "A recent review of 44 studies involving more than 60,000 men found that smoking was associated with reproductive dysfunction, including semen abnormalities and sexual dysfunction. The evidence indicated that men who smoke were more likely to have erectile dysfunction, ejaculation problems, and related issues such as absence of sperm in semen, poor sperm motility and abnormal sperm shape," it said.
Impact on treatments
For people using fertility treatment, tobacco smoking may reduce the chance of success. The publication cites earlier research from 21 studies, showing that cigarette smoking was linked to fewer live births and fewer pregnancies following assisted reproduction, such as in vitro fertilisation, with findings suggesting that the chances of successful outcomes may be roughly halved by cigarette smoking.
The WHO has recommended that healthcare providers inform individuals and couples planning a pregnancy about the reproductive risks of tobacco use and offer evidence-based support to help them quit. It also recommended that brief advice on quitting be consistently provided to all tobacco users in all healthcare settings.
